title: Why do we need UVM methodology?
answer:
The **Universal Verification Methodology (UVM)** is an IEEE standardized (IEEE 1800.2) methodology for verifying digital designs that facilitates developing reusable, modular, and well-structured verification testbenches.

**Key Reasons & Benefits:**

- **Reusability:** Provides a standardized class hierarchy (`uvm_driver`, `uvm_monitor`, `uvm_scoreboard`, `uvm_agent`, `uvm_env`) allowing verification components (UVCs) to be reused from block level to subsystem and SoC levels.

- **Factory Mechanism:** Enables overriding components or transactions without modifying testbench code.

- **Phasing Mechanism:** Standardizes testbench synchronization across components (`build`, `connect`, `run`, `check`, `report`), preventing race conditions.

- **TLM (Transaction-Level Modeling):** Decouples communication between testbench components, making them modular and plug-and-play.

- **Configuration Database (`uvm_config_db`):** Centralizes parameter and interface distribution across the testbench hierarchy.

- **Multi-vendor Support:** Supported by all major EDA simulators (Synopsys, Cadence, Siemens/Mentor).

---
solution:
**Key idea:** UVM (IEEE 1800.2) gives every team the same class library, the same testbench structure and the same simulation lifecycle. Verification components (UVCs) can then be reused from block to SoC level, reconfigured without editing their source, and driven by constrained-random, coverage-driven stimulus.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Problem["Ad-hoc SV testbench"]
    P1["initial blocks race each other"]
    P2["hard-coded classes, edit to change"]
    P3["every team invents its own structure"]
  end
  subgraph UVM["UVM provides"]
    U1["Phasing: build, connect, run, check, report"]
    U2["Factory overrides: swap types without editing code"]
    U3["Standard agent / env / test hierarchy"]
    U4["config_db, TLM, objections, RAL, reporting"]
  end
  P1 --> U1
  P2 --> U2
  P3 --> U3
  U3 --> U4
```

### Explanation
| Need | UVM mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Reuse across projects and levels | Standard base classes (`uvm_agent`, `uvm_env`, ...), active/passive agents |
| Change behavior without editing the TB | Factory (`type_id::create`, type/instance overrides) |
| Deterministic start-up and shutdown | Phases plus objections |
| Pass settings and interfaces down the hierarchy | `uvm_config_db` |
| Decoupled component communication | TLM ports and analysis ports |
| Stimulus as reusable, layered scenarios | Sequences, virtual sequences, sequence arbitration |
| Register verification | RAL (`uvm_reg_block`, adapters, predictors) |
| Consistent, filterable messages | `uvm_info/warning/error/fatal` with verbosity control |

- Because UVM is vendor-neutral, the same environment runs on VCS, Xcelium and Questa, and VIP from third parties plugs in.
- It separates test intent (tests, sequences) from testbench infrastructure (env, agents), so a new test is often just a new sequence plus a few overrides.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- UVM adds overhead. A tiny block with a handful of directed checks may not need a full UVM environment.
- Reuse only works when components are written for it: no hard-coded paths, and configuration delivered through config objects.

### Follow-ups
- *What came before UVM?* OVM and VMM. UVM grew mainly out of OVM and was standardized as IEEE 1800.2 in 2017.
- *Does UVM replace SystemVerilog?* No. It is a class library written in SystemVerilog.

title: Difference between `uvm_object` and `uvm_component`
answer:
*Refer: *[*Difference_between_uvm_component_and_uvm_object*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-class-hierarchy#Difference_between_uvm_component_and_uvm_object)

| Feature | `uvm_object` | `uvm_component` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Inheritance** | Base class for all UVM data objects | Derived from `uvm_object` (via `uvm_report_object`) |
| **Nature / Lifetime** | **Transient / Dynamic**: Created and destroyed on the fly during simulation | **Quasi-static**: Created at elaboration/build phase and exists throughout simulation |
| **Hierarchy** | No parent-child hierarchy | Strict parent-child hierarchy (`name` and `parent` required) |
| **Constructor** | `function new(string name="uvm_object");` | `function new(string name, uvm_component parent);` |
| **Phases** | Does **not** participate in UVM phases | Executes standard UVM phases (`build_phase`, `connect_phase`, etc.) |
| **Examples** | `uvm_sequence_item`, `uvm_sequence`, configuration objects | `uvm_driver`, `uvm_monitor`, `uvm_sequencer`, `uvm_scoreboard`, `uvm_env`, `uvm_test` |
| **Registration** | Registered via `` `uvm_object_utils(T) `` | Registered via `` `uvm_component_utils(T) `` |

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_component` is derived from `uvm_object`. Components are the quasi-static testbench structure: they are built once, have a parent and take part in phasing. Objects are transient data and configuration: they are created and discarded at any time, with no parent and no phases.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  OBJ["uvm_object"] --> TR["uvm_transaction"] --> SI["uvm_sequence_item"] --> SEQ["uvm_sequence_base / uvm_sequence"]
  OBJ --> RO["uvm_report_object"] --> COMP["uvm_component"]
  COMP --> D["uvm_driver"]
  COMP --> M["uvm_monitor"]
  COMP --> A["uvm_agent / uvm_env / uvm_test"]
  OBJ --> CFG["config objects, uvm_reg ..."]
```

### Explanation
| Feature | `uvm_object` | `uvm_component` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifetime | Dynamic: created and garbage-collected any time | Quasi-static: built in `build_phase`, lives for the whole simulation |
| Constructor | `new(string name = "...")` | `new(string name, uvm_component parent)` |
| Hierarchy | None (`get_full_name()` returns just the name) | Parent/child tree under `uvm_top` |
| Phasing | No phase methods | `build_phase`, `run_phase`, `report_phase`, ... |
| Factory macro | `` `uvm_object_utils `` | `` `uvm_component_utils `` |
| Overrides | Type override; instance override only through a context string | Type and instance override by hierarchical path |
| Examples | sequence items, sequences, config objects, register models | driver, monitor, sequencer, agent, scoreboard, env, test |

```systemverilog
class pkt extends uvm_sequence_item;
  `uvm_object_utils(pkt)
  function new(string name = "pkt"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

class my_drv extends uvm_driver #(pkt);
  `uvm_component_utils(my_drv)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- You cannot create a component after `build_phase` (end of elaboration). Creating one in `run_phase` is an error.
- Sequences are objects even though they "run". They borrow a component context through `m_sequencer`.

### Follow-ups
- *Why does a component need a parent?* The parent places it in the hierarchy. That position drives phasing order, config_db scoping and instance overrides.
- *Which class sits between them?* `uvm_report_object`, which gives components their reporting methods.

title: Difference between `uvm_transaction` and `uvm_sequence_item`
answer:
- **`uvm_transaction`:** Inherited from `uvm_object`. Adds basic timing, notification events, and transaction recording capabilities.

- **`uvm_sequence_item`:** Derived from `uvm_transaction`. Adds essential hooks and infrastructure for communicating with sequencers and drivers (e.g., `set_sequencer()`, `get_sequencer()`, `set_transaction_id()`, `get_transaction_id()`).

- **Modern Recommendation:** `uvm_transaction` is considered **deprecated** as a base class for user stimulus. All user-defined transaction classes should extend `uvm_sequence_item`.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_sequence_item` extends `uvm_transaction` and adds everything an item needs to travel through a sequencer: the parent sequence, the sequencer handle, and sequence/transaction IDs for routing responses. User stimulus should always extend `uvm_sequence_item`. ```mermaid flowchart LR O["uvm_object
copy, compare, print, pack"] --> T["uvm_transaction
begin_tr / end_tr, timestamps, recording, transaction_id"] T --> S["uvm_sequence_item
get_sequencer, get_parent_sequence, set_id_info, sequence_id"] S --> U["my_pkt (user item)"] ``` ### Explanation | | `uvm_transaction` | `uvm_sequence_item` | | --- | --- | --- | | Parent | `uvm_object` | `uvm_transaction` | | Adds | Transaction timing (`accept_tr`, `begin_tr`, `end_tr`), recording, events | `m_sequencer`, `m_parent_sequence`, `sequence_id`, `set_id_info()`, `get_full_name()` with the sequence path | | Can go through `start_item` / `finish_item`? | No | Yes | | Typical use | Rarely extended directly in modern code | All user stimulus and response items | - The driver must copy the IDs onto any response (`rsp.set_id_info(req)`), so the sequencer can route the response back to the sequence that issued the request. - Analysis-only items, such as a monitor's output, still usually extend `uvm_sequence_item`. That keeps one item type for both stimulus and observation. ```systemverilog class bus_item extends uvm_sequence_item; rand bit [31:0] addr, data; rand bit write; `uvm_object_utils_begin(bus_item) `uvm_field_int(addr, UVM_ALL_ON) `uvm_field_int(data, UVM_ALL_ON) `uvm_field_int(write, UVM_ALL_ON) `uvm_object_utils_end function new(string name = "bus_item"); super.new(name); endfunction endclass ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - An item extending `uvm_transaction` cannot be parameterized into `uvm_sequence #(T)` or `uvm_driver #(T)`, because those require a `uvm_sequence_item`. - The UVM documentation advises against extending `uvm_transaction` directly in user code. ### Follow-ups - *Is `uvm_sequence` also a sequence item?* Yes. `uvm_sequence_base` extends `uvm_sequence_item`, which is why sequences can be nested and arbitrated on a sequencer.

title: Difference between `create()` and `new()`
answer:
- **`new()` Method:** The native SystemVerilog constructor. It instantiates the exact class type specified at compile time. It does **not** query or support the UVM factory override mechanism.

- **`create()` Method:** A static factory method provided by the UVM factory registry wrapper (`type_id::create()`). When called, it queries the UVM factory table to check if any type or instance override has been configured (e.g., via `set_type_override_by_type` or `set_inst_override_by_type`). If an override exists, it constructs the derived/overridden class instead of the original class.

- **Summary:** Always use `<class_type>::type_id::create("name", parent)` in UVM testbenches to preserve polymorphism and enable testbench configurability without code edits.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `new()` is the plain SystemVerilog constructor and always builds the exact type written in the code. `type_id::create()` asks the UVM factory first, so a registered override can substitute a derived class without touching the original code. ```mermaid flowchart TD C["drv = my_drv::type_id::create('drv', this)"] --> F{"Factory: override for my_drv
at this path?"} F -->|"instance override"| I["construct err_drv for this path only"] F -->|"type override"| T["construct err_drv everywhere"] F -->|"none"| N["construct my_drv"] NW["drv = new('drv', this)"] --> X["always my_drv, factory bypassed"] ``` ### Explanation | | `new()` | `type_id::create()` | | --- | --- | --- | | Defined by | SystemVerilog language | `` `uvm_*_utils `` macro (static method of the type proxy) | | Override aware | No | Yes (type and instance overrides) | | Needs factory registration | No | Yes | | Use for | Ports/exports, TLM FIFOs, `uvm_event`, plain helper classes | Components, sequences, sequence items, config objects | ```systemverilog // in the test: swap the driver without editing env/agent code function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); super.build_phase(phase); my_drv::type_id::set_type_override(err_drv::get_type()); env = my_env::type_id::create("env", this); endfunction // in the agent drv = my_drv::type_id::create("drv", this); // returns an err_drv ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The override must be registered **before** `create()` runs. In practice that means in the test's `build_phase`, before the env is created. - The override type must derive from the original type, or the factory reports an error. - `create()` still calls `new()` internally. The class needs a constructor with the standard signature. ### Follow-ups - *Is `create()` virtual?* No. It is a static method of the type proxy (`type_id`). The factory picks the actual type to construct.

title: Difference between `copy()` and `clone()`
answer:
*Refer: *[*copy-and-clone-methods-in-uvm*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/copy-and-clone-methods-in-uvm)

- **`copy()`:** Copies data fields from a source object into an **already allocated** destination object. It performs a deep copy of the fields.

  ```systemverilog
  target_item = my_item::type_id::create("target_item");
  target_item.copy(source_item); // target_item must already exist
  ```

- **`clone()`:** First creates a new object using `create()`, and then internally calls `copy()` to duplicate the fields. It returns a handle of type `uvm_object`, which requires `$cast` into the target class handle.

  ```systemverilog
  $cast(target_item, source_item.clone()); // Allocates and copies in one step
  ```

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `copy()` fills an object that **already exists** with another object's field values. `clone()` **allocates a new object** with `create()`, then calls `copy()` into it. It returns a `uvm_object` handle, so you `$cast` the result.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User code
  participant S as src item
  participant D as dst item
  Note over U,D: copy()
  U->>D: dst = my_item::type_id::create("dst")
  U->>D: dst.copy(src)
  D->>S: read fields via do_copy
  Note over U,D: clone()
  U->>S: src.clone()
  S->>S: create() new object of same type
  S->>S: new_obj.copy(this)
  S-->>U: uvm_object handle
  U->>U: $cast(dst, handle)
```

### Explanation
| | `copy(rhs)` | `clone()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allocates memory | No, the destination must exist | Yes |
| Return value | `void` (function) | `uvm_object` |
| Needs `$cast` | No | Yes |
| Can be overridden | Override `do_copy()`, not `copy()` | `clone()` is virtual but rarely overridden |

```systemverilog
my_item a, b, c;
a = my_item::type_id::create("a");
void'(a.randomize());

b = my_item::type_id::create("b");
b.copy(a);                 // b already allocated

if (!$cast(c, a.clone()))  // c is a new, independent object
  `uvm_fatal("CAST", "clone cast failed")

// custom deep copy hook
virtual function void do_copy(uvm_object rhs);
  my_item r;
  super.do_copy(rhs);
  $cast(r, rhs);
  addr = r.addr;
  data = r.data;
  payload = r.payload;      // a dynamic array is copied by value
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- How deep the copy goes depends on `do_copy()` or the field macros. `uvm_field_object` with `UVM_DEEP` (the default) copies nested objects, while `UVM_REFERENCE` copies only the handle.
- Calling `copy()` on a null destination gives a null-handle runtime error.
- A monitor should send a clone, or a freshly created item, to analysis ports. That way the scoreboard never sees later mutations.

### Follow-ups
- *Can you clone a component?* No. `uvm_component::clone()` reports an error, because components cannot be duplicated.

title: Difference between `uvm_resource_db` and `uvm_config_db`
answer:
*Refer: *[*Difference_between_uvm_config_db_and_uvm_resource_db*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm_config_db-in-uvm#Difference_between_uvm_config_db_and_uvm_resource_db)

| Feature | `uvm_resource_db` | `uvm_config_db` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Relationship** | The underlying core database engine in UVM | A layered convenience API built on top of `uvm_resource_db` |
| **Lookup Mechanism** | String name lookup or type lookup (supports regex) | Hierarchical context + scope + field name lookup |
| **Precedence Resolution** | **Last write wins**: If two writes occur to the same key, the later one wins regardless of hierarchy | **Hierarchical precedence**: Higher-level components in the hierarchy (e.g., test or env) have higher precedence over lower-level components during `build_phase` |
| **Typical Usage** | Low-level resource sharing without hierarchical scoping | Standard UVM method for passing virtual interfaces, configuration objects, and knobs |

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_resource_db` is the low-level, name/type-based resource pool. `uvm_config_db` is a thin, type-safe wrapper on top of it. The wrapper scopes each set by component hierarchy and resolves conflicts by hierarchy during build, with the last write winning after build. ```mermaid flowchart LR T["uvm_test: config_db set(this, 'env.agt*', 'is_active', UVM_PASSIVE)"] --> CDB["uvm_config_db API
scope = cntxt.get_full_name() + inst_name"] CDB --> RP["uvm_resource_pool (global)"] RD["uvm_resource_db set('scope', 'name', val)"] --> RP RP --> G["agent: config_db get(this, '', 'is_active', v)"] ``` ### Explanation | | `uvm_resource_db` | `uvm_config_db` | | --- | --- | --- | | Relationship | Underlying database (resource pool) | Convenience layer over resource_db | | Key | Plain scope string, name, type | Context component + instance path + field name | | Scope | Scope string written by you (glob/regex) | Built from `cntxt.get_full_name()` and `inst_name` | | Conflict resolution | By resource precedence and queue order (`set_override` pushes a value to the front) | During build: the setter higher in the hierarchy wins. After build: the last set wins | | Typical use | Global, non-hierarchical resources shared by many | Virtual interfaces, config objects, knobs to specific components | ```systemverilog // config_db: hierarchical and component-relative uvm_config_db#(int)::set(this, "env.agt", "num_pkts", 100); uvm_config_db#(int)::get(this, "", "num_pkts", num_pkts); // resource_db: explicit scope string uvm_resource_db#(int)::set("*", "global_seed_mode", 1, this); void'(uvm_resource_db#(int)::read_by_name("*", "global_seed_mode", mode, this)); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Both are typed. A `set` with `#(int)` is not visible to a `get` with `#(bit[31:0])`. - Use `+UVM_CONFIG_DB_TRACE` / `+UVM_RESOURCE_DB_TRACE` to debug misses. ### Follow-ups - *Which should you use by default?* `uvm_config_db`. Reach for resource_db only for truly global, non-hierarchical data.

title: What is severity and verbosity in UVM?
answer:
Severity and verbosity control reporting and message filtering in UVM.

**1. Severity Levels (`uvm_severity`):** Indicates the criticality of a message:

- `UVM_INFO`: Informational message indicating simulation milestones or variable values.

- `UVM_WARNING`: Indicates non-fatal unexpected conditions that may require attention.

- `UVM_ERROR`: Indicates a verification failure (e.g., scoreboard mismatch, protocol violation). Simulation continues by default.

- `UVM_FATAL`: Indicates an unrecoverable failure. Terminates simulation immediately (`UVM_EXIT`).

**2. Verbosity Levels (`uvm_verbosity`):** Filters informational messages (`UVM_INFO`):

- `UVM_NONE` (0): Always printed; cannot be filtered out.

- `UVM_LOW` (100): High-level milestone messages.

- `UVM_MEDIUM` (200): Default verbosity level; standard progress reports.

- `UVM_HIGH` (300): Detailed debugging messages.

- `UVM_FULL` (400): Maximum verbosity (e.g., full transaction dumps).

- `UVM_DEBUG` (500): Granular step-by-step debug traces.

*Filter Rule:* A message is printed if `message_verbosity <= component_verbosity_threshold`.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** **Severity** says how serious a message is (INFO, WARNING, ERROR, FATAL) and decides the default action. **Verbosity** applies only to `UVM_INFO` and decides whether the message prints at all, compared against the component's verbosity threshold.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  M["uvm_info(ID, msg, UVM_HIGH)"] --> C{"message verbosity <= threshold?"}
  C -->|"yes"| P["print"]
  C -->|"no"| D["drop silently"]
  E["uvm_error(ID, msg)"] --> A["always processed: UVM_DISPLAY | UVM_COUNT"]
  F["uvm_fatal(ID, msg)"] --> X["UVM_DISPLAY | UVM_EXIT: ends simulation"]
```

### Explanation
| Severity | Default action | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UVM_INFO` | `UVM_DISPLAY` | Informational, filtered by verbosity |
| `UVM_WARNING` | `UVM_DISPLAY` | Unexpected but not a failure |
| `UVM_ERROR` | `UVM_DISPLAY \| UVM_COUNT` | Check failed. Simulation stops after `max_quit_count` errors (if set) |
| `UVM_FATAL` | `UVM_DISPLAY \| UVM_EXIT` | Unrecoverable failure, exits immediately |

| Verbosity | Value | Prints when threshold is `UVM_MEDIUM` (default)? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UVM_NONE` | 0 | Always |
| `UVM_LOW` | 100 | Yes |
| `UVM_MEDIUM` | 200 | Yes |
| `UVM_HIGH` | 300 | No |
| `UVM_FULL` | 400 | No |
| `UVM_DEBUG` | 500 | No |

```systemverilog
`uvm_info("DRV", $sformatf("sent %s", req.convert2string()), UVM_HIGH)
`uvm_error("SCB", "data mismatch")
// change threshold for one subtree
env.agt.set_report_verbosity_level_hier(UVM_DEBUG);
// or on the command line: +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_HIGH
// per component/ID: +uvm_set_verbosity=uvm_test_top.env.*,DRV,UVM_FULL,run
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Verbosity has no effect on warnings, errors and fatals. To change those, use `set_report_severity_action` or `set_report_severity_override`, for example to demote a known error.
- The macros check verbosity **before** evaluating `$sformatf`, so filtered messages cost almost nothing. A direct call to `uvm_report_info` does not skip that work.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you stop after N errors?* Use `+UVM_MAX_QUIT_COUNT=N` or `set_report_max_quit_count(N)`.

title: Difference between `sequence` and `sequencer`
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-sequence*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-sequence)* and *[*uvm-sequencer*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-sequencer)

- **`uvm_sequence`:**

  - A transient object extending `uvm_sequence_base` (`uvm_object`).

  - Contains procedural logic, generation algorithms, and timing flows to create stimulus transactions (`sequence_item`).

  - Not bound to the structural hierarchy; can call sub-sequences.

- **`uvm_sequencer`:**

  - A quasi-static structural component extending `uvm_sequencer_base` (`uvm_component`).

  - Acts as an arbiter and buffer between multiple running sequences and the driver.

  - Receives transaction requests from sequences via `start_item()` / `finish_item()` and forwards them to the driver via TLM `seq_item_export`.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** A **sequence** is a transient object that *generates* items in its `body()`. A **sequencer** is a permanent component that *arbitrates* between running sequences and hands the granted items to the driver. ```mermaid flowchart LR S1["seq A (uvm_object)
body: start_item / finish_item"] --> SQR S2["seq B (uvm_object)"] --> SQR SQR["sequencer (uvm_component)
arbitration queue, FIFO / priority / random"] -->|"seq_item_export"| DRV["driver: seq_item_port.get_next_item"] DRV --> DUT["DUT pins"] ``` ### Explanation | | Sequence (`uvm_sequence #(REQ,RSP)`) | Sequencer (`uvm_sequencer #(REQ,RSP)`) | | --- | --- | --- | | Base | `uvm_sequence_item` → `uvm_object` | `uvm_component` | | Lifetime | Created, started, finished, discarded | Built once in `build_phase` | | Role | Stimulus *content*: what items, in what order, with what constraints | Stimulus *routing*: who goes next, response routing | | Key methods | `body()`, `start()`, `start_item()`, `finish_item()`, `lock()`, `grab()` | `set_arbitration()`, `stop_sequences()`, `seq_item_export` | | Count | Many, possibly concurrent or nested | One per agent (plus optional virtual sequencer) | ```systemverilog // test or virtual sequence wr_seq w = wr_seq::type_id::create("w"); rd_seq r = rd_seq::type_id::create("r"); fork w.start(env.agt.sqr); // both run on the same sequencer, r.start(env.agt.sqr); // the sequencer interleaves their items join ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A sequence must be started on a sequencer (`start(sqr)`), or `start_item()` fails because `m_sequencer` is null. - The sequencer grants on item boundaries. A sequence that needs back-to-back items uses `lock()` or `grab()`. ### Follow-ups - *Can a sequence run without a driver?* A virtual sequence runs on a virtual sequencer, or on `null`, and only starts child sequences. It never calls `start_item` itself.

title: How to run any test case in UVM?
answer:
*Refer: *[*Execution_of_the_test*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-test#Execution_of_the_test)

There are two primary ways to run a test case in UVM:

1. **Explicitly in Top Module:**
   Hardcoding the test name in the top testbench module:

   ```systemverilog
   initial begin
     run_test("my_custom_test");
   end
   ```

2. **Via Command-Line Plusarg (Industry Standard):**
   Calling `run_test()` without an argument in `tb_top`, and supplying the test name at runtime:

   ```systemverilog
   initial begin
     run_test(); // No argument passed
   end
   ```

   Command line invocation:

   ```bash
   <simulator_run_command> +UVM_TESTNAME=my_custom_test
   ```

   *Advantage:* The testbench is compiled once, and any test can be run without recompilation.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** Call `run_test()` from the top module's `initial` block. Pass the test name either as a hard-coded argument or, preferably, with `+UVM_TESTNAME=<test>` at runtime, so one compiled image can run every test.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  TOP["tb_top: initial run_test()"] --> Q{"+UVM_TESTNAME given?"}
  Q -->|"yes"| N["use plusarg name (overrides the argument)"]
  Q -->|"no"| A{"argument given?"}
  A -->|"yes"| AN["use run_test('name')"]
  A -->|"no"| E["fatal: no test specified"]
  N --> F["factory creates uvm_test_top"]
  AN --> F
  F --> PH["phases: build ... final"]
  PH --> FIN["$finish (finish_on_completion)"]
```

### Solution
```systemverilog
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  `include "uvm_macros.svh"
  import my_test_pkg::*;          // makes test classes visible to the factory

  bit clk;
  always #5 clk = ~clk;
  dut_if vif(clk);
  dut    u_dut(.clk(clk), .data(vif.data) /* ... */);

  initial begin
    uvm_config_db#(virtual dut_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.*", "vif", vif);
    run_test();                    // test chosen by +UVM_TESTNAME
  end
endmodule
```

```bash
# compile once, run many tests
xrun -uvm -f files.f +UVM_TESTNAME=smoke_test  +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_LOW
xrun -uvm -f files.f +UVM_TESTNAME=stress_test +ntb_random_seed=1234
```

| Method | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `run_test("smoke_test")` | Simple for a single test | Recompile or edit to change tests |
| `run_test()` + `+UVM_TESTNAME` | One build runs all tests, works with regressions | Name must match a registered class exactly |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The test class must be registered with `` `uvm_component_utils `` and compiled into the image. Otherwise the factory cannot find it ("Requested test from command line +UVM_TESTNAME=... not found").
- If both are given, the plusarg wins.

### Follow-ups
- *What is the test instance called?* `uvm_test_top`, a child of `uvm_top`.

title: Write a simple UVM sequence template and explain each line
solution:
**Key idea:** A sequence is a factory-registered `uvm_object` whose `body()` repeatedly runs the item handshake: create, `start_item` (wait for a grant), randomize late, `finish_item` (wait for `item_done`).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant SEQ as my_sequence.body
  participant SQR as sequencer
  participant DRV as driver
  SEQ->>SQR: start_item(req) requests a grant
  DRV->>SQR: get_next_item()
  SQR-->>SEQ: grant (start_item returns)
  SEQ->>SEQ: req.randomize() late randomization
  SEQ->>SQR: finish_item(req)
  SQR-->>DRV: req
  DRV->>DRV: drive pins
  DRV->>SQR: item_done()
  SQR-->>SEQ: finish_item returns
```

### Code
```systemverilog
class my_sequence extends uvm_sequence #(my_seq_item);   // (1) REQ type sets req/rsp handles
  `uvm_object_utils(my_sequence)                          // (2) factory registration (object)

  rand int unsigned num_items = 10;                       // (3) knob, randomizable by the parent
  constraint c_num { num_items inside {[1:50]}; }

  function new(string name = "my_sequence");              // (4) object constructor: name only
    super.new(name);
  endfunction

  virtual task body();                                    // (5) the stimulus lives here
    repeat (num_items) begin
      req = my_seq_item::type_id::create("req");          // (6) factory create: overridable
      start_item(req);                                    // (7) arbitrate, wait for driver
      if (!req.randomize() with { addr < 32'h100; })      // (8) late randomization
        `uvm_error(get_type_name(), "randomize failed")
      finish_item(req);                                   // (9) send, block until item_done
      `uvm_info(get_type_name(), req.convert2string(), UVM_HIGH)
    end
  endtask
endclass

// usage (in a test's run_phase)
// my_sequence seq = my_sequence::type_id::create("seq");
// phase.raise_objection(this);
// if (!seq.randomize()) `uvm_fatal("TEST", "seq randomize")
// seq.start(env.agt.sqr);
// phase.drop_objection(this);
```

### Explanation
- `req` and `rsp` are inherited members typed from the class parameters, so there is no need to redeclare them. A local `my_seq_item req;` would shadow them.
- Randomizing after `start_item` lets constraints depend on state that exists only at grant time.
- `finish_item` returns once the driver calls `item_done()`. If a response is expected, call `get_response(rsp)` next.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Use `` `uvm_object_utils ``, not `` `uvm_component_utils ``. A sequence is an object.
- Forgetting `item_done()` in the driver hangs `finish_item` forever.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not `` `uvm_do ``?* Explicit calls are easier to debug and allow custom randomization or error handling.

title: How is scoreboard connected to different components?
answer:
The **UVM Scoreboard** receives transactions from monitors using TLM analysis ports and analysis exports/FIFOs:

1. **Direct Connection via `uvm_analysis_imp`:**
   The scoreboard declares an analysis implementation port (`uvm_analysis_imp #(item, scoreboard)`). In the `connect_phase` of the enclosing environment:

   ```systemverilog
   monitor.item_collected_port.connect(scoreboard.item_imp);
   ```

   The scoreboard must implement the `write(item t)` function.

2. **Connection via `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` (Recommended for multi-input scoreboards):**
   When comparing transactions from multiple monitors (e.g., ingress and egress), direct `write()` calls may create timing race conditions. Using TLM FIFOs decouples them:

   ```systemverilog
   // In env connect_phase:
   in_mon.item_port.connect(scb.in_fifo.analysis_export);
   out_mon.item_port.connect(scb.out_fifo.analysis_export);
   ```

   The scoreboard's `run_phase` can then independently `get()` from both FIFOs and compare results.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** Monitors publish observed transactions on `uvm_analysis_port`s. The scoreboard receives them through `uvm_analysis_imp`s, which call its `write_*()` functions, or through `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo`s that it drains in `run_phase`. The env wires everything up in `connect_phase`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph IN["input agent"]
    IM["in_mon.ap"]
  end
  subgraph OUT["output agent"]
    OM["out_mon.ap"]
  end
  IM -->|"write"| RM["reference model / predictor"]
  RM -->|"expected"| EF["scb.exp_fifo (uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo)"]
  OM -->|"actual"| AF["scb.act_fifo (uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo)"]
  EF --> CMP["scb.run_phase: get both, compare"]
  AF --> CMP
  IM -->|"write"| COV["coverage subscriber"]
```

### Explanation
**Option A: analysis imps (callback style)**
```systemverilog
`uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_exp)
`uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_act)
class my_scb extends uvm_scoreboard;
  uvm_analysis_imp_exp #(pkt, my_scb) exp_imp;
  uvm_analysis_imp_act #(pkt, my_scb) act_imp;
  pkt q[$];
  function void write_exp(pkt t); q.push_back(t); endfunction
  function void write_act(pkt t);
    pkt e;
    if (q.size() == 0) begin `uvm_error("SCB", "unexpected output") return; end
    e = q.pop_front();
    if (!t.compare(e)) `uvm_error("SCB", "mismatch")
  endfunction
  // new(): create exp_imp / act_imp with new("exp_imp", this)
endclass
```
**Option B: analysis FIFOs (thread style)**
```systemverilog
uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(pkt) exp_fifo, act_fifo;   // built with new("exp_fifo", this)
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  pkt e, a;
  forever begin
    act_fifo.get(a);
    exp_fifo.get(e);
    if (!a.compare(e)) `uvm_error("SCB", "mismatch")
  end
endtask
```
**Connection in the env**
```systemverilog
function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  in_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.exp_imp);            // A
  out_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.act_fifo.analysis_export); // B
  in_agt.mon.ap.connect(cov.analysis_export);    // same port fans out to many
endfunction
```

| | `uvm_analysis_imp` | `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Receives in | `write()` function (zero time) | Unbounded FIFO, then `get()` in a task |
| Multiple inputs | Needs `` `uvm_analysis_imp_decl `` suffixes | One FIFO per stream, no macros |
| Good for | Simple, in-order, immediate checks | Checks that wait or align two streams in time |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `write()` is a function and cannot block or wait.
- The monitor must send a new object each time (create or clone). Otherwise every queued entry points at the same, mutating item.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you check that nothing is left over?* In `check_phase`, report an error if the expected queue or FIFO is not empty (`exp_fifo.is_empty()`).

title: What is the UVM factory and what is its use?
answer:
The **UVM Factory** is a centralized object-creational registry based on the Factory Design Pattern.

**Key Uses:**

- Replaces direct constructor calls (`new()`) with polymorphic creation (`create()`).

- Allows replacing an object or component type with a derived type across the entire testbench (`set_type_override_by_type`) or for a specific instance path (`set_inst_override_by_type`) without editing existing testbench code.

- Essential for error injection tests, alternative protocol variations, and extending verification components.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** The UVM factory is a singleton lookup table from registered type names to type proxies (`type_id`). Creating everything through `type_id::create()` lets a test swap any registered class for a derived class, by type or by instance path, without editing or recompiling the environment. ```mermaid flowchart LR REG["uvm_component_utils(drv)
registers drv::type_id"] --> FAC["uvm_factory (singleton)
type table + override table"] TEST["test.build_phase:
set_type_override / set_inst_override"] --> FAC ENV["agent: drv::type_id::create('drv', this)"] --> FAC FAC -->|"no override"| D1["drv"] FAC -->|"override present"| D2["err_drv (extends drv)"] ``` ### Explanation - **Registration:** `` `uvm_object_utils(T) `` / `` `uvm_component_utils(T) `` create a `uvm_object_registry` / `uvm_component_registry` proxy called `type_id` and register it with the factory. - **Creation:** `T::type_id::create(name, parent)` asks the factory, which applies any matching override and constructs the final type. - **Override:** the test registers overrides before the env is built. ```systemverilog class err_test extends base_test; `uvm_component_utils(err_test) function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); // all packets become CRC-error packets pkt::type_id::set_type_override(crc_err_pkt::get_type()); // only agent 1's driver becomes a slow driver my_drv::type_id::set_inst_override(slow_drv::get_type(), "env.agt1.drv", this); super.build_phase(phase); // base test builds env afterwards endfunction endclass ``` | Typical use | Override | | --- | --- | | Error injection packet | Type override of the sequence item | | Different driver timing on one port | Instance override of a driver | | Different default sequence | Type override of a sequence | | Swap scoreboard or coverage model | Instance override | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Overrides affect only objects created with `create()` **after** the override is set. - Debug with `factory.print()` or `uvm_factory::get().print()`, and with `+uvm_set_type_override=orig,new`. ### Follow-ups - *Command-line override?* `+uvm_set_type_override=pkt,crc_err_pkt` or `+uvm_set_inst_override=my_drv,slow_drv,uvm_test_top.env.agt1.drv`.

title: Why phases are introduced in UVM? What are all phases present in UVM?
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-phases*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-phases)

**Why introduced:**
In traditional Verilog/SystemVerilog testbenches, components operated concurrently in unrestricted `initial` blocks, leading to race conditions during initialization, configuration, execution, and shutdown. UVM introduces structured phases to ensure all components transition synchronously through a deterministic lifecycle.

**Phases Present in UVM:**

1. **Build Phases (Functions - 0 simulation time, top-down):**

   - `build_phase`: Constructs components and distributes configurations.

   - `connect_phase`: Connects TLM ports and exports (bottom-up).

   - `end_of_elaboration_phase`: Finalizes topology and adjustments.

   - `start_of_simulation_phase`: Pre-run prints, banner display, and setup.

2. **Run Phase (Tasks - time-consuming, parallel):**

   - `run_phase`: Spans the active simulation time alongside 12 synchronized sub-phases:

     - *Reset:* `pre_reset` $	o$ `reset` $	o$ `post_reset`

     - *Configure:* `pre_configure` $	o$ `configure` $	o$ `post_configure`

     - *Main (Stimulus):* `pre_main` $	o$ `main` $	o$ `post_main`

     - *Shutdown:* `pre_shutdown` $	o$ `shutdown` $	o$ `post_shutdown`

3. **Cleanup Phases (Functions - 0 simulation time, bottom-up):**

   - `extract_phase`: Gathers state and counters.

   - `check_phase`: Validates that no transactions were dropped and checkers passed.

   - `report_phase`: Summarizes test results, pass/fail status, and coverage.

   - `final_phase`: Last-minute file closures and cleanups.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** Phases give every component the same ordered lifecycle: build, connect, run, check, report. Construction, connection, stimulus and checking then happen in a deterministic order instead of racing in `initial` blocks.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  subgraph BUILD["Build phases (functions, 0 time)"]
    B1["build (top-down)"] --> B2["connect"] --> B3["end_of_elaboration"] --> B4["start_of_simulation"]
  end
  subgraph RUN["Run-time phases (tasks, consume time)"]
    R0["run_phase (in parallel with the 12 sub-phases)"]
    R1["pre_reset / reset / post_reset"] --> R2["pre_configure / configure / post_configure"] --> R3["pre_main / main / post_main"] --> R4["pre_shutdown / shutdown / post_shutdown"]
  end
  subgraph CLEAN["Cleanup phases (functions, 0 time)"]
    C1["extract"] --> C2["check"] --> C3["report"] --> C4["final"]
  end
  B4 --> R0
  B4 --> R1
  R0 --> C1
  R4 --> C1
```

### Explanation
| Phase | Type | Order | Typical work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `build_phase` | function | top-down | create children, `config_db::get`, set overrides |
| `connect_phase` | function | bottom-up | connect TLM ports, assign RAL sequencer |
| `end_of_elaboration_phase` | function | bottom-up | print topology, final config checks |
| `start_of_simulation_phase` | function | bottom-up | banners, initial settings |
| `run_phase` | task | parallel | drive, monitor, run sequences |
| 12 run-time sub-phases | task | parallel per phase | finer-grained reset/config/main/shutdown flow |
| `extract_phase` | function | bottom-up | collect final data from scoreboards and coverage |
| `check_phase` | function | bottom-up | check that queues are empty, end-of-test checks |
| `report_phase` | function | bottom-up | print pass/fail summary |
| `final_phase` | function | bottom-up | close files, final cleanup |

- Every component's phase N finishes before any component starts phase N+1. For task phases, the phase ends when all objections are dropped.
- Custom phases and phase domains (`uvm_domain`) can be added, but they are rarely needed.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Mixing `run_phase` with the sub-phases in the same environment works, since they run in parallel, but it makes objection handling confusing. Many teams use only `run_phase`.
- Doing time-consuming work in a function phase is a compile error. You cannot call a task from a function.

### Follow-ups
- *Which phase builds the RAL model?* Usually `build_phase` of the env. The map's sequencer and adapter are set in `connect_phase`.

title: What approach does `build_phase` use and why?
answer:
`build_phase` uses a **top-down** approach.

**Reason:**
A parent component (e.g., `uvm_test` or `uvm_env`) must be instantiated and configured first before it can determine what child components (e.g., agents, scoreboards, drivers, monitors) are needed and instantiate them. Furthermore, configuration settings and virtual interfaces pushed into `uvm_config_db` by the parent must be available when child components build themselves.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `build_phase` runs **top-down**. A parent's `build_phase` creates its children, so a child cannot be built until its parent has run. The parent can also set overrides and `config_db` values before its children read them. ```mermaid flowchart TD T["1. test.build_phase
set overrides, config_db set, create env"] --> E["2. env.build_phase
get env_cfg, create agent + scoreboard"] E --> A["3. agent.build_phase
get is_active, create drv / sqr / mon"] E --> S["3. scb.build_phase"] A --> D["4. drv.build_phase: get vif"] A --> M["4. mon.build_phase: get vif"] ``` ### Explanation - **Existence:** the hierarchy is built by the phase itself. `env` only exists after `test.build_phase` calls `env = my_env::type_id::create("env", this)`, so the env's build can only run after that. - **Configuration flows down:** the test sets configuration (`uvm_config_db::set(this, "env.agt", "cfg", cfg)`) before creating the env. The agent can then `get` it in its own build_phase and decide, for example, whether to build a driver (active/passive). - **Overrides flow down:** factory overrides set in the test take effect when lower levels call `create()`. - **Precedence:** during build, a `config_db::set` from a higher component wins over one from a lower component. That works because higher components build first and are expected to be the authority. ```systemverilog function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); // in my_agent super.build_phase(phase); if (!uvm_config_db#(agent_cfg)::get(this, "", "cfg", cfg)) `uvm_fatal("CFG", "no agent_cfg") mon = my_mon::type_id::create("mon", this); if (cfg.is_active == UVM_ACTIVE) begin drv = my_drv::type_id::create("drv", this); sqr = my_sqr::type_id::create("sqr", this); end endfunction ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Children built in the same parent's build_phase are built breadth-first in creation order. Do not rely on sibling order. - Connecting ports in build_phase is wrong. Siblings might not exist yet, which is exactly why `connect_phase` is a separate, later phase. ### Follow-ups - *Which phases are bottom-up?* All other function phases: connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, extract, check, report, final.

title: Draw and explain the verification environment in UVM
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-testbench-top*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-testbench-top)

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                               tb_top                                   |
|  +--------------------+                     +-----------------------+  |
|  |     DUT Instance   |<=== Interface ====>| Virtual Interface (vif)|  |
|  +--------------------+                     +-----------+-----------+  |
|                                                         |              |
|  +------------------------------------------------------+-----------+  |
|  | uvm_test_top (uvm_test)                                          |  |
|  |   +------------------------------------------------------------+ |  |
|  |   | uvm_env                                                    | |  |
|  |   |  +-------------------------------------+  +--------------+ | |  |
|  |   |  | uvm_agent                           |  | Scoreboard   | | |  |
|  |   |  |  +-----------+     +------------+   |  |  (Checker &  | | |  |
|  |   |  |  | Sequencer |<--->|   Driver   |===|==> Reference    | | |  |
|  |   |  |  +-----------+     +------------+   |  |    Model)    | | |  |
|  |   |  |                         | (vif)     |  +-------^------+ | |  |
|  |   |  |                    +----+-------+   |          |        | |  |
|  |   |  |                    |  Monitor   |===|==========+        | |  |
|  |   |  |                    +------------+   |  +-------v------+ | |  |
|  |   |  +-------------------------------------+  | Coverage     | | |  |
|  |   |                                           | Collector    | | |  |
|  |   |                                           +--------------+ | |  |
|  |   +------------------------------------------------------------+ |  |
|  +------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Component Breakdown:**

- **`tb_top`:** Top SV module; instantiates DUT, interfaces, clock/reset generators, and calls `run_test()`.

- **`uvm_test`:** Configures environment topology, test-specific parameters, and selects default sequences.

- **`uvm_env`:** Encapsulates sub-environments, agents, scoreboards, and coverage collectors.

- **`uvm_agent`:** Groups protocol-specific components:

  - *Sequencer:* Controls sequence execution and arbitrates items.

  - *Driver:* Converts sequence items to signal-level activity on the interface.

  - *Monitor:* Samples interface signals and converts pin activity into transaction objects.

- **`uvm_scoreboard`:** Compares DUT outputs against expected outputs from an integrated reference model.

- **`Coverage Collector`:** Measures functional coverage points from sampled transactions.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** A static `tb_top` module holds the DUT, the interfaces and the clock/reset, then calls `run_test()`. The dynamic UVM hierarchy is `uvm_test_top → env → agents (sequencer, driver, monitor) + scoreboard + coverage`, joined to the DUT through virtual interfaces from `uvm_config_db`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph TOP["tb_top (module)"]
    CLK["clock / reset gen"]
    IF["dut_if"]
    DUT["DUT"]
    IF <--> DUT
  end
  subgraph TEST["uvm_test_top (my_test)"]
    subgraph ENV["env"]
      subgraph AGT["in_agent (ACTIVE)"]
        SQR["sequencer"] -->|"seq_item_port"| DRV["driver"]
        MON["monitor"]
      end
      subgraph OAGT["out_agent (PASSIVE)"]
        OMON["monitor"]
      end
      SCB["scoreboard + ref model"]
      COV["coverage subscriber"]
    end
    SEQ["sequences started by the test"] --> SQR
  end
  DRV -->|"vif"| IF
  IF -->|"vif"| MON
  IF -->|"vif"| OMON
  MON -->|"analysis port"| SCB
  MON -->|"analysis port"| COV
  OMON -->|"analysis port"| SCB
```

### Explanation
| Block | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `tb_top` | Instantiates DUT and interface, generates clock/reset, `config_db::set` of the vif, calls `run_test()` |
| Test | Picks configuration and overrides, builds env, starts the virtual sequence, raises and drops objections |
| Env | Builds agents, scoreboard and coverage, and connects their analysis ports |
| Agent | One interface/protocol. Active: sequencer + driver + monitor. Passive: monitor only |
| Sequencer | Arbitrates sequences and supplies items to the driver |
| Driver | Turns items into pin activity on the vif |
| Monitor | Samples pins, rebuilds transactions, writes them to its analysis port |
| Scoreboard | Predicts expected output (reference model) and compares it with actual |
| Coverage | Samples covergroups from monitored transactions |

```systemverilog
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*; import tb_pkg::*;
  logic clk = 0, rst_n;
  always #5 clk = ~clk;
  initial begin rst_n = 0; #50 rst_n = 1; end
  dut_if vif(clk, rst_n);
  my_dut u_dut(.clk, .rst_n, .bus(vif));
  initial begin
    uvm_config_db#(virtual dut_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.*", "vif", vif);
    run_test();
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Keep the agent free of DUT knowledge, so it can be reused at SoC level as a passive agent.
- The scoreboard should consume only monitor outputs, never the driver's items. That way it checks what actually reached the pins.

### Follow-ups
- *Where do RAL and the virtual sequencer go?* In the env. The RAL adapter and predictor connect to the bus agent's sequencer and monitor.

title: What all UVM phases take time?
answer:
Only **task-based** phases consume simulation time:

- `run_phase` (spans the entire active simulation duration).

- The 12 runtime sub-phases:

  - `pre_reset_phase`, `reset_phase`, `post_reset_phase`

  - `pre_configure_phase`, `configure_phase`, `post_configure_phase`

  - `pre_main_phase`, `main_phase`, `post_main_phase`

  - `pre_shutdown_phase`, `shutdown_phase`, `post_shutdown_phase`

*All other phases (**`build`**, **`connect`**, **`check`**, **`report`**, etc.) are functions and execute in zero simulation time.*

---
solution:
**Key idea:** Only **task** phases consume simulation time: `run_phase` and the 12 run-time sub-phases (pre_/post_ reset, configure, main, shutdown). Every other phase is a function and finishes in zero time. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Z1["0 sim time"] b["build"] --> c["connect"] --> e["end_of_elaboration"] --> s["start_of_simulation"] end subgraph T["consumes time (tasks)"] r["run_phase"] sub["pre_reset ... reset ... post_reset
pre_configure ... post_configure
pre_main ... main ... post_main
pre_shutdown ... shutdown ... post_shutdown"] end subgraph Z2["0 sim time"] x["extract"] --> k["check"] --> rp["report"] --> f["final"] end s --> r s --> sub r --> x sub --> x ``` ### Explanation | Time-consuming (task) phases | Notes | | --- | --- | | `run_phase` | Starts at the same time as `pre_reset_phase` and runs in parallel with all sub-phases | | `pre_reset`, `reset`, `post_reset` | Apply and release reset | | `pre_configure`, `configure`, `post_configure` | Program registers and configuration | | `pre_main`, `main`, `post_main` | Main traffic | | `pre_shutdown`, `shutdown`, `post_shutdown` | Drain traffic, final reads | - A task phase ends when every objection raised in that phase is dropped (plus drain time). - `run_phase` ends only when its own objections are dropped **and** the last sub-phase (`post_shutdown`) has ended, because they share the same end point before `extract`. ```systemverilog task main_phase(uvm_phase phase); phase.raise_objection(this); traffic_seq.start(env.agt.sqr); // time passes here phase.drop_objection(this); endtask ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A task phase with no raised objection ends after a delta cycle. Your `run_phase` thread is then killed when the phase moves on, which is a common "test ends at time 0" bug. - Functions such as `build_phase` cannot contain `#delay`, `@` or `wait`. ### Follow-ups - *Can a phase jump backwards?* Yes, the run-time sub-phases support `phase.jump(uvm_reset_phase::get())`, used for example in on-the-fly reset tests.

title: What all phases are functions and tasks in UVM?
answer:
*Refer: *[*How_does_UVM_phase_execution_start*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-phases#How_does_UVM_phase_execution_start)

- **Function Phases (Zero Simulation Time):**

  - `build_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - `connect_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - `end_of_elaboration_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - `start_of_simulation_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - `extract_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - `check_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - `report_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - `final_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

- **Task Phases (Time-Consuming):**

  - `run_phase(uvm_phase phase)`

  - All 12 runtime sub-phases (`reset`, `configure`, `main`, `shutdown`, and their `pre`/`post` counterparts).

---
solution:
**Key idea:** Phases that only build, connect or check are **functions** (zero time). Phases that interact with the DUT over time are **tasks**: `run_phase` and the 12 run-time sub-phases. | Phase | Kind | Execution order | | --- | --- | --- | | `build_phase` | function | top-down | | `connect_phase` | function | bottom-up | | `end_of_elaboration_phase` | function | bottom-up | | `start_of_simulation_phase` | function | bottom-up | | `run_phase` | **task** | all components in parallel | | `pre_reset`, `reset`, `post_reset` | **task** | parallel | | `pre_configure`, `configure`, `post_configure` | **task** | parallel | | `pre_main`, `main`, `post_main` | **task** | parallel | | `pre_shutdown`, `shutdown`, `post_shutdown` | **task** | parallel | | `extract_phase` | function | bottom-up | | `check_phase` | function | bottom-up | | `report_phase` | function | bottom-up | | `final_phase` | function | top-down | ```mermaid flowchart LR F1["8 function phases
uvm_bottomup_phase / uvm_topdown_phase"] --- T1["13 task phases
uvm_task_phase, forked per component"] ``` ### Explanation - In UVM source, function phases extend `uvm_topdown_phase` or `uvm_bottomup_phase` and run their `exec_func` in each component in order. Task phases extend `uvm_task_phase`, which forks `exec_task` for every component at the same time. - Prototypes: ```systemverilog virtual function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); virtual function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase); virtual task run_phase(uvm_phase phase); virtual task main_phase(uvm_phase phase); virtual function void report_phase(uvm_phase phase); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - `final_phase` is declared as a `uvm_topdown_phase` in UVM 1.2. Many tutorials list it as bottom-up, but it is top-down. - Writing `task build_phase` gives a compile error, because the prototype must match the virtual function in `uvm_component`. ### Follow-ups - *Why must build be a function?* It runs at time 0 to create the static hierarchy, so it has no reason to wait. Making it a function guarantees nothing can block elaboration.

title: Why do we use the `super` keyword in phases like `super.build_phase`, `super.main_phase` etc.?
answer:
- The `super` keyword calls the base class implementation of the method.

- In `build_phase`, calling `super.build_phase(phase)` executes `uvm_component::build_phase`, which automatically unpacks and assigns values from the `uvm_config_db` for fields registered with `uvm_field_*` macros.

- In other phases, it ensures any base-class behavior or safety checks are preserved.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `super.(phase)` runs the parent class's version of the phase. In `build_phase` this matters most: `uvm_component::build_phase` calls `apply_config_settings()`, which automatically pulls `config_db` values into fields registered with `` `uvm_field_* `` macros. Your own base classes also need `super` to keep their behavior, for example a base test that builds the env. ```mermaid flowchart TD D["my_test.build_phase"] -->|"super.build_phase(phase)"| B["base_test.build_phase
create env, cfg objects"] B -->|"super.build_phase(phase)"| U["uvm_component.build_phase
apply_config_settings: auto-get uvm_field_* fields"] D --> X["test-specific overrides / settings"] ``` ### Explanation | Phase | What skipping `super` breaks | | --- | --- | | `build_phase` | Auto-configuration of `uvm_field_*` fields from `config_db`, plus any user base-class building (env never created) | | `connect_phase`, `report_phase`, ... | Connections and reports implemented in your own base classes | | `run_phase` / `main_phase` | Threads started by the base class, such as reset handling or a heartbeat | ```systemverilog class base_test extends uvm_test; my_env env; function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); super.build_phase(phase); // uvm_component auto-config env = my_env::type_id::create("env", this); endfunction endclass class err_test extends base_test; function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); pkt::type_id::set_type_override(err_pkt::get_type()); // before env is built super.build_phase(phase); // builds env endfunction endclass ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - **Order matters.** Overrides and config sets that must influence children go *before* `super.build_phase()` in a derived test, because the base class creates the env. - For phases whose UVM base implementation is empty (for example `uvm_component::run_phase`), `super` does nothing harmful. Calling it is still a good habit. - Auto-config only applies to fields registered with field macros. Fields fetched with explicit `config_db::get` do not need it. ### Follow-ups - *Can you disable auto-config?* Yes. Override `apply_config_settings` or skip `super.build_phase`. Some teams avoid field macros entirely for performance.

title: Difference between `` `uvm_do `` and `` `uvm_rand_send ``
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm_do_example*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-sequence-macros#uvm_do_example)* and *[*uvm_rand_send_example*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-sequence-macros#uvm_rand_send_example)

- **`` `uvm_do(item/seq) ``:**
  Carries out the full item lifecycle:

  1. Creates the item using factory (`type_id::create()`).

  2. Calls `start_item()`.

  3. Randomizes the item (`randomize()`).

  4. Calls `finish_item()`.

- **`` `uvm_rand_send(item/seq) ``:**
  Requires the item to **already be created/allocated**.

  1. Calls `start_item()`.

  2. Randomizes the item (`randomize()`).

  3. Calls `finish_item()`.
     *(Does not create the object).*

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `` `uvm_do(item) `` **creates** the item through the factory, then runs start, randomize and finish. `` `uvm_rand_send(item) `` assumes the item **already exists** (made earlier with `` `uvm_create `` or `create()`) and only runs start, randomize and finish.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph DO["uvm_do(req)"]
    a1["create (factory)"] --> a2["start_item"] --> a3["randomize"] --> a4["finish_item"]
  end
  subgraph RS["uvm_rand_send(req)"]
    b2["start_item"] --> b3["randomize"] --> b4["finish_item"]
  end
  C["uvm_create(req) + set fields"] --> RS
```

### Explanation
| Macro | Creates? | Randomizes? | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `` `uvm_do(x) `` | yes | yes | Quick random item |
| `` `uvm_do_with(x, {c}) `` | yes | yes, with inline constraints | Quick constrained item |
| `` `uvm_create(x) `` | yes | no | Allocate, then set fields by hand |
| `` `uvm_send(x) `` | no | no | Send a pre-built directed item |
| `` `uvm_rand_send(x) `` | no | yes | Reuse one allocated item, re-randomize each time |
| `` `uvm_rand_send_with(x, {c}) `` | no | yes, with inline constraints | Same, with constraints |

```systemverilog
task body();
  `uvm_do_with(req, { addr == 'h10; })   // new object each time

  `uvm_create(req)                        // allocate once
  req.burst_len = 4;                      // pre-set non-rand fields
  repeat (5) `uvm_rand_send_with(req, { write == 1; })
endtask
```
The explicit equivalent of `` `uvm_rand_send(req) ``:
```systemverilog
start_item(req);
if (!req.randomize()) `uvm_warning("RND", "randomize failed")
finish_item(req);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Re-sending the **same** object with `` `uvm_rand_send `` is fine for the driver. Monitors and scoreboards must not store a handle to it, though, because its fields change on the next randomize.
- `` `uvm_rand_send `` on a null handle fails. Create the item first.
- On a sequence (not an item), these macros call `start()` with `call_pre_post = 0`, so `pre_body` / `post_body` are skipped.

### Follow-ups
- *Why do many teams ban the macros?* They hide the handshake, give poor error messages on randomize failure, and are hard to step through in a debugger.

title: What are bottom-up and top-down approaches in UVM phases?
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-phases*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-phases)

- **Top-Down Approach:**

  - Parent components execute before child components.

  - Used in: `build_phase`. (Parent must exist to instantiate and configure its children).

- **Bottom-Up Approach:**

  - Child components execute before their parent.

  - Used in: `connect_phase`, `end_of_elaboration_phase`, `start_of_simulation_phase`, `extract_phase`, `check_phase`, `report_phase`, and `final_phase`. (Subcomponents must finalize connections and check status before the parent aggregates them).

---
solution:
**Key idea:** Only `build_phase` (and `final_phase`) run **top-down**, because a parent must exist before it can create its children. The other function phases (connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, extract, check, report) run **bottom-up**, so children finish before parents summarize. Task phases run all components **in parallel**.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph TD["build_phase: top-down"]
    t1["1 test"] --> t2["2 env"] --> t3["3 agent"] --> t4["4 driver, monitor"]
  end
  subgraph BU["connect / check / report: bottom-up"]
    u4["1 driver, monitor"] --> u3["2 agent"] --> u2["3 env"] --> u1["4 test"]
  end
```

### Explanation
| Order | Phases | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Top-down | `build_phase`, `final_phase` | A parent creates and configures its children |
| Bottom-up | `connect`, `end_of_elaboration`, `start_of_simulation`, `extract`, `check`, `report` | Children are complete first. Parents connect sub-blocks and aggregate their results |
| Parallel | `run_phase` and the 12 run-time sub-phases | Every component's task is forked at once |

- Example: in `report_phase` each scoreboard prints its own counts first, then the test (last, at the top) prints the overall PASS/FAIL banner from the totals.
- In `connect_phase`, bottom-up means an agent can connect its driver to its sequencer before the env connects the agent's monitor port to the scoreboard. Connection really only needs every component to exist, though.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Siblings (children of the same parent) run in an order you should not depend on.
- Calling `create()` for components outside build_phase is an error ("cannot create components after build").

### Follow-ups
- *Does bottom-up matter for connect?* Not much functionally: all components exist after build. It matters more for end_of_elaboration checks and for reporting.

title: How do `uvm_config_db` set/get work?
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm_config_db-in-uvm*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm_config_db-in-uvm)

The `uvm_config_db` is a type-parameterized configuration database providing a centralized mechanism to store and retrieve parameters, configuration objects, and virtual interface handles across the UVM hierarchy.

#### 1. Syntax

```systemverilog
// Set method:
uvm_config_db #(TYPE)::set(uvm_component cntxt, string inst_name, string field_name, TYPE value);

// Get method:
uvm_config_db #(TYPE)::get(uvm_component cntxt, string inst_name, string field_name, ref TYPE value);
```

#### 2. Arguments Breakdown

- `cntxt`: The contextual component performing the set/get (usually `this` inside components, or `null` in `tb_top` / top module).

- `inst_name`: Relative hierarchical path matching target component instance(s). Can use wildcards (e.g., `"uvm_test_top.env.agent.*"`).

- `field_name`: Key/identifier string for the lookup.

- `value`: Variable holding the value being written (`set`) or read (`get`).

#### 3. Execution & Precedence Rules

- **Lookup Key:** Internally forms a lookup tuple combining context hierarchy, `inst_name`, and `field_name`.

- **Hierarchical Precedence in `build_phase`:** If multiple `set()` calls target the same variable, **the component higher up in the hierarchy wins** (e.g., a setting in `test` overrides a setting in `env`).

- **Same-level Precedence:** If two `set()` calls occur at the same hierarchical level, the **last write wins**.

- **Return Value of `get()`:** Returns `1` (true) on successful retrieval, `0` (false) if lookup fails or type mismatch occurs.

#### 4. Common Example: Virtual Interface Binding

```systemverilog
// In tb_top:
initial begin
  uvm_config_db #(virtual dut_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top*", "vif", vif);
  run_test();
end

// In driver build_phase:
virtual function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  super.build_phase(phase);
  if (!uvm_config_db #(virtual dut_if)::get(this, "", "vif", vif)) begin
    `uvm_fatal("NO_VIF", "Virtual interface not found in uvm_config_db")
  end
endfunction
```

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_config_db#(T)::set(cntxt, inst_name, field, value)` stores a typed value visible to the components whose path matches `cntxt.get_full_name() + "." + inst_name`. `get(this, "", field, var)` looks up the caller's own full path and returns 1 on success.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant TOP as tb_top (cntxt = null)
  participant TEST as uvm_test_top
  participant DB as config_db / resource pool
  participant DRV as uvm_test_top.env.agt.drv
  TOP->>DB: set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.agt*", "vif", vif)
  TEST->>DB: set(this, "env.agt", "cfg", cfg) scope = uvm_test_top.env.agt
  DRV->>DB: get(this, "", "vif", vif) lookup path = uvm_test_top.env.agt.drv
  DB-->>DRV: match on glob, returns 1
```

### Explanation
**Signatures**
```systemverilog
static function void set(uvm_component cntxt, string inst_name,
                         string field_name, T value);
static function bit  get(uvm_component cntxt, string inst_name,
                         string field_name, inout T value);
```
| Argument | `set` | `get` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cntxt` | Starting point of the scope (`null` means `uvm_root`, the top) | Usually `this` |
| `inst_name` | Relative path, wildcards allowed (`"env.agt*"`, `"*"`) | Usually `""` (myself) |
| `field_name` | Key string | Same key |
| value | Stored by value (handles for objects/vifs) | Output variable |

**Precedence**
| Situation | Winner |
| --- | --- |
| Two sets during `build_phase` from different levels | The component **higher** in the hierarchy (test beats env) |
| Two sets from the same component, or any sets after build | The **last** set |

```systemverilog
// tb_top
uvm_config_db#(virtual dut_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.agt*", "vif", vif);
// test
uvm_config_db#(int)::set(this, "env.agt.sqr.main_phase", "default_sequence_count", 20);
// driver
if (!uvm_config_db#(virtual dut_if)::get(this, "", "vif", vif))
  `uvm_fatal("NOVIF", {"vif not set for ", get_full_name()})
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The type parameter must match exactly. `#(int)` vs `#(int unsigned)` is a silent miss.
- `"env.agt"` matches only the agent itself, not its children. Use `"env.agt*"` or `"env.agt.*"` to reach the driver.
- A `get` before the matching `set` returns 0. Make sure the set happens earlier (top module before `run_test`, parents before children).
- Debug with `+UVM_CONFIG_DB_TRACE` and `uvm_config_db_options::turn_on_tracing()`.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you wait for a runtime value?* `uvm_config_db#(T)::wait_modified(this, "", "field")` blocks until a matching set happens.

title: What is an analysis port?
answer:
*Refer: *[*tlm_analysis_port_example*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/tlm/tlm-analysis-interface#tlm_analysis_port_example)

The `uvm_analysis_port #(T)` is a TLM-based communication channel that implements a **broadcast** (1-to-many or 1-to-0) pattern.

**Key Characteristics:**

- **Non-blocking `write()`:** Calling `ap.write(t)` is a function call that executes immediately without consuming simulation time.

- **Flexible Fan-out:** Can be connected to zero, one, or multiple subscribers (scoreboards, coverage collectors, loggers).

- If no subscribers are connected, calling `write()` safely does nothing without error.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_analysis_port #(T)` is a one-to-many broadcast port. A single `ap.write(t)` call, a non-blocking **function**, calls `write(t)` on every connected subscriber in zero time, and is harmless when nothing is connected. ```mermaid flowchart LR MON["monitor
ap.write(tr)"] --> SCB["scoreboard
analysis_imp write()"] MON --> COV["coverage
uvm_subscriber write()"] MON --> FIFO["uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo
analysis_export"] MON --> LOG["transaction logger"] ``` ### Explanation | Property | Analysis port | | --- | --- | | Method | `function void write(T t)` (cannot block) | | Fan-out | 0..N subscribers | | Response | None, one-way | | Endpoints | `uvm_analysis_imp`, `uvm_analysis_export` (hierarchical pass-through), `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo.analysis_export`, `uvm_subscriber.analysis_export` | ```systemverilog class my_mon extends uvm_monitor; uvm_analysis_port #(pkt) ap; function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); ap = new("ap", this); endfunction task run_phase(uvm_phase phase); forever begin pkt tr = pkt::type_id::create("tr"); // fresh object per transaction collect(tr); ap.write(tr); end endtask endclass // env.connect_phase agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.act_imp); agt.mon.ap.connect(cov.analysis_export); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Every subscriber gets the **same handle**. If one subscriber modifies the object, the others see the change. Subscribers should clone before modifying. - Subscribers are called one after another in the same time step, in an order that is not defined. Do not depend on scoreboard vs coverage order. - A slow consumer cannot apply back-pressure. Use an analysis FIFO if it needs to process the item later in a task. ### Follow-ups - *How do you connect through hierarchy?* Use a `uvm_analysis_port` at the agent level and connect `mon.ap.connect(agent.ap)` (port to port, child to parent). The env then connects `agent.ap` to the subscribers.

title: What are `pre_body` and `post_body` used in sequence?
answer:
*Refer: *[*start-a-sequence*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/start-a-sequence)

- `pre_body()` and `post_body()` are user-definable callback tasks in `uvm_sequence_base`.

- `pre_body()` executes immediately before `body()`.

- `post_body()` executes immediately after `body()`.

- **Critical Distinction:** They are called **only** when the sequence is started via `seq.start()`. They are **skipped** when the sequence is invoked via `` `uvm_do `` macros.

- Historically used to raise/drop objections, though modern best practice prefers managing objections in tests or virtual sequences.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `pre_body()` and `post_body()` are optional user hooks around `body()`. `start()` calls them only when its `call_pre_post` argument is 1, the default. They are skipped when a sequence is started as a child through `` `uvm_do `` (which passes 0), or when you call `start(sqr, this, -1, 0)`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  S["seq.start(sqr, parent, prio, call_pre_post)"] --> PS["pre_start (always)"]
  PS --> Q{"call_pre_post == 1?"}
  Q -->|"yes"| PB["pre_body"] --> B["body"]
  Q -->|"no"| B
  B --> Q2{"call_pre_post == 1?"}
  Q2 -->|"yes"| POB["post_body"] --> PST["post_start (always)"]
  Q2 -->|"no"| PST
```

### Explanation
- Full order inside `start()`: `pre_start` → (`pre_body`) → parent's `pre_do(0)` → parent's `mid_do` → `body` → parent's `post_do` → (`post_body`) → `post_start`. The `pre_do`/`mid_do`/`post_do` callbacks belong to the *parent* sequence.
- Typical old-style use: raise an objection in `pre_body` and drop it in `post_body`, but only for the top-level (root) sequence:

```systemverilog
task pre_body();
  uvm_phase p = get_starting_phase();      // UVM 1.2
  if (p != null) p.raise_objection(this);
endtask
task post_body();
  uvm_phase p = get_starting_phase();
  if (p != null) p.drop_objection(this);
endtask
```
- UVM 1.2 also offers `set_automatic_phase_objection(1)`, which raises and drops around `body()` for you.

| Hook | Called always? |
| --- | --- |
| `pre_start` / `post_start` | Yes |
| `pre_body` / `post_body` | Only if `call_pre_post == 1` |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Put logic that must always run (setup, cleanup) in `pre_start` / `post_start`, not in `pre_body` / `post_body`.
- Raising objections in every sub-sequence's `pre_body` costs performance and makes debugging harder. Raise them once in the test or the top virtual sequence.

### Follow-ups
- *Is `start()` blocking?* Yes. It returns after `post_start()` completes.

title: What is an active and passive agent?
answer:
- **Active Agent (`is_active = UVM_ACTIVE`):**

  - Actively drives stimulus onto the DUT pins.

  - Instantiates **sequencer**, **driver**, and **monitor**.

- **Passive Agent (`is_active = UVM_PASSIVE`):**

  - Passively observes DUT signals without driving anything.

  - Instantiates **only the monitor**.

  - Used for monitoring DUT output interfaces, or when verifying an SoC subsystem where another master IP drives the bus.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** An **active** agent drives the interface: it contains a sequencer, a driver and a monitor. A **passive** agent only observes: it contains a monitor only. The choice is the agent's `is_active` field, which is set through `config_db` or a config object.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph ACT["Active agent (UVM_ACTIVE)"]
    S1["sequencer"] --> D1["driver"]
    M1["monitor"]
  end
  subgraph PAS["Passive agent (UVM_PASSIVE)"]
    M2["monitor"]
  end
  D1 -->|"drives"| IF1["DUT input interface"]
  IF1 --> M1
  IF2["DUT output / internal bus"] --> M2
  M1 --> SCB["scoreboard / coverage"]
  M2 --> SCB
```

### Explanation
| | Active | Passive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Components | sequencer + driver + monitor | monitor only |
| Drives pins | Yes | No |
| Typical use | Block-level stimulus on DUT inputs | DUT outputs. Reusing a block agent at SoC level where real RTL now drives the bus |
| Default | `uvm_agent::is_active = UVM_ACTIVE` | Set explicitly |

```systemverilog
function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  super.build_phase(phase);          // picks up is_active from config_db
  mon = my_mon::type_id::create("mon", this);
  if (get_is_active() == UVM_ACTIVE) begin
    sqr = my_sqr::type_id::create("sqr", this);
    drv = my_drv::type_id::create("drv", this);
  end
endfunction
function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  if (get_is_active() == UVM_ACTIVE)
    drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export);
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Guard every reference to `drv` or `sqr` (connect, starting sequences) with the active check. Otherwise you get null-handle errors in passive mode.
- The monitor must be identical in both modes. That is what makes the vertical reuse trustworthy.

### Follow-ups
- *Can an agent be "reactive"?* Yes. A slave/responder agent is active, but its sequence waits for monitor requests and generates responses.

title: Difference between UVM subscriber and UVM scoreboard
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-subscriber*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-subscriber)* and *[*uvm-scoreboard*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-scoreboard)

- **`uvm_subscriber #(T)`:**

  - A specialized `uvm_component` designed as a convenient single-input consumer.

  - Comes with a built-in `uvm_analysis_imp` named `analysis_export` and defines a pure virtual `function void write(T t)`.

  - Primarily used for simple listeners, such as **coverage collectors**.

- **`uvm_scoreboard`:**

  - Extends `uvm_component` directly.

  - Designed for complex verification checking; typically instantiates multiple analysis ports, exports, or TLM FIFOs (e.g., input monitor stream vs output monitor stream).

  - Implements reference models, golden data predictors, queues/associative arrays, and data comparison logic.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_subscriber #(T)` is a ready-made, single-input listener: it comes with a built-in `analysis_export` and a pure virtual `write(T t)`, which is ideal for coverage. `uvm_scoreboard` is an empty `uvm_component` shell that you give several inputs (imps or FIFOs) plus checking logic. ```mermaid flowchart LR MON["monitor.ap"] --> SUB["uvm_subscriber #(pkt)
analysis_export, write(t): cg.sample()"] IN["in_mon.ap"] --> SCB["uvm_scoreboard
exp FIFO / imp"] OUT["out_mon.ap"] --> SCB SCB --> CHK["predict + compare + report"] ``` ### Explanation | | `uvm_subscriber #(T)` | `uvm_scoreboard` | | --- | --- | --- | | Base | `uvm_component` | `uvm_component` | | Built-in ports | `analysis_export` (an imp) | None | | Inputs | Exactly one stream of type T | Any number of streams and types | | Must implement | `function void write(T t)` | Whatever you design | | Typical use | Coverage collector, logger | Reference model and comparison, end-of-test checks | ```systemverilog class pkt_cov extends uvm_subscriber #(pkt); `uvm_component_utils(pkt_cov) pkt tr; covergroup cg; coverpoint tr.len { bins small = {[1:16]}; bins big = {[17:64]}; } coverpoint tr.kind; endgroup function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); cg = new(); endfunction function void write(pkt t); tr = t; cg.sample(); endfunction endclass ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A subscriber with two inputs means fighting the built-in single export. Use a plain component (or a scoreboard) with `` `uvm_analysis_imp_decl `` instead. - `uvm_scoreboard` adds no functionality over `uvm_component`. The name documents intent and lets tools classify the component. ### Follow-ups - *Where is the covergroup constructed?* In the constructor (`new`), since embedded covergroups must be built there or in a later function before sampling.

title: What is UVM objection and why do we need it?
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-objections*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-objections)

UVM Objections provide a standardized mechanism to coordinate the **end of simulation** in time-consuming phases (chiefly `run_phase`).

**How It Works:**

- Components/sequences raise an objection when starting an activity: `phase.raise_objection(this);`

- They drop the objection when the activity completes: `phase.drop_objection(this);`

- As long as the global objection count is $> 0$, the phase remains active.

- When all objections drop to $0$, UVM begins phase teardown (after an optional `set_drain_time()`) and advances to the cleanup phases (`extract`, `check`, `report`).

---

title: What are the different ways of exiting code execution?
answer:
1. **UVM Objections (Graceful & Recommended):** Dropping all objections allows UVM to finish the `run_phase` and proceed through `extract_phase`, `check_phase`, and `report_phase` to generate clean pass/fail summaries.

2. **`$finish` System Task:** Abruptly halts the simulator. Bypasses remaining UVM cleanup and reporting phases unless wrapped in specialized handlers.

3. **`uvm_fatal` / `uvm_report_fatal`:** Triggers `UVM_EXIT` action upon encountering an unrecoverable failure, exiting immediately.

4. **Phase Timeout (`set_timeout`):** Configured via `uvm_root::get().set_timeout(time)` to automatically terminate execution if a runaway sequence or deadlock prevents objections from dropping.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** The graceful way to end is to let all objections drop, so UVM runs extract, check, report and final and then calls `$finish`. The other exits (`uvm_fatal`, max-quit-count, global timeout, `$finish`) end abruptly. Some still print a report summary, while `$finish` skips everything.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  RUN["run_phase activity"] --> A{"how does it stop?"}
  A -->|"all objections dropped"| G["extract, check, report, final, then $finish"]
  A -->|"uvm_fatal or max_quit_count reached"| F["UVM_EXIT: report summary printed, die"]
  A -->|"global timeout (set_timeout)"| T["fatal PH_TIMEOUT: phase hung"]
  A -->|"$finish / $stop in user code"| X["immediate stop, no check or report"]
  A -->|"phase.jump / uvm_domain::jump_all"| J["skip to a later phase, e.g. extract"]
```

### Explanation
| Mechanism | Cleanup phases run? | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- |
