| Drop all objections | Yes | Normal test end |
| `` `uvm_fatal(ID, msg) `` | No (`die()` prints the report summary) | Unrecoverable condition (missing vif, bad config) |
| `+UVM_MAX_QUIT_COUNT=N` / `set_report_max_quit_count(N)` | No (summary only) | Stop after N errors in regressions |
| `uvm_top.set_timeout(t)` / `+UVM_TIMEOUT=t` | No (fatal) | Watchdog against hangs |
| `phase.jump(uvm_extract_phase::get())` | Yes, from the jump target | Abort the run but still check and report |
| `$finish` | No | Avoid in UVM code |

```systemverilog
initial begin
  uvm_top.set_timeout(5ms, 0);     // 0 = cannot be overridden later
  uvm_top.finish_on_completion = 1; // default: $finish after final_phase
  run_test();
end

// in a test: abort early but still run check/report
if (fatal_condition_seen)
  phase.jump(uvm_extract_phase::get());
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `$finish` from a driver or sequence bypasses the scoreboard's `check_phase`, so a test can "pass" with outstanding expected items.
- Setting `finish_on_completion = 0` keeps the simulator alive after `final_phase` (for example, to dump extra data or run the next stage in the same simulation).

### Follow-ups
- *How do you catch a fatal for a negative test?* Use a `uvm_report_catcher` that demotes the expected error or fatal, so the test can pass.

title: What is a sequence item in UVM?
answer:
*Refer: *[*sequence-items-in-uvm*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/sequence-items-in-uvm)

A **sequence item** (`uvm_sequence_item`) is the fundamental transaction object representing data exchanged between testbench components and the DUT at an abstracted protocol level (e.g., packet, bus cycle, frame).

**Contents:**

- Random variables (`rand bit [31:0] addr, data;`) representing pin-level stimulus fields.

- Protocol constraints and knobs.

- Utility automation macros (`` `uvm_field_* ``) or manual overrides for `do_copy()`, `do_compare()`, `do_print()`, and `do_pack()`.

- Sequence/sequencer routing identifiers (`transaction_id`).

---
solution:
**Key idea:** A sequence item is the transaction: a `uvm_sequence_item` subclass holding the randomizable fields, constraints and utility methods that describe one protocol operation (a bus read, a packet). Sequences generate items, drivers turn them into pins, and monitors rebuild them from pins.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SEQ["sequence: create + randomize item"] --> SQR["sequencer"] --> DRV["driver: item to pins"]
  DRV --> DUT["DUT"]
  DUT --> MON["monitor: pins to item"]
  MON --> SCB["scoreboard compares items"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class bus_item extends uvm_sequence_item;
  // stimulus fields
  rand bit [31:0] addr;
  rand bit [31:0] data;
  rand bit        write;
  rand int        delay;
  // response / observed fields
  bit             err;

  constraint c_align { addr[1:0] == 2'b00; }
  constraint c_delay { delay inside {[0:5]}; }

  `uvm_object_utils_begin(bus_item)
    `uvm_field_int(addr,  UVM_ALL_ON)
    `uvm_field_int(data,  UVM_ALL_ON)
    `uvm_field_int(write, UVM_ALL_ON)
    `uvm_field_int(delay, UVM_ALL_ON | UVM_NOCOMPARE)
    `uvm_field_int(err,   UVM_ALL_ON)
  `uvm_object_utils_end

  function new(string name = "bus_item"); super.new(name); endfunction

  function string convert2string();
    return $sformatf("%s addr=%h data=%h", write ? "WR" : "RD", addr, data);
  endfunction
endclass
```
| Part | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `rand` fields | Protocol content plus control knobs (delay, error inject) |
| Constraints | Keep stimulus legal by default. Tests add more with `randomize() with {}` |
| `do_copy` / `do_compare` / `do_print` / `convert2string` (or field macros) | Copying, scoreboard comparison, debug |
| IDs (`sequence_id`, `transaction_id`) | Inherited, used to route responses |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Keep timing knobs such as `delay` out of `compare()` (`UVM_NOCOMPARE`). The monitor cannot observe them, so the scoreboard would mismatch.
- Never put pins or a virtual interface inside an item. Items must be abstract and reusable.

### Follow-ups
- *Field macros or manual `do_*` methods?* Manual methods are faster and easier to debug. Macros are quicker to write.

title: Explain how the sequence starts
answer:
*Refer: *[*start-a-sequence*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/start-a-sequence)

A sequence is started by invoking its `start()` method:

```systemverilog
seq.start(m_sequencer, parent_sequence, priority, call_pre_post_body);
```

**Internal Execution Sequence:**

1. Sets the sequencer handle (`m_sequencer`).

2. Calls `pre_start()`.

3. Calls `pre_body()` (if `call_pre_post_body == 1`).

4. Executes the user's `body()` task (stimulus generation).

5. Calls `post_body()` (if `call_pre_post_body == 1`).

6. Calls `post_start()`.

7. Once `body()` and all handshakes with the driver conclude, `start()` unblocks and returns.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** A sequence runs when you call its blocking `start(sequencer, parent, priority, call_pre_post)` task. `start()` attaches the sequence to the sequencer, runs the hooks and `body()`, and returns once `body()` (and every item it sent) is done.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as test.run_phase
  participant S as seq
  participant Q as sequencer
  T->>S: seq = my_seq::type_id::create("seq")
  T->>S: seq.randomize() (optional knobs)
  T->>S: seq.start(env.agt.sqr)
  S->>S: set_sequencer, set_parent_sequence
  S->>S: pre_start()
  S->>S: pre_body() if call_pre_post
  S->>Q: body(): start_item / finish_item ...
  Q-->>S: items done
  S->>S: post_body() if call_pre_post
  S->>S: post_start()
  S-->>T: start() returns
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
virtual task start(uvm_sequencer_base sequencer,
                   uvm_sequence_base  parent_sequence = null,
                   int                this_priority   = -1,
                   bit                call_pre_post   = 1);
```
| Way to start | Example |
| --- | --- |
| From a test or virtual sequence | `seq.start(env.agt.sqr);` |
| As a child of another sequence | `sub.start(m_sequencer, this);` |
| With macros | `` `uvm_do_on(sub, p_sequencer.apb_sqr) `` |
| As a phase default sequence | `uvm_config_db#(uvm_object_wrapper)::set(this, "env.agt.sqr.main_phase", "default_sequence", my_seq::type_id::get());` |

```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  my_seq seq = my_seq::type_id::create("seq");
  phase.raise_objection(this);
  if (!seq.randomize() with { num_items == 20; }) `uvm_fatal("RND", "seq")
  seq.start(env.agt.sqr);
  phase.drop_objection(this);
endtask
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Passing `parent_sequence` is what links the child to the parent for priority, `pre_do`/`post_do` and lock inheritance.
- Starting the same sequence object twice concurrently is illegal. Create a new object per concurrent start.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you run sequences in parallel?* `fork s1.start(sqr); s2.start(sqr); join`, with the sequencer's arbitration mode deciding the interleaving.

title: How do sequence, driver, and sequencer communicate?
answer:
*Refer: *[*sequence-driver-sequencer-communication-in-uvm*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/sequence-driver-sequencer-communication-in-uvm)

Communication follows a bi-directional request-response TLM handshake:

```
Sequence                 Sequencer                 Driver
   |                         |                       |
   |-- start_item(req) ----->|                       |
   |   (requests grant)      |                       |
   |                         |<-- get_next_item(req)-|
   |                         |    (driver ready)     |
   |<- grants sequence ------|                       |
   |                         |                       |
   | [Late Randomization]    |                       |
   |-- finish_item(req) ---->|===> forwards req ====>|
   |   (sends item)          |                       |
   |   (blocks waiting)      |                       | [Pin Wiggling]
   |                         |                       |
   |                         |<-- item_done() -------|
   |<- unblocks finish_item -|                       |
```

1. **`start_item(req)`:** Sequence requests permission from sequencer.

2. **`get_next_item(req)`:** Driver indicates it is ready for the next transaction. Sequencer arbitrates among competing sequences and grants access.

3. **Randomization:** Sequence randomizes `req` with late state information.

4. **`finish_item(req)`:** Sequence passes `req` through the sequencer to the driver and suspends.

5. **Driver execution:** Driver translates transaction fields to interface pin signals.

6. **`item_done()`:** Driver notifies sequencer that item execution is complete, unblocking `finish_item()` in the sequence.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** The sequence and driver never talk directly. The sequence asks the sequencer for a grant (`start_item`) and hands over the item (`finish_item`). The driver pulls items through its `seq_item_port` (`get_next_item`) and signals completion (`item_done`), which unblocks the sequence. Optional responses flow back by sequence ID.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant SEQ as sequence
  participant SQR as sequencer
  participant DRV as driver
  DRV->>SQR: get_next_item(req) (blocks, driver ready)
  SEQ->>SQR: start_item(req) (request arbitration)
  SQR-->>SEQ: grant, start_item returns
  SEQ->>SEQ: randomize req (late)
  SEQ->>SQR: finish_item(req)
  SQR-->>DRV: get_next_item returns req
  DRV->>DRV: drive req on vif
  DRV->>SQR: item_done(rsp optional)
  SQR-->>SEQ: finish_item returns
  SEQ->>SQR: get_response(rsp) optional
```

### Explanation
**Connection (agent `connect_phase`)**
```systemverilog
drv.seq_item_port.connect(sqr.seq_item_export);
```
**Driver loop**
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  forever begin
    seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
    drive(req);                              // pin wiggling, consumes time
    rsp = my_item::type_id::create("rsp");
    rsp.set_id_info(req);                    // route response to the right sequence
    rsp.rdata = vif.rdata;
    seq_item_port.item_done(rsp);            // or item_done() with no response
  end
endtask
```
**Sequence**
```systemverilog
task body();
  req = my_item::type_id::create("req");
  start_item(req);
  void'(req.randomize());
  finish_item(req);
  get_response(rsp);                         // only if driver returns one
endtask
```
| Side | Blocking call | Unblocked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sequence `start_item` | waits for grant | Sequencer arbitration plus driver request |
| Sequence `finish_item` | waits for completion | Driver `item_done()` |
| Driver `get_next_item` | waits for an item | Sequence `finish_item` |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If `item_done()` is never called, the sequence hangs in `finish_item`. Calling `get_next_item()` twice without `item_done()` is an error.
- If the driver sends responses but the sequence never calls `get_response`, the response queue fills (depth 8 by default) and UVM reports an overflow error. Use `set_response_queue_error_report_disabled(1)` or consume the responses.

### Follow-ups
- *Alternative driver style?* `get(req)` followed by `put(rsp)`. Here `get` performs the `item_done` implicitly.

title: What are lock and grab methods?
answer:
*Refer: *[*lock-and-grab-methods-in-uvm-sequencer*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/lock-and-grab-methods-in-uvm-sequencer)

Both methods allow a sequence to request exclusive ownership of a sequencer, preventing other sequences from interleaving transactions:

- **`lock(sequencer)`:** Places an arbitration lock request into the sequencer's queue. It waits politely until all previously queued sequence items ahead of it finish. Once granted, no other sequence can access the sequencer until `unlock()` is called.

- **`grab(sequencer)`:** An aggressive, highest-priority lock. It takes effect immediately after the currently executing item finishes, jumping ahead of all other waiting sequences in the queue. Remains in effect until `ungrab()` is called.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `lock()` and `grab()` both give one sequence exclusive use of a sequencer until `unlock()` / `ungrab()`. **lock** joins the back of the arbitration queue and waits its turn. **grab** jumps to the front and takes effect at the next arbitration, right after the current item finishes.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as seq A (running)
  participant B as seq B (waiting)
  participant L as seq L (lock)
  participant G as seq G (grab)
  participant Q as sequencer
  A->>Q: item A1 in progress
  B->>Q: start_item queued
  L->>Q: lock() queued behind B
  G->>Q: grab() put at FRONT
  Q-->>G: granted after A1 completes
  G->>Q: G1, G2, G3 back-to-back
  G->>Q: ungrab()
  Q-->>B: B1 (B was ahead of L in queue)
  Q-->>L: lock granted
  L->>Q: L1, L2 back-to-back
  L->>Q: unlock()
```

### Explanation
| | `lock(sqr)` | `grab(sqr)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Queue position | Back of arbitration queue | Front of queue |
| Granted when | Its turn comes under the arbitration mode | Next arbitration (after the current item) |
| Release | `unlock()` | `ungrab()` |
| Blocking? | Yes, until granted | Yes, until granted |
| Use for | Atomic multi-item transfer that can wait (a register read-modify-write sequence) | Urgent traffic such as an interrupt service sequence |

```systemverilog
task body();
  lock(m_sequencer);              // or grab(m_sequencer)
  repeat (4) begin
    req = my_item::type_id::create("req");
    start_item(req);
    void'(req.randomize() with { burst == 1; });
    finish_item(req);
  end
  unlock(m_sequencer);            // always release
endtask
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Child sequences of the locking sequence can still use the sequencer, but unrelated sequences cannot.
- A grab or lock that is never released starves every other sequence, and the test hangs.
- If the sequencer is already locked, a grab waits until that lock is released. Grabs do not pre-empt existing locks.
- `is_blocked()` / `has_lock()` let you query the state.

### Follow-ups
- *Alternative without exclusivity?* Raise the sequence priority with arbitration `UVM_SEQ_ARB_STRICT_FIFO`. Items can still interleave, though.

title: What is the RAL model and its application?
answer:
The **Register Abstraction Layer (RAL)** provides an object-oriented representation of the DUT’s memory-mapped registers, register files, and memories.

**Key Applications:**

- **Named Access:** Read and write registers and fields by name (e.g., `regmodel.ctrl_reg.enable.write(status, 1)`) without hardcoding physical memory addresses.

- **Mirroring:** Automatically tracks desired values vs mirrored values (what hardware actually holds).

- **Pre-built Verification Sequences:** Includes turnkey UVM library sequences:

  - Reset check (`uvm_reg_hw_reset_seq`)

  - Bit-bash / walk 1s and 0s (`uvm_reg_bit_bash_seq`)

  - Register access check (`uvm_reg_access_seq`)

- **Functional Coverage:** Automatically generates register coverage models.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** RAL (UVM register layer) is an object model of the DUT's registers, fields and memories. Tests access registers **by name** (`regmodel.ctrl.en.write(...)`). The model keeps a **mirror** of the expected hardware value, and translates operations into bus transactions through an adapter, or into direct HDL accesses through backdoor paths. ```mermaid flowchart LR TEST["test / reg sequence
regmodel.ctrl.write(status, 'h5)"] --> RM["uvm_reg_block
uvm_reg / uvm_reg_field
desired + mirrored values"] RM --> MAP["uvm_reg_map (address map)"] MAP --> AD["adapter reg2bus / bus2reg"] AD --> SQR["bus agent sequencer"] --> DRV["driver"] --> DUT["DUT registers"] DUT --> MON["bus monitor"] --> PRED["uvm_reg_predictor"] -->|"update mirror"| RM RM -.->|"backdoor hdl path"| DUT ``` ### Explanation | Feature | Benefit | | --- | --- | | Named access (`read`, `write`, `set`/`update`, `mirror`, `peek`/`poke`) | Tests survive address-map changes and are reusable across buses | | Mirror and desired values | Built-in prediction: `mirror(status, UVM_CHECK)` compares the DUT against the model | | Front-door and back-door | Real bus traffic, or zero-time direct access | | Built-in sequences | `uvm_reg_hw_reset_seq`, `uvm_reg_bit_bash_seq`, `uvm_reg_access_seq`, `uvm_mem_walk_seq`, `uvm_reg_mem_built_in_seq` | | Coverage | Optional register/field coverage models | | Generated from spec | IP-XACT/RALF/CSV generators keep the model in sync with the design | ```systemverilog uvm_status_e st; uvm_reg_data_t val; regmodel.ctrl.enable.set(1); regmodel.ctrl.mode.set(2); regmodel.ctrl.update(st); // writes only if desired != mirrored regmodel.status.read(st, val); regmodel.status.mirror(st, UVM_CHECK); // read and compare against the mirror ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The mirror is only accurate if prediction is set up correctly: explicit prediction with a predictor on the bus monitor, or auto-predict. It must also know the field access policies (RO, W1C, RC, ...). - Volatile fields (hardware-updated status) must be marked volatile, or `mirror(UVM_CHECK)` reports false errors. ### Follow-ups - *What does the adapter do?* `reg2bus` converts a `uvm_reg_bus_op` into a bus sequence item, and `bus2reg` does the reverse for the predictor and read data.

title: What do you mean by front-door and back-door register access?
answer:
- **Front-Door Access:**

  - Accesses registers through the DUT's physical bus interface (e.g., APB, AXI).

  - Uses the driver to wiggle physical interface signals.

  - Consumes simulation time.

  - Verifies bus protocol, address decoders, and bus fabric.

- **Back-Door Access:**

  - Accesses registers directly using simulator DPI / HDL hierarchal register signal paths (`uvm_hdl_read` / `uvm_hdl_deposit`).

  - Bypasses physical bus logic.

  - Consumes **zero simulation time**.

  - Useful for fast register preloading during bring-up and sanity checking.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** **Front-door** access goes through the DUT's real bus interface (APB/AXI/...) via the adapter, sequencer and driver: it takes time and exercises the decode logic. **Back-door** access reads or writes the register storage directly through its HDL path (`uvm_hdl_*` / DPI): it takes zero time and bypasses the bus. ```mermaid flowchart LR REG["regmodel.ctrl"] -->|"path = UVM_FRONTDOOR"| AD["adapter"] --> SQR["bus sequencer"] --> DRV["driver"] --> BUS["APB pins"] --> DEC["address decode"] --> FF["ctrl flops"] REG -->|"path = UVM_BACKDOOR
uvm_hdl_deposit / uvm_hdl_read"| FF ``` ### Explanation | | Front-door | Back-door | | --- | --- | --- | | Path | Bus agent, real protocol | HDL hierarchical path (`add_hdl_path`, `configure` with path) | | Simulation time | Bus cycles | Zero | | Verifies | Bus protocol, address decode, access policies, side effects | Nothing about the bus. Just the storage value | | Side effects (W1C, RC, FIFO pops) | Happen | `write`/`read` with `UVM_BACKDOOR` emulate the policy. `poke`/`peek` do not | | Use for | Real register tests, functional configuration | Fast preload/init, checking a value without disturbing traffic, memory init | ```systemverilog // front-door regmodel.ctrl.write(st, 32'h1, UVM_FRONTDOOR); // back-door (needs hdl path) regmodel.ctrl.write(st, 32'h1, UVM_BACKDOOR); regmodel.ctrl.peek(st, val); // raw back-door read, no access-policy side effects regmodel.mem.poke(st, 'h40, 32'hDEAD_BEEF); // hdl path set-up in the reg block's build() ctrl.configure(this, null, "ctrl_q"); add_hdl_path("tb_top.u_dut.u_regs"); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A back-door write that bypasses the bus may desynchronize the mirror unless the model is updated. `write(UVM_BACKDOOR)` and `poke` do update it. - HDL paths can break after synthesis or renaming. Check them with `uvm_reg_mem_hdl_paths_seq`. - Back-door to a flop changing on the same edge can race with RTL. Prefer accessing when the DUT is idle. ### Follow-ups - *How do you verify a back-door write took effect?* Read it front-door and compare. That is exactly what `uvm_reg_access_seq` does.

title: What is TLM?
answer:
*Refer: *[*transaction-level-modeling-tlm*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/tlm/transaction-level-modeling-tlm)

**Transaction-Level Modeling (TLM)** is a standard modeling paradigm that abstracts signal-level communication (clocks, wires, handshakes) into discrete transaction objects.

**Key Features:**

- Standard ports (`uvm_blocking_put_port`, `uvm_nonblocking_get_port`, `uvm_analysis_port`).

- Standard interfaces: `put`, `get`, `peek`, `transport`, `write`.

- Decouples component implementation from communication transport, allowing modular testbench composition and SystemC integration.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** TLM (Transaction-Level Modeling) lets components exchange **whole transaction objects through method calls** (`put`, `get`, `peek`, `write`, `transport`) instead of wiggling signals. Components stay decoupled: the producer only knows its port, not who implements it. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["producer
uvm_blocking_put_port"] -->|"put(tr)"| C["consumer
uvm_blocking_put_imp
task put(tr)"] G["consumer2
uvm_blocking_get_port"] -->|"get(tr)"| F["uvm_tlm_fifo
get_export"] P2["producer2"] -->|"put"| F M["monitor
uvm_analysis_port"] -->|"write(tr)"| S1["subscriber 1"] M --> S2["subscriber 2"] ``` ### Explanation | Term | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Port | Initiator side: *calls* the method (`port.put(t)`) | | Export | Pass-through on the target side, forwarding to an inner imp | | Imp | Termination that *implements* the method in its parent component | | Blocking | `put`/`get`/`peek` are tasks and may wait | | Non-blocking | `try_put`/`try_get`/`can_put`/... are functions and return a status immediately | | Analysis | `write()` function, broadcast to 0..N subscribers | | Channels | `uvm_tlm_fifo`, `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo`, `uvm_tlm_req_rsp_channel` | ```systemverilog class producer extends uvm_component; uvm_blocking_put_port #(pkt) put_port; task run_phase(uvm_phase phase); pkt p = pkt::type_id::create("p"); put_port.put(p); // calls consumer.put() endtask endclass class consumer extends uvm_component; uvm_blocking_put_imp #(pkt, consumer) put_imp; task put(pkt p); `uvm_info("CONS", p.convert2string(), UVM_LOW) endtask endclass // env.connect_phase: prod.put_port.connect(cons.put_imp); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Every port must be connected (unless its min size is 0, as for analysis ports), or `end_of_elaboration` reports an error. - Objects pass by handle. Clone before handing off if the sender will reuse the object. ### Follow-ups - *TLM-1 vs TLM-2.0 in UVM?* TLM-1 is the put/get/analysis API. TLM-2.0 (`uvm_tlm_b_initiator_socket`, `b_transport`, generic payload) is for SystemC-style memory-mapped models.

title: What is TLM FIFO?
answer:
*Refer: *[*tlm-fifo*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/tlm/tlm-fifo)

A **`uvm_tlm_fifo #(T)`** is a transaction storage component that sits between an independent producer and consumer:

- Provides an internal storage queue of configurable depth.

- Exposes `put_export` on one side and `get_export` on the other.

- Decouples timing: A producer can push items (`put`) without waiting for the consumer, and a consumer can retrieve items (`get`) whenever ready.

- **`uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(T)`:** Extends `uvm_tlm_fifo` with an `analysis_export` on the write side, making it ideal for scoreboards to receive non-blocking broadcast items from monitors.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_tlm_fifo #(T)` is a channel component with a bounded queue (default depth 1, `0` = unbounded) between a producer and a consumer. It exposes `put_export` and `get_peek_export`, so the two sides run at their own pace, with back-pressure when the FIFO is full. ```mermaid flowchart LR PROD["producer
put_port"] -->|"put (blocks when full)"| PE["put_export"] subgraph FIFO["uvm_tlm_fifo #(pkt) size N"] PE --> Q["queue"] --> GE["get_peek_export"] end GE -->|"get / peek (blocks when empty)"| CONS["consumer
get_port"] ``` ### Explanation | Method | Blocking? | Behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | `put(t)` | yes | Waits while full | | `try_put(t)` | no | Returns 0 if full | | `get(t)` | yes | Waits while empty, removes the item | | `try_get(t)` | no | Returns 0 if empty | | `peek(t)` | yes | Waits while empty, does **not** remove | | `used()`, `size()`, `is_empty()`, `is_full()`, `flush()` | n/a | Status and management | ```systemverilog class env extends uvm_env; producer p; consumer c; uvm_tlm_fifo #(pkt) fifo; function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); p = producer::type_id::create("p", this); c = consumer::type_id::create("c", this); fifo = new("fifo", this, 4); // depth 4 endfunction function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase); p.put_port.connect(fifo.put_export); c.get_port.connect(fifo.get_peek_export); endfunction endclass ``` | | `uvm_tlm_fifo` | `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` | | --- | --- | --- | | Input | `put_export` (blocking put) | `analysis_export` (`write`, never blocks) | | Depth | Configurable, default 1 | Unbounded | | Typical use | Producer/consumer flow control | Scoreboard input buffering | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The default depth of 1 surprises people: the producer blocks after one item until the consumer gets it. - Use `check_phase` to report a FIFO that is not empty at end of test (`!fifo.is_empty()`). ### Follow-ups - *Why put a FIFO between monitor and scoreboard?* A monitor's analysis `write()` cannot block. An analysis FIFO buffers items so the scoreboard thread can `get()` them when ready.

title: What is `run_test`?
answer:
*Refer: *[*run_test_task*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-test#run_test_task)

`run_test` is a globally available UVM task defined in `uvm_globals.svh`:

1. Initializes the UVM phase engine and retrieves the `uvm_root` (`uvm_top`) singleton instance.

2. Checks if a test name was passed as an argument; if not, checks the command-line plusarg `+UVM_TESTNAME=<test_name>`.

3. Instantiates the selected test class via the factory as `uvm_test_top`.

4. Starts stepping through the UVM phase execution graph beginning with `build_phase`.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `run_test()` is the global task that starts UVM. It picks the test name (`+UVM_TESTNAME` overrides the argument), uses the factory to create the test as `uvm_test_top` under `uvm_root`, runs all the phases, and by default calls `$finish` at the end.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant TOP as tb_top initial
  participant ROOT as uvm_root (uvm_top)
  participant FAC as uvm_factory
  participant PH as phase engine
  TOP->>ROOT: run_test("opt_name")
  ROOT->>ROOT: read +UVM_TESTNAME (wins over argument)
  ROOT->>FAC: create_component_by_name(test, "", "uvm_test_top", uvm_root)
  FAC-->>ROOT: uvm_test_top
  ROOT->>PH: m_run_phases()
  PH->>PH: build, connect, ... run ... report, final
  PH-->>ROOT: all phases complete
  ROOT->>ROOT: report summary, $finish if finish_on_completion
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  initial begin
    // vif config_db sets must come BEFORE run_test (it does not return until the end)
    uvm_config_db#(virtual dut_if)::set(null, "*", "vif", vif);
    run_test();             // or run_test("base_test")
  end
endmodule
```
| Detail | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Declared in | `uvm_pkg` (`uvm_globals.svh`), calls `uvm_root::run_test` |
| Test instance name | `uvm_test_top` |
| Test selection | `+UVM_TESTNAME=name` > argument > none (fatal "No test specified") |
| End | `$finish` after `final_phase` if `uvm_top.finish_on_completion == 1` (default) |
| Command-line extras processed | `+UVM_VERBOSITY`, `+UVM_TIMEOUT`, `+UVM_MAX_QUIT_COUNT`, `+uvm_set_*` overrides |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Call `run_test()` only once, from one `initial` block. Calling it twice is a fatal error.
- Code after `run_test()` in the same initial block normally never runs, because `$finish` is called first.
- The test class must be compiled and registered, so import its package in `tb_top` or another compiled scope.

### Follow-ups
- *Can you run without a test?* `run_test()` with no name and no plusarg reports a fatal error and exits.

title: Explain generalized code structure for UVM monitor and scoreboard
What is an in-order and out-of-order scoreboard?
answer:
*Refer: *[*UVM_Scoreboad_types*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-scoreboard#UVM_Scoreboad_types)

- **In-Order Scoreboard:**

  - Expects output transactions to arrive in the exact same sequence as input stimuli were applied.

  - Implementation: Uses a standard FIFO queue (`exp_queue.push_back()` and `exp_queue.pop_front()`).

  - Suitable for FIFOs, pipelined buffers without arbitration, and simple streaming interfaces.

- **Out-of-Order Scoreboard:**

  - Accommodates designs where transactions may complete out of arrival order (e.g., AXI bus with independent read/write IDs, PCIe split transactions, network routers).

  - Implementation: Uses associative arrays or hash tables indexed by a transaction ID or tag (e.g., `exp_table[item.id] = item`). When an actual item arrives, it searches the table by key, compares contents, and deletes the matched entry.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** An **in-order** scoreboard expects outputs in the same order as the inputs, so a FIFO (`push_back` / `pop_front`) is enough. An **out-of-order** scoreboard is needed when the DUT can reorder outputs (multiple channels, AXI IDs, caches, arbiters). It stores expected items keyed by an ID or tag (an associative array) and matches each actual item by its key.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph IO["In-order"]
    I1["expected queue: A B C"] --> I2["actual A: pop_front A, match"]
    I2 --> I3["actual B: pop_front B, match"]
  end
  subgraph OOO["Out-of-order"]
    O1["exp[id]: id1=A id2=B id3=C"] --> O2["actual id3=C: exp.exists(3), match, delete"]
    O2 --> O3["actual id1=A: match, delete"]
  end
```

### Explanation
| | In-order | Out-of-order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data structure | Queue / TLM FIFO | Associative array (key: ID, address, tag), or queue + search |
| Match rule | Head of queue | Lookup by key |
| DUT examples | FIFO, pipeline, single-channel UART | AXI with IDs, NoC, crossbar, multi-port memory, packet switch |
| Error detection | Order and data errors | Data errors; order errors only within a key |

```systemverilog
// out-of-order: key by transaction ID, allow several per ID
pkt exp_q[int][$];
function void write_exp(pkt t); exp_q[t.id].push_back(t); endfunction
function void write_act(pkt t);
  pkt e;
  if (!exp_q.exists(t.id) || exp_q[t.id].size() == 0) begin
    `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("unexpected id %0d", t.id)) return;
  end
  e = exp_q[t.id].pop_front();          // in-order within one ID (AXI rule)
  if (!t.compare(e)) `uvm_error("SCB", "data mismatch")
  if (exp_q[t.id].size() == 0) exp_q.delete(t.id);
endfunction
function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  if (exp_q.num() != 0) `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("%0d ids never completed", exp_q.num()))
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using an out-of-order scoreboard on an in-order DUT hides ordering bugs. Match the checker to the spec.
- Items with no unique key (identical payloads) need a search-and-remove-first-match strategy.
- Always check for leftovers at end of test. A dropped packet is otherwise silent.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you add a latency check?* Timestamp the expected item on insert and compare `$time` at match against the allowed maximum.

title: Difference between `p_sequencer` and `m_sequencer`
answer:
| Feature | `m_sequencer` | `p_sequencer` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Definition** | Generic default sequencer handle built into `uvm_sequence_base` | User-defined, strongly-typed sequencer handle created in custom sequence |
| **Data Type** | `uvm_sequencer_base` | Specific user sequencer type (e.g., `my_custom_sequencer`) |
| **Availability** | Available by default in all sequences without declaration | Requires declaration via `` `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(my_custom_sequencer) `` |
| **Member Access** | Can only access standard methods of `uvm_sequencer_base` | Can directly access custom sequencer variables, handles, clocks, and sub-sequencers |
| **Virtual Sequences** | Inadequate for virtual sequences because it cannot see sub-sequencer handles | Essential in virtual sequences to coordinate child sequencers directly |

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `m_sequencer` is the generic `uvm_sequencer_base` handle every sequence gets automatically when started. `p_sequencer` is a **typed** handle, declared with `` `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(T) ``, that `$cast`s `m_sequencer` to your sequencer class. It is needed to reach custom members such as sub-sequencer handles or config. ```mermaid flowchart LR START["seq.start(env.vsqr)"] --> M["m_sequencer : uvm_sequencer_base
(set automatically)"] M -->|"m_set_p_sequencer: $cast"| P["p_sequencer : my_vsqr
(from uvm_declare_p_sequencer)"] P --> A["p_sequencer.apb_sqr"] P --> B["p_sequencer.axi_sqr"] P --> C["p_sequencer.cfg"] ``` ### Explanation | | `m_sequencer` | `p_sequencer` | | --- | --- | --- | | Type | `uvm_sequencer_base` | Your sequencer class | | Declared by | UVM (`uvm_sequence_item`) | `` `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(my_sqr) `` macro | | Set when | `start()` / `set_sequencer()` | Same moment, via `$cast` in `m_set_p_sequencer()` | | Access | Base methods only (`get_full_name`, arbitration, lock) | All members of `my_sqr` | | If types mismatch | n/a | Fatal "DCLPSQ" cast error at start | ```systemverilog class my_vsqr extends uvm_sequencer; `uvm_component_utils(my_vsqr) apb_sequencer apb_sqr; axi_sequencer axi_sqr; function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction endclass class top_vseq extends uvm_sequence; `uvm_object_utils(top_vseq) `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(my_vsqr) function new(string name = "top_vseq"); super.new(name); endfunction task body(); apb_cfg_seq cfg = apb_cfg_seq::type_id::create("cfg"); axi_traffic_seq t = axi_traffic_seq::type_id::create("t"); cfg.start(p_sequencer.apb_sqr, this); t.start(p_sequencer.axi_sqr, this); endtask endclass ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - `p_sequencer` ties the sequence to one sequencer type, which reduces reuse. Many teams prefer passing handles through a config object or plain sequence fields. - `p_sequencer` is null until the sequence is started. Do not use it in `new()`. ### Follow-ups - *Can you avoid the macro?* Yes: declare `my_sqr sqr;` and in `pre_start()` or `body()` do `if (!$cast(sqr, m_sequencer)) `uvm_fatal(...)`.

title: What is a virtual sequence? How is it used? Is it necessary to have a virtual sequencer for a virtual sequence?
answer:
*Refer: *[*virtual-sequence-and-virtual-sequencer*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/virtual-sequence-and-virtual-sequencer)

- **What is a Virtual Sequence?**
  A sequence that coordinates and orchestrates stimulus generation across **multiple interfaces/agents** simultaneously (e.g., configuring registers over APB while driving Ethernet packets into an ingress port).

- **How is it used?**
  It does **not** send sequence items directly to a driver. Instead, its `body()` task starts child sequences on different physical sequencers.

- **Is a virtual sequencer necessary?**
  **No, it is not strictly necessary.**

  - If a virtual sequencer is used, the virtual sequence accesses child sequencer handles via its `p_sequencer`.

  - Alternatively, the sub-sequencer handles can be passed directly to the virtual sequence from the test or configuration object before calling `seq.start(null)`, completely eliminating the need for a virtual sequencer component.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** A virtual sequence orchestrates stimulus across **several agents**. It sends no items itself: its `body()` starts child sequences on the agents' real sequencers, in order or in parallel. A virtual sequencer is **not required**: the sequencer handles can be passed in directly and the virtual sequence started on `null`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  TEST["test"] --> VS["virtual sequence body"]
  VS -->|"1. start"| CFG["apb_cfg_seq on apb_sqr"]
  VS -->|"2. fork"| ETH["eth_traffic_seq on eth_sqr"]
  VS -->|"2. fork"| INT["irq_service_seq on apb_sqr"]
  CFG --> APB["APB agent driver"]
  ETH --> EAG["ETH agent driver"]
  INT --> APB
```

### Explanation
**Option 1: with a virtual sequencer (`p_sequencer`)**
```systemverilog
class top_vseq extends uvm_sequence;
  `uvm_object_utils(top_vseq)
  `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(top_vsqr)
  task body();
    apb_cfg_seq     cfg = apb_cfg_seq::type_id::create("cfg");
    eth_traffic_seq eth = eth_traffic_seq::type_id::create("eth");
    cfg.start(p_sequencer.apb_sqr, this);   // configure first
    eth.start(p_sequencer.eth_sqr, this);   // then traffic
  endtask
endclass
// test: vseq.start(env.vsqr);
```
**Option 2: no virtual sequencer (handles assigned by the test)**
```systemverilog
class top_vseq extends uvm_sequence;
  `uvm_object_utils(top_vseq)
  apb_sequencer apb_sqr;
  eth_sequencer eth_sqr;
  task body();
    // same child starts, using apb_sqr / eth_sqr fields
  endtask
endclass
// test.run_phase:
vseq.apb_sqr = env.apb_agt.sqr;
vseq.eth_sqr = env.eth_agt.sqr;
vseq.start(null);
```
| | With virtual sequencer | Without |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extra component | Yes (`vsqr` in the env) | No |
| Handle wiring | env `connect_phase` | Test assigns fields, or a config object |
| `default_sequence` via config_db | Possible | Not possible (needs a sequencer) |
| Reuse into a bigger env | Nest virtual sequencers | Pass handles down |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- When started with `null`, `get_starting_phase()` is not set automatically, so raise objections in the test.
- Pass `this` as the parent of children so locks and priorities behave as expected.

### Follow-ups
- *Typical virtual sequence contents?* Reset, then register configuration, then parallel traffic on all interfaces, then end-of-test register checks.

title: Explain the virtual sequencer and its use
answer:
*Refer: *[*virtual-sequence-and-virtual-sequencer*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/virtual-sequence-and-virtual-sequencer)

- **What it is:** A `uvm_sequencer` subclass that contains handles pointing to real agent sequencers within the testbench environment.

- **Distinguishing characteristic:** It is **not** connected to any driver (`seq_item_port`).

- **Use:** Serves as a centralized lookup container. Virtual sequences can target this virtual sequencer using `` `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(v_sequencer_t) `` to obtain clean, typed access to all underlying sub-sequencers.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** A virtual sequencer is a `uvm_sequencer` with **no driver attached**. It holds handles to the real agent sequencers (and often the RAL model or config), so a virtual sequence started on it can reach every interface through `p_sequencer`. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph ENV["env"] VSQR["virtual sequencer
apb_sqr, axi_sqr, regmodel handles"] subgraph A1["apb_agent"] S1["apb_sqr"] --> D1["apb_drv"] end subgraph A2["axi_agent"] S2["axi_sqr"] --> D2["axi_drv"] end end VSEQ["virtual sequence"] -->|"start on"| VSQR VSQR -.->|"handle"| S1 VSQR -.->|"handle"| S2 ``` ### Explanation ```systemverilog class top_vsqr extends uvm_sequencer; // no driver, item type unused `uvm_component_utils(top_vsqr) apb_sequencer apb_sqr; axi_sequencer axi_sqr; my_reg_block regmodel; function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction endclass // env function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); vsqr = top_vsqr::type_id::create("vsqr", this); // agents built here too endfunction function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase); vsqr.apb_sqr = apb_agt.sqr; // assign handles, not TLM connections vsqr.axi_sqr = axi_agt.sqr; vsqr.regmodel = regmodel; endfunction ``` | Real sequencer | Virtual sequencer | | --- | --- | | Connected to a driver via `seq_item_export` | No driver connection | | Arbitrates items | Only a launch point for virtual sequences | | Inside an agent | Usually in the env (or a top-level env) | **Benefits** - One place to find every sequencer: the virtual sequence code stays independent of the env hierarchy paths. - Supports `default_sequence` configuration and phase-aware starting. - Nested envs: a top virtual sequencer can hold handles to sub-env virtual sequencers. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The handles are null until `connect_phase`. Starting a virtual sequence earlier, or forgetting to assign a handle, gives null-pointer errors in child `start()`. - Make sure the virtual sequencer does not get built inside a passive agent. It belongs at env level. ### Follow-ups - *Is it mandatory?* No. Handles can be put directly in the virtual sequence or a config object instead.

title: What is the UVM barrier and its usage?
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-barrier*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-barrier)

`uvm_barrier` is a synchronization class used to align multiple concurrent processes or threads across different components:

- Configured with a threshold count: `barrier.set_threshold(N);`

- When a process reaches a synchronization checkpoint, it calls `barrier.wait_for();` and blocks.

- Once $N$ processes have called `wait_for()`, the barrier trips, and all $N$ waiting processes are unblocked simultaneously.

---
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_barrier` is a rendezvous point. Each process calls `wait_for()` and blocks until the **threshold** number of processes have arrived, then all are released together. Use it to align independent threads (agents, sequences) at a common point.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",          "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "thread A",     "wave": "0=.....=.", "data": ["waiting","go"] },
  { "name": "thread B",     "wave": "0..=...=.", "data": ["waiting","go"] },
  { "name": "thread C",     "wave": "0......=.", "data": ["arrives+go"] },
  { "name": "waiters (thr=3)", "wave": "2=.=...2.", "data": ["0","1","2","0"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "all three released when the 3rd thread calls wait_for()" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
uvm_barrier b = new("sync_b", 3);    // threshold 3
// or b.set_threshold(3);

fork
  begin : a  cfg_seq.start(apb_sqr);  b.wait_for(); traffic_a.start(sqr_a); end
  begin : bb init_mem();              b.wait_for(); traffic_b.start(sqr_b); end
  begin : c  wait_link_up();          b.wait_for(); traffic_c.start(sqr_c); end
join
```
| Method | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `new(name, threshold)` / `set_threshold(n)` | Number of waiters needed |
| `wait_for()` | Block until threshold reached |
| `reset(wakeup = 1)` | Reset count, optionally releasing waiters |
| `set_auto_reset(1)` | Reset automatically after each release (default on), so it can be reused |
| `get_num_waiters()` | Debug |
| `cancel()` | Remove one waiter |

- To share it between components, store it in a `uvm_barrier_pool` (`uvm_barrier_pool::get_global("name")`) or pass it through `config_db`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If fewer than threshold processes ever arrive, everyone deadlocks. Pair it with a timeout or watchdog.
- Lowering the threshold below the current waiter count with `set_threshold` releases them immediately.

### Follow-ups
- *Barrier vs `uvm_event`?* An event is one-to-many notification (`trigger` / `wait_trigger`). A barrier is many-to-many with a count.

title: What is the UVM heartbeat and its usage?
answer:
*Refer: *[*uvm-heartbeat*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/uvm-heartbeat)

`uvm_heartbeat` is a liveness monitoring mechanism designed to prevent and diagnose simulation deadlocks or hangs:

- Monitored components trigger heartbeat signals (e.g., raising an event on each completed transaction or periodic activity).

- The heartbeat monitor checks that active components emit signals within a predefined window.

- If a component fails to emit a heartbeat within the allowable interval, the heartbeat monitor flags a timeout and terminates simulation with a detailed debug report.

---

title: What is a Singleton object and its usage?
answer:
*Refer: *[*singleton-object*](https://vlsiverify.com/uvm/singleton-object)

A **Singleton** is an object-oriented design pattern ensuring that only **one instance** of a specific class exists throughout the entire simulation, accessible via a global static method (e.g., `get()`).

**Usage in UVM:**

- `uvm_root` (`uvm_top`): The root component managing the entire testbench hierarchy and phase execution.

- `uvm_factory`: The global registry holding all type and instance overrides.

- Configuration and Resource databases (`uvm_config_db`, `uvm_resource_db`).

---

title: Given an IP, you are the owner of the IP, what are the steps you start with and when will it be signed off?
answer:
*Refer: *[*asic-verification-flow*](https://vlsiverify.com/asic-flows/asic-verification-flow)

#### Step-by-Step ASIC/IP Verification Flow:

1. **Specification Review:** Study architectural specs, register maps, interface timing diagrams, and protocol requirements.

2. **Verification Plan (vPlan) Creation:** Define features, test scenarios, coverage metrics, error cases, and corner conditions.

3. **Testbench Architecture & Environment Setup:**

   - Develop interfaces, UVC agents (driver, monitor, sequencer).

   - Implement scoreboards, reference models, and register models (RAL).

4. **Sanity & Bring-Up:** Develop reset sequence, register read/write tests, and basic smoke tests to ensure DUT is alive.

5. **Feature Verification:** Implement directed and constrained-random sequences targeting every feature in the vPlan.

6. **Error Injection & Stress Testing:** Test corner cases, backpressure, FIFO full/empty, invalid protocol handshakes, and illegal configurations.

7. **Coverage Analysis & Closure:**

   - **Functional Coverage:** Measure covergroups and coverpoints against the vPlan.

   - **Code Coverage:** Review line, branch, condition, toggle, and FSM coverage.

   - **Assertion Coverage:** Verify SVA protocol assertions.

8. **Regression Automation:** Run nightly randomized test suites across multiple seeds.

#### Sign-off Criteria:

- **100% Functional Coverage** achieved against the approved verification plan.

- **Target Code Coverage** reached (typically $>95-98\%$ with all unreached lines formally reviewed/waived).

- **100% Assertion Coverage** with zero assertion failures.

- **Zero Open Severity-1 / Severity-2 Bugs**.

- **Clean Regressions:** Multiple clean regression runs across random seeds without failures.
solution:
**Key idea:** Start from the spec and a reviewed **verification plan**, build a reusable testbench, bring up with sanity tests, close features with directed plus constrained-random tests, then drive coverage and regression to closure. Sign-off is a **measured** decision: the plan is fully covered, coverage targets are met with waivers reviewed, regressions are clean, and there are no open critical bugs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["1. Spec study + design/arch reviews, Q&A with designers"] --> B["2. Verification plan: features, checks, coverage model, stimulus, TB architecture"]
  B --> C["3. Build TB: agents, scoreboard/ref model, RAL, SVA, coverage"]
  C --> D["4. Bring-up: reset, register access, smoke tests"]
  D --> E["5. Feature tests: directed + constrained random, error injection"]
  E --> F["6. Regressions: many seeds, triage, bug tracking"]
  F --> G["7. Coverage analysis: code + functional + assertion, close holes"]
  G -->|"holes or new bugs"| E
  G --> H{"Sign-off criteria met?"}
  H -->|"no"| E
  H -->|"yes"| I["8. Sign-off review, hand-off to SoC (reuse agents passive)"]
```

### Explanation
| Sign-off criterion | Typical target |
| --- | --- |
| Verification plan items | 100% implemented and passing, reviewed with design and architecture |
| Functional coverage | 100% of planned covergroups and cover properties (exclusions justified) |
| Code coverage | Line/branch/condition/FSM/toggle about 95-100%, all holes reviewed and waived |
| Assertions | All pass, cover properties hit |
| Regression | N consecutive clean nightly runs, stable pass rate, no new bugs found |
| Bug status | No open P1/P2 bugs. Bug-discovery rate has flattened |
| Reviews | TB code review, test plan review, waiver review signed off |

- **Day 1 actions:** read the spec and list ambiguities, identify interfaces and protocols (reuse VIP), define the scoreboard strategy, write the plan with traceable feature IDs, and agree on milestones with design (RTL drops vs TB readiness).
- **Metrics over time:** track the bug-find rate, coverage trend and pass rate. A flat bug curve plus closed coverage is the signal to sign off.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- 100% coverage of a weak coverage model is not sign-off. The plan itself must be reviewed.
- RTL changes after sign-off (ECOs) need a delta regression and coverage re-check.
- Do not forget clock/reset variants, low-power modes, configuration parameters and CDC/lint/formal results as part of the sign-off package.

### Follow-ups
- *What if coverage is stuck at 97%?* Analyze holes: unreachable (waive with design approval), constraint gap (write directed or targeted tests), or a design bug.

title: Explain TLM ports and exports in UVM with examples
solution:
**Key idea:** TLM ports and exports connect **testbench components to each other**, never the testbench to the DUT; the DUT is reached only through virtual interfaces. A **port** is the initiator side: it calls methods such as `put`, `get` or `write`. An **export** passes the call down the hierarchy, and an **imp** is the end point that actually implements the method. The legal connection chain is port → (port) → (export) → imp.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph AGT["agent"]
    subgraph PROD["producer"]
      PP["put_port"]
    end
    AP["agent.put_port (port, pass-up)"]
  end
  subgraph ENV2["consumer_wrapper"]
    EX["put_export (export, pass-down)"]
    subgraph CONS["consumer"]
      IMP["put_imp: task put()"]
    end
  end
  PP -->|"port to port: child to parent"| AP
  AP -->|"port to export"| EX
  EX -->|"export to imp"| IMP
```

### Explanation
| Object | Role | Connect rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `uvm_*_port #(T)` | Calls the method (required interface) | `port.connect(port_of_parent / export / imp)` |
| `uvm_*_export #(T)` | Forwards the call into a sub-component (provided interface) | `export.connect(export_of_child / imp)` |
| `uvm_*_imp #(T, IMP)` | Ends the chain. Calls `IMP::put()` etc. | Leaf, never connects onward |

```systemverilog
class producer extends uvm_component;
  `uvm_component_utils(producer)
  uvm_blocking_put_port #(pkt) put_port;
  function new(string n, uvm_component p); super.new(n, p); put_port = new("put_port", this); endfunction
  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    pkt t = pkt::type_id::create("t");
    phase.raise_objection(this);
    void'(t.randomize());
    put_port.put(t);                    // executes consumer.put()
    phase.drop_objection(this);
  endtask
endclass

class consumer extends uvm_component;
  `uvm_component_utils(consumer)
  uvm_blocking_put_imp #(pkt, consumer) put_imp;
  function new(string n, uvm_component p); super.new(n, p); put_imp = new("put_imp", this); endfunction
  task put(pkt t);                      // the implementation
    `uvm_info("CONS", t.convert2string(), UVM_LOW)
    #10ns;                              // blocking put may consume time
  endtask
endclass

class env extends uvm_env;
  producer prod; consumer cons;
  function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    prod.put_port.connect(cons.put_imp);   // always call connect on the initiator side
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `connect()` is always called on the **initiator side** (`port.connect(export)`), never the reverse.
- An unconnected port, or connecting incompatible interfaces (blocking port to a non-blocking imp), is an elaboration error.
- One component with two imps of the same interface needs `` `uvm_blocking_put_imp_decl(_a) `` style suffixes.

### Follow-ups
- *Analysis port vs put port?* An analysis port broadcasts with a non-blocking `write()` to 0..N imps. A put port goes to exactly one imp and may block.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: How analysis ports/FIFOs and TLM ports/FIFOs differs? Explain the usecase of analysis ports/FIFOs being used in the testbench?
answer:
In UVM, **analysis ports and TLM (Transaction Level Modeling) ports** are both used for communication between UVM components, but they serve slightly different purposes.

**Analysis ports are used for one-to-many communication**, where a single UVM component sends data to multiple other components. An analysis port is typically implemented as a SystemVerilog interface with an associated `write` method. Components that want to receive the data connect to the analysis port using a **`` `uvm_analysis_port ``** object, which provides a **`write` method** that forwards the data to the **analysis port**. The analysis port then distributes the data to all connected components. Analysis ports are typically used for broadcasting events or passing data to multiple subscribers, such as for logging or coverage collection.

**TLM ports, on the other hand, are used for point-to-point communication** between UVM components. TLM ports are also implemented as SystemVerilog interfaces, but they typically provide a set of transaction-level methods (such as `write`, `read`, `peek`, etc.) that allow components to exchange transaction-level data directly. Components connect to TLM ports using a **`uvm_tlm_port`**`  or  `**`` `uvm_tlm_fifo ``** object. TLM ports are typically used for more fine-grained communication between components, such as passing transactions between a driver and a monitor.

Similarly, **analysis FIFOs and TLM FIFOs are used for one-to-many and point-to-point communication, respectively**. Analysis FIFOs are implemented as SystemVerilog interfaces with an associated `write` method that allows components to push data into the FIFO. Components that want to receive the data connect to the analysis FIFO using a **``uvm_analysis_fifo`** object, which provides a `get` method that retrieves the data from the FIFO. TLM FIFOs, on the other hand, are implemented as SystemVerilog classes that provide a set of transaction-level methods (such as `write`, `read`, `peek`, etc.) that allow components to exchange transaction-level data directly. Components connect to TLM FIFOs using a **``uvm_tlm_fifo`** object.

The use case of analysis ports/FIFOs and TLM ports/FIFOs in UVM depends on the specific needs of the design being tested. In general, analysis ports/FIFOs are useful for broadcasting events or passing data to multiple subscribers, while TLM ports/FIFOs are useful for fine-grained communication between specific pairs of components. **For example, analysis ports/FIFOs might be used to log data or collect coverage information from multiple components in a testbench, while TLM ports/FIFOs might be used to pass transaction-level data between a driver and a monitor.**
solution:
**Key idea:** **Analysis** ports/FIFOs are for *observation*: a one-to-many broadcast with a non-blocking `write()` function and no back-pressure, used from monitors to scoreboards and coverage. **TLM** ports/FIFOs (put/get/peek) are for *point-to-point flow control*: one producer to one consumer, possibly blocking, with a bounded FIFO. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph AN["Analysis path (observation)"] MON["monitor.ap"] -->|"write()"| AF["uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo
unbounded"] MON -->|"write()"| COV["coverage"] MON -->|"write()"| LOG["logger"] AF -->|"get() in task"| SCB["scoreboard thread"] end subgraph TL["TLM path (flow control)"] GEN["generator.put_port"] -->|"put() blocks when full"| TF["uvm_tlm_fifo depth N"] TF -->|"get()"| BFM["transactor"] end ``` ### Explanation | | Analysis port / `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` | TLM port / `uvm_tlm_fifo` | | --- | --- | --- | | Connectivity | 1 to 0..N | 1 to 1 | | Method | `write()` function, never blocks | `put`/`get`/`peek` tasks plus `try_*` functions | | Back-pressure | None | Yes (blocking put when full) | | FIFO depth | Unbounded | Configurable, default 1 | | Unconnected allowed | Yes | No (error) | | Typical use | Monitor to scoreboard, coverage, predictor | Stimulus pipelines, layered transactors, models | **Why analysis FIFOs in a scoreboard:** the monitor's `write()` happens in zero time, at whatever moment the bus completes. With two streams (expected and actual), the scoreboard needs to *wait* for the matching item. Analysis FIFOs buffer each stream, and a `run_phase` thread does blocking `get()`s to pair them. ```systemverilog class scb extends uvm_scoreboard; `uvm_component_utils(scb) uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(pkt) in_f, out_f; function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase); in_f = new("in_f", this); out_f = new("out_f", this); endfunction task run_phase(uvm_phase phase); pkt i, o; forever begin in_f.get(i); // blocks until input observed out_f.get(o); // blocks until DUT output observed if (!o.compare(predict(i))) `uvm_error("SCB", "mismatch") end endtask endclass // env: in_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.in_f.analysis_export); // out_agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.out_f.analysis_export); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - An analysis FIFO never applies back-pressure, so a stalled consumer grows it without bound. Check for leftovers in `check_phase`. - Subscribers share the same object handle. Do not modify it in place. ### Follow-ups - *Can a monitor use a TLM put port to the scoreboard?* It could, but a blocking put would let the scoreboard stall the monitor and miss bus activity. That is why monitors use analysis ports.

title: Sequence Vs Sequence item in UVM? Explain with Example
solution:
**Key idea:** A **sequence item** is *one* transaction (data plus constraints), for example a single bus write. A **sequence** is a *scenario generator*: its `body()` creates, randomizes and sends many items, or starts other sequences, in a particular order through a sequencer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph SEQ["write_read_seq (uvm_sequence)"]
    B["body()"] --> I1["item: WR addr=0x10"]
    B --> I2["item: WR addr=0x14"]
    B --> I3["item: RD addr=0x10"]
  end
  I1 --> SQR["sequencer"]
  I2 --> SQR
  I3 --> SQR
  SQR --> DRV["driver"]
```

### Explanation
| | Sequence item | Sequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base class | `uvm_sequence_item` | `uvm_sequence #(REQ, RSP)` (also derived from `uvm_sequence_item`) |
| Represents | One transaction | An ordered or random series of items or sub-sequences |
| Contains | `rand` fields, constraints, copy/compare/print | `body()` task, knobs, possibly constraints |
| Started by | `start_item` / `finish_item` inside a sequence | `seq.start(sequencer)` |
| Consumed by | Driver | Never reaches the driver itself |

```systemverilog
class bus_item extends uvm_sequence_item;            // ONE transaction
  rand bit [31:0] addr, data;
  rand bit        write;
  constraint c_al { addr[1:0] == 0; }
  `uvm_object_utils(bus_item)
  function new(string name = "bus_item"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

class write_read_seq extends uvm_sequence #(bus_item); // A SCENARIO
  `uvm_object_utils(write_read_seq)
  rand bit [31:0] base;
  function new(string name = "write_read_seq"); super.new(name); endfunction
  task body();
    bit [31:0] a;
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) send(1, base + 4*i);   // two writes
    send(0, base);                                      // read back first location
  endtask
  task send(bit wr, bit [31:0] a);
    req = bus_item::type_id::create("req");
    start_item(req);
    if (!req.randomize() with { write == wr; addr == a; }) `uvm_error("RND", "fail")
    finish_item(req);
  endtask
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Put protocol legality constraints in the item, and scenario intent (ordering, address ranges) in the sequence.
- Do not reuse one item handle across `finish_item` calls if anything downstream stores it.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a sequence be passed to `start_item`?* No. `start_item` is for items. Child sequences are run with `start()` (or `` `uvm_do ``).

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: Explain how uvm_transaction differs from a uvm_sequence_item in UVM with example
solution:
**Key idea:** Both are data objects, but `uvm_sequence_item` **extends** `uvm_transaction` and adds the hooks needed to flow through a sequencer to a driver: sequencer and parent-sequence handles, plus the sequence ID used for response routing. `uvm_transaction` only adds timing and recording on top of `uvm_object`. User items should extend `uvm_sequence_item`. ```mermaid flowchart TD O["uvm_object"] --> T["uvm_transaction
+ accept_tr, begin_tr, end_tr
+ transaction_id, recording, events"] T --> SI["uvm_sequence_item
+ m_sequencer, m_parent_sequence
+ sequence_id, set_id_info()
+ get_sequencer(), get_full_name with seq path"] SI --> MY["apb_item (user)"] SI --> SB["uvm_sequence_base"] ``` ### Explanation | Capability | `uvm_transaction` | `uvm_sequence_item` | | --- | --- | --- | | copy/compare/print/pack | ✓ (from `uvm_object`) | ✓ | | Transaction recording (`begin_tr`/`end_tr`) | ✓ | ✓ | | `start_item` / `finish_item` | ✗ | ✓ | | `uvm_driver #(T)` / `uvm_sequencer #(T)` parameter | ✗ | ✓ | | Response routing (`set_id_info`) | ✗ | ✓ | | Knows its sequence/sequencer | ✗ | ✓ | **Example: why it matters for responses** ```systemverilog class apb_item extends uvm_sequence_item; // NOT uvm_transaction rand bit [31:0] addr, wdata; bit [31:0] rdata; `uvm_object_utils(apb_item) function new(string name = "apb_item"); super.new(name); endfunction endclass // driver seq_item_port.get_next_item(req); drive(req); rsp = apb_item::type_id::create("rsp"); rsp.set_id_info(req); // copies sequence_id + transaction_id: only exists in sequence_item rsp.rdata = vif.prdata; seq_item_port.item_done(rsp); // sequencer routes rsp to the issuing sequence ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - UVM documentation states that user classes should not extend `uvm_transaction` directly. The library keeps it as an internal layer. - The "transaction_id" from `uvm_transaction` and the "sequence_id" from `uvm_sequence_item` are different. Both are copied by `set_id_info`. ### Follow-ups - *Should monitor output items also be sequence items?* Usually yes, reusing the same class. The extra fields are harmless and comparisons become simple.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: copy() Vs clone() Vs create() method in a UVM components?
solution:
**Key idea:** `create()` *builds* a new object through the factory (override-aware). `copy()` *overwrites* an existing object's fields with another's. `clone()` = `create()` of the same type + `copy()`, returned as a `uvm_object` handle that needs `$cast`. Note that `create`, `copy` and `clone` are for objects: components cannot be cloned. ```mermaid flowchart LR CR["create()
factory → new object
(fields default/random)"] CP["copy(src)
dst must exist
fields ← src"] CL["clone()
new object + copy
returns uvm_object"] CR --> CL CP --> CL ``` ### Explanation | Method | Allocates? | Copies data? | Factory override? | Return | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `T::type_id::create("n")` | Yes | No | Yes | `T` | | `dst.copy(src)` | No | Yes (`do_copy`) | n/a | void | | `src.clone()` | Yes, same *dynamic* type as `src` | Yes | Same type as the source object | `uvm_object` | ```systemverilog pkt a, b, c; a = pkt::type_id::create("a"); // may return an override type void'(a.randomize()); b = pkt::type_id::create("b"); b.copy(a); // b's fields = a's fields, b keeps its own name $cast(c, a.clone()); // brand new object, identical contents c.data = 0; // does not affect a ``` - Components: `uvm_component::clone()` and `copy` are not supported for components (`clone()` issues an error). Components are created only with `create(name, parent)` during build. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - `copy()` does not copy the instance name. `clone()` copies it (through `set_name(get_name())` internally). - If `do_copy` is not implemented and no field macros are used, `copy()` copies nothing beyond the base class fields. - A shallow copy of nested object handles shares sub-objects. Implement deep copy in `do_copy` when needed. ### Follow-ups - *When does a monitor use clone?* When it reuses one item for sampling: `ap.write(tr.clone())`-style hand-off. A better practice is to create a new item per transaction.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: How get_name() differs from get_full_name() method in a UVM?
solution:
**Key idea:** `get_name()` returns only the object's **leaf name** (the string given at construction). `get_full_name()` returns the **hierarchical path** from the top. For components that path is `uvm_test_top.env.agt.drv`. For objects (items, sequences) it is the leaf name, or the sequencer path plus sequence path for items in flight.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  ROOT["uvm_top (name '')"] --> T["uvm_test_top"]
  T --> E["env"] --> A["agt"] --> D["drv"]
  D --> N["drv.get_name() = 'drv'"]
  D --> F["drv.get_full_name() = 'uvm_test_top.env.agt.drv'"]
```

### Explanation
| Call | Component `drv` | Sequence `seq` started on `agt.sqr` | Plain object `cfg` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `get_name()` | `drv` | `seq` | `cfg` |
| `get_full_name()` | `uvm_test_top.env.agt.drv` | `uvm_test_top.env.agt.sqr.seq` | `cfg` |
| `get_type_name()` | `my_driver` | `my_seq` | `my_cfg` |

```systemverilog
function void end_of_elaboration_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  `uvm_info("NAME", $sformatf("name=%s full=%s type=%s",
            get_name(), get_full_name(), get_type_name()), UVM_LOW)
endfunction
// UVM_INFO ... [NAME] name=drv full=uvm_test_top.env.agt.drv type=my_driver
```
- `get_full_name()` is what `config_db` matches against and what instance overrides and `+uvm_set_verbosity` paths use. Messages print it automatically as the reporter path.
- For a sequence item, `get_full_name()` is built from its parent sequence and sequencer, which is handy for debug messages from inside `body()`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The constructor name must be unique among siblings, and should match the handle name to keep paths readable (`env = my_env::type_id::create("env", this)`).
- Do not use names with dots or spaces. They break path matching.

### Follow-ups
- *What is `uvm_top`'s full name?* An empty string. That is why the test's path is just `uvm_test_top`.

title: Explain the difference between UVM ACTIVE agent and UVM PASSIVE agent?
answer:
In the context of the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM), an **ACTIVE** agent is an agent that initiates transactions on its own, whereas a **PASSIVE** agent waits for the other side to initiate transactions.

An **ACTIVE** agent is responsible for generating transactions and driving them onto the bus or interface. It contains the logic to create the stimulus and control the timing of the transactions. ACTIVE agents are commonly used for stimulus generation, protocol checking, and coverage collection.

On the other hand, a **PASSIVE** agent is responsible for receiving transactions and responding to them. It waits for the other side to initiate transactions and reacts to them accordingly. PASSIVE agents are commonly used for monitoring the protocol, collecting protocol statistics, and checking for errors or violations.

An Agent is normally configured ACTIVE in a block level verification environment where stimulus is required to be generated. Same agent can be configured PASSIVE as we move from block level to chip level verification environment in which no stimulus generation is needed, but we still can use same for monitoring activity in terms of debug or coverage.

To summarize, the key difference between ACTIVE and PASSIVE agents in UVM is that ACTIVE agents initiate transactions, while PASSIVE agents wait for transactions to be initiated by the other side.
solution:
**Key idea:** An **ACTIVE** agent *drives* stimulus on its interface: it builds a sequencer and driver plus a monitor. A **PASSIVE** agent only *observes*: it builds just the monitor. Both still publish transactions to scoreboards and coverage. Active vs passive is about whether the testbench drives the pins, not about who initiates bus transfers; a slave or responder agent that drives responses is also ACTIVE. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph BL["Block level"] AA["uart_agent ACTIVE
sqr + drv + mon"] -->|"drives"| DUT1["UART IP"] end subgraph SOC["SoC level (same agent reused)"] CPU["CPU RTL drives the bus"] --> DUT2["UART IP"] PA["uart_agent PASSIVE
mon only"] -.->|"observes"| DUT2 end AA --> SCB1["scoreboard"] PA --> SCB2["scoreboard / coverage"] ``` ### Explanation | | ACTIVE (`UVM_ACTIVE`) | PASSIVE (`UVM_PASSIVE`) | | --- | --- | --- | | Builds | sequencer, driver, monitor | monitor | | Drives DUT pins | Yes (master requests or slave responses) | Never | | Sequences can run | Yes | No sequencer | | Typical place | Block-level inputs, response models | DUT outputs, internal buses, SoC reuse | | Default | `uvm_agent::is_active = UVM_ACTIVE` | Must be configured | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A passive agent must never touch the interface outputs. Its monitor must not assume the TB generated the traffic, so it should not read handles to driver items. - In passive mode, any code that references the driver or sequencer (connect, virtual sequencer handles, RAL `set_sequencer`) must be guarded. ### Follow-ups - *How is the mode chosen?* Via `uvm_config_db#(uvm_active_passive_enum)::set(this, "env.agt", "is_active", UVM_PASSIVE)` or an agent config object (see the next question).

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: How is an Agent configured as ACTIVE or PASSIVE?
answer:
UVM agents have a variable of type UVM_ACTIVE_PASSIVE_e which defines whether the agent is active (UVM_ACTIVE) with the sequencer and the driver constructed, or passive (UVM_PASSIVE) with neither the driver nor the sequencer constructed. This parameter is called active and by default, it is set to UVM_ACTIVE. This can be changed using set_config_int() while the agent is created in the environment class. The build phase of the agent should then have the code as below to selectively construct driver and sequencer.

```verilog
function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
if(m_cfg.active == UVM_ACTIVE) begin
//create driver, sequencer
end
endfunction
```

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: In UVM how a monitor differs from a scoreboard in UVM?
answer:
In the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM), monitors and scoreboards are two distinct components used for verifying the design under test (DUT).

A **monitor** is responsible for observing signals or transactions on the DUT’s interface and converting them into a higher-level abstraction that can be easily understood by the testbench. The monitor typically operates at the physical layer and captures the data being sent or received by the DUT. It can also perform additional tasks such as protocol checking, error detection, and data extraction.

On the other hand, a **scoreboard** is responsible for comparing the actual results generated by the DUT with the expected results provided by the testbench. It takes in the data produced by the monitor and performs comparisons against the expected data. The scoreboard typically operates at the transactional or functional layer and can identify errors such as incorrect data, missing transactions, or out-of-order transactions.

In summary, while both monitors and scoreboards are used for verification in UVM, they have distinct roles and operate at different layers of abstraction. The monitor captures the data being sent or received by the DUT, while the scoreboard performs comparisons against the expected results provided by the testbench.
solution:
**Key idea:** A **monitor** sits at the pin level. It samples one interface and converts signal activity into transactions, without judging them, apart from optional protocol checks. A **scoreboard** sits at the transaction level. It takes those transactions from several monitors, predicts expected results (reference model) and decides **pass or fail** on DUT functionality. ```mermaid flowchart LR IN["DUT input pins"] --> M1["input monitor
pins to txn"] OUT["DUT output pins"] --> M2["output monitor
pins to txn"] M1 -->|"ap.write"| RM["reference model / predictor"] RM -->|"expected"| SCB["scoreboard
compare, count, report"] M2 -->|"ap.write: actual"| SCB M1 --> COV["coverage"] ``` ### Explanation | | Monitor (`uvm_monitor`) | Scoreboard (`uvm_scoreboard`) | | --- | --- | --- | | Abstraction | Signal to transaction | Transaction only | | Connects to | Virtual interface, analysis port out | Analysis imps/FIFOs in, no vif | | Scope | One interface/protocol | End-to-end DUT behavior across interfaces | | Checks | Protocol rules on its bus (optional) | Data integrity, ordering, functional correctness | | Lives in | Agent (active and passive) | Env | | Reuse | With the agent, in any project using that protocol | DUT-specific | ```systemverilog // monitor: observe and publish only task run_phase(uvm_phase phase); forever begin pkt t; @(vif.cb iff vif.cb.valid && vif.cb.ready); t = pkt::type_id::create("t"); t.data = vif.cb.data; ap.write(t); end endtask // scoreboard: predict and judge function void write_act(pkt t); pkt e = exp_q.pop_front(); if (!t.compare(e)) `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("exp %s got %s", e.convert2string(), t.convert2string())) endfunction ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Do not put DUT-specific checking in the monitor. It destroys reuse. - The scoreboard should never sample the vif. It must stay timing-independent and only consume transactions. - When the expected queue is empty, the scoreboard still has to handle the incoming actual (report an "unexpected output" error) rather than popping an empty queue. ### Follow-ups - *Where do protocol assertions go?* In the interface (SVA) or the monitor. Functional checks go in the scoreboard.

title: What are pre_body() and post_body() functions in a sequence? Do they always get called?
answer:
pre_body() is a method in a sequence class that gets called before the body() method of a sequence is called. post_body() method in sequence gets called after the body() method is called.

The pre_body() and post_body() methods are not always called. The uvm_sequence::start() has an optional argument which if set to 0, will result in these methods not being called. Following are the formal argument of start() method in a sequence.

```
virtual task start (
uvm_sequencer_base sequencer, // Pointer to sequencer
uvm_sequence_base parent_sequencer = null, // parent sequencer
integer this_priority = 100, // Priority on the sequencer
bit call_pre_post = 1); // pre_body and post_body called
```
solution:
**Key idea:** `pre_body()` runs just before and `post_body()` just after `body()`, but **only when** `start()` is called with `call_pre_post = 1`, the default. They are skipped when a sequence is started with `call_pre_post = 0`, which is what the `` `uvm_do `` family does for child sequences. `pre_start()` and `post_start()` are always called.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph A["seq.start(sqr) : call_pre_post = 1"]
    a1["pre_start"] --> a2["pre_body"] --> a3["body"] --> a4["post_body"] --> a5["post_start"]
  end
  subgraph B["uvm_do(seq) or start(sqr, this, -1, 0)"]
    b1["pre_start"] --> b3["body"] --> b5["post_start"]
  end
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
virtual task start(uvm_sequencer_base sequencer,
                   uvm_sequence_base  parent_sequence = null,
                   int                this_priority   = -1,
                   bit                call_pre_post   = 1);
```
| Hook | Kind | Always called? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pre_start` / `post_start` | task | Yes |
| `pre_body` / `post_body` | task | Only if `call_pre_post == 1` |
| `pre_do` / `mid_do` / `post_do` | parent-sequence callbacks around each item or child | Yes, on the parent |

```systemverilog
class root_seq extends uvm_sequence #(pkt);
  task pre_body();
    if (get_starting_phase() != null) get_starting_phase().raise_objection(this);
  endtask
  task post_body();
    if (get_starting_phase() != null) get_starting_phase().drop_objection(this);
  endtask
endclass
```
- That objection pattern relies on `pre_body` being skipped for child sequences, so only the root sequence raises.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Cleanup that must always happen belongs in `post_start`, not `post_body`.
- Despite the question wording, these are **tasks**, not functions, so they may consume time.

### Follow-ups
- *UVM 1.2 replacement for the objection pattern?* `set_automatic_phase_objection(1)` in the sequence constructor.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: Is the start() method on a sequence blocking or nonblocking?
answer: The start() method is a blocking call. It blocks execution until the body() method of the sequence completes execution.
solution:
**Key idea:** `start()` is a **blocking task**. It returns only after the sequence's `body()`, and therefore every item it sent and every child sequence, has completed, along with `post_body`/`post_start`. To run sequences concurrently, wrap the calls in `fork`.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",               "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "test thread",       "wave": "2.......2..", "data": ["blocked in seq.start()","next stmt"] },
  { "name": "seq.body items",    "wave": "x=.=.=.=x..", "data": ["i0","i1","i2","i3"] },
  { "name": "driver item_done",  "wave": "0.1010101.0" }
],
  "head": { "text": "start() returns after the last item_done ends body()" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this);
  cfg_seq.start(env.apb_sqr);          // blocks: config finishes first
  fork                                  // concurrent traffic
    rd_seq.start(env.axi_sqr);
    wr_seq.start(env.axi_sqr);
  join                                  // wait for both
  fork
    bg_seq.start(env.irq_sqr);          // background, not waited for
  join_none
  phase.drop_objection(this);
endtask
```
| Call | Returns when |
| --- | --- |
| `seq.start(sqr)` | `body()` and the post hooks are done |
| `start_item(item)` | Sequencer grants the sequence |
| `finish_item(item)` | Driver calls `item_done()` |
| `fork ... join_none` around `start` | Immediately (sequence runs in background) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A `join_none` background sequence that is still running when the phase ends is killed, which can leave the driver mid-item. Stop it cleanly (a flag, or `kill()` followed by `stop_sequences()`).
- Because `start()` blocks, it can only be called from a task context such as `run_phase` or a sequence `body()`, not from `build_phase`.

### Follow-ups
- *Is `finish_item` blocking?* Yes, until `item_done`. In a pipelined driver it can return before the transfer completes on the bus.
