title: How can a sequence get exclusive access to a sequencer?
answer:
When multiple sequences are run on a sequencer, the sequencer arbitrates and grants access to each sequence on a sequence item boundary. Sometimes a sequence might want exclusive access to sequencer until all the sequence items part of it are driven to the driver

(for example: if you want to stimulate a deterministic pattern without any interruption).

There are two mechanisms that allow a sequence to get exclusive access to sequencer.

\1) **Using lock() and unlock( )**: A sequence can call the lock method of the sequencer on which it runs. The calling sequence will be granted exclusive access to the driver when it gets the next slot via the sequencer arbitration mechanism. If there are other sequences marked as a higher priority, this sequence needs to wait until it gets its slot. Once the lock is granted, no other sequences will be able to access the driver until the sequence issues an unlock() call on the sequencer which will then release the lock. The lock method is blocking and does not return until the lock has been granted.

\2) **Using grab() and ungrab(): **The grab method is similar to the lock method and can be called by the sequence when it needs exclusive access. The difference between grab and lock is that when grab() is called, it takes immediate effect and the sequence will grab the next sequencer arbitration slot, overriding any sequence priorities in place. The only thing that can stop a sequence from grabbing a sequencer is an already existing lock() or grab() condition on the sequencer.
solution:
**Key idea:** Normally the sequencer arbitrates **per item**, so items from concurrent sequences interleave. A sequence gets exclusive access with **`lock()`**/**`unlock()`**, which queues behind existing requests and waits its turn, or with **`grab()`**/**`ungrab()`**, which jumps to the front of the queue and wins the next arbitration. Either way, only that sequence (and its children) can send items until it releases.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant N as normal_seq
  participant X as atomic_seq
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant D as driver
  N->>Q: item N0
  Q->>D: N0
  X->>Q: lock() (waits for slot)
  Q-->>X: lock granted
  X->>Q: X0
  Q->>D: X0
  N->>Q: item N1 (blocked: sequencer locked)
  X->>Q: X1
  Q->>D: X1
  X->>Q: unlock()
  Q->>D: N1
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class atomic_rmw_seq extends uvm_sequence #(bus_item);
  `uvm_object_utils(atomic_rmw_seq)
  rand bit [31:0] addr;
  function new(string name = "atomic_rmw_seq"); super.new(name); endfunction
  task body();
    bus_item rd, wr;
    lock(m_sequencer);                    // grab(m_sequencer) for urgent traffic
    rd = bus_item::type_id::create("rd");
    start_item(rd); void'(rd.randomize() with { write == 0; addr == local::addr; }); finish_item(rd);
    get_response(rd);
    wr = bus_item::type_id::create("wr");
    start_item(wr); void'(wr.randomize() with { write == 1; addr == local::addr; data == rd.data | 1; }); finish_item(wr);
    unlock(m_sequencer);
  endtask
endclass
```
| | `lock` | `grab` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Queue position | End | Front |
| Respects priority / other waiting sequences | Yes | No (bypasses them) |
| Blocked by an existing lock/grab | Yes | Yes |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Always release. Put `unlock` on every exit path, including early returns, or every other sequence starves.
- If the locking sequence is killed while holding the lock, the sequencer stays locked unless `stop_sequences()` is used.
- Without `get_response` support in the driver (`item_done(rsp)`), this read-modify-write example would hang.

### Follow-ups
- *Non-exclusive alternative?* Set the arbitration mode (`UVM_SEQ_ARB_STRICT_FIFO`) and a higher priority. That favors the sequence but does not guarantee back-to-back items.

title: What is the difference between a pipelined and a non-pipelined sequence-driver model?
solution:
**Key idea:** A **non-pipelined** driver handles one transaction at a time: `get_next_item`, drive the whole transfer, then `item_done`, so the sequence is blocked for the full duration. A **pipelined** driver lets the next request start before the previous one completes, as AXI/AHB address/data phase overlap requires. It accepts items early and finishes their later phases in parallel threads, returning responses with `put()` and response routing.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",                 "wave": "p........." },
  {},
  { "name": "non-pipe addr",       "wave": "x3.x..4.x.", "data": ["A0","A1"] },
  { "name": "non-pipe data",       "wave": "x..3.x..4.", "data": ["D0","D1"] },
  {},
  { "name": "pipe addr",           "wave": "x34.5x....", "data": ["A0","A1","A2"] },
  { "name": "pipe data",           "wave": "x.345x....", "data": ["D0","D1","D2"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "pipelined: address of N+1 overlaps data of N" } }
```

### Explanation
**Non-pipelined**
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  forever begin
    seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
    drive_addr_phase(req);
    drive_data_phase(req);              // sequence is blocked all this time
    seq_item_port.item_done();
  end
endtask
```
**Pipelined (address and data phases as separate threads)**
```systemverilog
mailbox #(bus_item) data_q = new(2);   // depth bounds outstanding transfers

task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  fork
    addr_thread();
    data_thread();
  join
endtask

task addr_thread();
  forever begin
    seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
    drive_addr_phase(req);              // 1 cycle
    data_q.put(req);                    // hand to data thread
    seq_item_port.item_done();          // sequence may send next item now
  end
endtask

task data_thread();
  bus_item t, rsp;
  forever begin
    data_q.get(t);
    drive_data_phase(t);                // overlaps next address phase
    $cast(rsp, t.clone());
    rsp.set_id_info(t);
    seq_item_port.put(rsp);             // response routed by sequence id
  end
endtask
```
| | Non-pipelined | Pipelined |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outstanding transactions | 1 | N |
| `item_done` called | After full transfer | After request/address phase |
| Response path | `item_done(rsp)` or none | `put(rsp)` / `put_response`, matched by ID |
| Sequence side | `finish_item` = transfer done | `finish_item` = accepted; use `get_response` for completion |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The sequence must consume responses (`get_response` or `use_response_handler(1)` with `response_handler`), or the response queue overflows.
- Bound the outstanding depth to match the protocol, or the driver accepts more items than the DUT allows.

### Follow-ups
- *How does the sequence wait for completion?* Call `get_response(rsp, req.get_transaction_id())` in a forked thread, or use the response handler.

title: How do we make sure that if multiple sequences are running on a sequencer-driver, responses are send back from the driver to the correct sequence?
solution:
**Key idea:** Every item carries the **sequence ID** of the sequence that sent it, plus a transaction ID. The driver must copy them into its response with **`rsp.set_id_info(req)`**. The sequencer then uses the sequence ID to put the response into the right sequence's response queue, where `get_response()` picks it up.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as seq A (id 3)
  participant B as seq B (id 7)
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant D as driver
  A->>Q: req a (sequence_id 3)
  B->>Q: req b (sequence_id 7)
  Q->>D: req a
  D->>D: rsp.set_id_info(req a)
  D->>Q: item_done(rsp) / put(rsp) id 3
  Q-->>A: response queue of seq 3
  Q->>D: req b
  D->>Q: rsp with id 7
  Q-->>B: response queue of seq 7
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class my_driver extends uvm_driver #(bus_item);
  `uvm_component_utils(my_driver)
  virtual bus_if vif;
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction

  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);          // must be a task: get() blocks
    bus_item req, rsp;
    forever begin
      seq_item_port.get(req);               // get() = get_next_item + item_done
      drive_req(req);
      rsp = bus_item::type_id::create("rsp");
      rsp.set_id_info(req);                 // copy sequence_id + transaction_id
      rsp.rdata = vif.rdata;
      seq_item_port.put(rsp);               // sequencer routes by sequence_id
    end
  endtask
endclass

// in each sequence
task body();
  start_item(req); void'(req.randomize()); finish_item(req);
  get_response(rsp);                        // optionally get_response(rsp, req.get_transaction_id())
endtask
```
| Driver response method | When |
| --- | --- |
| `seq_item_port.item_done(rsp)` | After `get_next_item` |
| `seq_item_port.put(rsp)` | After `get()`, or later for pipelined responses |
| `rsp_port.write(rsp)` | Analysis-style response port on `uvm_driver` (connected to `sqr.rsp_export`) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Forgetting `set_id_info` causes a fatal or error ("Response has invalid sequence_id" or a dropped response), and the sequence hangs in `get_response`.
- Responses not consumed fill the per-sequence response queue (default depth 8) and raise an overflow error.
- Re-using the request object as the response works if IDs are already set, but creating a separate response object is clearer.

### Follow-ups
- *How to match responses to specific requests in a pipelined flow?* Pass `req.get_transaction_id()` to `get_response()`.

title: What is the difference between early randomization and late randomization while generating a sequence?
answer:
In **Early randomization**, a sequence object is first randomized using randomize() call and then the sequence calls start_item() to request access to a sequencer, which is a blocking call and can take time-based upon how busy the sequencer is. The following example shows an object (req) randomized first and then sequence waits for arbitration

```verilog
task body()
  assert(req.randomize());
  start_item(req); //Can consume time based on sequencer arbitration
  finish_item(req);
endtask

```

In **Late randomization,** a sequence first calls start_item() , waits until arbitration is granted from the sequencer, and then just before sending the transaction to sequencer/driver, randomize is called. This has the advantage that items are randomized just in time and can use any feedback from design or other components just before sending an item to driver. Following code shows late randomization of a request (req)

```verilog
task body()
  start_item(req); //Can consume time based on sequencer arbitration
  assert(req.randomivze());
  finish_item(req);
endtask

```
solution:
**Key idea:** **Early randomization** randomizes the item *before* `start_item()`, so the values are fixed before the sequence wins arbitration. **Late randomization** randomizes *after* `start_item()` returns, right before `finish_item()`. Constraints can then use state that is current at the moment the driver is ready, such as the latest response data or the DUT status. UVM recommends late randomization.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as sequence
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant D as driver
  Note over S: EARLY
  S->>S: req.randomize()
  S->>Q: start_item(req) may wait many cycles
  Q-->>S: grant (values possibly stale)
  S->>Q: finish_item(req)
  Note over S: LATE
  S->>Q: start_item(req)
  Q-->>S: grant (driver is ready now)
  S->>S: req.randomize() with current state
  S->>Q: finish_item(req)
  Q->>D: req
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// early
task body();
  req = item::type_id::create("req");
  if (!req.randomize()) `uvm_error("RND", "fail")
  start_item(req);                      // arbitration may take time
  finish_item(req);
endtask

// late (recommended)
task body();
  req = item::type_id::create("req");
  start_item(req);                      // granted: driver waiting
  if (!req.randomize() with { addr != last_addr; credit_ok == (p_sequencer.credits > 0); })
    `uvm_error("RND", "fail")
  finish_item(req);
  last_addr = req.addr;
endtask
```
| | Early | Late |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When values are chosen | Before arbitration | After grant |
| Can react to current DUT/TB state | No, can be stale | Yes |
| Typical use | Pre-computing a list of items, checking constraints before requesting | Default for reactive and stateful stimulus |
| `` `uvm_do `` macros | — | Use late randomization |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Never randomize *after* `finish_item`. The driver has already consumed the item.
- With late randomization, a randomization failure happens while holding the grant. Report it and still call `finish_item` (or handle the failure) so the driver does not stall.

### Follow-ups
- *Where does `mid_do` fit?* The parent's `mid_do(item)` is called inside `finish_item` just before the item is sent, another hook for last-moment changes.

title: What is the difference between get_next_item() and try_next_item() methods in UVM driver class?
answer:
The `get_next_item()` is a **blocking call** (part of the driver-sequencer API) which blocks until a sequence item is available for the driver to process, and returns a pointer to the sequence item.

The `try_next_item()` is a **nonblocking** version which returns a null pointer if no sequence item is available for driver to process.
solution:
**Key idea:** `get_next_item(req)` **blocks** until the sequencer has an item. `try_next_item(req)` does **not wait for an item**: if none is ready (after a few delta cycles of arbitration), it returns with `req == null`. The driver can then drive idle cycles. Both require `item_done()` after a successful fetch.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",              "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "seq item ready",   "wave": "0...1.0." },
  { "name": "get_next_item",    "wave": "2...3.2.", "data": ["blocked","item","blocked"] },
  { "name": "try_next_item req","wave": "4444344.", "data": ["null/idle","null/idle","null/idle","null/idle","item","null/idle","null/idle"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "try_next_item returns null each cycle with nothing ready, so the driver can idle" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// blocking style: bus idles implicitly while waiting
forever begin
  seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
  drive(req);
  seq_item_port.item_done();
end

// non-blocking style: protocol needs explicit idle cycles every clock
forever begin
  @(vif.cb);
  seq_item_port.try_next_item(req);
  if (req != null) begin
    drive(req);
    seq_item_port.item_done();
  end
  else
    drive_idle();                       // e.g. valid = 0, keep link alive
end
```
| | `get_next_item` | `try_next_item` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kind | task, blocks until an item | task, no wait for an item (only delta-cycle wait) |
| No item available | Waits | Returns `null` |
| Needs `item_done()` | Yes | Yes, only when non-null |
| Use when | Bus can just stall | Driver must do something every cycle (idle symbols, clock-driven protocols) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `try_next_item` waits a few delta cycles (`uvm_wait_for_nba_region`) so that sequences can respond in the same time step. It is still declared as a task.
- Calling `try_next_item` again without `item_done()` after a successful fetch is an error.

### Follow-ups
- *Can `has_do_available()` help?* Yes. `seq_item_port.has_do_available()` tells you whether any sequence is ready to send, without fetching an item.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is the difference between get_next_item() and get() methods in UVM driver class?
answer:
The `get_next_item()` is a **blocking call** to get the sequence item from the sequencer FIFO for processing by driver. Once the sequence item is processed by a driver, it needs to call `item_done()` to complete the handshake before a new item is requested using get_next_item().

The `get()` is also a **blocking call** which gets the sequence item from sequencer FIFO for processing by driver. However, while using `get()`, there is no need to explicitly call `item_done()` as the `get()` method completes the handshake implicitly.
solution:
**Key idea:** `get_next_item(req)` fetches an item but leaves the handshake **open**: the driver must call `item_done()` later, and `finish_item` in the sequence returns only then. `get(req)` fetches **and completes the handshake immediately** (it calls `item_done()` internally), so the sequence continues right away. Responses then go back with `put(rsp)`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as sequence
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant D as driver
  Note over S,D: get_next_item / item_done
  D->>Q: get_next_item(req)
  Q-->>D: req
  D->>D: drive (finish_item still blocked)
  D->>Q: item_done()
  Q-->>S: finish_item returns
  Note over S,D: get / put
  D->>Q: get(req)
  Q-->>D: req (item_done implied)
  Q-->>S: finish_item returns immediately
  D->>D: drive
  D->>Q: put(rsp)
  Q-->>S: get_response(rsp)
```

### Explanation
| | `get_next_item` | `get` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Removes item from sequencer | On `item_done()` | Immediately |
| Needs `item_done()` | Yes | No (calling it is an error) |
| Sequence `finish_item` returns | After driving completes | At once |
| Response method | `item_done(rsp)` or `put(rsp)` | `put(rsp)` |
| Good for | Simple blocking drivers, where finish_item means "done on the bus" | Pipelined or out-of-order drivers |

```systemverilog
// get + put style
forever begin
  seq_item_port.get(req);
  drive(req);
  rsp = item::type_id::create("rsp");
  rsp.set_id_info(req);
  seq_item_port.put(rsp);
end
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- With `get()`, `finish_item` no longer means the transfer finished. Sequences that need completion must wait on `get_response`.
- Mixing `get()` with `item_done()` gives "item_done called with no outstanding request".

### Follow-ups
- *What does `peek` add?* It returns the item without removing it (see next question).

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is the difference between get() and peek() methods of UVM driver class?
answer:
The `get()` method part of driver class is a **blocking call** which gets the sequence item from sequencer FIFO for processing by driver. It unblocks once an item is available and completes handshake with sequencer.

The `peek()` method is similar to `get()` and **blocks** until a sequence item is available. However, it will not remove the request from the sequencer FIFO. So calling `peek()` multiple times will return same sequencer item in driver.
solution:
**Key idea:** Both block until an item is available. **`get()`** *removes* it and completes the handshake. **`peek()`** returns the same item **without removing** it, so repeated `peek()` calls return the same item until a `get()` or `item_done()` consumes it. ```mermaid flowchart LR Q["sequencer: req0 pending"] -->|"peek(): look"| D1["driver sees req0
(still pending)"] Q -->|"peek() again"| D2["same req0"] Q -->|"get(): take"| D3["req0 removed
finish_item unblocked"] D3 --> N["next peek/get sees req1"] ``` ### Explanation ```systemverilog // decide before committing: e.g. wait for credit only if the item needs it forever begin seq_item_port.peek(req); // look at the head item, sequence still blocked if (req.needs_credit) wait (vif.credit > 0); seq_item_port.get(req); // now consume it (same item) drive(req); end ``` | | `get(req)` | `peek(req)` | | --- | --- | --- | | Blocking | Yes | Yes | | Removes item | Yes | No | | Unblocks sequence's `finish_item` | Yes | No | | Repeated calls | Return successive items | Return the same item | - A common pattern is `peek` then `get`. Another is `peek`, drive, `item_done()`, because `peek` behaves like `get_next_item` in leaving the handshake open. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - A driver that only peeks and never gets or calls `item_done` stalls the sequence forever. - Do not modify the item after `peek` if the sequence might still be relying on its values. It has not been handed over yet. ### Follow-ups - *Non-blocking variants?* `try_next_item` exists. There is no `try_peek` on the seq_item_port; use `has_do_available()` to test for availability.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is the difference in item_done() method of driver-sequencer API when called with and without arguments?
answer:
The `item_done()` method is a non blocking method in driver class that is used to complete handshake with the sequencer after a `get_next_item()` or `try_next_item()` is successful.

If there is no need to send a response back, `item_done()` is called with no argument which will complete the handshake without placing anything in the sequencer response FIFO. If there is a need to send a response back, `item_done()` is passed with a pointer to a response `sequence_item` as an argument. This response pointer will be placed in the sequencer response FIFO which can be processed by the sequence as a response to the request it drove.
solution:
**Key idea:** `item_done()` (a non-blocking **function**) closes the `get_next_item`/`try_next_item` handshake and unblocks `finish_item`. **Without** an argument, nothing goes back to the sequence. **With** `item_done(rsp)`, the response is also pushed into the sequencer's response queue, routed to the originating sequence (`set_id_info`), for `get_response()`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph NA["item_done()"]
    a1["driver"] -->|"handshake only"| a2["finish_item returns"]
  end
  subgraph WA["item_done(rsp)"]
    b1["driver: rsp.set_id_info(req)"] -->|"handshake + put_response"| b2["seq response queue"]
    b2 --> b3["get_response(rsp)"]
  end
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// driver
seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
drive(req);
if (req.is_read) begin
  rsp = item::type_id::create("rsp");
  rsp.set_id_info(req);
  rsp.rdata = vif.cb.rdata;
  seq_item_port.item_done(rsp);   // response returned
end
else
  seq_item_port.item_done();      // no response

// sequence
start_item(req); void'(req.randomize()); finish_item(req);
if (req.is_read) get_response(rsp);
```
| | `item_done()` | `item_done(rsp)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unblocks `finish_item` | Yes | Yes |
| Response queued | No | Yes |
| Sequence must call `get_response` | No | Yes (or use a response handler) |
| Equivalent to | — | `item_done()` + `put_response(rsp)` |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If responses are returned but never collected, the sequence's response queue (depth 8) overflows and UVM reports an error.
- If the sequence calls `get_response` but the driver never sends one, the sequence hangs.
- The driver can also update `req` in place (for example `req.rdata = ...`) without a separate response. The sequence then reads the updated `req` after `finish_item`. Simple, but not suitable for pipelined drivers.

### Follow-ups
- *Can `item_done` be called twice?* No. A second call without a new `get_next_item` is an error.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: Which of the following driver class methods are blocking calls and which are nonblocking?
answer:
\1) get()

\2) get_next_item()

\3) item_done()

\4) put()

\5) try_next_item()

\6) peek()

get(), get_next_item(), peek() are blocking calls.

try_next_item(), item_done(), and put() are nonblocking calls
solution:
**Key idea:** **Blocking:** `get()`, `get_next_item()`, `peek()`, which wait until an item exists. **Non-blocking:** `item_done()` (a function), `try_next_item()` (does not wait for an item; only delta-cycle waits) and `put()` (never waits in practice, since the response queue is not bounded by back-pressure).

| Method | Declared as | Waits for an item / consumes time? | Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `get(req)` | task | Yes, until an item is available | **Blocking** |
| `get_next_item(req)` | task | Yes | **Blocking** |
| `peek(req)` | task | Yes | **Blocking** |
| `try_next_item(req)` | task | No: returns `null` if nothing ready (may wait delta cycles) | **Non-blocking** |
| `item_done(rsp = null)` | function | No | **Non-blocking** |
| `put(rsp)` | task | No in practice (calls `put_response` immediately) | **Non-blocking** |
| `put_response(rsp)` | function | No | Non-blocking |
| `has_do_available()` | function | No | Non-blocking |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph B["Blocking: wait for sequencer"]
    g["get"]
    gn["get_next_item"]
    pk["peek"]
  end
  subgraph NB["Return immediately"]
    tn["try_next_item"]
    id["item_done"]
    pt["put"]
  end
```

### Explanation
- The blocking ones wait for a sequence to supply an item, so they can only be called from tasks such as `run_phase`.
- `try_next_item` is formally a task (it yields delta cycles to let sequences arbitrate) but never waits for *simulation time*, which is why it counts as non-blocking.
- `put` is formally a task in `uvm_sqr_if_base`, but it forwards to the function `put_response`, so it returns in zero time.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Calling `item_done` without an outstanding `get_next_item`/`try_next_item` is an error.
- Calling `get_next_item` twice without `item_done` is also an error ("get_next_item called twice").

### Follow-ups
- *Which pairs belong together?* `get_next_item`/`try_next_item` with `item_done`. `get` with `put`. `peek` followed by `get` or `item_done`.

title: How can you stop all sequences running on a sequencer?
answer: The sequencer has a method **`stop_sequences()` **that can be used to stop all sequences. However, this method does not check if the driver is currently processing any `sequence_items`. Because of this, if the driver calls an `item_done()` or `put()`, there can be a Fatal Error as the sequence pointer might not be valid. So a user needs to take care of making sure that once `stop_sequence()` is called, the sequencer thread is disabled (if started in a fork).
solution:
**Key idea:** Call `sequencer.stop_sequences()`. It kills every sequence (and child sequence) running on that sequencer and clears the arbitration queue and locks. The driver may still hold an item in flight, so it must be resynchronized too: finish or abandon the current item without calling `item_done` on a dead sequence. Typically you kill and restart the driver thread around the reset.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as test / reset handler
  participant Q as sequencer
  participant S as running sequences
  participant D as driver
  T->>Q: stop_sequences()
  Q->>S: kill() all, clear queues and locks
  T->>D: reset_driver(): disable drive thread
  D->>D: drop in-flight req, drive idle values
  T->>D: restart run thread after reset
  T->>Q: start new sequences
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// driver with a restartable main thread
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  forever begin
    @(negedge vif.rst_n);            // wait for reset assertion
    fork
      begin : main
        @(posedge vif.rst_n);        // wait for reset release
        forever begin
          seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
          drive(req);
          seq_item_port.item_done();
        end
      end
      @(negedge vif.rst_n);          // next reset kills main
    join_any
    disable fork;
    drive_idle();
  end
endtask

// test / env on reset
task handle_reset();
  env.agt.sqr.stop_sequences();      // kill all sequences on this sequencer
endtask
```
| Method | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `sqr.stop_sequences()` | Kills all sequences and children, clears requests, locks and grabs |
| `seq.kill()` | Kills one sequence (and children) |
| `phase.jump(...)` | Jumps phases and kills phase-started sequences |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the driver later calls `item_done()` or `put()` for an item whose sequence was killed, UVM may report errors. Kill the driver thread too, or skip `item_done` on reset.
- Objections raised by killed sequences may never drop. Raise objections in the test, not in sequences, when using kills.

### Follow-ups
- *Graceful alternative?* Have sequences poll a "stop" flag in the config object and exit their loops cleanly.

title: Which method in the sequence gets called when user calls sequence.print() method?
answer: **convert2string() : **It is recommended to implement this function which returns a string representation of the object (values of its data members). **This is useful to get debug information printed to simulator transcript or log file**.
solution:
**Key idea:** `print()` calls `sprint()`, which calls the **`do_print(uvm_printer printer)`** hook (plus any `` `uvm_field_* `` automation), and formats the output with the selected printer (table, tree or line). It does **not** call `convert2string()`. That method is a separate, user-implemented one-line summary used in your own `` `uvm_info `` messages.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["seq.print()"] --> SP["sprint(printer)"]
  SP --> FA["field macro automation (UVM_PRINT)"]
  SP --> DP["do_print(printer) : user hook"]
  DP --> OUT["uvm_table_printer output"]
  C["uvm_info(..., seq.convert2string(), ...)"] --> L["one-line string, user-defined"]
```

### Explanation
| Method | Called by | You implement | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `print(printer = null)` | User | No (non-virtual) | Prints `sprint()` result |
| `sprint(printer = null)` | `print()` | No | Formatted string |
| `do_print(uvm_printer printer)` | `sprint()` | Yes (or field macros) | Fields added to the printer |
| `convert2string()` | Only your code | Yes | Free-form string |

```systemverilog
class pkt extends uvm_sequence_item;
  rand bit [7:0] len; rand bit [31:0] addr;
  `uvm_object_utils(pkt)
  function new(string name = "pkt"); super.new(name); endfunction

  function void do_print(uvm_printer printer);
    super.do_print(printer);
    printer.print_field_int("addr", addr, 32, UVM_HEX);
    printer.print_field_int("len",  len,  8,  UVM_DEC);
  endfunction

  function string convert2string();
    return $sformatf("addr=%h len=%0d", addr, len);
  endfunction
endclass

p.print();                                          // table via do_print
p.print(uvm_default_line_printer);                  // single line, still do_print
`uvm_info("PKT", p.convert2string(), UVM_MEDIUM)    // convert2string
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Defining only `convert2string` and then calling `print()` shows just the header (name/type/size) with no fields.
- `print()` on a large object with the table printer is slow. Use `convert2string` in high-frequency messages.

### Follow-ups
- *Which other hooks follow the same pattern?* `copy`→`do_copy`, `compare`→`do_compare`, `pack`→`do_pack`, `record`→`do_record`.

title: How do we register an uvm_component class and uvm_sequence class with factory?
answer:
The uvm_sequence class is registered with the factory using uvm_object_utils() macro and passing the class name as an argument. An example below:

```verilog
class test_seq_c extends uvm_sequence;
`uvm_object_utils(test_seq_c)
```

The uvm_component class is registered with the factory using uvm_component_utils() macro and passing the class name as argument. An Example below:

```verilog
class test_driver_c extends uvm_component;
`uvm_component_utils(test_driver_c)
```
solution:
**Key idea:** Use **`` `uvm_component_utils(T) ``** for anything derived from `uvm_component` (test, env, agent, driver, ...), and **`` `uvm_object_utils(T) ``** for objects, which includes **sequences** and sequence items. Parameterized classes use the `_param_` variants. The constructor signature must match the kind.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["class test_c extends uvm_test"] -->|"uvm_component_utils(test_c)"| CR["uvm_component_registry #(test_c, 'test_c')"]
  S["class seq_c extends uvm_sequence #(pkt)"] -->|"uvm_object_utils(seq_c)"| OR["uvm_object_registry #(seq_c, 'seq_c')"]
  CR --> F["uvm_factory"]
  OR --> F
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class test_seq_c extends uvm_sequence #(pkt);
  `uvm_object_utils(test_seq_c)                 // object: no parent
  function new(string name = "test_seq_c");
    super.new(name);
  endfunction
endclass

class test_driver_c extends uvm_driver #(pkt);
  `uvm_component_utils(test_driver_c)           // component: needs parent
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent);
  endfunction
endclass

class fifo_seq #(int W = 8) extends uvm_sequence #(pkt);
  `uvm_object_param_utils(fifo_seq #(W))        // parameterized: no string name registered
  function new(string name = "fifo_seq"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass
```
| Class kind | Macro | Constructor | Created with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Component | `` `uvm_component_utils `` | `new(string name, uvm_component parent)` | `T::type_id::create("n", this)` |
| Object / sequence / item | `` `uvm_object_utils `` | `new(string name = "T")` | `T::type_id::create("n")` |
| Parameterized | `` `uvm_*_param_utils `` | same | by type only (no name-based lookup) |
| With field automation | `` `uvm_object_utils_begin ... _end `` | same | same |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `` `uvm_component_utils `` on a sequence fails to compile: the registry's `create` calls `new(name, parent)`.
- Object constructors need a **default** name argument, or factory creation by name fails.
- Parameterized classes are not registered by name, so `+UVM_TESTNAME` cannot select a parameterized test.

### Follow-ups
- *What does the macro expand to?* A `typedef uvm_*_registry #(T, "T") type_id;`, a static `get_type()`, `get_object_type()`, `get_type_name()` and `create()` support.

title: Why should we register a class with factory?
answer:
A factory is a special look-up table used in UVM for creating objects of component or transaction types. The benefit of object creation using the factory is that a testbench build process can decide at run-time which type of object has to be created. Based on this, a class type could be substituted with another derived class type without any real code change. To ensure this feature and capability, all classes are recommended to be registered with the factory. If you do not register a class with the factory, then you will not be able to use the factory `method::type_id::create()` to construct an object.

> [Concept of UVM Factory](https://theartofverification.com/concept-of-uvm-factory/)
solution:
**Key idea:** Registration puts the class in the factory's lookup table. Code that creates it with `type_id::create()` can then be redirected **at runtime** to a derived class, by type or instance override, by name from the command line, or by `+UVM_TESTNAME`. None of that needs edits to the env, agent or sequences. Unregistered classes can only be built with `new()`, which is fixed at compile time.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R["registered: uvm_component_utils(base_drv)"] --> F["factory table"]
  O["test: base_drv::type_id::set_type_override(err_drv::get_type())"] --> F
  A["agent: base_drv::type_id::create('drv', this)"] --> F
  F --> E["err_drv built, no agent edit"]
  N["agent: drv = new('drv', this)"] --> B["base_drv always: override impossible"]
```

### Explanation
| Benefit of registration | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Type/instance override | Error-injection driver in one test only |
| Test selection by name | `+UVM_TESTNAME=my_test` → `create_component_by_name` |
| Command-line overrides | `+uvm_set_type_override=pkt,big_pkt` |
| Create by string name | `factory.create_object_by_name("my_seq")` for table-driven tests |
| Debug | `factory.print()` lists registered types and overrides |
| Default sequences | `default_sequence` config takes a type wrapper (`my_seq::type_id::get()`) |

```systemverilog
// reusable env never changes
pkt p = pkt::type_id::create("p");      // registered + created via factory

// a test changes all packets to corrupted packets
class corrupt_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(corrupt_test)
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    pkt::type_id::set_type_override(corrupt_pkt::get_type());
    super.build_phase(phase);
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Registration alone is not enough. The code must also *create* through the factory, so one `new()` in the env defeats the override.
- The replacement type must extend the original type.

### Follow-ups
- *What is the cost?* A small runtime lookup per create, which is negligible except in extremely high-frequency object creation.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is meant by factory override?
answer: The UVM factory allows a class to be substituted with another derived class at the point of construction. This can be useful for changing the behavior of a testbench by substituting one class for another **without having the need to edit** or **re-compile the testbench code**.
solution:
**Key idea:** A factory override tells the UVM factory: *whenever someone asks for type A (everywhere, or at a specific path), build type B instead*, where B extends A. It changes testbench behavior from a test, or from the command line, **without editing or recompiling** the environment code that creates A.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Before["no override"]
    a1["agent: drv::type_id::create"] --> a2["drv"]
  end
  subgraph After["test: set_type_override(drv to err_drv)"]
    b1["agent: drv::type_id::create (unchanged)"] --> b2["err_drv (extends drv)"]
  end
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class err_drv extends my_drv;                         // must extend the original
  `uvm_component_utils(err_drv)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  virtual task drive(pkt p);
    if ($urandom_range(0, 9) == 0) p.crc = ~p.crc;  // inject CRC error 10% of the time
    super.drive(p);
  endtask
endclass

class crc_err_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(crc_err_test)
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    my_drv::type_id::set_type_override(err_drv::get_type());     // type override
    // or: set_type_override_by_type(my_drv::get_type(), err_drv::get_type());
    super.build_phase(phase);
  endfunction
endclass
```
| Override API | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| `orig::type_id::set_type_override(new::get_type())` | All instances |
| `orig::type_id::set_inst_override(new::get_type(), "env.agt1.*", this)` | Matching paths |
| `set_type_override_by_name("orig", "new")` | By string names |
| `+uvm_set_type_override=orig,new` | Command line |
| `+uvm_set_inst_override=orig,new,path` | Command line |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Overrides must be set **before** the target objects are created, usually in the test's `build_phase` before `super.build_phase` builds the env.
- Overriding with an unrelated type fails at create time. Overrides can chain (A→B, B→C gives C).

### Follow-ups
- *How do you confirm it worked?* Call `factory.print()` in `end_of_elaboration`, or `uvm_top.print_topology()` to see the actual type names.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is the difference between instance override and type override?
answer: A **type override **means that every time a component class type is created in a testbench hierarchy, a substitute type is created in its place. This applies to all instances of that component type. On the other hand, an **instance override **means, overriding only a specific instance of a component class. A specific instance of a component is referenced by the position of that component in the UVM component hierarchy. Since only UVM component classes can have a hierarchy in UVM test benches, only component classes can be overridden on an instance granularity while sequences (or UVM objects) can be the only type overridden.
solution:
**Key idea:** A **type override** replaces a class **everywhere** it is created through the factory. An **instance override** replaces it only for objects created at **matching hierarchical paths** (wildcards allowed). When both match, the instance override wins.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph ENV["env"]
    A0["agt0.drv"]
    A1["agt1.drv"]
    A2["agt2.drv"]
  end
  T["type override: drv to fast_drv"] -.-> A0
  T -.-> A1
  T -.-> A2
  I["instance override 'env.agt1.drv': drv to slow_drv"] ==> A1
  R["result: agt0 fast_drv, agt1 slow_drv (inst wins), agt2 fast_drv"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  // every my_drv becomes fast_drv
  my_drv::type_id::set_type_override(fast_drv::get_type());
  // only agent 1's driver becomes slow_drv (path relative to 'this' = the test)
  my_drv::type_id::set_inst_override(slow_drv::get_type(), "env.agt1.drv", this);
  super.build_phase(phase);
endfunction
```
| | Type override | Instance override |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Affects | All creations of the type | Creations whose full path matches |
| Path argument | None | Full or relative path, wildcards (`"env.agt*.drv"`) |
| Precedence | Lower | Higher (checked first) |
| Replace existing | `replace = 1` by default | Earlier-set instance overrides take precedence on matching paths |
| Factory API | `set_type_override_by_type(orig, new, replace)` | `set_inst_override_by_type(orig, new, full_inst_path)` |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- For instance overrides with `type_id::set_inst_override(..., path, this)`, the path is relative to `this`. With the raw factory API (`factory.set_inst_override_by_type`) you must pass the **full** path, e.g. `"uvm_test_top.env.agt1.drv"`.
- An instance override of an object (a sequence item) only matches if the object is created with a context path. Sequences do this automatically through the sequencer path (see next question).

### Follow-ups
- *Debug?* `factory.print(1)` shows all overrides. `factory.debug_create_by_type(my_drv::get_type(), "uvm_test_top.env.agt1", "drv")` shows the decision.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: Can instance override and type override be used for both uvm_component class and transaction types?
answer: No, only UVM_component classes are part of UVM testbench hierarchy and can be overridden on an instance granularity. The sequence items or sequences are not a part of UVM testbench hierarchy and hence can only be overridden using **type override** which will override all objects of that type.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Type overrides** work for both components and objects. **Instance overrides** are natural for components because they have a hierarchical path, but they also work for **objects** (sequences, sequence items) when the object is created with a **context path**. Sequences do this automatically: items created inside `body()` get the sequencer's full path as context. So the common answer "objects can only take type overrides" is too strong. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph C["Component"] c1["create('drv', this)
path = uvm_test_top.env.agt.drv"] end subgraph O["Object with context"] o1["create('req', , get_full_name())
or uvm_create / start_item path
= uvm_test_top.env.agt0.sqr.seq.req"] end subgraph N["Object without context"] n1["create('req')
path = 'req' only"] end IO["inst override '*.agt0.*'"] --> c1 IO --> o1 IO -.->|"cannot match a hierarchical path"| n1 ``` ### Explanation | | Type override | Instance override | | --- | --- | --- | | `uvm_component` | ✓ | ✓ (by hierarchical path) | | Sequence item / sequence | ✓ | ✓ only if created with a context string | ```systemverilog // only packets generated on agent 0's sequencer become error packets pkt::type_id::set_inst_override(err_pkt::get_type(), "env.agt0.sqr.*", this); // inside a sequence running on env.agt0.sqr: pass a context explicitly req = pkt::type_id::create("req", , get_full_name()); // get_full_name() = sqr path + seq name // `uvm_create(req) / `uvm_do(req) use the sequencer path automatically ``` - The factory builds the lookup path as `{contxt, ".", name}` for objects. With an empty context, the path is just the name, so an instance override written with a hierarchical path will not match. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Items created in the test or env with plain `create("req")` ignore path-based overrides. Pass `get_full_name()` as the context if you want them to apply. - Sequences started from the test are created there, so their own path is the test's context, not the sequencer's, unless you supply it. ### Follow-ups - *Simplest way to override a sequence for one agent only?* Instance override with a path matching that sequencer's sub-sequences, or just start a different sequence there.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is the concept of objections and where are they useful?
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_objection` is a shared counter. Components and sequences `raise_objection()` when they start work that must finish and `drop_objection()` when done. When the count goes from non-zero to **zero** (the "all dropped" condition), plus any drain time, the current task phase ends. Objections are how UVM decides when `run_phase` (or `main_phase`, ...) is over.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  P["run_phase starts, count = 0"] --> R1["test raises: count 1"]
  R1 --> R2["vseq raises: count 2"]
  R2 --> D1["vseq drops: count 1"]
  D1 --> D2["test drops: count 0, all_dropped"]
  D2 --> DT["drain time elapses"]
  DT --> PR["phase_ready_to_end callbacks (may re-raise)"]
  PR --> E["phase ends, go to extract / check / report"]
```

### Explanation
| Where useful | How |
| --- | --- |
| End of test | Test raises around the virtual sequence |
| Run-time sub-phases | Each of `reset`/`configure`/`main`/`shutdown` ends on its own objections |
| Delaying the end | A scoreboard re-raises in `phase_ready_to_end` until its queues drain |
| Drain time | `phase.phase_done.set_drain_time(this, 500ns)` for in-flight data |
| Debug | `+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE` shows every raise and drop |

```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this, "test running");
  vseq.start(env.vsqr);
  phase.drop_objection(this, "test done");
endtask
```
- Objections propagate up the hierarchy. Each component's count includes its children's, and the phase checks the total at `uvm_top`.
- UVM 1.2 sequences can use `set_automatic_phase_objection(1)`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- No raise means the phase ends at time 0 (the "test finished instantly" bug).
- A raise that is never dropped hangs until the timeout.
- Raising and dropping per item in drivers or monitors is slow and unnecessary.

### Follow-ups
- *Can objections be used outside phasing?* Yes. Any `uvm_objection` instance can coordinate custom events (for example the heartbeat's `uvm_callbacks_objection`).

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: How can we implement a simulation timeout mechanism in UVM methodology?
answer:
A simulation time out mechanism helps to stop the simulation if the test doesn’t progress because of some bug beyond a maximum time.

In UVM, **`set_global_timeout(timeout)` **– is a convenience function that sets **`uvm_top.phase_timeout` **variable with the timeout value. If the `run_phase()` doesn’t end before this timeout value, then the simulation is stopped and an error is reported. This function is called in the top-level module which also starts the test as follows

```verilog
module test;
  initial begin
    set_global_timeout(1000ns);
  end
  initial begin
    run_test();
  end
endmodule

```
solution:
**Key idea:** Set a global phase timeout so a hung test (an objection never dropped, a deadlock) ends with a clear fatal error instead of running forever. In UVM 1.2 use **`uvm_top.set_timeout(t, overridable)`** or the **`+UVM_TIMEOUT=<t>,<YES|NO>`** plusarg. `set_global_timeout()` is deprecated. The default is 9200 s. A test-level watchdog is a useful addition.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["run_test starts"] --> W["phase watchdog: timeout t"]
  S --> P["run-time phases"]
  P -->|"objections drop before t"| OK["extract / check / report"]
  W -->|"t reached first"| F["UVM_FATAL PH_TIMEOUT: 'Explicit timeout of t hit'"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  initial begin
    uvm_top.set_timeout(2ms, 1);   // 1 = may be overridden by +UVM_TIMEOUT
    run_test();
  end
endmodule
```
```bash
# command-line override (time in default time units; NO = later set_timeout calls ignored)
xrun ... +UVM_TESTNAME=stress_test +UVM_TIMEOUT=5000000,NO
```
**Test-specific watchdog (graceful: still runs check/report)**
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this);
  fork
    vseq.start(env.vsqr);
    begin
      #(cfg.max_test_time);
      `uvm_error("WDOG", $sformatf("test exceeded %0t", cfg.max_test_time))
    end
  join_any
  disable fork;
  phase.drop_objection(this);
endtask
```
| Mechanism | API | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global phase timeout | `uvm_top.set_timeout(t)` / `+UVM_TIMEOUT` | Fatal, no check/report phases |
| Deprecated | `set_global_timeout(t)` | Same, avoid in 1.2 |
| Watchdog in test | `fork ... join_any` with a delay | Error, then normal end of test |
| Per-phase drain | `set_drain_time` | Not a timeout, only delays the end |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The UVM timeout runs from the start of the run phases and covers all run-time phases together. Set it with margin for the longest legitimate test.
- With `overridable = 0`, `+UVM_TIMEOUT` cannot change it, which can surprise regression owners.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you find what is hanging?* Use `+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE`, or call `phase.get_objection().display_objections()` in a timeout handler, to list who still holds objections.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is the concept of phasing in UVM methodology and explain the different phases of a UVM Component
answer:
Please go through the below post to understand the Phasing concept in detail.

> [UVM Phasing](https://theartofverification.com/uvm-phasing/)
solution:
**Key idea:** Phasing gives every `uvm_component` the same ordered set of callback methods: **build** (create and configure), **connect** (wire TLM), **run** (time-consuming stimulus and checking), then **cleanup** (extract, check, report, final). The phase engine runs each phase across the whole hierarchy before moving to the next, so all components stay in step without races.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  subgraph BUILD["Build phases: functions, 0 time"]
    b1["build_phase (top-down)"] --> b2["connect_phase (bottom-up)"] --> b3["end_of_elaboration_phase"] --> b4["start_of_simulation_phase"]
  end
  subgraph RUN["Run-time phases: tasks"]
    r0["run_phase"]
    r1["pre_reset, reset, post_reset"] --> r2["pre_configure, configure, post_configure"] --> r3["pre_main, main, post_main"] --> r4["pre_shutdown, shutdown, post_shutdown"]
  end
  subgraph CLEAN["Cleanup phases: functions, 0 time"]
    c1["extract_phase"] --> c2["check_phase"] --> c3["report_phase"] --> c4["final_phase"]
  end
  b4 --> r0
  b4 --> r1
  r0 --> c1
  r4 --> c1
```

### Explanation
| Phase | Kind | What a component does here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `build_phase` | function, top-down | `config_db::get`, create children, set overrides |
| `connect_phase` | function, bottom-up | Connect ports/exports, assign handles |
| `end_of_elaboration_phase` | function | Print topology, sanity-check config |
| `start_of_simulation_phase` | function | Banners, final runtime settings |
| `run_phase` | task, parallel | Drivers/monitors loop, test starts sequences with objections |
| `reset` … `shutdown` (12) | task, parallel, in sequence | Optional finer control of reset/config/main/shutdown |
| `extract_phase` | function, bottom-up | Gather results, coverage numbers |
| `check_phase` | function, bottom-up | End-of-test checks (empty queues) |
| `report_phase` | function, bottom-up | Print summaries, PASS/FAIL |
| `final_phase` | function, top-down | Close files |

```systemverilog
class my_env extends uvm_env;
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);   agt = my_agent::type_id::create("agt", this); scb = my_scb::type_id::create("scb", this); endfunction
  function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase); agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.act_imp); endfunction
  function void report_phase(uvm_phase phase); `uvm_info("ENV", "done", UVM_LOW) endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Task phases end only through objections. Function phases end when the function returns in every component.
- `run_phase` runs in parallel with the 12 sub-phases. Use one style consistently.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you add a custom phase?* Extend `uvm_task_phase` or `uvm_topdown_phase`/`uvm_bottomup_phase` and insert it into the schedule with `uvm_domain::get_uvm_schedule().add(...)`. This is rarely needed.

title: Why is build_phase() executed top down in uvm_component hierarchy?
answer:
In UVM, all the testbench components like a test, Env, Agent, Driver, Sequencer are based on the `uvm_component` class and there is always a hierarchy for the testbench components. The `build_phase()` method is part of the `uvm_component` class and is used to construct all the child components from the parent component. So, to build the testbench hierarchy you always need to have a parent object first, which can then construct its children, and that can further construct its children using `build_phase`. Hence, `build_phase()` is always executed top-down.

For Example: The top level uvm_test class calls `build_phase` which should construct all the uvm_env components part of this test, and the `build_phase()` of each uvm_env class should construct all the uvm_agent components that are part of that uvm_env, and this goes on. For all other phases it really doesn’t matter in which order it is called. The `run_phase()` for all components runs in parallel.

additional reasons config_db needs to pass down from top and factory override must come first before the component create
solution:
**Key idea:** `build_phase` constructs the hierarchy, and a component can only be built after its parent has created it. Execution must therefore start at the root (`uvm_test_top`) and move **down**. Top-down order also lets parents push configuration and factory overrides that children read while building themselves.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as uvm_test_top
  participant E as env
  participant A as agent
  participant D as driver
  T->>T: build_phase: overrides, config_db set
  T->>E: create("env", this)
  E->>E: build_phase: get env_cfg
  E->>A: create("agt", this)
  A->>A: build_phase: get is_active
  A->>D: create("drv", this) if ACTIVE
  D->>D: build_phase: get vif
```

### Explanation
- **Existence:** before `test.build_phase` runs, `env` is just a null handle. The phase engine can only call `env.build_phase` once the test has created the env, so the traversal follows creation from the root downwards.
- **Configuration:** parents set `config_db` entries targeted at their subtree before creating children, so children always see the right config when they `get` it.
- **Overrides:** factory overrides from the test are in place before any lower-level `create()` call.
- **Structural decisions:** a parent can decide which children exist (active vs passive, number of agents from a config value). That decision has to come before the children are built.

```systemverilog
function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);          // my_env
  super.build_phase(phase);
  if (!uvm_config_db#(env_cfg)::get(this, "", "cfg", cfg)) `uvm_fatal("CFG", "no cfg")
  agts = new[cfg.num_agents];                         // decided top-down
  foreach (agts[i]) begin
    uvm_config_db#(agent_cfg)::set(this, $sformatf("agt%0d", i), "cfg", cfg.agt_cfg[i]);
    agts[i] = my_agent::type_id::create($sformatf("agt%0d", i), this);
  end
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Getting a config in a child that the parent sets **after** creating the child still works, because the child's build runs later. It is clearer to set before creating, though.
- Other function phases run bottom-up, because by then everything exists and results aggregate upward.

### Follow-ups
- *Is build_phase strictly depth-first?* UVM 1.2 traverses in levels: each component's build runs, then its newly created children's. Do not rely on sibling order.

title: What is the use of phase_ready_to_end() method in a uvm_component class?
answer:
**`phase_ready_to_end(uvm_phase phase)` **is a callback method available in a component class that gets called when all objections are dropped for that corresponding phase and the phase is going to end.

A component class can use this callback method to define any functionality that it needs to perform when the phase is about to end.

One example is if a component want to delay ending of phase until some condition even after all objections are dropped, it can be done using this callback method.

Another example is if an irritator or reactive sequence is running until a main sequence is complete, `phase_ready_to_end()` callback method in `main_phase()` can be used to stop those irritator sequences.
solution:
**Key idea:** `phase_ready_to_end(uvm_phase phase)` is a component callback that UVM calls when a task phase's objections all drop, **before** the phase actually ends. A component that still has work (a scoreboard waiting for in-flight transactions, a background sequence to stop) can **re-raise** an objection there to extend the phase, then drop it when finished. The callback can run again, up to 20 iterations by default.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as test
  participant P as run_phase
  participant S as scoreboard
  T->>P: drop_objection (count 0)
  P->>S: phase_ready_to_end(phase)
  S->>P: raise_objection (exp queue not empty)
  S->>S: wait until exp queue empty
  S->>P: drop_objection
  P->>S: phase_ready_to_end again
  S-->>P: nothing pending
  P->>P: phase ends, go to extract
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class my_scb extends uvm_scoreboard;
  pkt exp_q[$];
  virtual function void phase_ready_to_end(uvm_phase phase);
    if (phase.get_name() != "run") return;
    if (exp_q.size() != 0) begin
      phase.raise_objection(this, "waiting for outstanding packets");
      fork
        begin
          wait (exp_q.size() == 0);
          phase.drop_objection(this, "drained");
        end
      join_none
    end
  endfunction
endclass

// stopping a background irritator at the end of main_phase
virtual function void phase_ready_to_end(uvm_phase phase);
  if (phase.get_imp() == uvm_main_phase::get())
    irritator_seq.kill();
endfunction
```
| End-of-phase tool | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Drain time | Fixed extra delay after all-dropped |
| `phase_ready_to_end` | Conditional, data-dependent extension or cleanup |
| `phase_ended` | Notification after the phase is over (too late to extend) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- It is a **function**. Waiting must happen in a forked process, as shown.
- If no objection is re-raised, the phase ends immediately after the callback.
- A wait that never completes hangs the test, so pair it with a timeout.
- The re-entry limit is `max_ready_to_end_iterations` (default 20).

### Follow-ups
- *Drain time or ready_to_end?* Drain time is simpler for a known latency. `phase_ready_to_end` is exact for variable latency.

title: What is uvm_config_db and what is it used for?
answer:
The UVM configuration mechanism supports sharing of configurations and parameters across different testbench components. This is enabled using a configuration database called `uvm_config_db`. Any testbench component can populate the configuration database with variables, parameters, object handles, etc. Other testbench components can get access to these variables, parameters, and object handles from the configuration database without really knowing where it exists in the hierarchy. For Example, a top-level testbench module can store a virtual interface pointer to the `uvm_config_db`. Then any uvm_driver or a `uvm_monitor` component can query the `uvm_config_db` to get a handle to this virtual interface and use it for actually accessing the signals through the interface.

> [uvm_config_db and uvm_resource_db](https://theartofverification.com/uvm_config_db-and-uvm_resource_db/)
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_config_db` is UVM's typed, hierarchy-scoped configuration database. Higher-level code (the top module, test, env) **`set`s** values such as virtual interfaces, config objects, knobs and default sequences for a path. Lower components **`get`** them in `build_phase` without hard-coded handles between them.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  TOP["tb_top: set(null, 'uvm_test_top.*', 'vif', vif)"] --> DB[("uvm_config_db")]
  TEST["test: set(this, 'env', 'cfg', env_cfg)"] --> DB
  ENV["env: set(this, 'agt*', 'is_active', UVM_PASSIVE)"] --> DB
  DB --> DRV["driver.get: vif"]
  DB --> E2["env.get: cfg"]
  DB --> AG["agent.get: is_active"]
```

### Explanation
| Common use | Type |
| --- | --- |
| Virtual interfaces from the module world to classes | `virtual my_if` |
| Configuration objects (env/agent cfg) | `my_cfg` class handle |
| Scalar knobs | `int`, `bit`, enums such as `uvm_active_passive_enum` |
| Default sequences per phase | `uvm_object_wrapper` |
| RAL model handle | `my_reg_block` |

```systemverilog
// set
uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.agt*", "vif", bus_vif);
uvm_config_db#(env_cfg)::set(this, "env", "cfg", cfg);
// get
if (!uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if)::get(this, "", "vif", vif))
  `uvm_fatal("NOVIF", {"vif not set for ", get_full_name()})
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- It is typed: the `set` and `get` type parameters must match exactly.
- Prefer a few config **objects** over many scalar entries. Lookups are string-based and relatively slow, and objects are easier to manage.
- Check the return value of `get`. A silent miss leaves defaults or a null vif.

### Follow-ups
- *How are conflicts resolved?* During build, the higher component's set wins. Otherwise the last set wins.
- *Debug?* `+UVM_CONFIG_DB_TRACE`, and `uvm_top.check_config_usage()` for sets nobody read.

title: How do we use the get() and set() methods of uvm_config_db?
answer:
The get() and set() are the primary methods used to populate or retrieve information from the uvm_config_db. Any verification component can use the **set() **method to populate the config_db with some configuration information and can also control which other components will have visibility to the same information. It could be set to have global visibility or visible only to one or more specific testbench components. The get() function checks for a shared configuration from the database matching the parameters.

The syntax for the get() and set() methods are as follows:

```
uvm_config_db#(<type>)::set(uvm_component context, string inst_name, string field_name,<type> value)
uvm_config_db#(<type>)::get(uvm_component context, string inst_name, string field_name, ref value)
```

The *context *specifies the current class or component from which get/set is called.

The *inst_name *is the name of the instance of a component from which get/set is called.

The *field_name *is the name of the object or parameter or variable which is set/get in config_db.

The <type> identifies the type of the configuration information set/get in config_db. For object handles, this will have the class name while for other variables; it will be the type of that variable.
solution:
**Key idea:** `set(cntxt, inst_name, field_name, value)` stores a value visible to the components whose full path matches `cntxt.get_full_name() + "." + inst_name` (or `inst_name` alone if `cntxt` is null). `get(cntxt, inst_name, field_name, value)` looks up `cntxt`'s own path (with `inst_name` usually `""`), returns 1 and fills `value` on a match. ```mermaid flowchart LR S1["set(this, 'env.agt0', 'cfg', c0)
this = uvm_test_top"] --> K1["scope: uvm_test_top.env.agt0"] S2["set(this, 'env.*', 'mode', 2)"] --> K2["scope: uvm_test_top.env.*"] K1 --> G1["agt0.get(this, '', 'cfg', c) matches"] K2 --> G1 K2 --> G2["agt1.get(this, '', 'mode', m) matches"] K1 -.->|"no match"| G3["agt1.get(this, '', 'cfg', c) returns 0"] ``` ### Explanation ```systemverilog static function void set(uvm_component cntxt, string inst_name, string field_name, T value); static function bit get(uvm_component cntxt, string inst_name, string field_name, inout T value); ``` | Argument | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `cntxt` | Starting component, `null` = `uvm_root` (use in modules) | | `inst_name` | Path below `cntxt`, glob wildcards (`*`, `?`) allowed in set | | `field_name` | Key, must match exactly | | `value` | Typed by `#(T)` | ```systemverilog // test.build_phase: visibility control uvm_config_db#(int)::set(this, "*", "verbosity_knob", 1); // everyone under the test uvm_config_db#(int)::set(this, "env.agt0*", "num_pkts", 50); // agt0 and its children uvm_config_db#(int)::set(this, "env.agt1", "num_pkts", 10); // agt1 only (not its children) // in a sequence (objects have no hierarchy: use the sequencer path) if (!uvm_config_db#(int)::get(null, get_full_name(), "num_pkts", n)) n = 5; // or: uvm_config_db#(int)::get(m_sequencer, "", "num_pkts", n); ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - `"env.agt1"` does not match `env.agt1.drv`. Add `*` for subtrees. - `set` with `cntxt = this` in a component and `inst_name = ""` targets the component itself. - For values that change at runtime, `get` again or use `wait_modified()`. A `get` copies only the value at that moment (handles stay shared). ### Follow-ups - *Precedence?* In build_phase the higher component's set wins over a lower one. Same level or post-build: the last set wins.

title: Is it possible for a component lower in testbench hierarchy to pass a handle to a component in higher level of hierarchy using get/set config methods?
answer: This is not a recommended way of passing configuration objects in UVM. Normally the higher level component sets up configuration data base with handles and the lower level components do get them using get/set methods.
solution:
**Key idea:** It is *possible*: config_db is a global pool, so a child can `set` with a scope that matches its parent (for example `set(null, "uvm_test_top.env", "mon_h", this)` or `set(this, "..", ...)` with wildcards). It is **not recommended**, though. Configuration should flow top-down, and upward communication should use TLM/analysis ports, or a handle the parent reads directly.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  ENV["env"] -->|"recommended: config_db set down"| AGT["agent"]
  AGT -->|"recommended: analysis port up"| ENV
  AGT -.->|"possible but discouraged: config_db set to parent path"| ENV
  ENV2["env can also read child handle directly: agt.mon"]
```

### Explanation
| Approach | Works? | Recommended? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Child `set(null, "uvm_test_top.env", "h", this)`, parent `get` | Yes, if the get happens after the set | No | Breaks top-down build ordering. The parent builds first, so its build-phase `get` misses |
| Parent reads `agt.mon` directly in `connect_phase` | Yes | Yes | Parents know their children |
| Child publishes data via an analysis port | Yes | Yes | Decoupled, standard |
| Shared config object set top-down, child writes fields into it | Yes | Acceptable | One object, ownership stays at the top |

```systemverilog
// discouraged
// in agent.build_phase:
uvm_config_db#(my_agent)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env", "agt_h", this);
// env must get it AFTER build (e.g. connect_phase), since env.build ran first:
void'(uvm_config_db#(my_agent)::get(this, "", "agt_h", agt_h));

// preferred: env simply uses its own child handle
function void connect_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  agt.mon.ap.connect(scb.act_imp);
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Build-phase precedence favors higher components, so a child's set may be silently overridden by an ancestor's set of the same field.
- Upward sets create hidden dependencies that break when the child is reused under a different parent path.

### Follow-ups
- *How do two sibling components share something?* The common parent creates it and sets it to both (or assigns handles in connect_phase).

title: What is the recommended way of assigning virtual interfaces to different components in a UVM verification methodology?
solution:
**Key idea:** The top module that instantiates the interface **sets** the virtual interface into `uvm_config_db` before `run_test()`. Each component that needs pins (driver, monitor), or better its agent config object, **gets** it in `build_phase` and fails fatally if it is missing. Components never use hierarchical references to the module.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph MOD["tb_top (static module)"]
    IF["bus_if bus0(clk)"]
    DUT["dut u_dut(bus0)"]
  end
  IF -->|"config_db set(null, 'uvm_test_top.env.agt0*', 'vif', bus0)"| DB[("uvm_config_db")]
  DB -->|"get(this, '', 'vif', vif)"| DRV["agt0.drv"]
  DB -->|"get"| MON["agt0.mon"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
interface bus_if (input logic clk);
  logic [31:0] addr, data; logic valid, ready;
  clocking drv_cb @(posedge clk); output addr, data, valid; input ready; endclocking
  clocking mon_cb @(posedge clk); input  addr, data, valid, ready;      endclocking
endinterface

module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  logic clk = 0; always #5 clk = ~clk;
  bus_if bus0(clk);
  dut u_dut(.clk(clk), .bus(bus0));
  initial begin
    uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.agt0*", "vif", bus0);
    run_test();
  end
endmodule

class my_driver extends uvm_driver #(pkt);
  virtual bus_if vif;
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    super.build_phase(phase);
    if (!uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if)::get(this, "", "vif", vif))
      `uvm_fatal("NOVIF", {"virtual interface must be set for ", get_full_name()})
  endfunction
endclass
```
**Preferred for reusable VIP:** the test gets the vif once and stores it in the agent config object (`agt_cfg.vif = vif`), then sets the config object. Driver and monitor read `cfg.vif`, so there is one config_db lookup per agent and no scattered string paths.

| Approach | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Set directly to driver/monitor paths | Simple, many lookups |
| Set once, test packs into agent cfg | Recommended, scalable for many interface instances |
| Hierarchical reference `tb_top.bus0` in classes | Not reusable, avoid |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The `set` must run before the components' `build_phase`, which is guaranteed if it precedes `run_test()` in the same initial block.
- Parameterized interfaces need the matching parameterized virtual type: `virtual bus_if #(32)`.
- Multiple instances: use distinct scopes or field names (`"vif0"`, `"vif1"`), or a generate loop with `$sformatf`.

### Follow-ups
- *Why clocking blocks?* They give race-free sampling and driving relative to the DUT clock.

title: Explain how simulation ends in UVM methodology?
solution:
**Key idea:** The run-time phases end when **all objections are dropped**, after drain time and any `phase_ready_to_end` extensions. UVM then runs the zero-time cleanup phases (`extract`, `check`, `report`, `final`), prints the report summary, and calls `$finish` (if `finish_on_completion` is set). Abnormal endings are fatal errors, max-quit-count and the global timeout.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",               "wave": "p..........." },
  { "name": "test objection",    "wave": "01......0..." },
  { "name": "drain time",        "wave": "0.......1.0." },
  { "name": "phase",             "wave": "2=........=.", "data": ["build..sos","run_phase","extract/check/report/final"] },
  { "name": "$finish",           "wave": "0..........1" }
],
  "head": { "text": "objections drop, drain time, cleanup phases at 0 time, then $finish" } }
```

### Explanation
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["test drops last objection"] --> B["drain time"] --> C["phase_ready_to_end (may re-raise)"] --> D["run phases end (run_phase + post_shutdown)"]
  D --> E["extract"] --> F["check"] --> G["report"] --> H["final"] --> I["report summary + $finish"]
```
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this);
  vseq.start(env.vsqr);
  phase.drop_objection(this);
endtask
function void end_of_elaboration_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  uvm_run_phase::get().phase_done.set_drain_time(this, 200ns);
endfunction
function void report_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  uvm_report_server rs = uvm_report_server::get_server();
  if (rs.get_severity_count(UVM_ERROR) + rs.get_severity_count(UVM_FATAL) == 0)
    `uvm_info("RESULT", "** TEST PASSED **", UVM_NONE)
  else
    `uvm_info("RESULT", "** TEST FAILED **", UVM_NONE)
endfunction
```
| Ending | Cleanup phases run? |
| --- | --- |
| All objections dropped | Yes |
| `` `uvm_fatal `` / max quit count | No (summary printed) |
| Global timeout | No (fatal) |
| `$finish` in user code | No |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Forever loops in drivers and monitors are killed automatically when `run_phase` ends. They do not need objections.
- If you use run-time sub-phases, each one ends on its own objections, and `run_phase` ends together with `post_shutdown`.

### Follow-ups
- *Why did my test end at 0 ns?* No objection was raised in any run-time phase.

source.name: The Art of Verification – UVM Interview Questions

title: What is uvm_root class?
answer: The **uvm_root **class serves as the implicit top-level and phase controller for all UVM components. Users do not directly instantiate **uvm_root. **The UVM automatically creates a single instance of uvm_root that users can access via the global (uvm_pkg-scope) variable, **uvm_top **.
solution:
**Key idea:** `uvm_root` is the implicit, singleton top-level component. Every test sits under it, it runs the phasing (`run_test`), and it owns global settings such as the timeout and `finish_on_completion`. Users never instantiate it. They access it through the global `uvm_top` or `uvm_root::get()`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  ROOT["uvm_root (uvm_top), name ''"] --> T["uvm_test_top (your test)"]
  T --> E["env"]
  E --> A["agents ..."]
  ROOT -.-> R1["run_test()"]
  ROOT -.-> R2["set_timeout(), finish_on_completion"]
  ROOT -.-> R3["print_topology(), find(), find_all()"]
  ROOT -.-> R4["report handler for messages from non-components"]
```

### Explanation
| Feature | API |
| --- | --- |
| Access | `uvm_top`, `uvm_root::get()`, or `uvm_coreservice_t::get().get_root()` |
| Start the test and phases | `uvm_top.run_test("name")` (global `run_test` calls this) |
| Timeout | `uvm_top.set_timeout(1ms)` |
| Exit behavior | `uvm_top.finish_on_completion = 0` |
| Topology | `uvm_top.print_topology()` or `enable_print_topology = 1` |
| Find components | `uvm_top.find("*.agt0.drv")`, `find_all("*drv*", list)` |
| Implicit parent | Components created with `parent = null` become children of `uvm_top` |

```systemverilog
function void end_of_elaboration_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  uvm_component drv = uvm_top.find("uvm_test_top.env.agt0.drv");
  uvm_top.print_topology();
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `uvm_root` has an empty name, so the test's full name is just `uvm_test_top`.
- `uvm_top.find()` is handy for debug, but it bypasses the clean hierarchy. Avoid it in reusable code.
- `uvm_root` is a `uvm_component` and a singleton. Calling `new` on it is an error.

### Follow-ups
- *Where do messages from modules or sequences go?* `` `uvm_info `` outside a component uses `uvm_top`'s report handler, or the sequencer's for sequences.

title: What is the parent class for uvm_test?
answer:
`uvm_test` class is the top-level class that a user can implement and there is no explicit parent that is mentioned. However, UVM has a special component called `uvm_top` and it is assigned as the parent of the test class.

uvm_component <- uvm_test <- my_test
solution:
**Key idea:** Class inheritance and component hierarchy are different things. By **inheritance**, `uvm_test` extends `uvm_component` (`uvm_object → uvm_report_object → uvm_component → uvm_test → my_test`). In the **hierarchy**, the test's *parent component* is `uvm_top` (`uvm_root`), and `run_test()` creates it there with the name `uvm_test_top`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph INH["Inheritance (is-a)"]
    O["uvm_object"] --> RO["uvm_report_object"] --> C["uvm_component"] --> T["uvm_test"] --> B["base_test"] --> M["my_test"]
  end
  subgraph HIER["Component hierarchy (contains)"]
    R["uvm_root (uvm_top)"] --> UT["uvm_test_top : my_test"] --> E["env"] --> A["agent"]
  end
```

### Explanation
| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Base class of `uvm_test` | `uvm_component` |
| Base class of `my_test` | `uvm_test` (or your `base_test`) |
| Parent *instance* of the test | `uvm_top` (the `uvm_root` singleton) |
| Instance name | `uvm_test_top` |
| Full name | `uvm_test_top` (root's name is empty) |

```systemverilog
class base_test extends uvm_test;              // inheritance
  `uvm_component_utils(base_test)
  function new(string name = "base_test", uvm_component parent = null);
    super.new(name, parent);                   // run_test passes parent = uvm_root
  endfunction
  function void end_of_elaboration_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    `uvm_info("TEST", $sformatf("parent=%s", (get_parent() == uvm_root::get()) ? "uvm_top" : "?"), UVM_LOW)
  endfunction
endclass
```
- `uvm_test` itself adds almost nothing over `uvm_component`. It exists to mark intent and to be the thing `run_test` instantiates.
- A common practice is a project `base_test` that builds the env and default configuration, with each test extending it.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Do not confuse `get_parent()` (hierarchy) with `super` (inheritance) in interview answers.
- Creating the test yourself with `new` instead of through `run_test()` bypasses `+UVM_TESTNAME` and the standard `uvm_test_top` name.

### Follow-ups
- *What is `uvm_top`'s parent?* None (null). It is the root of the component tree.
