title: Plan black-box verification of a memory. Include address boundaries, read/write ordering, simultaneous operations, reset, and a reference model
answer:
**Answer. **I would first define the memory contract: depth, width, request acceptance, read latency, byte enables, reset behavior, and the result of a read and write to the same address. My scoreboard keeps an independent address-to-data model and updates it only on accepted writes. It predicts each accepted read using the specified ordering and compares the response at its expected time. For uninitialized locations, I track whether the contents are defined rather than inventing an expected zero.

Tests cover first/last addresses, every address bit, walking ones/zeros, all-zero/all-one/checkerboard data, back-to-back accesses, write-read-write ordering, byte masks, simultaneous port accesses, stalls, and reset with requests in flight. Assertions check acceptance and response counts, latency, stable stalled responses, and illegal accesses. Coverage crosses operation, address region, masks, collisions, and reset timing. Reset clears contents only if the specification says so.
solution:
**Key idea:** Pin down the memory *contract* first (depth, width, latency, byte enables, read-during-write and reset behavior), then build an independent reference model that updates **only on accepted writes** and predicts every accepted read. Stimulus covers the address space edges and the ordering cases; assertions and coverage close the gaps.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SEQ["sequences: directed + random"] --> DRV["driver"]
  DRV --> DUT["memory DUT"]
  DUT --> MON["monitor"]
  DRV -.-> IMON["request monitor"]
  IMON -->|accepted writes and reads| REF["reference model (assoc array + valid bits)"]
  REF -->|expected read data| SCB["scoreboard"]
  MON -->|actual read data| SCB
  IMON --> COV["coverage: op x region x mask x collision x reset"]
  SVA["SVA: latency, stable stall, illegal access"] -.-> DUT
```

### Solution
**1. Contract questions to settle before writing a test**

| Item | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Depth/width, address alignment | Defines boundary and illegal-address tests |
| Read latency (fixed / variable) | When the scoreboard expects data |
| Byte enables | Model must merge partial writes |
| Read and write to same address, same cycle | Old data, new data, or undefined |
| Reset | Contents cleared or retained? Outstanding requests dropped? |
| Uninitialized reads | Track "defined" bit instead of assuming 0 |

**2. Test list**
- Address: first, last, every address bit toggled (walking 1/0 on the address), aliasing check (write `A`, read `A ^ (1<<k)`).
- Data: all-0, all-1, checkerboard `0x55/0xAA`, walking ones, address-as-data (catches decoder aliasing).
- Ordering: write-read same address back-to-back, write-write-read, read-write-read, long random mix.
- Multi-port: simultaneous access to same/different addresses, read-during-write on both ports.
- Stalls/backpressure, reset with requests in flight, illegal/out-of-range accesses.

### Code
```systemverilog
class mem_txn extends uvm_sequence_item;
  rand bit        we;
  rand bit [9:0]  addr;
  rand bit [31:0] data;
  rand bit [3:0]  be;
  `uvm_object_utils(mem_txn)
  function new(string name = "mem_txn"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

class mem_scoreboard extends uvm_scoreboard;
  `uvm_component_utils(mem_scoreboard)
  uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(mem_txn) req_f;  // accepted requests, in order
  uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo #(mem_txn) rsp_f;  // observed read responses
  bit [31:0] model   [bit [9:0]];          // sparse reference memory
  bit [3:0]  written [bit [9:0]];          // per-byte "defined" flags

  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    req_f = new("req_f", this);
    rsp_f = new("rsp_f", this);
  endfunction

  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    mem_txn req, rsp;
    forever begin
      req_f.get(req);
      if (req.we) begin                       // merge byte enables
        if (!model.exists(req.addr)) begin model[req.addr] = '0; written[req.addr] = '0; end
        for (int b = 0; b < 4; b++)
          if (req.be[b]) begin
            model[req.addr][8*b +: 8] = req.data[8*b +: 8];
            written[req.addr][b] = 1'b1;
          end
      end else begin
        rsp_f.get(rsp);                       // in-order read responses assumed
        compare(req.addr, rsp.data);
      end
    end
  endtask

  function void compare(bit [9:0] a, bit [31:0] act);
    for (int b = 0; b < 4; b++) begin
      if (!written.exists(a) || !written[a][b]) continue;   // undefined byte: no check
      if (act[8*b +: 8] !== model[a][8*b +: 8])
        `uvm_error("MEM", $sformatf("addr %0h byte %0d exp %0h act %0h",
                   a, b, model[a][8*b +: 8], act[8*b +: 8]))
    end
  endfunction

  function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    if (req_f.used() || rsp_f.used())
      `uvm_error("MEM", "outstanding requests/responses at end of test")
  endfunction
endclass
```

```systemverilog
// Fixed 2-cycle read latency, response held during stall.
a_lat:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
           rd_req && rd_gnt |-> ##2 rd_valid);
a_stall: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
           rd_valid && !rd_ready |=> rd_valid && $stable(rd_data));
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Reset clears the model **only** if the spec says the memory clears.
- If reads can complete out of order, key the expected queue by tag, not by arrival order.
- A pure-random address stream almost never hits address-aliasing bugs; add address-as-data and walking-address tests.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you know you're done?* Coverage of every address bit 0/1, both boundaries, every collision type, and reset during each in-flight state, with a clean scoreboard.
- *Dual-port same-address write/write?* Spec must define the winner; the model follows the same rule, or flags it as an illegal access.

title: Verify fairness and correct grants in a round-robin arbiter, including persistent requests and contention
answer:
**Answer. **I model the round-robin priority pointer and compare every actual grant against the expected eligible winner. I check that grants are one-hot-or-zero, that a grant corresponds to a request, and that the pointer advances on the specified service event. If the winner stalls, the grant must remain stable when the interface requires it. An idle cycle must preserve or reset priority exactly as specified.

For fairness, hold all requests active and check that each requester is served within N accepted service opportunities for an N-way arbiter. A cycle bound requires a separate assumption that service can complete within a bounded time. Test single requests, every contention combination, newly arriving requests, withdrawn requests, pointer wraparound, reset, and long backpressure. Fixed priority can starve a low-priority requester; round-robin fairness depends on eligible requests and service progress.
solution:
**Key idea:** Keep a reference priority pointer and predict the winner each cycle. Checks: grant is one-hot or zero, a grant always has a matching request, the pointer moves after each service event, and with all requests held, every requester is served within N service opportunities.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",  "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "req[3:0]", "wave": "=....=..=..", "data": ["1111", "1010", "0001"] },
  { "name": "gnt[3:0]", "wave": "=========..", "data": ["0001", "0010", "0100", "1000", "0001", "0010", "1000", "0010", "0001"] },
  { "name": "ptr",      "wave": "==========.", "data": ["0", "1", "2", "3", "0", "1", "2", "0", "2", "1"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "4-way RR: after granting i, requester i+1 has top priority" } }
```

### Explanation
**Reference model** (pointer = requester with highest priority):
```systemverilog
function automatic int rr_predict(bit [3:0] req, int ptr);
  for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) begin
    int idx = (ptr + k) % 4;
    if (req[idx]) return idx;
  end
  return -1;                       // no request -> no grant
endfunction
// after a grant to w is *accepted*: ptr = (w + 1) % 4
```

**Assertions:**
```systemverilog
a_onehot: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $onehot0(gnt));
a_valid:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) (gnt & ~req) == '0);
a_work:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) |req |-> |gnt);
// Fairness: requester 0 held high is granted within 4 grant opportunities
a_fair0:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
            req[0] && !gnt[0] |-> ##[1:4] gnt[0]);
a_hold:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
            gnt[1] && !done |=> gnt[1]);   // grant stable until done, if the spec requires it
```
`a_fair0` uses a cycle bound, which is only valid when each grant finishes in one cycle. With multi-cycle service, count **service events**, not cycles.

**Stimulus:**
| Scenario | What it catches |
| --- | --- |
| All requests held forever | Starvation, pointer not advancing |
| Every 2^N request mask (small N) | Priority calculation errors |
| Request drops before grant | Granting a non-requester |
| Single requester repeatedly | Pointer wrap / stuck priority |
| Requester arrives just after its turn | Correct wait of up to N-1 grants |
| Downstream stall / reset mid-grant | Grant stability, reset pointer value |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Should an idle cycle hold the pointer or reset it? Follow the spec exactly.
- Some designs move the pointer to `winner+1` and others to `ptr+1`. These give different fairness, so the model must match the spec.
- Fixed priority starving a low requester is expected behavior there, not a bug.

### Follow-ups
- *Weighted RR?* Keep a credit counter per requester in the model; check grants are proportional to the weights over a window.
- *Coverage?* Cross winner x request mask x previous winner, plus max-wait histogram bins.

title: Build a FIFO verification plan. Test reset, empty/full, simultaneous push/pop, wraparound, overflow/underflow, and data order
answer:
**Answer. **I use a queue reference model. Each accepted push appends data and each accepted pop removes and compares the oldest item. The occupancy changes by accepted_push minus accepted_pop. The model must follow the specified full/empty and simultaneous push/pop policy, including whether a full FIFO can accept a replacement push when a pop succeeds and whether an empty FIFO supports bypass.

Test reset, one element, fill to full, drain to empty, repeated pointer wraparound, push/pop together at every occupancy, overflow/underflow attempts, and distinct data patterns. Check no loss, duplication, or reordering; flag accuracy; blocked operations; output stability; and read latency. Cross occupancy boundary, operation combination, stalls, and reset. For an asynchronous FIFO, also vary independent clocks, clock phase, stopped clocks, and reset sequencing.

title: Explain the UVM factory and compare factory-based create() against direct new()
solution:
**Key idea:** `type_id::create()` asks the **factory** which class to build, so a test can override it. `new()` calls one specific constructor and bypasses all overrides. Use `create()` for anything a test might want to swap: components, transactions, sequences.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["packet::type_id::create('p')"] --> F{"factory: any override for packet?"}
  F -->|no| P["new packet object"]
  F -->|"yes: packet -> err_packet"| E["new err_packet object (returned as packet handle)"]
  B["new('p')"] --> P2["always packet, overrides ignored"]
```

### Explanation
| | `type_id::create()` | `new()` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goes through factory | Yes | No |
| Honors type/instance overrides | Yes | No |
| Requires registration | `` `uvm_object_utils`` / `` `uvm_component_utils`` | No |
| Sets hierarchical name/parent for components | `create("drv", this)` | `new("drv", this)` also does, but no override |
| Typical use | Components, sequence items, sequences | Small helpers, TLM FIFOs, ports, covergroups |

```systemverilog
class packet extends uvm_sequence_item;
  `uvm_object_utils(packet)
  function new(string name = "packet"); super.new(name); endfunction
endclass

// In a component's build_phase
drv = my_driver::type_id::create("drv", this);   // overridable
p   = packet::type_id::create("p");              // overridable
p   = new("p");                                  // NOT overridable
```

- The factory returns the *derived* object through a *base* handle. Virtual methods give the new behavior.
- `create()` works on the requested type and its registered overrides. Without the registration macro, the class cannot be created by the factory, and string-based lookups (`+uvm_set_type_override`) will not find it.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Overrides must be set **before** the `create()` call. Objects already built are not changed.
- Ports, exports, and analysis FIFOs are normally built with `new()`, which is correct. They are not factory objects.
- The override class must extend the original type. If it doesn't, you get a factory error or a cast failure.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is the constructor signature fixed?* The factory calls `new(name)` for objects and `new(name, parent)` for components, so extra arguments must have defaults.
- *How to debug?* `factory.print()` or `uvm_top.print_topology()` shows active overrides and the real types.

title: Distinguish type overrides from instance overrides
answer:
**Answer. **A type override replaces requests for a registered base type wherever they match. An instance override replaces that type only at a matching creation path. A matching instance override takes precedence over a type override. The replacement should extend the requested class so callers can use the same interface.

```systemverilog
base_driver::type_id::set_type_override(error_driver::get_type());
base_driver::type_id::set_inst_override(
  error_driver::get_type(), "uvm_test_top.env.agent0.drv");
```

For components, the instance path follows the parent hierarchy and creation name. For objects, a useful path requires an appropriate creation context. Set overrides before create(). Reference: [UVM factory reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_factory.svh)
solution:
**Key idea:** A **type override** replaces a type everywhere it is created through the factory. An **instance override** replaces it only for a matching hierarchical path. When both match, the instance override wins.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  C["base_driver::type_id::create('drv', agent0)"] --> I{"instance override matches path?"}
  I -->|yes| IO["use instance override type"]
  I -->|no| T{"type override for base_driver?"}
  T -->|yes| TO["use type override type"]
  T -->|no| B["use base_driver"]
```

### Explanation
| | Type override | Instance override |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Every factory `create` of that type | Only matching full path (wildcards allowed) |
| API | `set_type_override(new_type)` | `set_inst_override(new_type, "path")` |
| Precedence | Lower | Higher |
| Typical use | "All drivers inject errors" | "Only agent0's driver injects errors" |

```systemverilog
class err_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(err_test)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    // every base_driver in the env becomes error_driver
    base_driver::type_id::set_type_override(error_driver::get_type());
    // but agent1 gets a slow_driver (instance wins over type)
    // path is relative to 'this' (uvm_test_top) when a parent is passed
    base_driver::type_id::set_inst_override(slow_driver::get_type(),
                                            "env.agent1.drv", this);
    super.build_phase(phase);           // env is created after the overrides
  endfunction
endclass
```

Result: `agent0.drv` is `error_driver`, `agent1.drv` is `slow_driver`.

- The path in `set_inst_override(type, path, parent)` is relative to `parent` when one is given (here it becomes `uvm_test_top.env.agent1.drv`). With `parent = null`, pass the full path.
- For objects, the path is the context passed to `create(name, parent, contxt)`. A sequence item created with no context has only a name, so give it a context (for example `get_full_name()`) if you want instance overrides on objects.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Call the override before the target is created. The usual mistake is calling it after `super.build_phase()` when the parent creates the env there.
- A path typo matches nothing and gives no error. Check with `factory.print()`.
- `replace = 0` in `set_type_override` keeps an earlier override in place.

### Follow-ups
- *Command line?* `+uvm_set_type_override=base_driver,error_driver` and `+uvm_set_inst_override=base_driver,slow_driver,uvm_test_top.env.agent1.drv`.
- *Override by name?* `set_type_override_by_name("base_driver","error_driver")`. This works only for registered classes.

title: Identify the entry point that starts a UVM test
solution:
**Key idea:** `run_test()`, called from an `initial` block in the top module, starts UVM. It creates the test named by `+UVM_TESTNAME` (or by its string argument) as `uvm_test_top`, runs all phases, and then calls `$finish`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant TOP as tb_top module
  participant ROOT as uvm_root
  participant F as factory
  participant T as uvm_test_top
  TOP->>TOP: config_db set vif
  TOP->>ROOT: run_test()
  ROOT->>F: create +UVM_TESTNAME
  F-->>ROOT: my_test instance
  ROOT->>T: build -> connect -> end_of_elab -> start_of_sim
  ROOT->>T: run_phase (objections)
  ROOT->>T: extract -> check -> report -> final
  ROOT->>TOP: $finish
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  `include "uvm_macros.svh"
  logic clk = 0;
  always #5 clk = ~clk;
  bus_if bus(clk);
  dut u_dut(.clk(clk), .bus(bus));

  initial begin
    uvm_config_db#(virtual bus_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.*", "vif", bus);
    run_test();              // test chosen by +UVM_TESTNAME=my_test
  end
endmodule
```
Simulator: `vsim tb_top +UVM_TESTNAME=my_test +UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_MEDIUM`

- If `+UVM_TESTNAME` is given, it overrides the string argument in `run_test("default_test")`.
- The test must be registered with `` `uvm_component_utils`` so the factory can create it by name.
- `run_test` ends only after every phase finishes. By default it calls `$finish` (controlled by `uvm_root::finish_on_completion`).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Set virtual interfaces **before** `run_test()`, or at least before time 0 ends. Build phase runs in the same time step.
- No test name and no argument gives `UVM_FATAL` "No test specified".
- Only call `run_test()` once.

### Follow-ups
- *Where does phase execution start?* `uvm_root::run_test` calls `uvm_phase::m_run_phases()` after it creates the test.
- *Why is it named uvm_test_top?* That fixed instance name gives every config_db/override path a stable root.

title: Explain virtual interfaces and how class-based components gain access to DUT signals
answer: **Answer. **An interface is a statically instantiated container for signals, clocking blocks, and modports. A virtual interface is a handle that lets dynamically created classes access that instance. The top passes the handle through configuration; the driver and monitor retrieve it. A clocking block gives explicit sampling and driving timing to avoid races with RTL. A virtual interface does not create another interface or another copy of its signals.

title: Explain a virtual sequencer and when coordinating multiple agents requires one
answer: **Answer. **A virtual sequencer usually holds handles to the sequencers of several agents. A virtual sequence uses those handles to coordinate traffic such as programming registers before starting data transfers. The virtual sequencer normally has no driver and does not drive pins itself. It is optional. The test can pass agent sequencer handles directly to a virtual sequence and start that sequence on null.
solution:
**Key idea:** A virtual sequencer is a container of **handles** to real agent sequencers. It has no driver and no items of its own. Virtual sequences run on it so one place can coordinate traffic across agents, for example "program registers over APB, then start AXI data, then poll an interrupt." It is optional: a virtual sequence can also run on `null` with its handles set directly by the test.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  T["test"] -->|"vseq.start(env.vsqr)"| VS["virtual sequencer"]
  VS -->|p_sequencer.apb_sqr| A["APB agent sequencer"] --> AD["APB driver"]
  VS -->|p_sequencer.axi_sqr| X["AXI agent sequencer"] --> XD["AXI driver"]
  VS -->|p_sequencer.irq_sqr| I["IRQ agent sequencer"] --> ID["IRQ driver"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class soc_vsqr extends uvm_sequencer;          // no item type needed
  `uvm_component_utils(soc_vsqr)
  apb_sequencer apb_sqr;
  axi_sequencer axi_sqr;
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
endclass

// env.connect_phase
vsqr.apb_sqr = apb_agt.sqr;
vsqr.axi_sqr = axi_agt.sqr;

class init_then_traffic_vseq extends uvm_sequence;
  `uvm_object_utils(init_then_traffic_vseq)
  `uvm_declare_p_sequencer(soc_vsqr)
  function new(string name = "init_then_traffic_vseq"); super.new(name); endfunction
  task body();
    apb_cfg_seq cfg = apb_cfg_seq::type_id::create("cfg");
    axi_rand_seq dat = axi_rand_seq::type_id::create("dat");
    cfg.start(p_sequencer.apb_sqr);       // serial dependency
    dat.start(p_sequencer.axi_sqr);
  endtask
endclass
```

**When you need one**
| Situation | Virtual sequencer? |
| --- | --- |
| Single agent | No |
| Multi-agent, ordering between agents (config before data) | Yes, or a vseq with handles |
| Reusable env where tests should not know the agent paths | Yes, it hides the hierarchy |
| Need to share config/events among coordinated sequences | Convenient place to put them |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Handles must be assigned in `connect_phase`. If they are null, `start()` gives a fatal error.
- `uvm_declare_p_sequencer` does a `$cast`. Starting the vseq on the wrong sequencer type is fatal.
- Calling `start_item` on a virtual sequencer does not work because no driver is connected.

### Follow-ups
- *Vseq on null?* `vseq.apb_sqr = env.apb_agt.sqr; vseq.start(null);`. This works fine, but the sequence can't use `p_sequencer`.
- *Exclusive access?* Use `lock()`/`grab()` on the *real* sequencer for atomic multi-item operations.

title: Classify UVM phases as tasks or functions. Explain the purpose of check_phase
answer:
**Answer. **build_phase, connect_phase, end_of_elaboration_phase, start_of_simulation_phase, extract_phase, check_phase, report_phase, and final_phase are functions. run_phase and the runtime subphases are tasks. check_phase performs final consistency checks such as an empty scoreboard, no outstanding transactions, and no accumulated failures. It cannot wait for a late response; drain traffic during a task phase before checking.

Reference: [UVM phase reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_common_phases.svh)
solution:
**Key idea:** Only `run_phase` and its 12 runtime sub-phases are **tasks**, because they consume simulation time. Every other phase is a zero-time **function**. `check_phase` is a function for end-of-test consistency checks (scoreboard empty, nothing outstanding). It cannot wait, so traffic must be drained before it runs.

| Phase | Kind | Order | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| build_phase | function | top-down | create children, get config |
| connect_phase | function | bottom-up | connect TLM ports |
| end_of_elaboration_phase | function | bottom-up | topology print, sanity |
| start_of_simulation_phase | function | bottom-up | banners, initial config display |
| **run_phase** | **task** | parallel | stimulus, monitoring |
| pre_reset ... post_shutdown (12) | **task** | parallel, in sequence | optional runtime sub-phases |
| extract_phase | function | bottom-up | pull final data from monitors/scoreboards |
| **check_phase** | function | bottom-up | verify end state |
| report_phase | function | bottom-up | print pass/fail summary |
| final_phase | function | top-down | close files |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B["build"] --> C["connect"] --> E["end_of_elab"] --> S["start_of_sim"] --> R["run (task)"] --> X["extract"] --> CK["check"] --> RP["report"] --> FN["final"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  super.check_phase(phase);
  if (exp_q.size() != 0)
    `uvm_error("SCB", $sformatf("%0d expected items never observed", exp_q.size()))
  if (outstanding_reqs != 0)
    `uvm_error("SCB", "requests still pending at end of test")
endfunction
```

- The ordering is extract (collect) -> check (judge) -> report (print).
- Late responses must be handled in run_phase: keep the objection raised, or use `phase_ready_to_end` / drain time.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A scoreboard that compares in run_phase can still have leftover items. That is exactly what check_phase is for.
- Calling `#` or `@` inside check_phase is a compile error (it is a function).

### Follow-ups
- *Why separate extract and check?* So every component's data is final before anyone judges.
- *Is final_phase guaranteed?* It runs before `$finish` when phasing completes normally.

title: Draw a complete UVM testbench and trace the sequencer-to-driver request and completion protocol. Include test, env, agents, monitor, scoreboard, predictor and optional coverage
Implement a monitor that collects data while valid is asserted and publishes a completed transaction when valid falls
Launch five concurrent threads; once four have finished, terminate the remaining thread
solution:
**Key idea:** Spawn the five workers inside a **supervisor** process. Each worker posts a token to a mailbox when it finishes. After four `get()` calls, `disable fork` kills the supervisor's remaining children only. The mailbox counts correctly even when several workers finish in the same time slot.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as supervisor
  participant W as workers 0..4
  participant M as mailbox done
  S->>W: fork x5 (join_none)
  W->>M: put(2) t=10
  W->>M: put(0) t=15
  W->>M: put(4) t=15
  W->>M: put(1) t=30
  S->>M: get x4 complete
  S->>W: disable fork (kills worker 3)
```

### Solution
```systemverilog
task automatic work(int id);
  #($urandom_range(10, 100));
  $display("[%0t] worker %0d done", $time, id);
endtask

task automatic run_five();
  mailbox #(int) done = new();
  int id;
  fork
    begin : supervisor               // isolates disable fork from caller's other threads
      for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) begin
        automatic int k = i;         // capture loop index per child
        fork
          begin
            work(k);
            done.put(k);
          end
        join_none
      end
      repeat (4) begin
        done.get(id);
        $display("[%0t] got completion from %0d", $time, id);
      end
      disable fork;                  // kill the remaining worker(s)
    end
  join
endtask
```

**Trace example**
| time | event | tokens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | worker 2 done | 1 |
| 15 | workers 0 and 4 done (same slot) | 3 |
| 30 | worker 1 done | 4, then `disable fork` kills worker 3 |

### Explanation
- **Why the outer `fork ... join`?** `disable fork` kills *all* descendants of the calling process. Wrapping the workers in their own process means only the workers are killed, not unrelated threads started by the caller.
- **Why a mailbox and not `count++`?** Either works in practice, since SV threads don't preempt each other. The mailbox, however, lets the supervisor *block* until four are done without polling, and keeps the ids.
- An alternative is `process` handles plus `p[i].kill()` on the one whose `status()` is not `FINISHED`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the fifth worker finishes in the same time slot as the fourth, there may be nothing left to kill. That is fine.
- A killed thread does not run cleanup code. Semaphore keys it held are **not** returned, and objections it raised are not dropped.
- Without `automatic int k`, every worker would see `i == 5`.

### Follow-ups
- *Kill only the slowest?* Same as above, since after 4 completions only the slowest is left.
- *First one to finish wins?* `fork ... join_any; disable fork;` inside an isolating wrapper.

title: Distinguish task-based and function-based phases
answer: **Answer. **Function phases complete without consuming simulation time and are suited to construction, connections, and final checks. Task phases can wait for clock edges, delays, or events and perform concurrent stimulus and monitoring. UVM starts run_phase tasks for components concurrently. Keep a task phase alive with an objection until stimulus ends and required responses drain. A forever loop in a monitor does not keep the phase alive.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Function phases** run in zero simulation time and handle structure: build, connect, and final checks. **Task phases** (`run_phase` and the runtime sub-phases) can consume time with `@`, `#`, and `wait`, and run in parallel in every component. Objections control how long they last.

| | Function phases | Task phases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Examples | build, connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, extract, check, report, final | run_phase; reset/configure/main/shutdown (+pre/post) |
| Consumes time | No | Yes |
| Execution | One component after another (top-down or bottom-up) | All components' tasks forked in parallel |
| Ends when | function returns | all objections dropped (+ drain time) |
| Typical content | create, connect, check end state | drive, monitor, sequences |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph F1["function phases (0 time)"]
    B["build"] --> C["connect"] --> E["end_of_elab"] --> S["start_of_sim"]
  end
  subgraph T1["task phases (time advances)"]
    R["run_phase || reset -> configure -> main -> shutdown"]
  end
  subgraph F2["function phases (0 time)"]
    X["extract"] --> K["check"] --> P["report"] --> Q["final"]
  end
  F1 --> T1 --> F2
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this);       // keep the phase alive
  seq.start(env.agt.sqr);
  phase.drop_objection(this);        // phase ends when the count reaches 0
endtask
```

- A monitor's `forever` loop does **not** keep the phase alive. When the last objection drops, UVM kills all run_phase processes.
- `run_phase` runs **in parallel** with the runtime sub-phases, not before or after them.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- No objection raised means run_phase ends at time 0 and the test passes while doing nothing.
- Raising objections per transaction in the driver works but is slow. Raising them in the test or virtual sequence is typical.
- Use `phase.phase_done.set_drain_time(this, 100ns)` to let in-flight responses finish.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a function phase call a task?* No. A function can't call a task that consumes time (you can fork one, but that's poor practice).
- *Why would you use the sub-phases?* Reset in the middle of a test or phase jumping (`phase.jump(uvm_reset_phase::get())`).

title: Identify top-down versus bottom-up UVM phase traversal
answer:
**Answer. **build_phase traverses top-down, so parents configure and create children before the children build. connect_phase, end_of_elaboration_phase, start_of_simulation_phase, extract_phase, check_phase, and report_phase traverse bottom-up. final_phase traverses top-down. Task phases launch concurrent component processes, so their execution should not depend on a parent-before-child runtime ordering.

Reference: [UVM phase reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_common_phases.svh)
solution:
**Key idea:** `build_phase` goes **top-down**, because a parent must create its children before they can build. `final_phase` is also top-down. All other function phases (`connect`, `end_of_elaboration`, `start_of_simulation`, `extract`, `check`, `report`) go **bottom-up**, so children are ready before their parents use them. Task phases run in parallel.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  T["uvm_test_top"] --> E["env"]
  E --> A["agent"]
  A --> D["driver"]
  A --> M["monitor"]
```

**Order trace for this tree**
| Phase | Visit order |
| --- | --- |
| build (top-down) | test -> env -> agent -> driver -> monitor |
| connect (bottom-up) | driver -> monitor -> agent -> env -> test |
| end_of_elaboration / start_of_simulation | bottom-up, same as connect |
| run (task) | all `run_phase` tasks forked at the same time |
| extract / check / report | bottom-up |
| final | top-down |

### Explanation
- Top-down build lets a parent call `uvm_config_db::set` and factory overrides **before** its children are created and read them.
- Bottom-up connect means a parent's connect can rely on child ports that already exist and are connected inside the child.
- Bottom-up report: leaf scoreboards print their results before the test prints the overall summary.
- For task phases, never depend on the parent's `run_phase` starting before the child's. They are forked in parallel.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Calling `config_db::set` for a child **after** creating it still works in build. Setting it after the child's build_phase has already run has no effect.
- Siblings run in name (alphabetical) order inside a level. Don't depend on that order either.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is final top-down?* It is cleanup, so parents close top-level resources and can tell children to shut down.
- *Can you create components in connect_phase?* No. After build completes, new components are illegal (UVM error).

title: Compare uvm_config_db and uvm_resource_db
answer:
**Answer. **uvm_config_db is a typed, hierarchy-oriented configuration interface built on uvm_resource_db. Its context and instance path make it a natural choice for virtual interfaces and agent configuration. uvm_resource_db provides more general named or type-based resource access. Prefer config_db for component configuration; check every get() result and avoid an overly broad wildcard that assigns the wrong interface to several agents.

During build, higher-level config settings have greater precedence; settings at the same level use last-set-wins. After build, settings use the default precedence with last-set-wins behavior. Reference: [UVM configuration reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_config_db.svh)

title: Explain how factory overrides allow replacing implementations without editing the parent test
answer:
**Answer. **A parent creates a base component through base_driver::type_id::create(). A derived test registers an override before that creation, so the same parent code receives a derived driver through the base-class handle. Virtual methods provide the replacement behavior. The parent must use factory creation, and the replacement must implement the expected contract.

```systemverilog
function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  base_driver::type_id::set_type_override(stress_driver::get_type());
  super.build_phase(phase); // Parent may create the environment here.
endfunction
```

Both classes must be factory-registered. If the parent builds an object with new(), an override will not affect it. Reference: [UVM factory reference](https://github.com/accellera-official/uvm-core/blob/main/src/base/uvm_factory.svh)
solution:
**Key idea:** The parent builds through the factory, for example `drv = base_driver::type_id::create("drv", this)`. A derived test registers an override **before** that call, so the same parent code gets a `stress_driver` through its `base_driver` handle. Virtual methods give the new behavior. No line of the env or agent changes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T["stress_test.build_phase: set_type_override(base_driver -> stress_driver)"] --> S["super.build_phase creates env"]
  S --> A["agent.build_phase: base_driver::type_id::create('drv', this)"]
  A --> F{"factory lookup"}
  F --> D["stress_driver object in base_driver handle"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class base_driver extends uvm_driver #(item_t);
  `uvm_component_utils(base_driver)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  virtual task drive(item_t t);             // virtual: the hook that gets replaced
    /* normal protocol */
  endtask
  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    forever begin
      seq_item_port.get_next_item(req);
      drive(req);
      seq_item_port.item_done();
    end
  endtask
endclass

class stress_driver extends base_driver;
  `uvm_component_utils(stress_driver)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  virtual task drive(item_t t);
    repeat ($urandom_range(0, 5)) @(posedge vif.clk);   // random idle gaps
    super.drive(t);
  endtask
endclass

class stress_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(stress_test)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction
  function void build_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    base_driver::type_id::set_type_override(stress_driver::get_type());
    super.build_phase(phase);              // env/agent/driver created here
  endfunction
endclass
```

| Requirement | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Parent uses `type_id::create` | `new()` skips the factory |
| Both classes registered | Factory needs the proxies |
| Replacement extends the original | Must fit the base handle (`$cast` inside factory) |
| Override set before create | Already-built components are not changed |
| Behavior in `virtual` methods | Otherwise the base handle calls base code |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Putting the override *after* `super.build_phase()` does nothing when the base test creates the env there.
- Overriding a parameterized class needs the exact specialization (`base_driver#(32)`).

### Follow-ups
- *Swap only one agent's driver?* `set_inst_override` with that path.
- *Without recompiling?* `+uvm_set_type_override=base_driver,stress_driver` on the command line.

title: Explain virtual sequences and how they coordinate multiple sequencers
solution:
**Key idea:** A virtual sequence doesn't generate items itself. It **starts other sequences** on several agent sequencers, serially to enforce dependencies and with `fork/join` to make concurrent traffic. It gets the sequencer handles from a virtual sequencer (`p_sequencer`) or from fields the test fills in.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant V as virtual sequence
  participant B as bus_sqr (APB)
  participant D as data_sqr (AXI-S)
  V->>B: cfg_seq.start() - program DUT
  B-->>V: done
  par concurrent traffic
    V->>D: tx_seq.start()
  and
    V->>B: poll_seq.start() - status polling
  end
  V->>B: check_seq.start() - read counters
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
class top_vseq extends uvm_sequence;
  `uvm_object_utils(top_vseq)
  apb_sequencer  bus_sqr;          // filled by test (or use p_sequencer)
  axis_sequencer data_sqr;
  function new(string name = "top_vseq"); super.new(name); endfunction

  task body();
    apb_cfg_seq   cfg   = apb_cfg_seq  ::type_id::create("cfg");
    axis_tx_seq   tx    = axis_tx_seq  ::type_id::create("tx");
    apb_poll_seq  poll  = apb_poll_seq ::type_id::create("poll");
    apb_check_seq check = apb_check_seq::type_id::create("check");

    cfg.start(bus_sqr, this);         // 1) configure first (parent = this)
    fork                              // 2) concurrent
      tx.start(data_sqr, this);
      poll.start(bus_sqr, this);
    join
    check.start(bus_sqr, this);       // 3) final checks
  endtask
endclass

// test run_phase
top_vseq v = top_vseq::type_id::create("v");
v.bus_sqr  = env.apb_agt.sqr;
v.data_sqr = env.axis_agt.sqr;
phase.raise_objection(this);
v.start(null);                        // no virtual sequencer needed
phase.drop_objection(this);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Use **separate** child sequence objects for concurrent starts. Starting the same object twice at once is illegal.
- Two sequences on one sequencer interleave items. If a multi-item operation must be atomic, use `lock()`/`grab()`.
- Passing `this` as parent keeps the sequence tree and its priority/response routing correct.
- `fork ... join_none` without a later `wait fork` lets the vseq return while children still run.

### Follow-ups
- *Wait for an event across agents?* Share a `uvm_event` through config_db, or poll a status register.
- *Virtual sequencer vs null start?* Same capability. The virtual sequencer hides the env layout from tests.

title: Pass a virtual interface from the top-level testbench through uvm_config_db
Explain reactive sequences, driver responses, response queues, and preserving sequence IDs
[Meta] Share 10 units among four recipients with each getting at least one, using constraints
solution:
**Key idea:** Four random amounts, each `>= 1`, summing to 10. Bound each one to `[1:7]`. 7 is the real maximum, since the other three need at least 1 each, and the bound also stops 32-bit wraparound from producing "solutions" such as `0xFFFF_FFFD + ...`.

| amount[0] | amount[1] | amount[2] | amount[3] | sum |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 7 | 10 |
| 2 | 3 | 4 | 1 | 10 |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 10 |
| 4 | 4 | 1 | 1 | 10 |

### Solution
```systemverilog
class shares;
  rand int unsigned amount[4];
  constraint c_share {
    foreach (amount[i]) amount[i] inside {[1:7]};
    amount.sum() with (int'(item)) == 10;
  }
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    shares s = new();
    repeat (5) begin
      if (!s.randomize()) $fatal(1, "randomize failed");
      $display("%p", s.amount);
    end
  end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- `sum() with (int'(item))` sets the width of the reduction. Without a cast, the sum of `bit [3:0]` elements would be 4 bits wide and overflow.
- Number of solutions: stars and bars, C(10-1, 4-1) = C(9,3) = **84** distinct distributions. The solver picks among them, though not necessarily uniformly.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If `amount` were `bit [7:0]`, `amount.sum() == 10` is evaluated in 8 bits. `200+50+10+6 = 266 = 10 mod 256` would pass. Always cast the item.
- Total < number of recipients is infeasible, so `randomize()` returns 0. Check the return value.

### Follow-ups
- *At most 4 each?* Change the range to `[1:4]`. Still feasible since 4x4 >= 10.
- *Variable N recipients and total T?* `rand int unsigned amount[]; amount.size() == N; foreach ... inside {[1:T-N+1]}; sum == T;`.

title: [NVIDIA] Constrain a 32-bit word to prevent runs of five identical bits, without post_randomize
Split 15 distinct integers into three nonempty queues, preserving each exactly once, using constraints
In a ten-element array, require one value to appear exactly three times and all others to be distinct
Match parity of every array item to the parity of its index
solution:
**Key idea:** Parity is the LSB. Constrain `a[i][0] == i[0]` for each element: even index gives an even value, odd index gives an odd value. Using bit 0 instead of `% 2` also works for negative numbers, where `-3 % 2 == -1` in SystemVerilog.

| i | i[0] | example a[i] | a[i][0] |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 14 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | -7 | 1 |
| 2 | 0 | 102 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 33 | 1 |

### Solution
```systemverilog
class parity_match;
  rand int a[10];
  constraint c_parity {
    foreach (a[i]) a[i][0] == i[0];
  }
endclass
```

### Explanation
- `foreach` index variables are `int`, so `i[0]` is a legal bit-select.
- Equivalent arithmetic form, for non-negative values only: `a[i] % 2 == i % 2`.
- Two's complement: `-7 = ...11111001`, LSB 1 means odd. The bit test is always correct.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `a[i] % 2 == 1` fails for negative odd numbers (result `-1`). That is a classic trap.
- Dynamic arrays: add `a.size() inside {[...]}`. The constraint itself doesn't change.

### Follow-ups
- *Opposite parity?* `a[i][0] != i[0]`.
- *Value divisible by its index?* `if (i > 0) a[i] % i == 0;` (watch out for negative values and solver cost).

title: Generate a 32-bit word differing from the previous result in exactly two bit positions
Manage fork/join_any, selectively cancel one thread, and wait for others
answer:
**Answer. **join_any returns after the first child finishes. It leaves the others running. To cancel only a selected child, capture its process handle and call `kill();` then `wait fork` for the remaining children. This follows the process-class example in IEEE 1800 section 9.7.

```verilog
task automatic selective_cancel();
  process p[3];
  fork begin                      // isolate wait fork from caller's children
    fork
      begin p[0] = process::self(); work(0); end
      begin p[1] = process::self(); work(1); end
      begin p[2] = process::self(); work(2); end
    join_any
    wait (p[1] != null);          // handle may not be assigned yet
    if (p[1].status() != process::FINISHED) p[1].kill();
    wait fork;                    // wait for the survivors
  end join
endtask
```

`join_any` resumes the parent as soon as any child finishes. If `work(0)` takes zero time, worker 0 can finish before worker 1 has run `process::self()`, and calling `status()` on a null handle is a fatal error. `wait (p[1] != null)` prevents that. If worker 1 was the first finisher, it is already complete and the status check skips `kill()`. The outer `fork begin ... end join` isolates wait fork from unrelated children of the caller. disable fork would cancel all remaining descendants of the calling process, so it is inappropriate for selecting just worker 1.

For N threads, spawn in a loop with join_none and an automatic copy of the index, because `join_none` children run after the loop variable has moved on. Then wait for the first finisher with p[x].await() or a mailbox.

Shorter alternative for a fixed set of threads: name each block and disable the selected one by name.

```verilog
task automatic selective_cancel();
  fork begin
    fork
      begin : t0  work(0); end
      begin : t1  work(1); end
      begin : t2  work(2); end
    join_any
    disable t1;
    wait fork;
  end join
endtask
```

This has three limits. First, disable acts on a block's static scope, so it kills every active instance of t1, including those in other concurrent calls of the task. p[1].kill() affects only the one process its handle refers to. Second, threads spawned in a loop share one block name, so you cannot select a single one. Third, if t0 finishes in zero time before t1 starts, disable t1 has nothing to disable and t1 runs to completion. In an interview, give this version for "three threads, cancel one", then say you would switch to process handles for reentrant tasks or N threads.
solution:
**Key idea:** `join_any` resumes the parent after the **first** child finishes and leaves the rest running. To cancel one specific child, keep its `process` handle and call `kill()`, then `wait fork` for the rest. Wrap the block in its own `fork ... join` so `wait fork` doesn't also wait on unrelated threads of the caller.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "work(0)", "wave": "1..0....." },
  { "name": "work(1)", "wave": "1..0....." },
  { "name": "work(2)", "wave": "1......0." },
  { "name": "parent",  "wave": "0..=...=.", "data": ["join_any: p[1].kill()", "wait fork returns"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "worker 0 finishes first; worker 1 is killed; parent waits for worker 2" } }
```

### Solution
```systemverilog
task automatic selective_cancel();
  process p[3];
  fork begin                                   // isolation wrapper
    fork
      begin p[0] = process::self(); work(0); end
      begin p[1] = process::self(); work(1); end
      begin p[2] = process::self(); work(2); end
    join_any
    wait (p[1] != null);                       // handle might not be set yet
    if (p[1].status() != process::FINISHED)
      p[1].kill();
    wait fork;                                 // only waits for p[0], p[2]
  end join
endtask
```

**N threads, cancel thread `x`:**
```systemverilog
task automatic cancel_one_of_n(int n, int x);
  process p[] = new[n];
  fork begin
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) begin
      automatic int k = i;
      fork begin p[k] = process::self(); work(k); end join_none
    end
    wait (p[x] != null);
    if (p[x].status() != process::FINISHED) p[x].kill();
    wait fork;
  end join
endtask
```

### Explanation
| Mechanism | Kills | Problem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `disable fork` | **all** remaining children | not selective |
| `disable t1;` (named block) | every active instance of block `t1` | not reentrant-safe, can't select in a loop |
| `p[1].kill()` | exactly that process | needs the handle |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A child may finish in zero time before another has run `process::self()`. Calling `status()` on a null handle is fatal, hence the `wait (p[1] != null)`.
- If the target was itself the first to finish, `kill()` is skipped by the status check.
- A killed process doesn't release semaphores it held and doesn't drop its objections.

### Follow-ups
- *Wait for a specific thread?* `p[2].await();`.
- *Suspend instead of kill?* `p[i].suspend()` / `resume()`.

title: Explain how loop-index capture affects processes launched using fork/join_none
solution:
**Key idea:** `fork ... join_none` children don't start until the parent **blocks or finishes**. By then the loop has completed and the shared variable `i` equals 5, so every child prints 5. Declare an `automatic` copy in the loop body **before** the `fork`, so each iteration gets its own variable.

| Version | Variable each child reads | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared `i` | one `i`, final value 5 | `5 5 5 5 5` |
| `automatic int k = i;` before fork | separate `k` per iteration | `0 1 2 3 4` (order not guaranteed) |
| `fork begin automatic int k = i; ... end join_none` (inside the child) | assigned when the child starts (i already 5) | `5 5 5 5 5` |
| `fork automatic int k = i; $display(k); join_none` (fork's own declaration) | initialized by the parent before spawning | `0 1 2 3 4` |

### Solution
```systemverilog
module tb;
  initial begin
    // Correct
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) begin
      automatic int k = i;        // evaluated now, by the parent
      fork
        $display("k=%0d", k);
      join_none
    end
    wait fork;

    // Bug
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
      fork
        $display("i=%0d", i);     // runs later; sees i == 5
      join_none
    wait fork;
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as parent loop
  participant C as children
  P->>P: i=0: k0=0, spawn C0 (queued)
  P->>P: i=1: k1=1, spawn C1 (queued)
  P->>P: ... i=5 loop exits
  P->>C: wait fork: parent blocks, children run
  C-->>P: C0 prints k0=0, C1 prints k1=1 ...
```

### Explanation
- The loop variable of a `for` statement is a single variable for the whole loop. Each `begin ... end` iteration, however, creates a new automatic `k` that stays alive as long as a child refers to it.
- Inside a class method or an `automatic` task, block variables are already automatic. You still need the copy, because `i` itself is shared.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A `#0` inside the loop after the fork also "works", but it relies on scheduling. Don't use it.
- In a `static` task you need the `automatic` keyword explicitly.

### Follow-ups
- *`foreach` with join_none?* Same issue and same fix.
- *Why does `fork begin automatic int k = i; ... end join_none` fail but `fork automatic int k = i; ... join_none` work?* Declarations in the fork's own item list are initialized by the parent before any child is spawned (IEEE 1800-2017 9.3.2). Declarations inside the child's `begin...end` run only when that child starts, after the loop has moved on.

title: [Meta] Constrain a 2D pixel array using each pixel's four immediate neighbors
solution:
**Key idea:** For each pixel, compare it with the **sum of the neighbors that exist** (up, down, left, right). Out-of-range neighbors contribute 0. Cast every term to `int` so four 16-bit values can't overflow a 16-bit sum. The rule assumed here, since the source didn't fix it, is `pixel < sum of neighbors`.

| neighbors per cell (4x5) | c0 | c1 | c2 | c3 | c4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| r0 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 |
| r1 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 |
| r2 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 |
| r3 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 2 |

### Solution
```systemverilog
class pixels #(int R = 4, int C = 5);
  rand bit [15:0] p[R][C];
  constraint c_nbr {
    foreach (p[r, c])
      int'(p[r][c]) <
          ((r > 0)   ? int'(p[r-1][c]) : 0) +
          ((r < R-1) ? int'(p[r+1][c]) : 0) +
          ((c > 0)   ? int'(p[r][c-1]) : 0) +
          ((c < C-1) ? int'(p[r][c+1]) : 0);
  }
endclass
```

### Explanation
- The ternaries are guarded, so an out-of-range index such as `p[-1][c]` is never evaluated as a real constraint term.
- Every cell has at least 2 neighbors, so a constant image such as all 5s is a valid solution (5 < 10). That proves the system can be solved.
- Other boundary policies: wrap-around (`p[(r+R-1)%R][c]`), constraint on interior cells only, or fixed padding.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Without the `int'` casts, `p[r-1][c] + p[r+1][c] + ...` is evaluated in 16 bits and can wrap, so a large pixel could look smaller than its "sum."
- A 1x1 image has no neighbors, so `p < 0` has no solution.
- Coupled constraints over a big image (1920x1080) are far too slow for the solver. Generate tiles, or generate procedurally and check with constraints.

### Follow-ups
- *Each pixel differs from all 4 neighbors?* `if (r+1 < R) p[r][c] != p[r+1][c]; if (c+1 < C) p[r][c] != p[r][c+1];` (each pair checked once).
- *Pixel equals the average of its neighbors?* Multiply instead of dividing: `n_count * p == sum`.

Verify synchronous and asynchronous FIFO behavior, pointer comparisons, Gray-code crossing, and non-power-of-two depth
answer:
**Answer. **For a synchronous FIFO, check accepted push/pop operations against a queue and compute occupancy exactly in its clock domain. A counter or wrap-aware pointers can detect empty/full. For a conventional power-of-two asynchronous FIFO, keep binary pointers locally for RAM addressing, convert them to Gray code for crossing, and synchronize each Gray pointer into the opposite clock domain.

For that conventional design, empty compares the next local read Gray pointer with the synchronized write Gray pointer; full compares the next local write Gray pointer with the synchronized read pointer with its two most significant Gray bits inverted. Confirm whether flags use current or next pointers in the actual RTL. Local one-step Gray transitions must change one bit, but a synchronized pointer may skip several source increments and need not differ by only one bit between destination samples. Flags can be pessimistic because of synchronizer latency. Check CDC structure and physical skew constraints in addition to simulation. A binary counter wrapping directly at a non-power-of-two depth does not generally give a one-bit Gray wrap. Use a reviewed arbitrary-depth scheme or a power-of-two physical ring with separately enforced logical capacity. Changing the modulus alone does not work.

title: Calculate FIFO depth for different producer/consumer clock rates and burst occupancy
solution:
**Key idea:** Depth = **maximum backlog** = peak of `writes_so_far - reads_so_far` over the worst-case burst, not just a ratio of clock frequencies. Work it out over the burst window, using effective **word rates** (accounting for idle cycles), and add margin for synchronizer latency and read start-up delay.

**Classic worked example:** burst of 120 words. Writer: 100 MHz, 1 word every cycle. Reader: 80 MHz, 1 word every cycle.

| quantity | value |
| --- | --- |
| burst write time | 120 / 100 MHz = 1200 ns |
| words read in 1200 ns | 1200 ns x 80 MHz = 96 |
| backlog at end of burst | 120 - 96 = **24** |
| + read start delay (2-FF sync, about 3 rclk) | about 3 words |
| depth to build | 27, rounded up to 32 |

**With idle cycles:** writer 1 word every 2 cycles at 200 MHz (100 Mw/s), reader 1 word every 4 cycles at 320 MHz (80 Mw/s). The effective rates are the same, so the answer is the same 24 words plus margin.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["write rate Rw (words/s)"] --> B["backlog growth = (Rw - Rr) x T_burst"]
  R["read rate Rr (words/s)"] --> B
  B --> M["+ latency margin (sync, startup)"]
  M --> D["depth (round to 2^n for Gray FIFO)"]
```

### Solution
A small SystemVerilog model to measure peak occupancy for any pattern:
```systemverilog
module fifo_depth_calc;
  timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
  realtime TW = 10ns, TR = 12.5ns;       // 100 MHz writer, 80 MHz reader
  int      BURST = 120, RD_DELAY = 3;    // read starts 3 rclk late (sync latency)
  int      occ = 0, peak = 0, written = 0;

  initial fork
    begin : writer
      repeat (BURST) begin #TW; occ++; written++; if (occ > peak) peak = occ; end
    end
    begin : reader
      #(RD_DELAY * TR);
      forever begin #TR; if (occ > 0) occ--; if (written == BURST && occ == 0) break; end
    end
  join_any
  final $display("peak occupancy = %0d", peak);
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- Formula for one burst with the reader running throughout: `depth = B - floor(B * Rr / Rw)` when `Rw > Rr`.
- Back-to-back bursts: if the long-run average write rate exceeds the read rate, **no** finite FIFO is enough. You need backpressure or a guaranteed gap between bursts that lets the FIFO drain.
- Classic trick: "the writer sends 80 words in any 100-cycle window." The worst case is 80 words at the end of one window followed by 80 at the start of the next, so 160 back-to-back writes. Size the FIFO for that 160-word burst.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Use **word throughput**, not clock frequency, when the interface has idle cycles.
- Async FIFOs need power-of-two depth (Gray pointers), so round up.
- Pessimistic full/empty flags hide 2 to 3 entries of usable space. Add them to the depth.

### Follow-ups
- *Reader faster than writer?* Depth 1 to 2 is in theory enough. You still need sync margin.
- *Verify it?* Coverage on peak occupancy plus an assertion that `full && push` never happens when no backpressure exists.

title: Explain blocking versus nonblocking assignment scheduling and race conditions
solution:
**Key idea:** A blocking `=` updates **immediately**, so later statements in the same block see the new value. A nonblocking `<=` evaluates the right side now and updates in the **NBA region** after all active processes finish. Every flop therefore samples "old" values, which is how real flip-flops behave. Rule: `<=` in clocked logic, `=` in combinational logic.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",               "wave": "p..." },
  { "name": "a (nonblocking)",   "wave": "1.0." },
  { "name": "b (nonblocking)",   "wave": "0..." },
  { "name": "c (nonblocking)",   "wave": "0.1." },
  { "name": "a (blocking)",      "wave": "1.0." },
  { "name": "c (blocking)",      "wave": "0..." }
],
  "head": { "text": "start a=1,b=0,c=0; at the edge: NB rotates (a,b,c)=(0,0,1); blocking gives (0,0,0)" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// Starting a=1, b=0, c=0
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  a <= b; b <= c; c <= a;      // RHS sampled first: a=0, b=0, c=1  (rotate)
end

always @(posedge clk) begin
  a = b; b = c; c = a;         // a=0, b=0, c=a(new)=0   (value lost)
end
```

**Scheduling regions in one time step (simplified):**
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Preponed: assertions / clocking block inputs sample"] --> A["Active: always blocks, = updates, <= RHS evaluated"]
  A --> I["Inactive (#0)"]
  I --> N["NBA: <= updates applied"]
  N -->|triggers more events| A
  N --> O["Observed: assertions evaluated"]
  O --> R["Reactive: program blocks / TB"]
  R --> PP["Postponed: $strobe, $monitor"]
```

**Race example:** two `always @(posedge clk)` blocks, one writing `x = 1` and the other reading `y = x`. Active-region order isn't defined, so `y` can see the old or new `x`. With `x <= 1` the reader always sees the old value.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Mixing `=` and `<=` on the same variable in different blocks causes simulation/synthesis mismatches.
- Blocking in sequential logic can still be "correct" if you write the statements in reverse order, but it's fragile. Avoid it.
- Testbench driving with `=` on the same edge the DUT samples gives a race. Use a clocking block (`output #1` skew) or drive on the opposite edge.
- `$display` shows pre-NBA values. Use `$strobe` to see the values after updates.

### Follow-ups
- *Combinational always with `<=`?* It simulates, but it adds extra delta cycles and can mislead. Use `=` in `always_comb`.
- *What does `#0` do?* It moves the process to the Inactive region. It is a hack, not a fix for races.

title: Test fixed-priority and round-robin arbiters
answer:
**Answer. **For fixed priority, predict the highest-priority asserted eligible request and compare it with the grant. For round-robin, add a reference priority pointer and update it at the defined service event. Both need one-hot-or-zero grants, no grants to nonrequesters, correct reset state, and stability while a selected transfer stalls.

Exercise all requester masks for a small arbiter, persistent contention, intermittent high-priority requests, changing eligibility, reset mid-service, and pointer wraparound. Fixed-priority starvation can be expected behavior; round-robin should bound wait in service opportunities under persistent requests and eventual downstream progress. Cross winner, contention mask, previous winner, and stalls. Measure fairness only under the assumptions the implementation promises.

title: Verify valid/ready pipeline stages and backpressure under stalls
solution:
**Key idea:** A transfer happens only on a clock edge with `valid && ready`. Once `valid` is asserted, the source must hold `valid` and `data` **stable** until `ready`. The source must not wait for `ready` before raising `valid`. A pipeline stage accepts input when it is empty or when its output leaves in the same cycle. The verification model is an ordered queue of accepted inputs compared against accepted outputs.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "valid", "wave": "01....0.." },
  { "name": "ready", "wave": "0.1.010.." },
  { "name": "data",  "wave": "x=.==.x..", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2"] },
  { "name": "xfer",  "wave": "0.1.010.." }
],
  "head": { "text": "D0 waits one cycle for ready; D1 sent; D2 held while ready=0, then sent" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// One-entry elastic stage (combinational ready path)
assign in_ready = !out_valid || out_ready;
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) out_valid <= 1'b0;
  else if (in_ready) begin
    out_valid <= in_valid;
    if (in_valid) out_data <= in_data;
  end

// Protocol assertions on the output side
a_hold:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
           out_valid && !out_ready |=> out_valid && $stable(out_data));
a_noX:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) out_valid |-> !$isunknown(out_data));
// Liveness (bounded): a stalled item eventually leaves if ready eventually returns
a_live:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
           out_valid |-> ##[0:100] out_ready);
```

**Test matrix**
| Scenario | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| Single transfer, idle gaps | latency, no extra beats |
| Full rate (ready always 1) | throughput 1/clk, no bubbles |
| Random ready (10% to 90%) | no loss, duplication, or reorder |
| Long stall then release | data stability, no overwrite |
| Simultaneous in and out transfer while full | stage refilled in the same cycle |
| Reset while holding data | valid drops, model flushed |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The `in_ready` path above is combinational from `out_ready`. Long pipelines then get long ready paths. A **skid buffer** (2 entries) registers ready without losing throughput.
- The checker must sample on the same edge as the design and use `valid && ready` only. Counting beats on `valid` alone double-counts stalls.
- AXI forbids `valid` depending combinationally on `ready` at the same interface.

### Follow-ups
- *Why 2 entries in a skid buffer?* With registered ready, the upstream sees `ready=0` one cycle late and sends one more beat. The second slot catches it.
- *Coverage?* Stall length bins, back-to-back transfers, ready toggling every cycle.

title: Select safe CDC methods for slow-to-fast and fast-to-slow crossings
answer:
**Answer. **For a single level that stays stable long enough, use a destination-domain synchronizer, commonly two flip-flops. A slow-to-fast pulse can be sampled only if its width and the destination clock behavior guarantee capture. A short fast-to-slow pulse can be missed entirely, so use pulse stretching with a stated bound, a toggle scheme with a rate bound, or a request/acknowledge handshake.

A handshake is appropriate when every event must arrive despite variable clock ratios. A toggle can lose events if it changes twice before the destination observes the first change. Use a data-stable handshake or an asynchronous FIFO for multibit payloads; independently synchronizing each data bit does not preserve coherence. Also test stopped clocks and reset recovery, rather than assuming clock ratio alone proves a safe crossing.
solution:
**Key idea:** Pick the scheme by **what** crosses and **how often**. A slow, stable single-bit level uses a 2-FF synchronizer. A pulse going fast to slow can be missed, so stretch it, convert it to a toggle, or use req/ack. Multi-bit data never goes through per-bit synchronizers. Use a handshake with stable data, or an async FIFO.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "fast_clk",  "wave": "p..........." },
  { "name": "pulse",     "wave": "0.10........" },
  { "name": "slow_clk",  "wave": "P.....P....." },
  { "name": "naive_q",   "wave": "0..........." },
  { "name": "toggle",    "wave": "0..1........" },
  { "name": "sync_tog",  "wave": "0.....1....." }
],
  "head": { "text": "1-cycle fast pulse falls between slow edges and is lost; a toggle level is captured" } }
```

| Crossing | Safe method | Condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level, slow to fast | 2-FF sync | level stable for at least 2 dest cycles (usually true) |
| Pulse, slow to fast | 2-FF sync + edge detect | pulse longer than 1 dest period + margin |
| Pulse, fast to slow | pulse stretch | stretch width >= about 1.5 dest periods (known ratio) |
| Pulse, fast to slow | toggle sync + edge detect | events at least 2 to 3 dest cycles apart |
| Pulse, any ratio, must not be lost | req/ack handshake | throughput limited by round trip |
| Multi-bit, occasional | handshake / MUX-recirculation with stable data | data held until ack |
| Multi-bit stream | async FIFO (Gray pointers) | depth sized for bursts |
| Counter value | Gray code + 2-FF | changes by 1 per source clock |

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// Toggle synchronizer for single-cycle events
always_ff @(posedge src_clk) if (src_pulse) src_tog <= ~src_tog;
always_ff @(posedge dst_clk) {dst_q3, dst_q2, dst_q1} <= {dst_q2, dst_q1, src_tog};
assign dst_pulse = dst_q3 ^ dst_q2;         // one dst-cycle pulse per event
```
"Slow to fast" isn't automatically safe. If the clock ratio is close to 1 or the slow clock may run faster in some modes, apply the same analysis.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A toggle loses events if it changes twice before the destination samples it (the two flips cancel). Use a rate limit or a handshake.
- Independently synchronized bits of a bus can arrive in different cycles. That breaks **coherence**.
- Verify with CDC structural tools plus simulation with random phase and jitter, stopped clocks, and resets in each domain.

### Follow-ups
- *How many flops?* 2 is typical. 3 for very high frequency or low-voltage corners (MTBF).
- *Back-to-back pulses fast to slow?* An async FIFO of events, or a counter crossed with Gray code.

title: Compare synchronized handshake, recirculation mux, and asynchronous FIFO for wide buses
answer:
**Answer. **A synchronized request/acknowledge handshake transfers a stable data word with explicit acknowledgment and backpressure. A recirculation mux keeps the destination register unchanged until a synchronized load control tells it to capture the held source data. That mux arrangement still needs a data-stability protocol and timing constraints; it is not sufficient on its own. An asynchronous FIFO buffers multiple words and supports sustained streams with independent clocks.

Choose a handshake for infrequent configuration or status transfers, and an asynchronous FIFO for a stream that needs buffering and throughput. In a bundled-data handshake, hold the payload until acknowledgment and ensure the data reaches the destination before capture. Check reset alignment and do not reuse a handshake slot prematurely. The wide data bus usually bypasses per-bit synchronizers because its coherence comes from holding it stable while the control crosses safely.
solution:
**Key idea:** All three keep a wide bus **coherent** by synchronizing only a *control* signal while the data stays stable.
- **Handshake (req/ack):** one word per round trip, with explicit flow control. Good for configuration or status.
- **Recirculation mux:** a synchronized load-enable that selects new data into a destination register (otherwise the register feeds back to itself). It's the capture side of a handshake, not a full protocol.
- **Async FIFO:** buffers many words for continuous streams.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph SRC["source domain"]
    D["data reg (held stable)"]
    REQ["req toggle"]
  end
  subgraph DST["destination domain"]
    S["2-FF sync of req"] --> P["edge detect = load_en"]
    M["recirculation mux"] --> Q["dest data reg"]
    Q --> M
    A["ack"]
  end
  D -->|"wide bus, no sync"| M
  REQ --> S
  P --> M
  P --> A
  A -->|"2-FF sync back"| SRC
```

| | Handshake | Recirculation mux | Async FIFO |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Throughput | 1 word per about 4 to 6 slow cycles | same as its control protocol | up to 1 word per cycle |
| Buffering | 1 word | 1 word | depth N |
| Backpressure | ack | needs protocol | full/empty |
| Area | small | small (mux + regs) | RAM + Gray logic |
| Typical use | config, status, rare events | wide registers updated rarely | streaming data |
| Key constraint | data stable from req to ack | data stable while load_en is in flight | Gray-pointer skew, depth sizing |

### Explanation
- In bundled-data schemes the data path has no synchronizer. Correctness relies on the data settling **before** the synchronized control arrives: 2 or more destination cycles later. Constrain the data path with `set_max_delay -datapath_only` so it is shorter than the sync latency.
- Don't reuse the handshake until ack has returned. Otherwise the source changes data mid-capture.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A recirculation mux with no ack-back to the source lets the source overwrite data too early. It needs a protocol around it.
- A reset in one domain alone can leave req/ack half-done. Reset both sides together or design an abort.
- CDC tools must be told about the "qualifier" relation (data qualified by synchronized enable), or they flag every data bit.

### Follow-ups
- *4-phase vs 2-phase handshake?* 4-phase (req high, ack high, req low, ack low) is simpler. 2-phase (toggle) is about twice as fast.
- *Wide counter?* Gray-encode it and use a 2-FF sync. That's coherent with no handshake if it increments by 1.

title: Explain metastability, reset synchronization, reconvergence, and CDC constraint consistency
answer:
**Answer. **Metastability occurs when a flip-flop samples near a transition and may take longer than usual to settle. Synchronizer stages give extra resolution time and reduce the probability of a metastable value reaching functional logic; they do not eliminate it. RTL simulation cannot measure analog metastability or prove a physical MTBF.

Reset may assert asynchronously when required, but deassert it synchronously in each destination clock domain. Check recovery/removal timing and interactions between independently reset domains. Reconvergence occurs when related signals cross through separate synchronizers and later meet with inconsistent latency; transfer them coherently or use a protocol that tolerates the skew. Keep CDC and STA clock/reset definitions consistent. Review clock groups, generated clocks, synchronizer placement, Gray-bus skew/max-delay requirements, reset paths, and justified waivers. A false path is a timing-analysis instruction, not evidence that a crossing is functionally safe.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Metastability:** a flop sampled during its setup/hold window can hang near mid-rail for an unbounded (but probabilistically decaying) time. Synchronizer stages add resolution time to reduce failure probability: `MTBF = e^(t_r / tau) / (T_0 * f_clk * f_data)`. They don't remove the effect. **Reset:** assert asynchronously, deassert synchronously in each domain. **Reconvergence:** separately synchronized related signals can arrive one cycle apart, so the logic that recombines them sees an inconsistent state. **Constraints:** CDC and STA setups must describe the same clocks, groups, and exceptions.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",      "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "async_d",  "wave": "0.1...." },
  { "name": "ff1",      "wave": "0.x1..." },
  { "name": "ff2",      "wave": "0...1.." },
  { "name": "rst_n_in", "wave": "1.0.1.." },
  { "name": "rst_sync", "wave": "1.0...1" }
],
  "head": { "text": "ff1 may be metastable for a cycle; ff2 output is clean. Reset asserts at once, releases 2 edges later" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// Reset synchronizer: async assert, sync deassert
module rst_sync (input logic clk, rst_n_in, output logic rst_n_out);
  logic q1;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n_in)
    if (!rst_n_in) {rst_n_out, q1} <= 2'b00;
    else           {rst_n_out, q1} <= {q1, 1'b1};
endmodule
```

| Topic | Risk | Fix / check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metastability | functional logic sees an unsettled value | 2 to 3 FF sync, no logic between stages, placed close together |
| Reset release | recovery/removal violation, flops leave reset in different cycles | reset synchronizer per domain, recovery/removal timing |
| Reconvergence | `a_sync` and `b_sync` skewed by 1 cycle | cross one encoded signal, or a handshake/FIFO |
| Gray bus skew | multiple bits change at the destination | `set_max_delay -datapath_only` <= 1 source period |
| Constraints | false path hides a real crossing | CDC tool review, matching clock groups, justified waivers |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- RTL simulation can't show analog metastability. Use CDC tools, and optionally inject random 1-cycle delay at synchronizers in simulation to expose reconvergence bugs.
- `set_false_path` only tells STA to ignore a path. It doesn't make the crossing functionally safe.
- Glitchy combinational logic **before** a synchronizer can create pulses the source never meant to send. Register the signal in the source domain first.

### Follow-ups
- *Effect of a 3rd flop?* Adds a full period of resolution time, so MTBF grows by about `e^(T/tau)`.
- *Reset domain crossing (RDC)?* An async reset of one domain can corrupt flops in another domain that sample it. Use isolation or sequenced reset.

title: Distinguish setup and hold analysis and debug clock skew
solution:
**Key idea:** **Setup**: the *latest* data must arrive before the next capture edge minus `t_setup`. **Hold**: the *earliest* data change must arrive after the *same* capture edge plus `t_hold`. Skew (`capture clock arrival - launch clock arrival`) helps setup when positive and hurts hold by the same amount.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "launch clk",  "wave": "p...." },
  { "name": "capture clk", "wave": "p....", "phase": -0.2 },
  { "name": "D at FF2",    "wave": "x.=x.", "data": ["valid window"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "data must be stable from (edge - t_setup) to (edge + t_hold) at the skewed capture edge" } }
```

### Explanation
Same-frequency, single-cycle path:
- **Setup:** `T + skew >= t_cq,max + t_comb,max + t_setup` gives slack `= T + skew - (t_cq + t_comb + t_su)`
- **Hold:** `t_cq,min + t_comb,min >= t_hold + skew`

**Worked example:** `T = 2.0 ns`, `t_cq = 0.15`, `t_setup = 0.10`, `t_hold = 0.05`, `skew = +0.20 ns`

| path | t_comb (max/min) | setup slack | hold slack |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 1.60 / 1.60 | 2.0+0.2-(0.15+1.60+0.10) = **+0.35** | (0.15+1.60)-(0.05+0.2) = +1.50 |
| B | 2.10 / 0.02 | 2.2-2.35 = **-0.15** (setup fail) | 0.17-0.25 = **-0.08** (hold fail) |

**Debug flow**
| Violation | Look at | Fixes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setup | worst path logic depth, net delay, clock latency | restructure logic, upsize, pipeline, useful skew, slower clock |
| Hold | shortest path, clock skew on capture | insert delay buffers, reduce capture latency |
| Both on same path | large skew | fix the clock tree first |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Lowering frequency does not fix hold.** The hold check doesn't involve the period.
- Setup is checked at slow corners, hold at fast corners, each with OCV derates and clock uncertainty.
- A multicycle path `-setup 2` also moves the hold check unless you add `-hold 1`.
- Hold fixes are mandatory before tape-out. Setup failures only lower the achievable frequency.

### Follow-ups
- *Negative skew?* It hurts setup and helps hold.
- *Why does hold matter for a shift register with no logic?* `t_cq,min` alone has to cover `t_hold + skew`. Clock skew between adjacent flops can break it.
