| Testbench timestamp checker | spacing of TB-driven events (e.g. async interface spec) | behavioral |

### Code: cell model with a timing check
```verilog
`timescale 1ns/1ps
module dff_tc (input D, CLK, output reg Q);
  reg notifier;
  always @(posedge CLK) Q <= D;
  always @(notifier)    Q <= 1'bx;          // corrupt output on violation
  specify
    (posedge CLK => (Q +: D)) = (0.10, 0.12);
    $setuphold(posedge CLK, D, 0.08, 0.04, notifier);  // setup 80 ps, hold 40 ps
  endspecify
endmodule
```

### Code: behavioral spacing checker (for an async interface spec)
```systemverilog
module setuphold_mon #(realtime TSU = 2ns, THD = 1ns) (input logic clk, d);
  realtime t_d = -1ns, t_clk = -1ns;
  always @(d)   begin
    t_d = $realtime;
    if (t_clk >= 0 && (t_d - t_clk) < THD) $error("hold violation %t", $realtime);
  end
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    t_clk = $realtime;
    if (t_d >= 0 && (t_clk - t_d) < TSU) $error("setup violation %t", $realtime);
  end
endmodule
```

### Pitfalls
- RTL simulation has zero delay; a "passing" RTL test says nothing about timing.
- Timing checks on synchronizer flops fire by design → disable them there (or use `+no_notifier`-style options per instance) so X does not propagate.

### Follow-ups
- *Why GLS if STA exists?* Catch unconstrained paths, wrong constraints/exceptions, reset/X issues, and SDF-annotated async behavior.

title: Digital Design: FSM for a Digital Lock with RTL and Assertions
answer: Missing the lock code and timing policy. Model the longest matching prefix of the accepted key sequence, transition only on a valid key event, and define wrong-key, timeout, and reset behavior. Assert unlock occurs only after the complete sequence and for the specified duration. Test partial matches, repeated keys, overlaps, wrong keys, and timeout at boundary cycles.

title: Computer Architecture: ROB and CFC - Out-of-Order Execute with In-Order Commit
answer: A reorder buffer tracks instructions in program order while execution completes out of order. Commit only completed, exception-free instructions at the head, preserving precise architectural state. Squash younger work after a branch misprediction or exception. CFC is ambiguous in this title. If it means a committed register file, it stores retired state; confirm the course's definition before assigning a specific role.
solution:
**Key idea:** The **reorder buffer (ROB)** is a FIFO of in-flight instructions in program order. Instructions *execute and complete* out of order, writing results into their ROB entry (or a physical register), but they **commit (retire) in order from the head**, and only if complete and exception-free. That keeps architectural state precise: on a mispredict or exception, everything younger is squashed. "CFC" is not a standard acronym; most course material that pairs it with a ROB means the **committed (architectural) register file / state** — the copy that is updated only at commit and used for recovery. Confirm the definition before answering in detail.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["decode / rename"] -->|allocate at tail| ROB["ROB (program order)"]
  D --> RS["reservation stations"]
  RS --> EX["execution units (any order)"]
  EX -->|"result + done bit"| ROB
  ROB -->|"commit from head, in order"| ARF["committed state (ARF / CFC)"]
  ROB -->|"exception or mispredict at head"| FL["flush younger entries"]
```

### Trace

| Instr (program order) | Latency | Completes at | Commits at |
|---|---|---|---|
| I1 `div x1, x2, x3` | 20 | cycle 21 | 21 |
| I2 `add x4, x5, x6` | 1 | cycle 3 | 22 (waits for I1) |
| I3 `ld  x7, 0(x8)` | page fault | cycle 5 (marked exception) | at head (23): trap, squash I3 and younger |

I2 finished early but its result becomes architectural only after I1 retires; I3's exception is taken precisely, with I1 and I2 committed and nothing after them.

### Explanation
- ROB entry: PC, destination (arch reg + physical reg/value), done, exception code, branch info.
- Commit: write committed state (ARF or retirement RAT), free the old physical register, release store to memory (stores leave the store buffer only after commit).
- Recovery: restore speculative mapping from committed state or checkpoints, reset ROB tail to the faulting/mispredicted entry.

### Pitfalls
- Stores must not update memory before commit (otherwise imprecise).
- Commit width (instructions per cycle) limits throughput even if execution is fast.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not commit out of order?* An older instruction might fault or be on a mispredicted path — state would not be precise.

title: Computer Architecture: Two Kinds of RAT and What They Solve
answer: A speculative RAT maps architectural registers to the newest allocated physical registers, removing WAR/WAW name dependencies. A retirement RAT records the committed mapping, supporting precise state and recovery. Checkpointed speculative maps can speed branch recovery. Physical-register reclamation must wait until older mappings are no longer needed. Terminology and exact recovery structures vary by implementation.
solution:
**Key idea:** With register renaming there are two map tables: the **speculative (front-end) RAT**, updated at rename, which maps each architectural register to its *newest* physical register — eliminating WAR/WAW false dependencies; and the **retirement (architectural) RAT**, updated at commit, which holds the *committed* mapping and is used to restore precise state after an exception or mispredict.

### Worked example (renaming)

| Program | After rename | Spec. RAT change | Retire RAT change (at commit) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `r1 = r2 + r3` | `p10 = p2 + p3` | r1 → p10 | r1 → p10 (free old p1) |
| `r4 = r1 * 2` | `p11 = p10 * 2` | r4 → p11 | r4 → p11 (free p4) |
| `r1 = r5 - 1` (WAW with #1, WAR with #2) | `p12 = p5 - 1` | r1 → p12 | r1 → p12 (free p10) |

The third instruction can execute before #2 reads `r1`, because they now use different physical registers (p12 vs p10).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  REN["rename stage"] -->|"update at rename"| SRAT["speculative RAT"]
  COM["commit stage"] -->|"update at retire"| RRAT["retirement RAT"]
  RRAT -->|"copy on flush"| SRAT
  CK["branch checkpoints"] -->|"fast restore"| SRAT
```

### What each solves

| Table | Problem solved |
|---|---|
| Speculative RAT | WAR and WAW name dependencies; lets younger instructions find the right producer |
| Retirement RAT | precise exceptions; knows which physical registers hold architectural values; frees physical regs safely |
| Checkpoints (optional) | branch-mispredict recovery in 1 cycle instead of waiting for the branch to reach the head |

### Explanation
- A physical register can be freed when the *next* writer of the same architectural register commits (its old mapping is no longer reachable).
- Recovery: on exception at ROB head, copy retirement RAT → speculative RAT and reset the free list.

### Pitfalls
- Freeing a physical register at rename (instead of commit) breaks recovery.
- Terminology varies (front-end RAT / F-RAT, R-RAT, architectural map table).

### Follow-ups
- *Alternative to two RATs?* ROB-based renaming (values in ROB, ARF at commit) as in P6.

title: Computer Architecture: Purpose of CFC in Tomasulo Machine
answer: Classic Tomasulo uses reservation stations, tag-based dependency tracking, and a common data bus for result broadcast. CFC is not a universal Tomasulo term. If the source means a committed register file, its purpose is to retain committed architectural values for precise recovery; a ROB controls retirement. The exact CFC answer needs the original diagram or acronym definition.
solution:
**Key idea:** Classic Tomasulo removes RAW stalls and WAR/WAW hazards with **reservation stations** (renaming to RS tags), a **register status table** (which tag will produce each register), and a **common data bus (CDB)** broadcasting results to waiting stations and the register file. The original algorithm has **no precise exceptions**. "CFC" is not part of the standard Tomasulo vocabulary; if your material uses it for a committed register file / commit structure, its purpose is to keep the **committed architectural values** so the machine can recover precisely, while a ROB orders retirement. Confirm the acronym with the source figure.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  IQ["instruction queue"] --> RS["reservation stations (Vj, Vk, Qj, Qk)"]
  RF["register file + status (Qi)"] --> RS
  RS --> FU["FUs: add, mul, load"]
  FU --> CDB["common data bus (tag, value)"]
  CDB --> RS
  CDB --> ROB["ROB (if added)"]
  ROB -->|"in-order commit"| CRF["committed register file"]
```

### Structures

| Structure | Holds | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Reservation station | op, Vj/Vk values or Qj/Qk tags | wait for operands; renaming |
| Register status (Qi) | tag of the latest producer per register | route consumers to the right producer |
| CDB | (tag, value) broadcast | wake up dependants, update RF |
| ROB | results in program order | in-order commit, precise state |
| Committed RF / "CFC" | architectural values | restore on mispredict/exception |

### Worked example
`F2 = load` (tag Load1), `F4 = F2 * F0` (Mult1 waits on Qj = Load1), `F2 = F6 + F8` (Add1, writes register status F2 → Add1). When Load1 broadcasts, Mult1 captures the value; the RF ignores it for F2 because status now says Add1 — WAW handled by tags.

### Follow-ups
- *CDB bottleneck?* Only one (or few) result per cycle; multiple CDBs cost wiring and comparators.
- *Why add a ROB?* Speculation past branches and precise interrupts.

title: Computer Architecture: MOESI vs MESI - The O State and Performance
answer: MOESI adds Owned to MESI. An Owned cache has the dirty shared copy and is responsible for supplying or eventually writing back it; other caches may hold Shared copies while memory remains stale. This can avoid an immediate memory writeback on a remote read of dirty data. Ownership and invalidation still enforce a single writer.
solution:
**Key idea:** MOESI adds **Owned (O)** to MESI: a line that is dirty *and* shared. When another cache reads a line held in M, MESI must write the data back to memory (M→S), but MOESI lets the holder go M→**O** and supply data cache-to-cache, keeping memory stale. The O cache is responsible for supplying the line and writing it back on eviction. This saves memory bandwidth and latency for read-sharing of dirty data.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C0 as "Core0 (M)"
  participant C1 as "Core1 (I)"
  participant MEM as "Memory"
  C1->>C0: BusRd (snoop)
  Note over C0,MEM: MESI: C0 flushes line to memory, C0 M to S, C1 I to S
  Note over C0,C1: MOESI: C0 sends data to C1 only, C0 M to O, C1 I to S, memory stays stale
```

### States

| State | Dirty? | Other copies? | Supplies data on snoop | Write-back on evict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M | yes | no | yes | yes |
| O | yes | may be S copies | yes | yes |
| E | no | no | optional | no |
| S | maybe (if an O exists) | yes | no (O or memory supplies) | no |
| I | – | – | – | – |

### Performance
- Avoids a memory write each time a modified line becomes shared (producer/consumer patterns, e.g. one core writes a buffer, several read it).
- Cache-to-cache transfer is usually faster than DRAM.
- Costs: one more state, the owner must answer snoops; on eviction of O the write-back still happens (just later, often once instead of many times).

### Pitfalls
- O is still not writable: a write in O must invalidate sharers (O→M).
- Only one cache may be O for a line.

### Follow-ups
- *MESIF?* Intel's alternative adds Forward (clean shared designated responder) instead of O.

title: Computer Architecture: MOESI State Transition Table for 4-Core CMP
answer: For a snooping write-back model: local read miss I→S if shared, otherwise E; local write E→M and S/O→M after invalidating sharers. A remote read of M makes the holder O and requester S; a remote read of E makes both S. Remote ownership requests invalidate other copies, with dirty data supplied by M/O. Exact transient states require the chosen bus/directory specification.
solution:
**Key idea:** For a snooping, write-back, invalidate-based MOESI protocol, list each state's reaction to **local** events (PrRd, PrWr, eviction) and **remote/snooped** events (BusRd from another core, BusRdX/BusUpgr = another core wants to write). The same table applies to every core of a 4-core CMP; the bus (or directory) serializes requests so all cores see one order.

### Transition table (stable states)

| State | PrRd | PrWr | Evict | Snoop BusRd | Snoop BusRdX / BusUpgr |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | issue BusRd → **S** if any other copy, else **E** | issue BusRdX → **M** | – | – | – |
| **S** | hit, stay S | issue BusUpgr → **M** (others invalidate) | silent drop → I | stay S | → **I** |
| **E** | hit | silent → **M** (no bus) | silent → I | → **S** (may supply data) | → **I** |
| **O** | hit | issue BusUpgr → **M** | write back → I | supply data, stay **O** | supply data (for RdX) → **I** |
| **M** | hit | hit | write back → I | supply data → **O** | supply data → **I** |

Data source on a miss: the M or O holder if one exists, otherwise memory (or an E holder if the design allows).

### Worked example (4 cores, line X)

| Step | Event | C0 | C1 | C2 | C3 | Memory |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | C0 read | E | I | I | I | valid |
| 2 | C0 write | M | I | I | I | stale |
| 3 | C1 read | O | S | I | I | stale |
| 4 | C2 read | O | S | S | I | stale |
| 5 | C3 write (BusRdX, C0 supplies) | I | I | I | M | stale |
| 6 | C3 evicts | I | I | I | I | updated |

### Explanation
- Real implementations add **transient states** (e.g. IS_D: waiting for data, SM_A: waiting for upgrade ack) to handle races such as an invalidation arriving while an upgrade is pending — the main source of coherence bugs.
- Invariants to check in DV: single writer (≤1 of M/E per line, and M/E exclude any other valid copy), at most one O, every read returns the value of the last write.

### Follow-ups
- *Directory version?* Same stable states; the directory tracks sharers and sends point-to-point invalidations instead of broadcast snoops.

title: Verilog Macro Define Inside if-else
answer: A macro is processed before simulation. A runtime `if/else` does not conditionally execute a `define`; the preprocessor sees directives independently of runtime control flow. Use `ifdef/`ifndef for preprocessing, parameters and generate-if for elaboration, and ordinary if-statements for runtime behavior. Check include order, macro scope, and duplicate definitions.
solution:
**Key idea:** `` `define `` is handled by the **preprocessor** before elaboration or simulation, as plain text substitution in file order. A `` `define `` inside a runtime `if/else` is **not** conditional: both definitions are processed in textual order and the last one wins for all later text. Use `` `ifdef `` for compile-time choices, `parameter` + generate-if for elaboration-time choices, and ordinary `if` for run-time behavior.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SRC["source files (in compile order)"] --> PP["preprocess: define, ifdef, include"]
  PP --> EL["elaborate: parameters, generate"]
  EL --> SIM["simulate: if/else, case at run time"]
```

### Example
```systemverilog
module tb;
  bit mode = 0;
  initial begin
    if (mode) begin
      `define WIDTH 8
    end else begin
      `define WIDTH 16      // redefinition warning; this one wins (later in the text)
    end
    $display("WIDTH = %0d", `WIDTH);   // prints 16, whatever 'mode' is
  end
endmodule
```

### Do this instead

| Need | Construct |
|---|---|
| Choose code at compile time (per build) | `` `ifdef FAST_SIM ... `else ... `endif `` with `+define+FAST_SIM` |
| Choose structure per instance | `parameter int WIDTH = 16;` and `if (WIDTH == 8) begin : g8 ... end` (generate) |
| Choose behavior while running | `if (mode) ...` on a variable, or `$test$plusargs` / `$value$plusargs` |

### Pitfalls
- Macros are **global** to the compilation unit after their definition: a `` `define `` in one file leaks into files compiled later (order-dependent). Use `` `undef `` or prefixes.
- Separate compilation units (`-mfcu` vs per-file) change macro visibility between tools.
- Macros with arguments: always parenthesize — `` `define SQ(x) ((x)*(x)) ``.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a parameter be used in `ifdef`?* No — `ifdef` only tests macro names.
- *How to pass a define from the command line?* `+define+NAME=VALUE` (VCS/Xcelium/Questa).

title: Clock Divider Progression & Clock Gating
answer: A toggle flip-flop divides by two; cascaded toggles divide further but create multiple clock domains. A counter can generate enables or divided clocks. Clock gating removes selected pulses without changing the remaining edge times. Use a glitch-free ICG, generated-clock constraints, and test enable support. Prefer a clock enable when the implementation and power goals permit it.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** division changes the repeating clock rate; gating suppresses selected clock pulses. A toggle register produces divide-by-two, while a clock enable lets ordinary registers update less often without creating another clock domain.

| Input rising edge | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Toggle Q, initially 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Divide-by-four enable | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

### Implementation
```systemverilog
module divide2(input logic clk, rst_n, output logic q);
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) q <= 1'b0;
    else q <= ~q;
endmodule
```
Q has one complete period per two input periods. Cascading toggle outputs creates ripple clocks; their edges accumulate clock-to-Q delay and need separate timing treatment. A synchronous counter with an enable is usually easier to analyze when the goal is simply slower state updates.

For power gating of a clock tree, use an approved integrated clock-gating cell. It holds the enable stable during the active clock phase, preserving complete pulses. Include test-enable behavior and generated-clock constraints where required.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
An arbitrary combinational AND of clock and enable can create short pulses. Division by an odd number with a 50% duty cycle needs a specified architecture, often both edges or a dedicated clock resource. Verify reset phase, minimum pulse width, and transitions into and out of gating.

title: Max Operating Frequency & Hold Violation
answer: Maximum frequency follows the worst setup path: `fmax ≈ 1/(tcq_max+tcomb_max+tsetup-skew+uncertainty)`. Hold checks the shortest path between same-cycle edges and is mostly independent of clock period. Fix hold with inserted delay, routing, or skew correction; a slower clock usually helps setup only. Evaluate every mode and process/voltage/temperature corner.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** setup limits the available cycle time; hold protects the same-edge sampling window. Reducing frequency generally fixes neither a short data path nor excessive capture-clock lateness.

Let skew be capture-clock arrival minus launch-clock arrival. For a one-cycle path:

| Check | Required inequality |
|---|---|
| Setup | T >= tcq_max + tdata_max + tsetup - skew + Usetup |
| Hold | tcq_min + tdata_min >= thold + skew + Uhold |

### Worked example
With 80 ps clock-to-Q, 600 ps logic, 70 ps setup, 30 ps positive skew and 20 ps setup uncertainty, the minimum period is 740 ps, or approximately 1.35 GHz. These numbers are illustrative; real signoff uses library corners and propagated clocks.

For hold, suppose the minimum data arrival is 50 ps, hold time is 30 ps, positive skew is 40 ps, and uncertainty is 10 ps. The requirement is 80 ps, so at least 30 ps additional effective delay is needed. Increasing the period does not alter this same-edge inequality.

### Fixes and follow-up
Setup fixes include logic reduction, pipelining, stronger cells, and useful skew. Hold fixes include delay cells, route adjustment, or clock-skew correction. A change helping one check can hurt the other. Recheck all modes, corners, recovery/removal paths, and clock relationships after implementation; the scalar formulas do not replace full STA.

title: Dual Sequence Detector FSM (10111 & 10010)
answer: Build states for the distinct proper prefixes of 10111 and 10010, sharing common prefixes. After each input, retain the longest suffix that is a prefix of either pattern. A Mealy output fires on the final bit; retain suffix state for overlaps. Verify both patterns, overlap combinations, near matches, and reset against a shift-register reference model.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** track the longest suffix of received bits that is also a proper prefix of either `10111` or `10010`. Shared prefixes eliminate duplicated states, and suffix fallback preserves overlaps.

| State (matched prefix) | Input 0 → next | Input 1 → next | Detection |
|---|---|---|---|
| empty | empty | 1 | none |
| 1 | 10 | 1 | none |
| 10 | 100 | 101 | none |
| 101 | 10 | 1011 | none |
| 1011 | 10 | 1 | 10111 on 1 |
| 100 | empty | 1001 | none |
| 1001 | 10 | 1 | 10010 on 0 |

### Explanation
Start in empty. For `10010`, follow empty→1→10→100→1001, then emit the second-pattern pulse and retain `10`. Retaining that suffix matters: it can begin a new match without discarding accepted bits. Similarly, completing `10111` retains `1`.

A Mealy detector computes the detection from the current state and accepted input. Register that indication if a full-cycle, glitch-free pulse is required; clear the pulse on every subsequent nonmatching edge. An input-valid enable must gate both state updates and detection so idle cycles do not count as bits.

### Verification and follow-up
Compare each accepted five-bit window with the two literal patterns. Test consecutive overlaps, repeated ones/zeros, interruptions, and reset during a partial match. A Moore machine adds detection states and needs explicitly documented observation latency. Do not reset to empty after every match unless the specification forbids overlap.

title: 4-Input 1024-bit Sorting Network with CAS
answer: Use five compare-and-swap units in three layers: compare pairs (0,1) and (2,3), then (0,2) and (1,3), then (1,2). This sorts four keys. If each item is a 1024-bit record, compare its specified key and swap the whole record; if the entire value is the key, use 1024-bit comparisons. Define signedness and equal-key stability; pipeline layers if timing requires it.

title: Saturating PE Unit a*b+c
answer: Compute the signed or unsigned product at full precision, extend c, then add with enough width to retain carry/sign. For signed W-bit output, clamp above `2^(W-1)-1` or below `-2^(W-1)`; otherwise return the low W bits. Specify scaling, rounding, and pipeline latency. Verify extrema, exact saturation boundaries, and mixed signs.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** saturate the full mathematical result, not an already truncated product or sum. This example specifies signed 8-bit operands and an 8-bit signed result.

| a | b | c | Exact a*b+c | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 12 | 7 | 127 | 127 |
| 10 | 12 | 8 | 128 | 127 |
| -16 | 8 | -1 | -129 | -128 |
| -16 | 8 | 1 | -127 | -127 |

```systemverilog
module sat_mac8(input logic signed [7:0] a,b,c,
                output logic signed [7:0] y);
  logic signed [15:0] product;
  logic signed [16:0] sum;
  always_comb begin
    product = a*b;
    sum = $signed({product[15],product})
        + $signed({{9{c[7]}},c});
    if (sum > 17'sd127) y = 8'sh7f;
    else if (sum < -17'sd128) y = 8'sh80;
    else y = sum[7:0];
  end
endmodule
```
### Explanation
The product retains 16 bits, and both addends are sign-extended before the 17-bit addition. Signed comparisons against explicit bounds select either a rail or the representable result. Unsigned saturation instead clamps to zero through `2^W-1` and needs a different arithmetic contract.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
For fixed-point operands, define binary-point alignment and rounding before saturation. Pipeline latency and valid behavior are separate requirements. Verify exact rails, one beyond each rail, minimum-negative operands, and cancellation where a large product is brought back into range by c.

title: Async FIFO Gray Code SDC Constraint
answer:
Gray coding assumes adjacent pointer transitions cannot arrive as several independent changes. Constrain delay/skew from source Gray registers to the first destination synchronizer stage to a suitable bound, often the faster clock period, using the target STA flow. Mark synchronizers and prevent retiming. A false-path alone removes timing analysis but does not enforce bus coherence.

Reference: [AMD bus-skew constraints](https://docs.amd.com/r/2024.2-English/ug903-vivado-using-constraints/About-Bus-Skew-Constraints?contentId=kXqymQdxWW597oxcQ4ClQw)
solution:
> Completed by Codex.
> Reviewed and corrected by Claude.

**Key idea:** Gray coding limits each source increment to one changing bit, but routing must preserve that property at the receiving synchronizer. Declaring unrelated clocks alone does not bound pointer-bus skew.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G["Registered Gray pointer"] --> P["Bounded delay and bus skew"]
  P --> S1["Destination sync stage 1"]
  S1 --> S2["Destination sync stage 2"]
  S2 --> F["Local FIFO flag logic"]
```
### Constraints
Constrain the registered Gray outputs to the first destination synchronizer inputs using the implementation tool's supported maximum-delay and/or bus-skew mechanism. The bound must prevent transitions from consecutive source updates from being observed as an incoherent combination; a conservative design often uses the faster clock period. [Intel's dual-clock FIFO guidance](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/programmable/683082/22-1/dual-clock-fifo-timing-constraints.html) explicitly calls for skew constraints in addition to clock-domain treatment.

Example for the write-pointer crossing, assuming wclk = 4 ns and rclk = 6 ns, so the bound is min(4, 6) = 4 ns (cell names are illustrative; repeat for the read pointer going into wclk):

```tcl
# Synopsys-style SDC (DC / PrimeTime): bound the Gray bus explicitly.
# Do NOT also cover these paths with set_false_path or
# set_clock_groups -asynchronous: both take precedence over set_max_delay.
set_max_delay 4.0 -from [get_cells {u_wptr/wgray_reg[*]}] \
                  -to   [get_cells {u_w2r_sync/q1_reg[*]}]

# Vivado XDC equivalent (same pattern as the XPM CDC Gray macros):
set_max_delay -datapath_only 4.0 -from [get_cells {u_wptr/wgray_reg[*]}] \
                                 -to   [get_cells {u_w2r_sync/q1_reg[*]}]
set_bus_skew 4.0 -from [get_cells {u_wptr/wgray_reg[*]}] \
                 -to   [get_cells {u_w2r_sync/q1_reg[*]}]
```

Do not copy a generic SDC exception without checking precedence: broad asynchronous clock groups can override maximum-delay checks in some flows. Inspect exception reports and the actual timed endpoints after synthesis and routing. Keep the first-to-second synchronizer path normally timed in the destination domain, mark synchronizer registers, and prevent harmful retiming.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Gray coding does not eliminate metastability, and receiving a later pointer while skipping intermediate values is legal. Verify pointer registration, wrap behavior, reset assumptions, and both crossing directions. The commands above are a template: the real bound comes from the actual clock periods, and the exact options and exception precedence must be checked in the target STA tool's documentation and exception reports.

title: Sequence Detector Optimization
answer: Represent states as matched prefixes, share identical behavior, and remove unreachable or equivalent states. Compare Moore and Mealy latency, state encoding, and output glitch requirements. One-hot can reduce decode depth while binary can reduce flip-flop count. Optimize using synthesis timing/area results, then prove equivalence and test overlaps; fewer states do not automatically mean faster hardware.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** optimize the observable behavior and implementation cost, not just the number of state labels. Start with a correct overlap-aware detector and preserve its output timing.

| Choice | Potential benefit | Cost or risk |
|---|---|---|
| Prefix sharing | Removes duplicated history | Needs correct suffix fallback |
| State minimization | Reduces equivalent states | Must include output behavior |
| Binary encoding | Fewer registers | More decoding depth |
| One-hot encoding | Simpler local transitions | More registers and clock power |
| Mealy output | Detects final bit immediately | Input-dependent glitches |
| Registered output | Clean cycle indication | Timing contract may change |

### Procedure
List reachable states and partition states with different outputs. Refine partitions until states in each group transition into the same groups for every input. Merge only those equivalent states. For sequence matching, represent states as useful prefixes and retain the longest useful suffix after each input.

Synthesize multiple encodings under the same constraints. Compare worst-path delay, area, clock load, and switching activity. A reduced binary FSM can be slower than a larger one-hot machine because decoding, fanout, and placement matter.

### Verification and follow-up
Use a shift-register reference over accepted input bits, checking both positive detections and absence of false positives. Exercise overlapping matches and reset from every reachable state. If pipelining a detection output, explicitly update the latency specification and scoreboard rather than calling the change behaviorally equivalent.

title: Serial Divisibility-by-5 FSM
answer: For MSB-first serial bits, let state r be the remainder 0..4. On each accepted bit b, set `r_next=(2*r+b)%5`; divisible means remainder zero at the specified observation point. Define whether leading zeros and the empty input count. For LSB-first input, track bit-position weight modulo 5 instead. Verify with a software modulo reference.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** for an MSB-first binary stream, appending bit b changes value N into `2*N+b`; only its remainder modulo five is needed.

| Current remainder | Next on 0 | Next on 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | 4 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 2 |
| 4 | 3 | 4 |

```systemverilog
module div5_stream(input logic clk,rst_n,clear,valid,bit_in,
                   output logic divisible);
  logic [2:0] rem5;
  logic seen;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin rem5<=0; seen<=0; end
    else if (clear) begin rem5<=0; seen<=0; end
    else if (valid) begin
      rem5 <= ((int'(rem5)*2)+int'(bit_in))%5;
      seen <= 1;
    end
  end
  assign divisible = seen && (rem5==0);
endmodule
```
### Example and contract
The input `1010` gives remainders 1→2→0→0: decimal ten is divisible by five. The output describes all bits accepted since clear. `seen` makes the empty stream false; a nonempty string of zeros is true. Observe the registered result after the sampling edge.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
An LSB-first stream needs the positional weight as additional state because appending a bit no longer doubles the accumulated value. Define packet boundaries, output qualification, and backpressure. The modulus is constant and the input bounded to 0..9; a synthesis tool can reduce this to the five-state transition table.

title: Single-Port vs Dual-Port SRAM Interface
answer: Single-port SRAM supports one access on its port per cycle. Simple dual-port often gives one write port and one read port; true dual-port can allow reads/writes on both. Specify independent clocks, latency, and collision behavior. Check same-address read/write and dual writes against the macro datasheet; they may be undefined. Port count trades area/power for throughput.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** SRAM port names describe access capability, but latency and collisions are part of the macro contract. “Dual-port” alone is insufficient to write a correct controller.

| Organization | Typical operations per cycle | Important restriction |
|---|---|---|
| Single-port 1RW | One read or one write | Cannot independently do both |
| Simple dual-port 1R1W | One read and one write | Read/write collision semantics |
| True dual-port 2RW | Up to two independent accesses | Same-address writes may be illegal |

### Example
A producer writes address 12 while a consumer reads address 5. A 1R1W memory can support this concurrently; a single port needs arbitration or time multiplexing. If both target address 12, the returned value might be old data, new data, unspecified, or prohibited depending on the macro. Do not infer that behavior from a behavioral array's simulation ordering.

Document address width, byte enables, output-register latency, chip enable, clock domains, and power/sleep sequencing. A controller must hold or pipeline response metadata so read data stays associated with its request.

### Verification and follow-up
Test independent accesses, collisions, byte-mask overlap, disabled cycles, and boundary addresses. For separate clocks, test near-coincident edges according to the vendor's collision window. More ports generally increase physical cost; banked single-port memories may improve throughput but introduce bank conflicts and arbitration requirements.

title: create_generated_clock SDC
answer: Declare the primary clock, then describe the generated clock at its output pin with a source pin and transformation, for example `create_generated_clock -name div2 -source [get_pins u_div/CK] -divide_by 2 [get_pins u_div/Q]`. Real pin names and master selection depend on the netlist. Use edge lists or inversion options for more complex waveforms, then inspect reported clocks and timing.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** a generated clock preserves the relationship between a primary clock and a derived waveform. It is not an unrelated clock with a coincidentally matching frequency.

```tcl
# Illustrative netlist names; adapt to the actual design.
create_clock -name sys_clk -period 10.0 [get_ports clk]
create_generated_clock -name div2   -source [get_pins u_div/CK]   -divide_by 2 [get_pins u_div/Q]
```

| Clock | Rising-edge spacing | Example nominal rate |
|---|---|---|
| sys_clk | 10 ns | 100 MHz |
| div2 | 20 ns | 50 MHz |

### Explanation
The source pin identifies where the parent clock is observed; the target pin identifies the generated clock origin. `-divide_by 2` expresses the waveform transformation. STA uses the common relationship when evaluating crossings, clock latency, and edge selection. A plain independent `create_clock` on Q would lose that intended relationship.

For muxed sources, multiple masters, inversion, phase shifts, or nonuniform waveforms, the required master selection, edge list, and add options depend on the STA tool and implementation. The example assumes a conventional divide-by-two toggle output.

### Verification and follow-up
Inspect reported period, waveform, source, and clock propagation. Check that target collections resolve to real pins and no unintended paths are unconstrained. Generated-clock definitions do not replace clock-gating checks or asynchronous reset release analysis; nor do they model arbitrary data-dependent clock behavior.

title: MSI / MESI / MOESI Cache Coherence Protocols
answer: MSI has Modified, Shared, Invalid. MESI adds Exclusive for a clean unshared line, allowing a silent E→M local write. MOESI adds Owned so dirty data can be shared without immediate memory writeback. Coherence serializes writes to each line; it is distinct from memory consistency and synchronization between different addresses.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** MESI and MOESI add states to reduce unnecessary traffic while preserving a coherent value for each cache line. Coherence does not define ordering across different addresses.

| State | Data status | Other cached copies | Memory current? |
|---|---|---|---|
| M: Modified | Dirty owner | No valid peer copies | Usually no |
| E: Exclusive | Clean exclusive copy | None | Yes |
| S: Shared | Clean/shared role | May exist | Yes in MSI/MESI; not necessarily MOESI |
| O: Owned | Dirty shared owner | Shared copies may exist | No |
| I: Invalid | Unusable | Irrelevant | Irrelevant |

### Example
CPU0 reads a line that no other cache holds. MESI can grant E. Its later local store changes E→M without broadcasting an invalidation, because exclusivity is already known. MSI initially uses S, so it generally needs an ownership transaction before writing.

If CPU1 later reads CPU0's modified line, MESI typically makes the data clean/shared through the protocol's writeback mechanism. MOESI can let CPU0 become O and supply dirty data while CPU1 holds S. The owner retains responsibility for eventually writing back the current value.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Exact messages and transient states depend on the implementation. Avoid saying every Shared line implies memory is current in MOESI. Verification must check one writable owner, data forwarding, invalidation acknowledgements, eviction races, and retry handling. Atomic operations and memory fences impose additional requirements beyond stable-state coherence.

title: Booth Algorithm for Multiplication
answer: Radix-2 Booth examines the multiplier's current bit and previous bit. Pair 01 adds the multiplicand; 10 subtracts it; 00 and 11 do nothing, followed by an arithmetic right shift. It compresses runs of ones and supports signed multiplication with proper extension. Radix-4 uses -2,-1,0,+1,+2 multiples and roughly halves partial-product count. Verify negative operands and minimum signed values.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** radix-2 Booth recoding replaces runs of multiplier ones with signed boundary operations, then uses arithmetic shifts to preserve sign.

| Pair (current multiplier bit, previous bit) | Operation before shift |
|---|---|
| 00 | None |
| 01 | Add multiplicand |
| 10 | Subtract multiplicand |
| 11 | None |

### Worked example
For multiplier `0111` (7), append an initial previous bit of zero and inspect from least significant upward. The first boundary is `10`, contributing `-1` times the multiplicand. The high boundary is `01`, contributing `+8` times the multiplicand. Therefore `7*M = (8-1)*M`, replacing three positive partial products with two signed terms.

An iterative implementation maintains the accumulator, multiplier, and previous-bit register. Perform the selected add/subtract and arithmetic-right-shift the combined register each iteration. Use enough sign-extension width to represent the negation of the minimum signed multiplicand; a W-bit `-(-2^(W-1))` overflows if kept at W bits.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Logical shifts break signed results. Specify whether both operands are signed and preserve a 2W-bit final product. Exhaustive testing is practical for small widths and catches minimum-negative corner cases. Radix-4 Booth examines overlapping three-bit groups to select 0, ±M, or ±2M, reducing the number of partial products approximately by half.

title: Two-Stage Pipeline ac + bc with Power Optimization
answer: Use distributivity: `a*c+b*c=(a+b)*c`, subject to exact-width and signedness rules. Stage one can register the widened sum; stage two multiplies by c delayed to align. One multiplier may reduce area and switching, but its input is wider. Finite-width truncation or intermediate saturation can invalidate the rewrite. Check equivalence, latency, and actual switching/power reports.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** distributivity replaces two multipliers with one, but the widened sum and delayed c must preserve exact arithmetic and sample alignment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["a and b"] --> S["Widened sum register"]
  C["c"] --> D["Delay register"]
  S --> M["Multiplier"]
  D --> M
  M --> Y["Result register"]
```

```systemverilog
module factored_mac(input logic clk,rst_n,
  input logic signed [7:0] a,b,c,
  output logic signed [16:0] y);
  logic signed [8:0] sum_ab;
  logic signed [7:0] c_d;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin sum_ab<=0; c_d<=0; y<=0; end
    else begin
      sum_ab <= $signed({a[7],a}) + $signed({b[7],b});
      c_d <= c;
      y <= sum_ab*c_d;
    end
  end
endmodule
```
### Explanation
Eight-bit signed a and b require a nine-bit sum. Multiplying that by signed eight-bit c fits in 17 bits. Inputs sampled at edge k produce y after edge k+1: there are two register boundaries including the input computation stage. A streaming interface should pipeline its valid bit identically.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
The identity may fail if the original design independently rounds, saturates, or truncates each product. One wider multiplier is not automatically lower power than two smaller optimized multipliers. Compare synthesized cells and realistic switching activity; clock enables or operand isolation can reduce idle switching further. Verify equivalence using full precision and explicitly specified latency.

title: SRAM Configuration Power Analysis
answer: Power depends on depth, width, ports, access rate, banking, supply, and macro design. Compare implementations using the foundry macro's characterized leakage and energy per read/write, with realistic activity. Banking can reduce switched capacitance but adds decode/mux overhead. Unused banks can sleep if supported. No numerical ranking is possible without the candidate configurations and workload.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** compare characterized energy under the same workload. SRAM capacity alone cannot determine which depth/width/banking configuration consumes less power.

| Contributor | Estimate | Required information |
|---|---|---|
| Read activity | reads/s × joules/read | Macro characterization |
| Write activity | writes/s × joules/write | Mask and data activity |
| Leakage | Sum of active/sleep leakage | Mode residency and PVT |
| Surrounding logic | Decoder/mux/clock power | Implementation and toggles |

### Worked example
Suppose candidate A consumes 10 pJ/read and 20 µW leakage; B consumes 6 pJ/read and 50 µW leakage. At one million reads/s, their simplified powers are 30 µW and 56 µW. At ten million reads/s, they are 120 µW and 110 µW. The preferred candidate changes with activity. These are illustrative numbers, not measured macro results.

Banking can reduce the capacitance activated per access, but adds selection logic and may change timing. Wider accesses can fetch unnecessary bits; narrower accesses may require more cycles. Compare equal useful throughput and account for read-modify-write operations and port conflicts.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
The candidate configurations and workload are missing, so no numerical ranking is defensible. Include voltage, frequency, temperature, sleep entry/exit energy, retention requirements, and wake latency. Verification should ensure disabled banks really stop unnecessary accesses without losing required state.

title: 4-bit x 4-bit Array Multiplier FA/HA Count
answer: For one conventional unsigned 4x4 array, generate 16 partial products with AND gates, then reduce and add them; a common textbook layout uses 8 full adders and 4 half adders. The exact count changes with the reduction topology or signed implementation. Draw the weighted bit columns and count compressors to justify the chosen layout rather than treating the count as universal.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** generate 16 unsigned partial-product bits, then count the adders in a specified reduction layout. “4×4 multiplier” alone does not uniquely determine its adder count.

| Weight column | Initial partial-product count |
|---|---|
| 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 3 |
| 3 | 4 |
| 4 | 3 |
| 5 | 2 |
| 6 | 1 |

### Conventional row-add construction
Let row j be the four bits `a[i]&b[j]`, shifted left by j. Add row 0 to row 1 using one HA at weight 1, two FAs at weights 2 and 3, and one HA at weight 4. Next add row 2 to the remaining upper result using one HA at weight 2 and three FAs at weights 3..5. Add row 3 using one HA at weight 3 and three FAs at weights 4..6.

This construction uses **16 AND gates, 4 half adders, and 8 full adders**, producing an eight-bit product. Each carry moves to the next higher weight; a half adder has no carry input.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Wallace/Dadda compression, optimized final adders, and signed Baugh-Wooley/Booth structures can change the count. Do not silently apply the unsigned layout to signed operands. Verify all 256 input pairs against integer multiplication and inspect the actual netlist when the question asks about synthesized rather than textbook cell counts.

title: Latchup Effect in CMOS
answer: Latchup is unintended conduction through the parasitic PNPN structure formed by CMOS wells/substrate. Once triggered, it can sustain a large supply-to-ground current. Reduce risk with well/substrate contacts, guard rings, spacing, suitable processes, and limits on injected current or over/undershoot. This is a physical electrical effect, not an RTL latch.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** CMOS latchup is a parasitic, self-sustaining supply-current path. It is unrelated to accidentally inferring an RTL latch.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["Injected current or supply disturbance"] --> P["Parasitic bipolar devices turn on"]
  P --> R["Regenerative PNPN conduction"]
  R --> C["Large supply-to-ground current"]
  C --> H["Heating and possible damage"]
```

### Explanation
The well and substrate structures form coupled parasitic bipolar devices. A disturbance can trigger positive feedback; if the available current exceeds the holding requirement, conduction can persist after the initiating disturbance disappears. Removing power or sufficiently reducing current may be necessary to end it. This mechanism and its qualification tests are described in [TI's latchup white paper](https://www.ti.com/lit/wp/scaa124/scaa124.pdf).

Layout mitigations include frequent well/substrate contacts, guard rings, appropriate spacing, and processes designed to isolate devices. System mitigations constrain pin injection current, overshoot, undershoot, and problematic power sequencing according to the component specification.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
An ESD event can trigger latchup, but ESD and latchup are different failure mechanisms. A logic simulation cannot prove latchup immunity. Use foundry layout rules and device qualification data, then investigate abnormal current with electrical measurements. The exact trigger and holding conditions depend on the physical process and geometry; there is no universal safe current threshold for all CMOS devices.

title: Tristate Buffer Circuit and Applications
answer: A tristate buffer drives 0/1 when enabled and high impedance when disabled. It supports shared buses, especially I/O pins, if only one driver is enabled. Floating buses need a defined bias or keeper where appropriate. Internal FPGA tristates typically synthesize to muxes. Verify no overlapping enables and define behavior when every driver is off.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** high impedance means the output driver is disconnected. It is neither logic zero nor a stored logic value.

| Enable | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 or 1 | Z |
| 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |

```systemverilog
module tristate_pin(input logic enable, data,
                     inout wire pad);
  assign pad = enable ? data : 1'bz;
endmodule
```
### Shared bus example
Two devices may connect to the same pad if ownership ensures only one actively drives it. Before ownership changes, define a turnaround interval so the outgoing driver releases the bus before the incoming driver enables. If every driver is off, a pull resistor or keeper can establish the required idle behavior.

In four-state simulation, conflicting strong zero and one drivers typically resolve to X. Electrically the conflict can cause large current, so functional correctness alone is insufficient. A keeper is weak state preservation, not permission for two strong drivers to contend.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Internal FPGA tristates commonly become multiplexers; external I/O resources support actual high impedance. A floating input can be noisy and consume excess current. Verify one-hot-or-zero drive enables, idle behavior, turnaround, reset ownership, and unknown enable conditions. Open-drain buses are a related case where devices actively drive only low and a pull-up supplies high.

title: 2-Stage Synchronizer: Metastability, Design, and Analysis
answer: The first destination flop can become metastable; the second samples after a resolution interval. More stages increase MTBF but add latency. Use a recognized synchronizer structure, close placement, and only the final-stage output. It is suitable for a slowly changing single-bit level; short pulses and coherent multibit words need different protocols. Simulation cannot model the real analog failure probability.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** two destination-clock registers give a metastable first stage time to resolve before downstream logic uses the signal. They reduce failure probability rather than guaranteeing zero failures.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Asynchronous level"] --> S1["First destination flop"]
  S1 --> S2["Second destination flop"]
  S2 --> L["Destination logic"]
```

```systemverilog
module sync_level(input logic dst_clk,rst_n,async_level,
                  output logic level);
  (* ASYNC_REG = "TRUE" *) logic s1,s2;
  always_ff @(posedge dst_clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) begin s1<=0; s2<=0; end
    else begin s1<=async_level; s2<=s1; end
  assign level=s2;
endmodule
```
### Design reasoning
Only s2 feeds functional logic. Keep the interstage route short so most of the destination period remains available for resolution, and time that path normally. A typical MTBF model grows exponentially with available resolution time and decreases with destination frequency and input transition rate; the constants come from library characterization.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Assume reset deassertion meets the destination-domain reset methodology. A short source pulse can be missed entirely; use pulse stretching, a toggle protocol, or a handshake. Independently synchronizing word bits does not ensure coherent data. RTL simulation cannot reproduce analog metastability probability. Verify structural CDC rules, implementation placement, reset release, and the level's required minimum persistence; use additional stages when the system reliability target requires them.

title: Gray Code Binary Conversion & CDC Use Case
answer: Binary to Gray is `g=b^(b>>1)`. Gray to binary uses prefix XOR: MSB is unchanged and each lower binary bit is the XOR of Gray bits above and including it. Adjacent reflected-Gray values differ by one bit, making FIFO pointers safer to synchronize. Physical delay/skew constraints still matter, and sampled pointers can legitimately skip intermediate values.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** reflected Gray code changes exactly one bit between adjacent counter values. Conversion uses XOR; it does not make arbitrary multibit data safe to cross clock domains.

| Binary | Gray = binary XOR (binary >> 1) |
|---|---|
| 000 | 000 |
| 001 | 001 |
| 010 | 011 |
| 011 | 010 |
| 100 | 110 |

```systemverilog
module gray_convert(input logic [3:0] binary,gray,
                    output logic [3:0] encoded,decoded);
  assign encoded = binary ^ (binary >> 1);
  always_comb begin
    decoded[3]=gray[3];
    for (int i=2;i>=0;i--) decoded[i]=decoded[i+1]^gray[i];
  end
endmodule
```
### CDC application
An asynchronous FIFO keeps local binary pointers for memory addressing and registers the corresponding Gray pointer before crossing. Each destination bit uses a synchronizer, then local logic compares the received pointer to its own pointer. Delayed remote visibility creates conservative full/empty behavior.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
A combinational Gray encoder can glitch as binary counter bits change; cross a registered Gray result. Routing skew must preserve the intended one-transition behavior. A destination can skip several source values, so consecutive observed Gray samples may differ in multiple bits even when the crossing is correct. Check one-hot changes in the source clock domain, not across arbitrarily spaced received samples. Arbitrary jumps or a nonstandard wrap require a separate proof.

title: Async FIFO Data Path Handling
answer: Store payload in a dual-port memory. The write domain writes data before publishing the advanced write pointer; the read domain observes the synchronized pointer before treating that entry as available. Synchronize Gray pointers, not every payload bit. Respect RAM read latency and ensure an entry is not overwritten before consumption. Verify data order across unrelated clocks and reset sequences.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** FIFO payload travels through dual-port storage. Pointer synchronization controls when a stored word is safe to consume; synchronizing every payload bit separately would destroy coherence.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["Write clock: accept data"] --> M["Dual-port memory"]
  W --> P["Publish advanced Gray pointer"]
  P --> S["Read-domain synchronizer"]
  S --> E["Read-domain empty logic"]
  E --> R["Read request"]
  M --> R
  R --> O["Output valid and data"]
```

### Ordering argument
On an accepted write, the write port stores the payload at the current address and advances its local pointer. The read domain sees that advancement only after synchronization latency. Until then, it conservatively treats the location as unavailable. Once visible, the word remains owned by the reader until an accepted read advances the read pointer; the writer learns about that release later through its own synchronizer.

Memory timing still matters. A synchronous read RAM returns data after its specified latency, so the controller must align output-valid and metadata. A first-word-fall-through interface needs explicit prefetch logic or a compatible memory implementation.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
The reasoning assumes a correctly constrained pointer crossing and supported independent-clock memory behavior. Never overwrite unread entries or read from empty. Verify a reference queue across unrelated clock ratios, simultaneous operations, wrap, backpressure, and coordinated reset. Resetting only one pointer domain without an agreed flush protocol can expose stale data or corrupt occupancy.

title: Async FIFO Architecture
answer: An asynchronous FIFO uses local binary pointers for memory addresses and Gray pointers for crossing domains. Each domain synchronizes the other pointer, computes its own full/empty state, and accepts operations only when permitted. Typical reflected-Gray implementations use power-of-two depth and one extra wrap bit. Flags are conservative because remote updates take time to arrive.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** each domain owns its binary address pointer and local status flag; only registered Gray pointers cross the boundary.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["Write pointer and full logic"] --> RAM["Dual-port RAM"]
  RAM --> R["Read pointer and empty logic"]
  W --> WS["Gray sync into read clock"]
  WS --> R
  R --> RS["Gray sync into write clock"]
  RS --> W
```

### Pointer equations
For depth `2^A`, use A address bits plus one wrap bit. On accepted operations, advance the local binary pointer and derive its Gray encoding as `b ^ (b >> 1)`. Empty is equality between the next local read Gray pointer and the synchronized write Gray pointer. In the usual reflected-Gray full test, compare the next write Gray pointer against the synchronized read Gray pointer with its **top two bits inverted** and the remaining bits unchanged.

An operation is accepted only when its local permission allows it. Compute registered next flags consistently with the accepted increment, rather than mixing current and next pointer conventions.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
This full-test description assumes the conventional power-of-two FIFO with appropriate pointer width. Remote updates arrive late, so a flag may remain asserted for extra cycles after space or data becomes available; that is safe conservatism. Verify no overflow/underflow, ordering, every wrap boundary, reset coordination, memory read latency, synchronizer placement, and Gray-bus timing constraints.

title: Same Frequency, Different Phase - Why CDC Still Needed
answer: Equal nominal frequencies do not guarantee a safe sampling relationship. Independent clocks can drift in phase and violate setup/hold. Use CDC structures if their relationship is unconstrained. If both clocks have a known fixed relationship generated from a common source, constrain and time the paths as related clocks instead. Frequency equality alone does not establish that relationship.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** safe synchronous timing requires a guaranteed edge relationship, not just equal numbers on two frequency labels.

| Clock relationship | Correct treatment |
|---|---|
| Same source, defined phase and uncertainty | Related-clock STA |
| Independent sources, nominally equal frequency | Asynchronous CDC |
| Common frequency but phase may change | Analyze the actual phase-control contract |

### Example
Two oscillators are each described as 100 MHz, but one is slightly faster. Their relative phase gradually sweeps through all values, including the receiving register's setup/hold aperture. Even perfectly equal frequencies would be unsafe if their arbitrary fixed phase placed the data transition inside that aperture.

For a stable single-bit level, use a destination synchronizer. For events use a suitable handshake/toggle scheme; for data streams use an asynchronous FIFO. These protocols accommodate uncertain sampling latency rather than assuming a particular edge separation.

If both clocks come from a common source with a documented fixed phase shift, describe that relationship in timing constraints. STA can then check the correct launch/capture edges, insertion delay, jitter, and setup/hold requirements. A synchronizer is not inherently required for every crossing with a different clock name.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Clock muxing, PLL relock, spread spectrum, and dynamic phase changes can invalidate a steady-state relationship. Establish which operating modes are supported and verify safe transitions. Frequency matching by measurement does not prove the required bound on phase.

title: FIFO with Non-Power-of-2 Depth
answer: A synchronous FIFO can explicitly wrap pointers at DEPTH-1 and use occupancy. A conventional Gray-pointer asynchronous FIFO cannot simply truncate the sequence at arbitrary depth because wrap may change several bits. Use a proven arbitrary-depth scheme or a power-of-two physical FIFO with a safely enforced lower logical capacity. Verify wrap and remote visibility carefully.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** arbitrary-depth synchronous FIFOs are straightforward, but abruptly wrapping a conventional Gray counter can break an asynchronous FIFO's CDC assumption.

| Binary sequence for depth 6 | Gray value |
|---|---|
| 0 | 000 |
| 1 | 001 |
| 2 | 011 |
| 3 | 010 |
| 4 | 110 |
| 5 | 111 |
| Wrap to 0 | 000: three bits change |

### Synchronous design
Use an explicit address wrap at `DEPTH-1`, plus an occupancy count ranging from zero through DEPTH. Update occupancy according to accepted write/read operations. Simultaneous accepted operations leave occupancy unchanged, while their memory-collision behavior still follows the storage implementation.

### Asynchronous design
Do not reuse that truncated Gray sequence with ordinary bit synchronizers. One option is a proven arbitrary-depth pointer protocol. Another is a power-of-two physical FIFO with a smaller logical occupancy limit. For the latter, preserve the full power-of-two binary/Gray pointer cycle and derive a conservative write-domain occupancy from the synchronized read pointer; do not wrap addresses at the logical limit. This approach needs explicit modular-distance and reset reasoning.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
The extra physical entries and conservative status latency affect usable throughput. Verify every physical wrap, logical-limit boundary, extreme clock ratio, and stale remote pointer condition. If minimum storage area is critical, use a validated architecture rather than inventing a shorter Gray cycle from binary truncation.

title: FIFO Registered Output and Empty Flag Design
answer: Distinguish memory occupancy from output-valid state. A registered RAM read returns data later, so reserve or pop the entry at request acceptance and assert output valid when data arrives. A first-word-fall-through interface instead prefetches the head. Define whether empty means no stored words or no externally available word. Check the last read, backpressure, and simultaneous refill.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** accepting a read and presenting its result are distinct events when memory has registered output. Track pending responses and externally visible valid data separately from stored occupancy.

| Edge | Action | Memory occupancy | Output state |
|---|---|---|---|
| k | Accept last read request | Becomes 0 | Response pending |
| k+1 | RAM response arrives | 0 | Valid word available |
| k+2 | Consumer accepts word | 0 | No valid word |

The table assumes a one-cycle response path and a ready consumer at k+2. Different RAM primitives require different alignment.

### Interface choices
In a request/response FIFO, empty can prohibit new read requests while an earlier request still has data pending. In a first-word-fall-through FIFO, the consumer sees the head word with an output-valid indication and pops it using a handshake. Prefetch logic fills that output slot ahead of consumption.

A prefetched word still counts toward total logical FIFO contents until the interface's defined consumption event. Conversely, if a request already reserves an entry, do not let another request reserve it again. Capacity accounting must include all holding registers and pending memory transactions according to the architecture.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Check the final word under backpressure, refill while empty, simultaneous pop/push, and reset with a pending response. Never equate “RAM has no unread entries” with “output has no valid data” without proving those states are identical in the chosen implementation.

title: AXI Valid-Ready Handshake FSM
answer:
Transfer occurs only on a clock edge with VALID and READY high. A source asserts VALID independently of READY, and holds VALID and payload stable while stalled. A registered source needs an output slot that can be replaced when empty or consumed. AXI's channels handshake independently; the write address and data need not arrive together.

Reference: [Arm AXI protocol specification](https://documentation-service.arm.com/static/63ff0ebd56ea36189d4e7ee7)
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** transfer occurs at a rising edge with VALID and READY both high. Once VALID is asserted, the source must preserve VALID and payload while READY is low.

```wavedrom
{"signal":[{"name":"clk","wave":"p....."},{"name":"valid","wave":"01..0."},{"name":"ready","wave":"0..1.."},{"name":"data","wave":"x=..x.","data":["A"]}],"head":{"text":"A remains stable throughout the stall"}}
```

### One-entry source buffer
```systemverilog
module elastic #(parameter int W=32)(input logic clk,rst_n,
  input logic in_valid, input logic [W-1:0] in_data,
  output logic in_ready, output logic out_valid,
  output logic [W-1:0] out_data, input logic out_ready);
  assign in_ready = !out_valid || out_ready;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin out_valid<=0; out_data<='0; end
    else if (in_ready) begin
      out_valid<=in_valid;
      if (in_valid) out_data<=in_data;
    end
  end
endmodule
```
This generic ready/valid buffer replaces its word when empty or when the current word is consumed. The output cannot change while stalled. It contains a combinational backward READY path; an AXI boundary requiring no input-to-output combinational path needs a registered-ready/skid-buffer architecture instead.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
The source must not wait for READY before initially offering VALID. AXI write address and write data are independent channels: do not require simultaneous arrival. Verify sustained throughput, arbitrary stalls, reset, and payload stability. Include sideband fields in the held payload, and check channel-specific AXI dependencies separately.

title: Flip-Flop vs Latch
answer: A flip-flop samples at an edge. A latch is transparent while its enable level is active and holds afterward. Latches can allow time borrowing but require careful phase/hold analysis. In RTL, use `always_ff` for registers and `always_latch` for intentional latches. An incomplete combinational assignment can infer an unintended latch.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** a flip-flop samples at a clock edge; a latch follows its input throughout an active enable level and holds the last value when that interval closes.

| Property | Positive-edge flip-flop | Active-high latch |
|---|---|---|
| Sampling | Rising edge | Entire enable-high interval |
| Held state | Between edges | While enable is low |
| Timing opportunity | Fixed edge boundaries | Time borrowing across stages |
| Main hazard | Setup/hold violation | Race-through and closing-edge timing |

```systemverilog
module storage_examples(input logic clk,en,d,
                        output logic q_ff,q_latch);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) q_ff <= d;
  always_latch if (en) q_latch <= d;
endmodule
```
### Explanation
The latch intentionally has no assignment when disabled, because storage is its purpose. In contrast, a supposedly combinational block with an unassigned path can accidentally infer a latch. Coding intent and synthesis results must agree.

Latch-based pipelines can let a slow stage use part of the next phase's available interval. That benefit comes with phase constraints, hold checks, and careful handling of overlapping enables. Two same-phase transparent latches in succession can allow a value to race through both.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
A latch is not universally smaller or lower power once clocking and timing constraints are included. Establish the target library and pipeline architecture. Explain setup/hold relative to the latch's closing edge, and verify reset behavior, transparency, and whether downstream logic can tolerate changes during the open interval.

title: Avoiding Unintended Latches in RTL
answer: Assign every combinational output on every path. Set defaults at the top of `always_comb`, then override in if/case branches; include appropriate default cases. Use blocking assignments in combinational logic. A register retaining its value in a clocked block is intentional state and is not a latch. Inspect synthesis warnings and lint for incomplete assignments.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** combinational logic must assign every output on every execution path. Defaults followed by explicit overrides make the intended behavior visible.

```systemverilog
module comb_example(input logic valid,sel,
  input logic [7:0] a,b, output logic [7:0] y,
  output logic ready);
  always_comb begin
    y = '0;
    ready = 1'b0;
    if (valid) begin
      ready = 1'b1;
      if (sel) y = a;
      else y = b;
    end
  end
endmodule
```

| Condition | y | ready |
|---|---|---|
| valid=0 | 0 | 0 |
| valid=1, sel=0 | b | 1 |
| valid=1, sel=1 | a | 1 |

### Explanation
Without the initial assignments, an inactive valid branch could retain the previous values. Hardware then needs storage. Merely declaring `always_comb` communicates intent and enables tool checks; it does not fill missing assignments with zeros.

Use blocking assignments for combinational computations, including intermediate variables. In an FSM, default next-state to current-state and default every combinational output before decoding transitions. That self-loop describes next-state logic feeding a separate register, not an inferred latch.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
An incomplete case statement, partially assigned vector, or loop that executes zero times can also retain values. Avoid self-assignment as a combinational default. Lint and synthesis should report no unexpected latch cells. A clocked register without an else intentionally holds state; that is a flip-flop enable, not an unintended latch.

title: Pipeline Waveform - always @(posedge clk) A=en?1:C; B=A; C=B;
answer: With blocking assignments in the single shown process, A gets `en?1:old_C`, then B gets new A, and C gets new B. All three end with the same value on that edge; it is not a three-stage pipeline. With nonblocking assignments, B gets old A and C gets old B. The exact waveform still needs initial values and en over time.

title: CDC Multi-bit Transfer - Why Not 2-FF Synchronizer?
answer: Independent bit synchronizers can deliver bits from different source updates, producing an incoherent word. For stable bundled data, synchronize a request and hold data until acknowledgement. Use an asynchronous FIFO for streams or Gray coding for suitable counters. Synchronizing bits independently is only acceptable when those bits are genuinely independent controls and reconvergence is safe.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** separate synchronizers protect individual bits from metastability propagation; they do not preserve which source word those bits belonged to.

| Source update | Bit 1 seen early? | Bit 0 seen late? | Possible received word |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01 → 10 | 1 | 1 | 11, never transmitted |
| 01 → 10 | 0 | 0 | 00, never transmitted |

### Bundled-data handshake
The source captures a complete word into a holding register and changes a request indicator. The destination synchronizes the request, captures the stable word only after the protocol's settling requirement is met, and returns an acknowledgement through another synchronizer. The source keeps the word unchanged until acknowledgement permits reuse.

This protocol must constrain the data path relative to the request visibility; “hold until ack” alone does not justify an arbitrarily slow data route. Reset must initialize request/acknowledgement consistently so no phantom transaction occurs.

For sustained throughput, an asynchronous FIFO decouples producer and consumer clocks. For a monotonically incrementing pointer, registered Gray encoding can be appropriate with physical skew constraints. Independent status flags may use separate synchronizers only if there is no unsafe reconvergent relationship.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
A two-bit encoded state is a coherent word, not two independent controls. Check that the destination captures each requested word exactly once and the source cannot overwrite a pending transfer. Analyze latency, backpressure, reset during transfer, and maximum input event rate.

title: 128-bit Priority Arbiter with Logic Depth Analysis
answer: For lowest-index priority, derive each grant from its request and absence of all higher-priority requests. A naive serial prefix chain has O(N) depth; a balanced prefix/tree encoder gives approximately O(log2 N), or seven combining levels for 128 inputs, plus output decode. Area and exact delay depend on fanout, cell mapping, and output encoding. Fixed priority can starve low-priority requests.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** priority selection can be expressed as a prefix OR, but physical depth depends on whether that prefix is built serially or as a balanced tree.

For lowest-index priority, `grant[i] = request[i] & ~OR(request[i-1:0])`.

| Structure | Combining depth for 128 inputs | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Linear prefix chain | Up to 127 | Simple, potentially slow |
| Balanced prefix/tree | About 7 levels | More wiring/fanout management |
| Hierarchical groups | Local select + group select | Placement-friendly partitioning |

### Behavioral specification
```systemverilog
module priority128(input logic [127:0] req,
                    output logic [127:0] grant);
  logic found;
  always_comb begin
    grant='0;
    found=0;
    for (int i=0;i<128;i++) begin
      if (req[i] && !found) begin
        grant[i]=1;
        found=1;
      end
    end
  end
endmodule
```
This code specifies priority correctly but does **not** guarantee a balanced implementation. Constrain and inspect synthesis, or explicitly instantiate a balanced prefix architecture when required.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Seven OR-combining levels is an abstract structural estimate, not seven total cell delays: output masking, encoding, wire load, and fanout add cost. Verify one-hot-or-zero grants, grant subset of requests, and no lower-priority winner while a higher-priority request exists. A fixed-priority arbiter can starve request 127 indefinitely; round-robin arbitration needs state and a different fairness specification.

title: Cache - CPU Write, Set Mapping, PLRU
answer: A cache address splits into byte offset, set index, and tag. A write hit changes the data and marks dirty for write-back; a write miss follows the allocation policy. For tree PLRU, update bits along the accessed way's path and use them to select a victim, with invalid ways preferred. Exact index bits require capacity, line size, associativity, and address width.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** first derive the address mapping, then apply write and replacement policies. Cache geometry and policy are missing, so the following numbers are an explicit example.

For a 32 KiB, four-way cache with 64-byte lines and 32-bit byte addresses, there are `32768/(4*64)=128` sets.

| Address field | Bits | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Offset | [5:0] | Byte within line |
| Index | [12:6] | One of 128 sets |
| Tag | [31:13] | Identify resident line |

### Write behavior
On a write-back hit, merge the enabled bytes and mark the line dirty. On a miss, write-allocate fetches or obtains ownership of a line before the store; no-write-allocate forwards the store without installing a line. A dirty victim needs writeback, and a coherent cache must obtain write permission before modifying a shared line.

### Tree PLRU
Four ways require three tree bits. Define each bit to point toward the less-recently-used subtree. Accessing a way updates every bit on its root-to-leaf path to point away from that way. Victim selection follows the stored directions, unless an invalid way can be chosen first.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Tree PLRU approximates recency and is not exact LRU. Document bit polarity, update timing, and concurrent miss behavior. Verify partial stores, dirty eviction, invalid-way preference, and address aliases. Different capacities, line sizes, or associativities change the field boundaries.

title: Packet Stream Interface Signals
answer: A streaming interface commonly has data, valid, ready, start/end-of-packet, byte-valid/keep, and optional ID/destination/error metadata. Define which side drives each signal and what remains stable under backpressure. A beat transfers on valid&&ready. Specify partial last beats, empty packets, interleaving, reset, and error behavior. The title does not identify one particular protocol.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** define a beat-level transfer contract and packet boundaries separately. The title does not specify AXI-Stream or any other particular protocol.

| Signal | Typical owner | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| data | Producer | Beat payload |
| valid | Producer | Payload and metadata are valid |
| ready | Consumer | Can accept a beat |
| sop/eop or last | Producer | Packet boundary metadata |
| keep | Producer | Valid byte lanes |
| id/destination/error | Producer | Optional routing/status |

### Example
A ten-byte packet on a four-byte-wide bus needs three accepted beats. Their valid-byte masks might be `1111`, `1111`, `0011`, assuming byte lane zero comes first. Only the third beat carries EOP. If READY drops during that final beat, DATA, KEEP, EOP, and other metadata remain stable with VALID asserted until transfer.

Define whether packet starts are explicit or inferred from the previous end. Also specify whether packets can interleave, whether empty packets exist, and whether errors terminate or annotate a packet.

### Verification and follow-up
Check beat stability during stalls, exactly one packet termination, byte count, and reset handling for partial packets. A scoreboard reconstructs packets from accepted beats, never from clock cycles alone. “Valid is high for three cycles” does not imply three transfers if the consumer stalls. Credit-based and non-backpressured streams require different overflow and flow-control rules.

title: Implement AND Gate Using 2-to-1 MUX
answer: For `y=a&b`, use select a, input 0 tied to 0, and input 1 connected to b: `y = a ? b : 1'b0`. Either operand may be the select. Verify the four input combinations.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** a two-input mux implements Shannon expansion. Select on a and choose the appropriate constant/function for each value of a.

For `y=a&b`, when a=0 the result must be zero; when a=1 it must equal b.

| a (select) | b | Selected mux input | y |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | D0=0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | D0=0 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | D1=b | 0 |
| 1 | 1 | D1=b | 1 |

```systemverilog
module and_using_mux(input logic a,b, output logic y);
  assign y = a ? b : 1'b0;
endmodule
```

### Explanation
The mux equation is `y=(~a & D0) | (a & D1)`. Substitution gives `(~a & 0) | (a & b)=a&b`. Since AND is commutative, b can instead be the select with D0=0 and D1=a.

### Pitfalls and follow-up
Check which physical mux pin is selected when select is high; swapping D0 and D1 changes the function. This is a logical construction, not a guarantee that synthesis retains a mux cell: optimization may map it to an AND gate. The same method implements OR with D0=b and D1=1, or inversion with D0=1 and D1=0. Compare truth tables before optimizing timing or cell area.

title: Race Condition in Verilog initial Blocks
answer: Separate initial blocks run concurrently in the active region; their ordering is unspecified. If one writes a variable and another reads it at the same time, the result can be race-dependent. Put ordered operations in one process, use an event/handshake, or sample in a suitable clocking region. A #0 delay is not a robust general race fix.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** separate initial blocks are concurrent. Their active-region execution order is unspecified, so a read racing a write at the same simulation time is nondeterministic.

```systemverilog
module ordered_initialization;
  int value;
  initial begin
    value = 5;
    $display("value=%0d", value);
  end
endmodule
```

| Structure | Guaranteed result? |
|---|---|
| One initial writes; another immediately displays | No ordering guarantee |
| Write followed by display in one process | Yes, displays assigned value |
| Clocked nonblocking update followed by active-region display | Display sees pre-NBA value |
| Appropriate postponed observation | Can see settled same-time updates |

### Explanation
The simplest fix for initialization with a required order is to express that order in one process. If independent processes must coordinate, use a persistent condition, mailbox, or a properly designed handshake. A bare event trigger can be missed if the listener has not started waiting, so it needs its own ordering argument.
