```systemverilog
// returns number of beats that fit before the next 4KB boundary (aligned start)
function automatic int unsigned beats_to_4k(input longint unsigned addr, input int unsigned bytes);
  longint unsigned aligned = addr & ~(longint'(bytes) - 1);
  return (4096 - (aligned & 'hFFF)) / bytes;
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- 12-bit arithmetic overflows: `addr[11:0] + 64` wraps to a small number and the check passes falsely — widen.
- Using `addr + total` instead of the aligned base mis-handles unaligned starts.
- Bursts ending exactly at `0x...FFF` are legal (`<= 4096`, not `< 4096`).
- AXI4 INCR allows up to 256 beats, so with 128-B beats a single burst can be 32 KB — the 4 KB rule is the real limit.

### Follow-ups
- *AHB equivalent?* 1 KB boundary.
- *Coverage?* Bursts ending exactly at the boundary, one byte before it, and every size.

title: Carry-Select Adder: Design and Timing Analysis
answer: A carry-select adder computes each upper block twice, assuming carry-in 0 and 1, then selects using the real carry. The low block computes the first carry normally. This trades extra area/power for a shorter carry path. Select block sizes from actual gate delays; uniform blocks are not always optimal. Verify addition and carry-out across block boundaries.
solution:
**Key idea:** Split the adder into blocks. Each upper block computes its sum **twice in parallel** — once assuming carry-in 0 and once assuming 1 — and a mux picks the right one when the real carry arrives. The critical path becomes *first block ripple + one mux per block* instead of a full-width ripple, at the cost of ~2x adder area/power.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B0["block 0 (bits 3:0) RCA"] -->|c4| M1["mux"]
  subgraph BLK1["block 1 (bits 7:4)"]
    S10["RCA cin=0"]
    S11["RCA cin=1"]
  end
  S10 --> M1
  S11 --> M1
  M1 -->|c8| M2["mux"]
  subgraph BLK2["block 2 (bits 11:8)"]
    S20["RCA cin=0"]
    S21["RCA cin=1"]
  end
  S20 --> M2
  S21 --> M2
  M2 -->|c12| M3["mux block 3"]
```

### Timing analysis (16-bit, t_c = 1 per bit of ripple, t_mux = 1)
| Architecture | Critical path | Delay |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ripple-carry 16 | 16 carry stages | **16** |
| Carry-select, 4 uniform 4-bit blocks | 4 (block 0) + 3 muxes | **7** |
| Carry-select, variable blocks 2-2-3-4-5 | 2 + 4 muxes, each block ready exactly when its select arrives | **6** |

Variable sizing: block k's internal ripple finishes at the same time as its select arrives, so block size grows by 1 each stage → delay ≈ sqrt(2N).

### Code (parameterized, uniform blocks)
```systemverilog
module csel_adder #(
  parameter int N = 16,
  parameter int B = 4                       // N % B == 0
) (
  input  logic [N-1:0] a, b,
  input  logic         cin,
  output logic [N-1:0] sum,
  output logic         cout
);
  localparam int NB = N / B;
  logic [NB:0] c;
  assign c[0] = cin;

  for (genvar k = 0; k < NB; k++) begin : g_blk
    logic [B:0] s0, s1;                     // B-bit sum + carry
    if (k == 0) begin : g_first             // block 0: real carry-in, no duplication
      assign s0 = a[B-1:0] + b[B-1:0] + cin;
      assign sum[B-1:0] = s0[B-1:0];
      assign c[1]       = s0[B];
    end else begin : g_sel
      assign s0 = a[k*B +: B] + b[k*B +: B];          // assume carry-in 0
      assign s1 = a[k*B +: B] + b[k*B +: B] + 1'b1;   // assume carry-in 1
      assign sum[k*B +: B] = c[k] ? s1[B-1:0] : s0[B-1:0];
      assign c[k+1]        = c[k] ? s1[B]     : s0[B];
    end
  end
  assign cout = c[NB];
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `s0 = a[..] + b[..]` must be assigned to a (B+1)-bit target so the carry is kept (context-determined width).
- Uniform blocks are not optimal; real block sizes come from actual gate delays (mux vs FA carry).
- Verification: exhaustive for small N, random + directed carry-propagate patterns (`a = 0xFFFF, b = 1`, carries rippling exactly across block boundaries), compare to `a + b + cin`.

### Follow-ups
- *Carry-select vs carry-lookahead?* CLA computes generate/propagate trees (log delay, less area than duplicating); carry-select duplicates sums.
- *Conditional-sum adder?* Carry-select applied recursively down to single bits.

title: 1-bit D Flip-Flop Without always Block - Verilog RTL
answer: An edge-triggered flip-flop cannot be described by a simple combinational assign. Instantiate a flip-flop cell or build a structural master-slave latch circuit with feedback and appropriate primitives. Synthesis support and timing depend on the technology. A latch-like feedback expression is not automatically a valid DFF. The exact permitted implementation depends on whether primitives or library cells are allowed.

title: Transaction Constraints and Burst Statistics
answer: Put legality constraints in the transaction and traffic-distribution choices in the sequence/test. Bound burst length, size, address, and payload size; enforce alignment and boundary rules. Use `dist` for desired weights, but sample resulting distributions because constraints can bias outcomes. Coverage should include lengths, command types, alignment, and crossings. Exact constraints require the transaction fields and protocol.

title: Constraint: Address Alignment with CMD Signal
answer: Use a conditional constraint, for example `if (cmd==WRITE) addr % ALIGN == 0;`, with ALIGN nonzero. For power-of-two alignment, constrain the low address bits to zero. If other commands need different alignment, state those branches explicitly. Bound command values and address range, check randomize return status, and cover each command/alignment combination.

title: Constraint: Dynamic Array Sum and 2D Array Row Constraint
answer: Constrain dynamic-array size and elements, then use `a.sum() with (int'(item)) == target;` so small element widths do not truncate the total. For each 2D row, constrain its size/value range and sum if supported by the simulator, or use a compatible helper representation. Check feasibility before invoking the solver. The target and row rules are missing here.

title: Constraint: Various Array Constraints
answer: Use `size()` for dynamic arrays, foreach for per-element/range relations, pairwise inequality or `unique` for uniqueness, and widened reduction methods for sums/counts. Bound sizes before applying pairwise constraints to control solver cost. Check feasibility, randomize success, and corner distributions. The title alone does not specify a unique set of constraints.
solution:
**Key idea:** Array constraints are built from a few patterns: **size** (`size()`), **per-element** (`foreach`), **pairwise** (`foreach` + `foreach` with `i < j`, or `unique`), **reduction** (`sum/product/and/or/xor with (...)`, widened), and **adjacent** relations (`a[i]` vs `a[i-1]`). Always bound the size first so pairwise constraints stay tractable.

### Pattern cookbook
| Goal | Constraint |
| --- | --- |
| size in range | `a.size() inside {[5:10]};` |
| element range | `foreach (a[i]) a[i] inside {[0:99]};` |
| all unique | `unique {a};` or `foreach (a[i]) foreach (a[j]) if (i < j) a[i] != a[j];` |
| ascending | `foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0) a[i] > a[i-1];` |
| sum | `a.sum() with (int'(item)) == 100;` |
| count of value 7 is 3 | `a.sum() with (int'(item == 7)) == 3;` |
| no two adjacent equal | `foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0) a[i] != a[i-1];` |
| even elements at even index | `foreach (a[i]) (i % 2 == 0) -> a[i] % 2 == 0;` |
| palindrome | `foreach (a[i]) a[i] == a[a.size()-1-i];` |
| element equals index squared | `foreach (a[i]) a[i] == i * i;` |
| at least one element > 90 | `a.sum() with (int'(item > 90)) >= 1;` |
| max element is 50 | `foreach (a[i]) a[i] <= 50; a.sum() with (int'(item == 50)) >= 1;` |

### Code
```systemverilog
class arr_demo;
  rand int unsigned a[];
  rand int unsigned b[];

  constraint c_size  { a.size() inside {[5:10]}; b.size() == a.size(); }
  constraint c_range { foreach (a[i]) a[i] inside {[0:99]}; foreach (b[i]) b[i] inside {[0:99]}; }
  constraint c_uniq  { unique {a}; }                                    // all a distinct
  constraint c_sort  { foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0) a[i] > a[i-1]; }       // strictly ascending
  constraint c_sumb  { b.sum() with (longint'(item)) == 150; }
  constraint c_cnt   { b.sum() with (int'(item == 7)) == 2; }          // exactly two 7s in b
  constraint c_adj   { foreach (b[i]) if (i > 0) b[i] != b[i-1]; }      // no adjacent repeats
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    arr_demo d = new();
    repeat (3) begin
      if (!d.randomize()) $fatal(1, "randomize failed");
      $display("a=%p\nb=%p", d.a, d.b);
    end
  end
endmodule
```

### Example output
| a (unique, ascending) | b (sum 150, two 7s, no adjacent repeats) |
|---|---|
| 3 18 22 61 77 90 | 7 40 7 66 12 18 |

### Explanation
- `unique` is concise and lets the solver use an efficient all-different encoding; the `foreach` pair form is O(N^2) constraints.
- `item == 7` in a `with` clause is a 1-bit result; casting to `int` before summing counts correctly.
- Strict ascending implies unique — `c_uniq` is redundant here but harmless; redundant constraints sometimes help solver performance, sometimes hurt.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Infeasible combos: 10 unique values in `[0:5]`; ascending + sum too small.
- Unbounded `size()` with pairwise constraints can blow up solve time.
- Use `longint'` for sums of 32-bit elements.

### Follow-ups
- *Shuffle instead?* Generate a legal multiset then `a.shuffle()` in `post_randomize` — fast but breaks positional constraints.

title: SV Constraint: 1D/2D Array Size, Value, and Ordering
answer: Constrain dynamic dimensions first, values second, and ordering with adjacent relations such as `foreach(a[i]) if(i>0) a[i]>=a[i-1];`. For a 2D array, define whether ordering applies per row, per column, or flattened. Strict order needs enough distinct legal values. Fixed packed dimensions are declared in the type, not randomized with size().

title: SV Constraint: Dynamic Array with Sum Equal to 20
answer: Declare `rand int a[];`, constrain `a.size()` to a legal bounded range, constrain elements, and use `a.sum() with (longint'(item)) == 20;`. The widening avoids overflow for large values. Decide whether negative values are allowed; without bounds the solver has a much wider space. Test minimum/maximum lengths and check every randomization result.
solution:
**Key idea:** `rand int a[];` + bounded `a.size()` + element bounds + `a.sum() with (longint'(item)) == 20`. Widening the reduction avoids overflow/wrap, and element bounds (e.g. non-negative) keep the solution space meaningful.

### Code
```systemverilog
class sum20;
  rand int a[];

  constraint c_size { a.size() inside {[1:10]}; }
  constraint c_val  { foreach (a[i]) a[i] inside {[0:20]}; }     // decide: negatives allowed?
  constraint c_sum  { a.sum() with (longint'(item)) == 20; }
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    sum20 s = new();
    repeat (4) begin
      if (!s.randomize()) $fatal(1, "randomize failed");
      $display("size=%0d a=%p sum=%0d", s.a.size(), s.a, s.a.sum() with (longint'(item)));
    end
    // corner: force min and max length
    if (!s.randomize() with { a.size() == 1;  }) $fatal(1, "fail"); $display("%p", s.a); // '{20}
    if (!s.randomize() with { a.size() == 10; }) $fatal(1, "fail"); $display("%p", s.a);
  end
endmodule
```

### Example results
| size | a | sum |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 | 20 |
| 3 | 7, 0, 13 | 20 |
| 5 | 4, 4, 2, 9, 1 | 20 |
| 10 | 2, 0, 3, 1, 5, 0, 2, 4, 1, 2 | 20 |

### Explanation
- Without `c_val`, `int` elements may be negative and huge: `'{2147483647, -2147483627}` is a legal solution — legal but probably not what you want.
- Without the widening cast, `a.sum()` is computed in `int` (32-bit) and can wrap: `'{2147483647, 2147483647, ... }` could "sum" to 20 modulo 2^32.
- The `with` clause also allows conditional sums, e.g. sum of even-index elements: `a.sum() with ((item.index % 2 == 0) ? longint'(item) : 0)`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `a.size()` unconstrained → solver may pick huge sizes or fail; always bound it.
- If elements must be ≥ 1, the size must be ≤ 20 to be feasible.
- Check the return of `randomize()`.

### Follow-ups
- *Uniform distribution over all compositions?* SV solvers aim for uniform over the solution space, but `size` interacts — add `solve a.size() before a` hints only if the size distribution must be uniform.

title: SV Constraint: Non-Overlapping Rectangle Regions in 2D Array
answer: For positive-width axis-aligned rectangles, constrain x/y bounds and require each pair to be disjoint: `x1+w1<=x2 || x2+w2<=x1 || y1+h1<=y2 || y2+h2<=y1`. These are half-open bounds, so touching edges is allowed. Change inequalities if touching is forbidden. Widen additions and check packing feasibility.
solution:
**Key idea:** Represent each rectangle by `(x, y, w, h)` with **positive** width/height, keep it inside the grid (`x + w <= W`, `y + h <= H`), and for every pair require **separation on at least one axis**: `x_i+w_i <= x_j || x_j+w_j <= x_i || y_i+h_i <= y_j || y_j+h_j <= y_i`. These are half-open intervals, so touching edges is allowed; use `<` to forbid touching.

### Example (8x8 grid, 3 rectangles)
```text
      x: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
y=0      1 1 1 . . . . .      R1: x=0 y=0 w=3 h=2
y=1      1 1 1 . 2 2 2 2      R2: x=4 y=1 w=4 h=3
y=2      . . . . 2 2 2 2      R3: x=1 y=4 w=2 h=4
y=3      . . . . 2 2 2 2
y=4      . 3 3 . . . . .
y=5      . 3 3 . . . . .
y=6      . 3 3 . . . . .
y=7      . 3 3 . . . . .
```

| pair | separating axis |
|---|---|
| R1, R2 | x: 0+3 = 3 <= 4 |
| R1, R3 | y: 0+2 = 2 <= 4 |
| R2, R3 | x: 1+2 = 3 <= 4 |

### Code
```systemverilog
class rect_place #(int W = 8, int H = 8, int N = 3);
  rand int unsigned x[N], y[N], w[N], h[N];
  int grid[H][W];                                   // 0 = empty, k = rectangle k

  constraint c_bounds {
    foreach (x[i]) {
      w[i] inside {[1:W]};  h[i] inside {[1:H]};
      x[i] < W;             y[i] < H;
      x[i] + w[i] <= W;     y[i] + h[i] <= H;       // all values bounded -> no overflow
    }
  }
  constraint c_disjoint {
    foreach (x[i]) foreach (x[j])
      if (i < j)
        (x[i] + w[i] <= x[j]) || (x[j] + w[j] <= x[i]) ||
        (y[i] + h[i] <= y[j]) || (y[j] + h[j] <= y[i]);
  }

  function void post_randomize();
    foreach (grid[r, c]) grid[r][c] = 0;
    foreach (x[k])
      for (int r = y[k]; r < y[k] + h[k]; r++)
        for (int c = x[k]; c < x[k] + w[k]; c++) begin
          assert (grid[r][c] == 0) else $error("overlap at (%0d,%0d)", c, r);  // independent check
          grid[r][c] = k + 1;
        end
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Explanation
- Two axis-aligned rectangles overlap iff their x-intervals overlap **and** their y-intervals overlap; the negation is the 4-way OR above.
- The `post_randomize` fill gives an independent overlap check (don't trust the constraint you are testing).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `w` or `h` of 0 makes "rectangles" that can sit anywhere — require ≥ 1.
- Packing feasibility: total area ≤ W x H is necessary but not sufficient (e.g. three 5x5 squares in 8x8 fail).
- With `int` (signed) and no lower bound, negative coordinates appear; with narrow unsigned types `x + w` can wrap — bound or widen.

### Follow-ups
- *Minimum gap of 1 cell?* Use `x_i + w_i < x_j` (strict) on each term.
- *Rectangles must not touch even at corners?* Same strict form — it already rejects corner contact.

title: SV Constraint: Exactly One Consecutive Run of 1s in 16-bit Value
answer: Choose start s and length l with `0<=s<16`, `1<=l<=16`, and `s+l<=16`, then constrain the vector to a widened mask `((32'h1<<l)-1)<<s`. This creates exactly one nonempty contiguous run. Alternatively, on a 17-bit zero-extended value, require exactly two transitions against its shifted copy. Specify whether the all-zero value is excluded.

title: SV Constraint: rand bit Array with Odd Number of 1s
answer: For a bit array, constrain `a.sum() with (int'(item)) % 2 == 1`, plus a legal size. For a packed vector, `$countones(v)%2==1` or reduction XOR equal to 1 expresses odd parity. Widen array sums because summing bit elements without casting can truncate. Verify count parity independently after randomization.
solution:
**Key idea:** Odd parity = count of 1s is odd. For an unpacked/dynamic bit array: `a.sum() with (int'(item)) % 2 == 1` (widen, otherwise the sum of 1-bit items is 1-bit). For a packed vector: `$countones(v) % 2 == 1` or simply `^v == 1'b1`.

### Code
```systemverilog
class odd_ones;
  rand bit       a[];          // unpacked dynamic bit array
  rand bit [7:0] v;            // packed vector

  constraint c_size  { a.size() inside {[1:12]}; }
  constraint c_a_odd { (a.sum() with (int'(item))) % 2 == 1; }
  constraint c_v_odd { ^v == 1'b1; }                  // reduction XOR = odd parity
  // equivalent: $countones(v) % 2 == 1;

  function void post_randomize();
    int n = 0;
    foreach (a[i]) n += a[i];
    assert (n % 2 == 1)        else $error("a has even ones: %p", a);   // independent check
    assert ($countones(v) % 2) else $error("v has even ones: %b", v);
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Trace: why the cast matters
| a | `a.sum()` (1-bit context) | `a.sum() with (int'(item))` | odd? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,1,1 | 1 (3 mod 2) | 3 | yes |
| 1,1 | 0 | 2 | no |
| 1,1,1,1,1 | 1 | 5 | yes |

Here the 1-bit sum happens to equal parity, but the same habit breaks for "exactly 3 ones" (`a.sum() == 3` can never be true in 1 bit) — always widen.

### Explanation
- `^v` is a single XOR tree — the cheapest constraint for the solver.
- For a fixed-size array, `a.size()` is not needed; for a dynamic array, size must be ≥ 1 (an empty array has 0 ones, which is even).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Without `with`, the result type of `a.sum()` is the element type (1 bit for `bit`), so any count larger than 1 is lost; the cast removes all doubt.
- Exactly-K ones: `a.sum() with (int'(item)) == K`, with K ≤ size.

### Follow-ups
- *Even parity for a byte plus parity bit?* `^{v, p} == 0`.

title: SV Constraint: 300-Element Array, Values 0-5, Each = 40 Times, No Consecutive 0s
answer: As stated, the constraint is impossible: six values appearing 40 times each account for only 240 elements, not 300. Clarify whether the array has 240 entries, each value occurs 50 times, or 60 entries may use additional values. Only then add count constraints and `if(i>0) !(a[i]==0 && a[i-1]==0)`. Do not hide the contradiction with a solver workaround.

title: SV Constraint: 300-Element Array, 0 May Repeat, Non-Zero Values Must Not Be Consecutive
answer: Clarify whether adjacent nonzero values cannot be equal or whether no two nonzero elements may be adjacent. For no equal adjacent nonzero values, use `if(i>0 && a[i]!=0 && a[i-1]!=0) a[i]!=a[i-1];`. For no adjacent nonzeros at all, require `a[i]==0 || a[i-1]==0`. Zero repetition remains allowed in both interpretations.
solution:
**Key idea:** "Non-zero values must not be consecutive" is ambiguous. Interpretation A: two **adjacent non-zero values must not be equal** (e.g. `3,3` illegal, `3,4` OK). Interpretation B: **no two non-zero values may be adjacent at all** (every non-zero is followed by 0). Zeros may repeat in both. State the interpretation and constrain accordingly.

| sequence | A: adjacent non-zeros differ | B: no adjacent non-zeros |
|---|---|---|
| 0 0 3 4 0 | legal | **illegal** (3,4) |
| 0 3 3 0 0 | **illegal** (3,3) | **illegal** |
| 5 0 0 2 0 | legal | legal |
| 0 0 0 0 0 | legal | legal |

### Code (one named block per interpretation, selected with `constraint_mode`)
```systemverilog
class arr300_nz2;
  rand bit [3:0] a[300];
  constraint c_range  { foreach (a[i]) a[i] inside {[0:9]}; }
  constraint c_diffnz { foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0 && a[i] != 0 && a[i-1] != 0) a[i] != a[i-1]; } // A
  constraint c_isolnz { foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0) (a[i] == 0 || a[i-1] == 0); }                  // B
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    arr300_nz2 o = new();
    o.c_isolnz.constraint_mode(0);              // run interpretation A
    if (!o.randomize()) $fatal(1, "A failed");
    o.c_isolnz.constraint_mode(1);
    o.c_diffnz.constraint_mode(0);              // run interpretation B
    if (!o.randomize()) $fatal(1, "B failed");
    $display("%p", o.a[0:15]);
  end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- B implies at least ~half the array is zero (at most 150 non-zeros in 300 slots).
- Constraints are written with `if (i > 0 ...)` guards so `a[i-1]` never indexes out of bounds.
- Prefer two named constraint blocks over one with a knob: clearer and each interpretation can be turned on/off by tests.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Distribution: under B the solver may produce mostly zeros; add `dist` on `a[i] == 0` if you need a certain density.
- Check the first element and the wrap-around (is `a[299]`, `a[0]` adjacent? usually not — state it).

### Follow-ups
- *Also forbid three zeros in a row?* `if (i > 1) !(a[i] == 0 && a[i-1] == 0 && a[i-2] == 0)`.

title: SV Constraint: Memory Access with Excluded Range
answer: For a forbidden half-open interval [L,H), a single address must satisfy `addr<L || addr>=H`. A whole access of n bytes must satisfy `addr+n<=L || addr>=H`, with n>0, widened addition, and address-space bounds. Merely excluding the starting address does not prevent overlap. Include alignment and legal transfer sizes.
solution:
**Key idea:** For a forbidden half-open range `[L, H)`, a **single address** needs `addr < L || addr >= H`, but a **whole access** of `n` bytes must not overlap: `addr + n <= L || addr >= H`. Only constraining the start address lets an access start below L and run into the hole.

### Number line (L = 0x2000, H = 0x3000, n = 0x100)
| access start | bytes | start-only check | full-range check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0x1E00 | 0x1E00–0x1EFF | OK | OK |
| 0x1F80 | 0x1F80–0x207F | OK (start < L) | **illegal** (overlaps hole) |
| 0x2800 | 0x2800–0x28FF | illegal | illegal |
| 0x3000 | 0x3000–0x30FF | OK | OK |

### Code
```systemverilog
class mem_access;
  localparam longint unsigned SPACE = 64'h1_0000;   // 64 KB address space
  rand bit [31:0] addr;
  rand bit [15:0] len;                              // bytes, > 0
  bit [31:0] L = 32'h2000, H = 32'h3000;            // forbidden [L, H) — can be changed by tests

  constraint c_len   { len inside {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256}; }
  constraint c_align { (addr & (32'(len) - 1)) == 0; }            // natural alignment (power-of-2 len)
  constraint c_space { 64'(addr) + len <= SPACE; }                // stay inside the space, widened
  constraint c_hole  { (64'(addr) + len <= L) || (addr >= H); }   // whole access avoids [L, H)
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    mem_access m = new();
    repeat (1000) begin
      if (!m.randomize()) $fatal(1, "randomize failed");
      assert ((64'(m.addr) + m.len <= m.L) || (m.addr >= m.H))
        else $error("overlap: addr=%h len=%0d", m.addr, m.len);
    end
  end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- Widening (`64'(addr) + len`) prevents `0xFFFF_FF00 + 0x200` from wrapping to a small value and passing.
- Multiple holes: one OR-clause per hole, ANDed together (e.g. a `foreach` over a list of `{lo, hi}` pairs).
- Bias toward the edges to test boundaries: `addr dist {L - len := 10, H := 10, [0:SPACE-1] :/ 80}`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Inclusive vs exclusive `H`: `[L, H]` inclusive needs `addr > H`.
- `len == 0` makes every address legal — exclude it.
- Feasibility: if the hole covers the whole space, randomize fails — expected.

### Follow-ups
- *Generate accesses *inside* the hole for error tests?* Disable `c_hole` and add `addr >= L && 64'(addr) + len <= H` inline.

title: SV Constraint: Repeatedly Randomize Non-Overlapping Memory Regions Until Full
answer: Maintain allocated intervals outside the randomized transaction. Constrain each new positive-size region to fit the address space and not overlap any prior region, then update the allocator only after successful randomization. Stop when no legal fit remains, not only when total allocated bytes equals capacity. Random sizes can fragment space; use fixed slots or a free-interval allocator if exact filling is required.

title: SV Constraint: Symmetric Array Using Helper Function
answer: If symmetry means transpose symmetry, constrain `a[i][j]==a[j][i]` on a square array. If it means mirror symmetry, use the correct reflected index. Prefer direct foreach relations. A helper function in a constraint can impose solve-order restrictions and must be side-effect free; do not assume the solver inverts arbitrary procedural code.

title: Constraint Inheritance and constraint_mode()
answer: Inherited constraints are active together. A derived constraint block with the same name replaces the inherited block; a different name adds restrictions. `constraint_mode(0)` disables a selected block, while `rand_mode(0)` freezes a variable. Inline constraints add to active constraints and do not automatically override conflicting hard constraints. Inspect solver failure before changing modes.
solution:
**Key idea:** A derived class inherits **all** constraint blocks of its base, and all active blocks are solved together (AND). A derived block with the **same name overrides** (replaces) the base block; a **different name adds** to it. `constraint_mode(0)` turns a named block off; `rand_mode(0)` turns a variable into a state variable. Inline `with {}` constraints are **added**, they never override hard constraints.

### Code
```systemverilog
class base_t;
  rand bit [7:0] len;
  rand bit [7:0] addr;
  constraint c_len  { len inside {[1:16]}; }
  constraint c_addr { addr < 8'h80; }
endclass

class derived_t extends base_t;
  constraint c_len  { len inside {[32:64]}; }     // SAME name -> replaces base c_len
  constraint c_even { addr % 2 == 0; }            // NEW name   -> added to c_addr
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    derived_t d = new();
    base_t    b = d;                              // base handle, derived object

    if (!d.randomize()) $fatal(1, "fail");      // len 32..64, addr even and < 0x80
    $display("len=%0d addr=%0h", d.len, d.addr);

    d.c_addr.constraint_mode(0);                  // turn off base block in this object
    if (!d.randomize() with { addr > 8'hF0; })    // now feasible
      $fatal(1, "fail");

    d.len.rand_mode(0); d.len = 5;                // len is now state; 5 violates derived c_len [32:64]
    if (!d.randomize()) $display("expected failure: state len=5 violates c_len");

    $display("c_len mode = %0d", d.c_len.constraint_mode());   // query form returns 1/0
  end
endmodule
```

### Behavior summary
| Situation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| derived block, same name | base block replaced (polymorphic, even via base handle) |
| derived block, new name | both apply |
| `obj.blk.constraint_mode(0)` | that block ignored for this object only |
| `obj.var.rand_mode(0)` | variable not randomized, its current value must satisfy constraints |
| inline `with {}` | added; conflict with active hard constraint → randomize fails |
| `soft` base constraint | yields to conflicting later/inline constraints |

### Explanation
- Overriding is resolved by name, like virtual methods: `b.randomize()` on a `derived_t` object uses the derived `c_len`.
- `constraint_mode` is per object instance; static constraint blocks (`static constraint`) are shared across all instances.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Turning off constraints to "make randomize pass" hides a real conflict — inspect the solver message first.
- `rand_mode(0)` variables still participate as constants; an illegal current value makes the whole randomize fail.
- Calling `constraint_mode` on a name that doesn't exist is a compile error; `c_len.constraint_mode()` with no argument queries.

### Follow-ups
- *Avoid overriding entirely?* Make the base default `soft` so tests can redirect with inline constraints.

title: Consecutive Uniqueness & Cross-Array Common Element
answer: Adjacent uniqueness is `if(i>0) a[i]!=a[i-1]`; it is weaker than global uniqueness. For two arrays sharing exactly one distinct value, explicitly choose a shared value and constrain membership plus all other cross-array pairs to differ, accounting for duplicates within each array. If only at least one common element is required, a selected matching index pair suffices.

title: std::randomize Return Value Bug
answer: `std::randomize(...)` returns 1 for success and 0 for failure. Write `if (!std::randomize(x) with {...}) $fatal(...)`; do not treat zero as success or ignore the result. Failure does not mean a legal new value was generated. Distinguish std::randomize variables from object.randomize and check which constraints are actually active.

title: Sudoku 9x9 Grid Constraint
answer: Constrain every cell to 1..9. Require pairwise uniqueness within each row, column, and 3x3 box. For two distinct cells in the same unit, values must differ. Add clue constraints only where a given cell is nonzero. Check conflicting clues and solver performance. Multiple solutions are legal unless the task requires uniqueness of the entire puzzle.

title: Dynamic Array - Sum, Consecutive Ones, Unique in Range
answer: Combine bounded size, widened sum, and value-range constraints. If exactly one run of consecutive ones is required, introduce start/length and map each position to 1 inside the run and 0 outside. If only a certain number of adjacent pairs is required, count that instead. Global uniqueness of a bit array severely limits size; confirm these are separate exercises before combining them.

title: Static Array Uniqueness - With and Without unique
answer: For a fixed array, `unique {a};` expresses distinct elements when supported. Without unique, use `foreach(a[i]) foreach(a[j]) if(i<j) a[i]!=a[j];`. Bound the element range to contain at least as many values as elements. Pairwise constraints scale quadratically, so use a shuffled legal set for large permutation tasks if allowed.

title: Alternating READ/WRITE Transactions Using post_randomize
answer: Keep a non-rand next-command state, constrain cmd to that state, then toggle the state in post_randomize. Successful calls alternate READ and WRITE. Do not overwrite cmd afterward in a way that breaks related randomized constraints. Define the initial command and reset behavior. Failed randomization must not advance the expected alternation.

title: 1D Array - Unique Elements Without unique, Sum Constraint
answer: Use pairwise `a[i]!=a[j]` for i<j, bound size/range, and a widened `a.sum()` constraint. Check that the requested sum lies between the minimum and maximum sums of the permitted number of distinct elements. Sorted construction plus shuffle can be an alternative if procedural generation is allowed; it may have a different distribution.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Combine pairwise distinctness with a widened array reduction and a feasible sum.

| Distinct values in 0..9 | Sum |
| --- | --- |
| Minimum: 0,1,2,3 | 6 |
| Example: 1,4,6,9 | 20 |
| Maximum: 6,7,8,9 | 30 |

### Explanation
The original title does not supply a length, domain, or target. This concrete instance uses four elements, values zero through nine, and a total of twenty. Four distinct integers in this domain can sum only between six and thirty; checking those bounds quickly detects impossible requirements. The cast inside the reduction widens each term before addition.

### Code
```systemverilog
class distinct_sum;
  rand bit [3:0] a[4];
  constraint legal_c {
    foreach (a[i]) a[i] inside {[0:9]};
    foreach (a[i]) foreach (a[j]) if (i < j) a[i] != a[j];
    a.sum() with (int'(item)) == 20;
  }
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
A narrow reduction may overflow before comparison, so casting only the completed sum is insufficient. Distinctness does not impose ordering. Bounds are necessary but not sufficient for arbitrary sparse domains: a sum inside the min/max interval may still be unreachable. Always check solver success.

### Follow-ups
If N values are selected from consecutive integers L..U, the minimum sum is N*L+N*(N-1)/2, and the maximum is N*U-N*(N-1)/2.

title: 1KB Address Space - Non-Overlapping 32-byte Stride Regions
answer: A 1KB space contains 32 aligned 32-byte slots. Represent a region by a slot index 0..31 and address `slot*32`. Unique slot indices guarantee nonoverlap for 32-byte regions. For variable lengths, constrain full interval disjointness instead. Limit the number of simultaneous regions and account for whether 1KB is the entire space or an offset within larger memory.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Represent each aligned 32-byte allocation as one of 32 distinct slots in a 1024-byte space.

| Slot | Base address | Occupied bytes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0x000 | 0x000–0x01f |
| 1 | 0x020 | 0x020–0x03f |
| 31 | 0x3e0 | 0x3e0–0x3ff |

### Explanation
With fixed size and alignment, interval disjointness reduces to slot uniqueness. This example chooses four simultaneous allocations. Addresses are calculated from the chosen slots, so there is no redundant address solver state. The last slot is valid because its final byte is 1023. For a nonzero memory base, add the base after this offset calculation and ensure the containing address type is wide enough.

### Code
```systemverilog
class regions;
  rand bit [4:0] slot[4];
  constraint distinct_c { unique {slot}; }
  function int unsigned base_addr(int unsigned i);
    return int'(slot[i]) * 32;
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The alignment simplification assumes every region is exactly 32 bytes. If lengths differ, unique starting addresses do not guarantee nonoverlap: check end_i < start_j or end_j < start_i with widened arithmetic. More than 32 live regions is impossible. Randomizing repeatedly does not preserve nonoverlap across calls unless existing allocations are included as state.

### Follow-ups
For a real allocator, keep a free-slot bitmap and release slots explicitly; randomization should choose among currently free slots.

title: 8-bit Vector - No Cyclic Right Shift
answer: To reject rotations of reference r, constrain v different from each of its eight circular rotations, including rotation zero if equality is forbidden. If two generated values must not be rotations, compare all rotations of one against the other. Symmetric references can have fewer than eight distinct rotations.

title: Generate 4-bit Value with Exactly 4 Ones - No countones
answer: A 4-bit vector with exactly four ones has only one legal value: `v==4'b1111`. If the intended width is larger, sum individually widened bits to four, or use an allowed helper count. Do not present a randomized distribution for a singleton solution.

title: Array with if-else Constraint, then shuffle()
answer: Solve the conditional value constraints first, check success, then call `a.shuffle()`. Shuffling preserves the multiset and sum, but can violate ordering, adjacency, or index-dependent constraints. Use shuffle only when those positional conditions are irrelevant, or revalidate after it.

title: 7x7 Pixel Image - No All-D 3x3 Submatrix (Parameterized)
answer: For every legal top-left coordinate of a 3x3 window, require at least one of its nine pixels to differ from D. Bound the pixel alphabet and parameterized dimensions, and skip windows when either dimension is smaller than three. A nested constraint or explicit nine-term OR can express the condition. Verify every overlapping window independently.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Every possible overlapping 3×3 window must contain at least one pixel different from D.

| 7×7 image | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Possible top-left rows | 0 through 4 |
| Possible top-left columns | 0 through 4 |
| Windows checked | 25 |

### Explanation
Assume two pixel values, D=1 and not-D=0. For each top-left location whose complete window fits, OR the nine tests for a non-D pixel. This forbids an all-D window without forbidding large numbers of D pixels elsewhere. The nested foreach iterates all cells, while the guard restricts actual window checks. Parameters must be positive.

### Code
```systemverilog
class image_bits #(int R = 7, int C = 7);
  rand bit pixel[R][C];
  constraint window_c {
    foreach (pixel[i,j]) if ((i < R-2) && (j < C-2)) {
      !pixel[i][j]     || !pixel[i][j+1]     || !pixel[i][j+2] ||
      !pixel[i+1][j]   || !pixel[i+1][j+1]   || !pixel[i+1][j+2] ||
      !pixel[i+2][j]   || !pixel[i+2][j+1]   || !pixel[i+2][j+2];
    }
  }
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
Disjoint 3×3 tiles are insufficient: a forbidden window may straddle tile boundaries. For R<3 or C<3 there are no fitting windows, so this rule imposes no restriction. A multi-symbol alphabet requires pixel != D rather than logical negation and a separate alphabet constraint.

### Follow-ups
A checker should scan the 25 windows independently and count D pixels in each; it must reject a deliberately inserted all-D window even when it overlaps previously checked windows.

title: Overriding a Constraint in Child Class - Three Methods
answer: Three useful approaches are a same-name derived constraint block, disabling the inherited block with constraint_mode and adding a replacement, or declaring a base default as soft so an inline/derived constraint can supersede it. These have different semantics. An inline hard constraint alone cannot override a conflicting inherited hard constraint.

title: SVA: Analyze a Complex Property
answer: Identify clock and disable condition, then expand each delay/repetition into sampled-cycle obligations. Distinguish implication, sequence concatenation, overlapping matches, and strong/weak completion. Check vacuous passes when the antecedent never occurs. Build a cycle table with one passing and one failing trace before claiming a specific interpretation.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** The source contains no actual complex property, so its precise behavior cannot be reconstructed. Analyze a clearly labeled example instead.

| Cycle | req | ack | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 1 | 0 | Antecedent triggers |
| 1 | 0 | 0 | Earliest response slot |
| 2 | 0 | 1 | Response match: pass |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | Latest slot if no prior match |

### Explanation
For the illustrative property below, each sampled req starts an independent obligation for ack at one of the next three samples. |-> begins the consequent at the triggering sample, and ##[1:3] moves the response into future samples. A level req held high starts a new obligation every clock; replacing it with $rose(req) changes the contract to rising-edge requests.

### Code
```systemverilog
// Illustrative example only; the original property was not supplied.
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 req |-> ##[1:3] ack);
cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                req ##3 ack);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
No req means a vacuous pass, not evidence of handshake correctness. A single ack may satisfy multiple outstanding attempts. disable iff aborts existing attempts during reset. To analyze the missing source property, obtain its full text, clock, reset polarity, and signal definitions; do not infer timing from its title.

### Follow-ups
For a real complex property, expand each sequence match into a cycle table, inspect repetition endpoints, then test an early response, a late response, no response, and overlapping triggers.

title: SVA: Glitch Detection - Signal HIGH for Less Than 2.5 ns
answer: Use event timestamps to measure actual pulse width: record `$realtime` on the rising edge and check `$realtime-rise_time >= 2.5ns` on the falling edge. Track whether a valid rise was observed, define reset and initial-high behavior, and use sufficient timeprecision. A posedge-clocked assertion misses glitches between samples. Add a watchdog if a maximum width is also required.

title: SVA: valid Must Remain High Until ready
answer: A standard sampled rule is `valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(payload)`, with reset disabled. It repeats for each stalled cycle and includes the cycle when ready finally rises. If only valid persistence is required, omit payload stability. Add a bounded-progress requirement only if the protocol guarantees eventual ready; otherwise indefinite backpressure can be legal.

title: SVA: Sequence Assertion - cat Followed by 3 or 4 dogs
answer: Assuming cat and dog are one-cycle Boolean events and dogs must be consecutive starting next cycle: `cat |=> dog[*3:4]`. This allows a 3- or 4-cycle match; it does not forbid a fifth dog or force exactly four when a fourth occurs. Exact-length behavior needs an ending condition such as !dog plus clear overlap rules.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Distinguish “at least a three- or four-cycle match” from an exact run that must end after three or four dogs.

| Cycle after cat | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Three dogs | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | — |
| Four dogs | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 |

### Explanation
Assume cat is a one-cycle event and dog is a Boolean sampled every clock. The first property requires dog on the next three samples; a four-sample run also qualifies. The second additionally requires the run to end, thereby rejecting five consecutive dogs. The termination sample follows the final dog sample. If cat can remain high, it starts overlapping checks on every high cycle; use $rose(cat) if the intended trigger is an edge.

### Code
```systemverilog
// A 3-or-4-cycle match; longer dog runs can still satisfy this.
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  cat |=> dog[*3:4]);
// Exact run of 3 or 4 dogs beginning on the next sample.
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  cat |=> dog[*3:4] ##1 !dog);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The exact property does not forbid dog before cat or unrelated runs later. It also does not make cat and dog mutually exclusive on the trigger sample. Decide those rules separately. With no cat, both implications pass vacuously.

### Follow-ups
If “dogs” are separated events rather than consecutive high samples, use event counting with explicit gap and timeout rules; consecutive repetition [*] would implement the wrong protocol.

title: SVA: Clock Period Verification - Within 5% of Expected Period
answer: On each eligible clock edge, measure the interval from the prior edge using realtime. Check `0.95*expected <= measured && measured <= 1.05*expected`. Skip the first edge, define reset and whether the expected period is fixed for the interval, and add a no-edge watchdog for a stopped clock. Period checking alone does not verify duty cycle.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** A 100 MHz clock has a 10 ns period; with ±5% tolerance the acceptable interval is 9.5–10.5 ns.

| Successive rises | Period | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10, 20 ns | 10 ns | Pass |
| 20, 30.5 ns | 10.5 ns | Pass at boundary |
| 30.5, 41.1 ns | 10.6 ns | Fail |

### Explanation
Measure successive rising edges with realtime rather than integer time so fractional nanoseconds are retained. The first edge after reset initializes history and makes no comparison. EXPECTED specifies the nominal rising-edge period, not the half period. For the 100 MHz question, the frequency is fixed but no tolerance was given; this example explicitly chooses ±5%, which should be replaced by the design requirement.

### Code
```systemverilog
module period_checker(input logic clk, rst_n);
  timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
  parameter realtime EXPECTED = 10ns;
  realtime previous_edge, measured;
  bit history = 0;
  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) history = 0;
    else begin
      if (history) begin
        measured = $realtime - previous_edge;
        assert (measured >= 0.95*EXPECTED &&
                measured <= 1.05*EXPECTED)
          else $error("Bad period: %0t", measured);
      end
      previous_edge = $realtime;
      history = 1;
    end
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
A checker triggered only by clock edges cannot fail if the clock stops permanently. Use an independent reference-clock or timed watchdog for that case. Period alone says nothing about duty cycle: a 1 ns high and 9 ns low waveform still has a 10 ns period. X/Z clock transitions can also trigger edge-sensitive processes; establish a known-clock policy.

### Follow-ups
For 50% duty cycle verification, measure rising-to-falling and falling-to-rising intervals separately, each against its own tolerance.

title: SVA: Clock Period Check When expected_clock_period Is Async
answer: An asynchronous expected period can change mid-interval. Define whether a change takes effect immediately, at the next edge, or only after a stable-mode handshake. Snapshot the accepted expectation for each interval or suppress the explicitly permitted transition interval. Do not compare a completed interval with an unrelated latest value.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Define when the asynchronous expected period takes effect, then compare each interval with the expectation assigned to that interval.

| Event | Expected value | Checker action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Edge at 0 ns | 10 ns | Capture 10 ns |
| Config changes at 4 ns | 20 ns | Do not rewrite prior interval |
| Edge at 10 ns | 20 ns | Check prior 10 ns; capture 20 ns |
| Edge at 30 ns | 20 ns | Check 20 ns |

### Explanation
This example adopts a next-edge policy: the expected value captured at one rising edge applies to the interval ending at the following edge. A configuration update within an interval therefore affects the next complete interval. This is a verification contract, not a physical synchronizer. The environment must make the value stable around the sampling edge, or provide a mode-change handshake and settling indication.

### Code
```systemverilog
timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
realtime previous_edge, interval_expected;
bit have_edge = 0;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
  if (!rst_n) have_edge = 0;
  else begin
    if (have_edge)
      assert ($realtime-previous_edge >= 0.95*interval_expected &&
              $realtime-previous_edge <= 1.05*interval_expected);
    previous_edge = $realtime;
    interval_expected = expected_clock_period;
    have_edge = 1;
  end
end
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
Comparing against the newest value at the end of an interval wrongly rejects a legal old-mode interval. Updating configuration in the same simulation region as this checker creates a race. If hardware permits one transitional interval, explicitly identify and exempt that interval; indefinite suppression can hide a broken clock.

### Follow-ups
For a PLL, use a synchronized mode/lock indication and check steady-state periods only after the specified settling window; separately verify that lock arrives within its deadline.

title: SVA: APB Protocol Assertion - PSEL to PENABLE to PREADY
answer: APB setup has PSEL=1 and PENABLE=0; the following cycle enters access with both high. While PREADY is low, keep address/control/write data stable and stay in access. Completion occurs when PSEL&&PENABLE&&PREADY. The next cycle must leave access, though PSEL may stay high for back-to-back transfers. Add PSLVERR and PSTRB rules for the relevant APB version.

title: SVA: B Toggles 2 Cycles After A Toggles
answer: For a change in A requiring a change in B two sampled cycles later: `$changed(A) |-> ##2 $changed(B)`. This does not prohibit earlier or extra B toggles; add separate properties if required. Define simultaneous triggers, reset history, and whether X transitions count. Use `$rose`/`$fell` instead when only one edge polarity should trigger.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Use a sampled change in A to require a sampled change in B exactly two clock samples later.

| Sample | A | B | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | History |
| 1 | 1 | 0 | A changes |
| 2 | 1 | 0 | One cycle later |
| 3 | 1 | 1 | B changes: obligation met |

### Explanation
|-> starts the consequent at the current sample; ##2 therefore selects the sample two cycles after the trigger. Each A change creates a separate attempt. Consecutive A changes require B changes on consecutive corresponding samples. The rule requires a change at the target sample but does not prohibit B from changing earlier or at other times.

### Code
```systemverilog
bit past_valid = 0;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) past_valid <= 0;
  else past_valid <= 1;
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  past_valid && $changed(A) |-> ##2 $changed(B));
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The history flag prevents an initialization comparison from being treated as a real trigger. $changed detects sampled value changes, including four-state changes; reject unknowns separately if only 0/1 edges are meaningful. Transitions between sampling edges are invisible to this property.

### Follow-ups
For rising edges only, replace both $changed calls with $rose. To forbid unsolicited B changes, add a reverse correspondence using guarded $past($changed(A),2).

title: req => ack Handshake Protocol
answer: Clarify whether req/ack are pulses or a four-phase level handshake. For a level protocol, req rises, ack eventually rises, req falls, then ack falls. Check bounded response latency if guaranteed, persistence before acknowledgement, and no unsolicited ack. For pipelined requests, an outstanding counter or tagged model is needed instead of a single pending bit.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** First choose a handshake contract; this example uses a four-phase, one-outstanding, level handshake with bounded acknowledgement.

| Phase | req | ack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Idle | 0 | 0 |
| Request waiting | 1 | 0 |
| Acknowledged | 1 | 1 |
| Cleanup | 0 | 1 |
| Idle again | 0 | 0 |

### Explanation
Assume ack must rise one through eight samples after req rises, the requester holds req until acknowledgement, and no new request begins until ack is low again. The latency bound is illustrative because the title gives none. The persistence rule checks the accepting sample too. The cleanup rules intentionally permit ack to stay high while req is high and after req falls until the next check requires its fall.

### Code
```systemverilog
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $rose(req) |-> !ack ##[1:8] $rose(ack));
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req && !ack |=> req);
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $rose(ack) |-> req);
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  ack && req |=> ack);
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $fell(req) |=> !ack);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
This illustrative suite still needs a rule preventing a new req during cleanup and a reset/history policy for edge functions. It cannot model pipelined requests with a single pending phase. A no-request test can pass vacuously, so cover completed transactions and the latency extremes.

### Follow-ups
For pulse req/ack, use an outstanding counter or transaction IDs; holding req high is then a wrong requirement.

title: AHB-Lite Burst Must Not Cross 1KB Boundary
answer: AHB bursts must not cross a 1KB address boundary. Track accepted beats, HSIZE, HBURST, and start address, while accounting for HREADY stalls and address/control pipelining. Compute the last byte of incrementing bursts or each accepted address; wrapping bursts use their defined wrap window. A start-address-only assertion is insufficient.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** A burst must remain inside its original 1 KB region, including every transferred byte of every accepted beat.

| Start | Beat bytes | Beats | Last byte | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x3f0 | 4 | 4 | 0x3ff | Legal |
| 0x3f4 | 4 | 4 | 0x403 | Illegal |

### Explanation
For a fixed-length incrementing burst, compute last_byte = start + beats*bytes_per_beat - 1 with widened unsigned arithmetic. Compare start and last_byte after shifting right by ten. For indefinite INCR bursts and wrapping bursts, track the actual accepted address sequence instead. Only accepted address phases advance the tracker: HREADY must be high and HTRANS must be NONSEQ or SEQ. BUSY and IDLE do not count as data beats.

### Code
```systemverilog
function automatic bit incr_fits_1k(
  input longint unsigned start,
  input int unsigned beats,
  input int unsigned bytes_per_beat);
  longint unsigned last_byte;
  if (beats == 0 || bytes_per_beat == 0) return 0;
  last_byte = start + longint'(beats)*bytes_per_beat - 1;
  if (last_byte < start) return 0; // arithmetic overflow
  return (start >> 10) == (last_byte >> 10);
endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
This helper assumes legal aligned addresses and a known incrementing burst length; it is not a complete AHB monitor. Check HSIZE against bus width, alignment, HREADY stalls, and wrap-address calculation separately. Avoid counting the data phase as another accepted address.

### Follow-ups
For accepted SEQ beats, compare address[ADDR_W-1:10] with the NONSEQ start region and check the final byte's region too; retain state through BUSY cycles.

title: Check Clock Frequency is 100 MHz
answer: 100MHz has a 10ns period. Measure successive edges with realtime and compare to 10ns using the specified tolerance and timeprecision. Check high and low widths separately for duty cycle, and add a timeout because a period checker triggered only by edges cannot detect a permanently stopped clock.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** A 100 MHz clock has a 10 ns period; with ±5% tolerance the acceptable interval is 9.5–10.5 ns.

| Successive rises | Period | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10, 20 ns | 10 ns | Pass |
| 20, 30.5 ns | 10.5 ns | Pass at boundary |
| 30.5, 41.1 ns | 10.6 ns | Fail |

### Explanation
Measure successive rising edges with realtime rather than integer time so fractional nanoseconds are retained. The first edge after reset initializes history and makes no comparison. EXPECTED specifies the nominal rising-edge period, not the half period. For the 100 MHz question, the frequency is fixed but no tolerance was given; this example explicitly chooses ±5%, which should be replaced by the design requirement.

### Code
```systemverilog
module period_checker(input logic clk, rst_n);
  timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
  parameter realtime EXPECTED = 10ns;
  realtime previous_edge, measured;
  bit history = 0;
  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n) history = 0;
    else begin
      if (history) begin
        measured = $realtime - previous_edge;
        assert (measured >= 0.95*EXPECTED &&
                measured <= 1.05*EXPECTED)
          else $error("Bad period: %0t", measured);
      end
      previous_edge = $realtime;
      history = 1;
    end
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
A checker triggered only by clock edges cannot fail if the clock stops permanently. Use an independent reference-clock or timed watchdog for that case. Period alone says nothing about duty cycle: a 1 ns high and 9 ns low waveform still has a 10 ns period. X/Z clock transitions can also trigger edge-sensitive processes; establish a known-clock policy.

### Follow-ups
For 50% duty cycle verification, measure rising-to-falling and falling-to-rising intervals separately, each against its own tolerance.

title: Simple Fell-Triggered Assertion
answer: `$fell(a)` detects a sampled transition from 1 to 0 according to four-state sampling semantics. For example, `$fell(a) |=> b` requires b on the following sample. Define reset and establish valid past history before evaluating startup transitions.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** $fell detects a sampled transition whose current least-significant bit is zero and whose previous bit was one, X, or Z.

| Previous sampled a | Current a | $fell(a) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | 1 |
| X | 0 | 1 |
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 0 | 1 | 0 |

### Explanation
For a known one-bit signal, the familiar case is 1→0. Four-state semantics also allow X/Z→0, so the source note describing only 1→0 is incomplete. The example requires b at the sample following a detected fall. A history flag avoids treating the first post-reset sample as a meaningful transition from an uninitialized historical value. For vectors, $fell examines the least-significant bit rather than detecting an arbitrary falling bit.

### Code
```systemverilog
bit have_history = 0;
always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) have_history <= 0;
  else have_history <= 1;
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  have_history && $fell(a) |=> b);
// Strict known 1-to-0 interpretation:
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  have_history && ($past(a) === 1'b1) && (a === 1'b0) |=> b);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The two properties are alternatives for different contracts, not necessarily checks to enable together. A fall between clock samples can be missed. Check b for X explicitly if the diagnostic should distinguish unknown from false.

### Follow-ups
For a same-sample requirement use |-> b. For a response two cycles later use |-> ##2 b; do not accidentally add another cycle with |=> ##2.

Reference: [Accellera SystemVerilog 3.1a, sampled-value functions](https://eecs.umich.edu/courses/eecs578/eecs578.f15/miniprojects/SVAproject/manuals/SVA_manual.pdf).

title: Complete req-ack Handshake Suite
answer: Check request detection, legal acknowledgement, required latency bounds, request persistence, acknowledgement pulse/level width, cleanup order, and reset cancellation. Add coverage for minimum/maximum latency and consecutive handshakes. Use a pending flag for one outstanding request or a queue/counter for several. Avoid claiming completion from a suite that permits vacuous passes with no requests.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** A complete handshake suite needs safety, bounded progress, reset behavior, and coverage tied to a stated protocol.

| Requirement | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Request accepted once | Track one outstanding request |
| Ack legal | Requires pending request |
| Latency | Ack in specified window |
| Cleanup | No stale ack/new request overlap |
| Exercise | Cover short and long legal latency |

### Explanation
For a one-outstanding pulse protocol, maintain pending and age state. On req, reject an existing pending request and start age at zero. On ack, require pending and check age against the agreed latency range. Increment age while pending; clear on ack and reset. Define whether simultaneous ack and a new req is supported before ordering these updates. This reference model is often clearer than trying to make one property encode ownership and timing simultaneously.

### Code
```systemverilog
// Illustrative temporal subset: pulse req, response in 2..5 cycles.
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req |=> !req);
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  ack |=> !ack);
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req |-> ##[2:5] ack);
cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req ##2 ack);
cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req ##5 ack);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The temporal subset alone is not complete: one ack can satisfy overlapping req attempts, and unsolicited acks are not rejected. The pending/age model supplies those missing checks. Reset cancels outstanding work only if that is the specified hardware contract.

### Follow-ups
For tagged out-of-order traffic, replace pending with a map from tag to acceptance timestamp; reject duplicate outstanding tags and report leftovers at end of test.

title: Detect Short Glitch Pulses Shorter Than 2.5 ns
answer: Measure rise-to-fall duration with realtime rather than only a slower reference clock. Flag widths below 2.5ns, including narrow pulses between reference edges. Specify startup/reset behavior, event polarity, and X/Z treatment. Sufficient timeprecision is necessary.

title: req/gnt 4-Way Handshake - Concurrent and always Block
answer: For four-phase req/gnt, enforce req rise before gnt rise, req high until gnt, req fall after grant, then gnt fall before a new request. Encode sampled obligations with SVA and model states IDLE, WAIT_GRANT, WAIT_REQ_LOW, WAIT_GRANT_LOW procedurally. Specify timeouts and legal same-cycle transitions so both implementations check the same protocol.

title: Immediate assertion vs Concurrent Assertion
answer: An immediate assertion executes procedurally when control reaches it and checks a Boolean expression, typically `assert(expr)`. A concurrent assertion describes behavior across sampled events using sequences/properties, such as `assert property (@(posedge clk) req |=> ack)`. It samples/evaluates in defined assertion regions. Choose immediate for local procedural checks and concurrent for temporal protocol rules.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Immediate assertions check a procedural instant; concurrent assertions check sampled temporal behavior.

| Feature | Immediate | Concurrent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical syntax | assert(expr) | assert property(...) |
| Execution | When process reaches statement | On declared sampling event |
| Time relationship | Boolean now | Sequences across samples |

### Explanation
An immediate assertion is useful after a calculation or transaction comparison. It sees values available in its current scheduling region. A concurrent property samples signals at its clock event and evaluates temporal obligations using assertion scheduling rules. It can therefore express “request now implies acknowledgement next cycle” without manually saving history. Both kinds should have actionable diagnostics.

### Code
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  assert (!$isunknown(select)) else $error("Unknown select");
end
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 req |=> ack)
  else $error("Expected acknowledgement after request");
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
An immediate assert inside an always @(posedge clk) does not automatically gain concurrent assertion sampling semantics; it can observe pre-NBA values and race with blocking testbench drives. X/Z in a Boolean assertion expression is not true and causes failure. A temporal implication can pass vacuously when its trigger never occurs, so pair it with coverage.

### Follow-ups
Can an immediate assertion check a protocol? Yes, using explicitly maintained history/state; concurrent syntax normally makes the intended clock relationship clearer.

title: Blocking vs Nonblocking Assignments and Race Avoidance
answer: Blocking updates the variable immediately in the process. Nonblocking evaluates the RHS now and schedules the update in NBA, so clocked registers sample old values together. Use blocking for combinational calculations and nonblocking for sequential state. Avoid two processes writing the same variable and use clocking blocks for testbench races.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Blocking assignment updates immediately; nonblocking assignment schedules the update after right-hand sides have been evaluated.

| Before edge | Statements | After NBA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a=1, b=0 | a <= b; b <= a; | a=0, b=1 |
| a=1, b=0 | a = b; b = a; | a=0, b=0 |

### Explanation
For a clocked register pipeline, each stage must capture the previous stage's old value on the same edge. Nonblocking assignments provide that behavior within and across clocked processes. Blocking assignments are appropriate for ordered combinational calculations where later statements intentionally use newly computed values. These conventions describe intended hardware and reduce races, but assignment choice alone does not resolve multiple writers.

### Code
```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
  if (!rst_n) begin stage1 <= 0; stage2 <= 0; end
  else begin stage1 <= din; stage2 <= stage1; end
end
always_comb begin
  sum = a + b;
  result = sum ^ mask;
end
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
Do not drive the same variable from unrelated processes. A testbench that drives din with a blocking assignment at the active clock edge can race with the sequential block even though the DUT uses NBA. Use a clocking block or an agreed different drive edge. Combinational blocks need complete assignments to avoid latches.

### Follow-ups
Does NBA make execution parallel? RHS expressions still execute in processes; deferred updates make register sampling behave as simultaneous old-state capture.

title: SystemVerilog Task vs Function
answer: A function cannot consume simulation time and cannot call a time-consuming task. It may return a value or be void. A task may wait, delay, and return values through arguments. Both can be automatic and have input/output/ref arguments. Use functions for calculations and tasks for protocol activity.

title: display, strobe, monitor, and write
answer: $display prints with a newline when executed; $write does the same without adding a newline. $strobe reports at the end of the time slot, after nonblocking updates. $monitor schedules end-of-slot reporting when its monitored arguments change, with one active monitor list.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Choose the print task according to when values must be observed and whether a newline is needed.

| Task | Timing | Newline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $display | At execution | Yes |
| $write | At execution | No |
| $strobe | End of current time slot | Yes |
| $monitor | End of slot after monitored change | Yes |

### Explanation
Nonblocking updates are deferred, so a display immediately following an NBA normally sees the old value. A strobe in that same slot reports the final value after updates. monitor installs a change-driven reporting list; calling it again replaces the active list instead of adding an independent monitor. Use monitoron and monitoroff to control that list when needed.

### Code
```systemverilog
module prints;
  logic q = 0;
  initial begin
    $monitor("monitor q=%0b", q);
    #1;
    q <= 1;
    $display("display q=%0b", q); // 0
    $strobe("strobe q=%0b", q);   // 1
    $write("prefix: ");
    $display("message");
    #1 $finish;
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The relative order of multiple end-of-slot messages should not be treated as a protocol guarantee. Use $time or $realtime plus instance and transaction identifiers for useful diagnostics. A display in an assertion action can show current rather than sampled signal values; use $sampled when reporting the values checked by a concurrent property.

### Follow-ups
For printing a multi-part line use $write, but concurrent processes can interleave their output; build one string before logging when message integrity matters.

title: case, casez, casex, and Priority Encoders
answer: case matches four-state values exactly. casez treats Z and ? as wildcards; casex also masks X, which can hide bugs and is generally unsafe. Priority encoders need explicit ordering, often if/else or a qualified case. `unique`/`priority` add checking and synthesis assumptions but do not repair incomplete assignments. Define behavior for no request.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Use exact case matching by default; wildcard forms can hide unknown inputs, and priority must be explicit.

| Construct | Wildcards |
| --- | --- |
| case | None: X/Z match literally |
| casez | Z and ? |
| casex | X, Z and ? |

### Explanation
This four-request priority encoder assigns the highest index first and supplies complete defaults. It avoids wildcard interpretation entirely. With unknown request bits, ordinary if conditions may still choose a lower known request, so an independent known-value check is useful in verification. The valid flag distinguishes index zero selected from no request.

### Code
```systemverilog
always_comb begin
  valid = 1'b1;
  index = 2'd0;
  if      (req[3]) index = 2'd3;
  else if (req[2]) index = 2'd2;
  else if (req[1]) index = 2'd1;
  else if (req[0]) index = 2'd0;
  else            valid = 1'b0;
end
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 !$isunknown(req));
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
casex can interpret an X caused by an uninitialized or conflicting driver as a useful wildcard and conceal a bug. casez also treats Z bits in the selector as wildcards. unique and priority supply runtime checking and synthesis intent; they do not fill in missing assignments or make overlapping priority patterns mutually exclusive.

### Follow-ups
For a one-hot input, unique case may express the contract, but assert $onehot0(req) separately when zero is legal and reject unknowns explicitly.

title: Streaming Operators and Flattening a 2D Packed Array
answer: Packed multidimensional arrays are already one contiguous packed bit vector and can be assigned to an equal-width vector. Streaming operators reorder chunks: `{>>{a}}` preserves the stream direction and `{<<8{a}}` reverses byte-sized chunks. Unpacked arrays may need explicit packing, and endianness must match the interface.

title: Associative Arrays in a UVM Scoreboard
answer: An associative array keyed by transaction ID or address supports sparse/out-of-order lookup. Store expected data plus metadata and timeout state; on an observed response, check exists(), compare, then delete after successful completion. Detect duplicate IDs, duplicate responses, and leftovers. If IDs can repeat while outstanding, store a queue per ID.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** An associative array maps each outstanding transaction ID to the expected response, allowing out-of-order completion.

| Event | Outstanding IDs |
| --- | --- |
| Issue ID 7 | 7 |
| Issue ID 2 | 7,2 |
| Receive ID 2 | 7 |
| Receive ID 7 | Empty |

### Explanation
The key must uniquely identify a live transaction. Store a value snapshot or clone of mutable objects so later producer edits cannot change the expectation. On a response, first check existence, then compare, report, and consume according to the scoreboard policy. This example consumes even a mismatching response after reporting it, avoiding a second misleading leftover error for an already completed transaction.

### Code
```systemverilog
class response_model;
  bit [31:0] expected[int unsigned];
  function void issue(int unsigned id, bit [31:0] data);
    if (expected.exists(id)) $error("Duplicate outstanding ID %0d", id);
    else expected[id] = data;
  endfunction
  function void receive(int unsigned id, bit [31:0] data);
    if (!expected.exists(id)) $error("Unexpected ID %0d", id);
    else begin
      if (data !== expected[id]) $error("Mismatch ID %0d", id);
      expected.delete(id);
    end
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
Use four-state data if X detection is required; bit inputs coerce unknowns. Check leftover entries in check_phase and add acceptance timestamps for timeout diagnostics. If multiple requests may share an ID, a single array element overwrites information; use a queue per ID or a composite key.

### Follow-ups
How does reset affect outstanding work? Flush it only when the architecture cancels requests; otherwise retain and validate the defined reset-completion behavior.

title: fork...join, join_any, join_none, and Safe Cleanup
answer: join waits for every child; join_any waits for one; join_none lets the parent continue, with children starting when the parent blocks or ends. After join_any, remaining children keep running unless explicitly stopped. Put competing workers/timeouts inside an isolated wrapper process before disable fork so cleanup cannot kill unrelated descendants.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** join controls when the parent resumes; surviving child processes require a deliberate lifetime policy.

| Join form | Parent resumes |
| --- | --- |
| join | After every child completes |
| join_any | After any child completes |
| join_none | Immediately; children start when parent suspends or ends |

### Explanation
For a worker-versus-timeout race, isolate the competition inside one child process, then disable that child's descendants. The outer join waits only for the isolated wrapper. This prevents disable fork from killing unrelated children that the original caller may have started earlier. The example uses delays only to make the control flow runnable.

### Code
```systemverilog
module race_example;
  timeunit 1ns; timeprecision 1ps;
  task automatic race_work();
    fork
      begin
        fork
          begin #3ns; $display("work done"); end
          begin #10ns; $error("timeout"); end
        join_any
        disable fork;
      end
    join
  endtask
  initial race_work();
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
disable fork terminates active descendants of the calling process, not just the nearest textually visible fork block. A completed worker may have spawned its own background process; cancellation should account for those descendants too. If both branches finish in the same time slot, define whether timeout at the boundary is legal rather than relying on scheduling luck.

### Follow-ups
For independent cancellation, retain process handles or use a scoped worker controller; avoid broadly disabling a shared named block during concurrent task invocations.

title: Unique Constraints for a 2D Random Array
answer: Flatten index pairs or compare every distinct pair of cells with foreach and `a[i][j]!=a[k][l]` when their coordinates differ. The legal value range must contain at least rows*columns distinct values. If the requirement is row-only uniqueness, do not overconstrain across rows.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Global uniqueness across a 2D array requires comparisons across different rows as well as within each row.

| 2×2 array | Global unique? |
| --- | --- |
| Row 0: 1,2; row 1: 3,4 | Yes |
| Row 0: 1,2; row 1: 2,3 | No: 2 occurs twice |

### Explanation
A flattened ordinal i*C+j supplies an ordering on cells, so every unordered pair is compared exactly once. This avoids a[i][j] != a[i][j] and cuts duplicate comparisons. The example uses six elements chosen from eight values. If the intended requirement is per-row uniqueness only, use a different constraint; global uniqueness would remove otherwise legal arrays.

### Code
```systemverilog
class unique_grid;
  rand bit [2:0] a[2][3];
  constraint unique_c {
    foreach (a[i,j]) foreach (a[k,l])
      if ((i*3+j) < (k*3+l)) a[i][j] != a[k][l];
  }
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
The domain must contain at least R*C distinct values. For large matrices the pairwise solver cost grows quadratically in the number of cells. Unsigned bit fields avoid accidental negative domain values, but a constrained domain is still needed when its size is not a power of two. Check randomization success before using the matrix.

### Follow-ups
For a full permutation of a known legal set, initialize a flat array, shuffle it, and map back into rows; this is procedural construction rather than a solver-enforced invariant.

title: SystemVerilog cast: Purpose, Dynamic Downcast, and Failure Handling
answer: A static cast such as `int'(x)` changes representation/type without a runtime check. `$cast(derived,base)` performs checked dynamic casting for class handles; it returns success in function form. On failure, do not use the target. Prefer an explicit failure report and avoid unnecessary downcasts by exposing needed virtual base methods.

title: OOP: Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Singleton Pattern
answer: Inheritance reuses a base contract; virtual methods let derived implementations run through base handles. A singleton uses a static stored handle, a restricted (local/protected) constructor, and a static accessor that creates the instance once. In testbenches, global singleton state can contaminate tests.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** Inheritance defines a shared contract, virtual dispatch chooses the runtime implementation, and a singleton centralizes one instance.

| Concept | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Inheritance | packet extends transaction |
| Polymorphism | base handle invokes packet override |
| Singleton | one registry handle returned by get() |

### Explanation
These concepts solve different problems. Inheritance alone does not make a method call dynamically dispatch; the base method must be virtual. A singleton uses a restricted constructor so callers cannot directly create additional instances, plus a static handle shared by the class. The accessor initializes that handle on first use. Keep global mutable state small because it can couple otherwise independent tests.

### Code
```systemverilog
class transaction;
  virtual function string kind(); return "transaction"; endfunction
endclass
class packet extends transaction;
  virtual function string kind(); return "packet"; endfunction
endclass
class registry;
  local static registry instance;
  local function new(); endfunction
  static function registry get();
    if (instance == null) instance = new;
    return instance;
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
A class handle assignment does not copy the object. Singleton lifetime normally spans the simulation, so resetting a DUT does not automatically reset singleton contents. A private constructor also prevents ordinary external factory construction; do not apply this pattern blindly to UVM components.

### Follow-ups
When is dependency injection preferable? When tests need independent state or alternative implementations, pass an interface/base handle through configuration instead of reading a global singleton.

title: OOP: UVM Sequence Bug Analysis
answer: Common problems include reusing one item handle across asynchronous consumers, ignoring randomize failure, missing start_item/finish_item pairing, starting one sequence object concurrently, and using a sequencer with incompatible item type. Trace creation, handle ownership, arbitration, request delivery, and response routing before changing code.
solution:
> Completed by Codex.

**Key idea:** The actual buggy sequence is absent; diagnose ownership and sequencer protocol without inventing a source-specific fix.

| Checkpoint | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Creation | Fresh item or mutable shared handle? |
| Arbitration | start_item before randomize/finish_item? |
| Solve | Failure checked? |
| Completion | Driver calls item_done exactly once? |

### Explanation
A safe baseline creates an item per iteration, waits for arbitration through start_item, randomizes, and delivers it with finish_item. This limits accidental reuse by consumers that retain references. The example assumes a separately defined my_item and a sequencer parameterized with that same item type. It illustrates the correct flow rather than claiming to reproduce the missing code.

### Code
```systemverilog
class safe_sequence extends uvm_sequence #(my_item);
  `uvm_object_utils(safe_sequence)
  function new(string name="safe_sequence"); super.new(name); endfunction
  task body();
    repeat (10) begin
      my_item item;
      item = my_item::type_id::create("item");
      start_item(item);
      if (!item.randomize()) `uvm_fatal("RAND", "Item randomization failed")
      finish_item(item);
    end
  endtask
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
Do not insert simulation-time delays between start_item and finish_item without understanding the sequencer contract. A driver that retains an item after item_done must establish safe ownership. Starting the same sequence object concurrently also shares its execution state; use separate instances.

### Follow-ups
To locate the real bug, obtain the source sequence and driver, then trace one item handle from creation through arbitration, delivery, completion, and any queued analysis consumers.
