> Generated by Gemini via agy. **Key idea:** SoC verification focuses on integration, cross-block concurrency, memory map routing, and system-level data flows between CPU, DMA, and peripherals, contrasting with block-level verification which targets deep microarchitectural corner cases. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph SoC Interconnect Fabric CPU["CPU Subsystem
(C firmware / PSS / VIP)"] --> BUS["System Interconnect / NoC"] DMA["Multi-channel DMA Engine"] --> BUS BUS --> MEM["DDR / System SRAM"] BUS --> PERIPH1["High-speed Peripheral (PCIe / USB)"] BUS --> PERIPH2["Low-speed Peripheral (UART / SPI)"] end subgraph SoC Verification Components MON["System Bus Monitor & Scoreboard"] -.-> BUS INTC["Interrupt Controller Checker"] -.-> CPU end ``` ### Explanation - **Block-Level vs SoC-Level Scope:** - *Block-Level Verification:* Exhaustive functional verification of individual IPs using UVM agents, constrained random stimulus, and protocol assertions. Focuses on internal FIFOs, FSM transitions, and interface protocol compliance. - *SoC-Level Verification:* Assumes blocks are functionally clean. Focuses on system integration, multi-master arbitration, memory mapping, interrupt routing, and clock/reset sequencing. - **Core SoC Verification Focus Areas:** 1. *Address Mapping & Routing:* Ensure CPU and DMA accesses reach the correct peripheral addresses and that unmapped regions trigger standard bus aborts (DECERR). 2. *Concurrent Data Paths & QoS:* Stress multiple DMA channels and CPU memory transactions contending simultaneously for shared DDR bandwidth. 3. *End-to-End Data Flows:* Peripheral receives external data $\to$ DMA transfers to DDR $\to$ CPU processes data $\to$ DMA sends to output peripheral. 4. *Power and Reset Integration:* Verify power domain crossing, low-power sleep/wake sequences (UPF/CPF), and subsystem reset isolation. - **Methodology:** Combines C-based firmware sequences running on the embedded CPU with external UVM VIPs driving chip boundaries. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - **Cache Coherency:** DMA writing to memory while CPU caches hold stale data, or CPU writing without cache flushing before DMA transmission. - **Interrupt Deadlocks:** Peripherals generating interrupts that require multi-step clear sequences; verify interrupt line deassertion prevents CPU lockup. ### Follow-ups - What is Portable Stimulus Standard (PSS)? A standard enabling abstract verification intent to generate tests for both block-level UVM and SoC-level C firmware. - Why are full UVM scoreboards rarely used at SoC level? High abstraction and simulation runtime make lightweight end-to-end memory checkers more practical.

title: Verification: Test Plan for Address-Based Routing DUT (A/B Client)
answer: Build an independent address-to-client routing model. Monitor requests and responses, preserving IDs. Test each region's first/last address, gaps, illegal addresses, overlapping decode priorities, outstanding traffic, errors, and backpressure.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy.

**Key idea:** Testing an address-based router requires verifying address decoding at boundary edges, ensuring unmapped address holes generate decode errors without leaking data, and checking that concurrent backpressure on one client does not stall traffic to the other.

| Test Category | Target Scenario | Stimulus Strategy | Checker & Expected Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Boundary Decoding | Start and end addresses of Client A & B | Targeted writes/reads to $Addr_{min}$, $Addr_{max}$, and adjacent words | Correct destination port asserted; zero misrouted packets |
| Address Gaps & Holes | Unmapped address regions between clients | Random access to unmapped memory holes | Decode Error (DECERR/SLVERR); no packet forwarded to A or B |
| Priority & Overlap | Overlapping region decode priority | Transactions targeting shared prefix address ranges | Router routes strictly according to defined priority rule |
| Cross-Port Backpressure | Client A stalls (`ready=0`), Client B open | Continuous burst to Client A interleaved with Client B | Client B traffic proceeds without head-of-line blocking |

### Explanation
- **Address Decode Logic:** Verify that each client's base address and address mask correctly route incoming transactions. Validate boundary transitions: the last address of Client A ($A_{max}$) and the first address of Client B ($B_{min}$).
- **Scoreboard Architecture:**
  - Connect a monitor on the upstream input interface and monitors on both downstream client interfaces (Client A and Client B).
  - The scoreboard maintains an internal reference address map.
  - When an input item arrives, the scoreboard predicts the destination port. If routed to Client A, it pushes the item to `client_a_expected_queue`; if unmapped, it asserts that an error response is generated.
- **Flow Control & Congestion:** Verify that if Client A asserts backpressure (e.g., slave FIFO full), transactions destined for Client B can still bypass or proceed (unless the DUT architecture explicitly specifies head-of-line blocking).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Partial Word Writes:** Sub-word byte enables (`strb`) on address boundaries must not trigger spurious decode errors.
- **Outstanding Pipelined Requests:** Verify correct tracking when multiple requests to Client A and Client B are in flight simultaneously.

### Follow-ups
- How to handle dynamic address remapping? If base address registers (BARs) are programmable, reconfigure BARs mid-test and verify immediate routing updates.
- What if an illegal address is accessed? The DUT must return a bus slave error and prevent data corruption in adjacent client domains.

title: Async FIFO vs Circular FIFO vs Sync FIFO
answer: A synchronous FIFO has one clock; an asynchronous FIFO crosses independent clocks with Gray-coded synchronized pointers. Circular FIFO describes wraparound storage organization, so it can be sync or async.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy.

**Key idea:** Synchronous and asynchronous FIFOs differ in clocking domains and pointer synchronization schemes, whereas circular FIFO describes the ring-buffer storage topology that can be implemented synchronously or asynchronously.

| Attribute | Synchronous FIFO | Asynchronous FIFO | Circular FIFO |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clock Domains | Single common clock (`clk`) | Independent write (`wclk`) and read (`rclk`) | Single or Dual (describes topology) |
| Pointer Encoding | Binary counters | Gray code (for CDC synchronization) | Binary index with modulo wrap |
| Full/Empty Check | Direct pointer comparison in same domain | Pointers synchronized across domains via 2-FF | Direct or synchronized pointer comparison |
| Latency to Flag | Instantaneous (1 cycle) | Multi-cycle synchronization latency | Dependent on sync implementation |
| Primary Use Case | Pipeline buffering, rate matching | Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) | Streaming ring buffers, audio/video frames |

### Explanation
- **Synchronous FIFO:**
  - Both read and write operations use the same clock.
  - Pointers are simple binary counters. Full and empty conditions are detected instantly by comparing the write pointer and read pointer (typically using an extra MSB wrap bit to distinguish full from empty).
- **Asynchronous FIFO:**
  - Operates across two asynchronous, unrelated clock domains (`wclk` and `rclk`).
  - Pointers must cross clock domains to evaluate full (in write domain) and empty (in read domain).
  - To prevent CDC metastability and multi-bit transition skews, pointers are converted to Gray code (where only 1 bit changes per increment) and passed through 2-stage flip-flop synchronizers.
- **Circular FIFO:**
  - Refers to the architectural organization of storage memory where the buffer address wraps around modulo the FIFO depth. Both sync and async FIFOs are almost universally implemented as circular ring buffers.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Pessimistic Flags in Async FIFO:** In async FIFOs, empty and full flags are conservative: a full flag may persist for a few write cycles after a read occurs because of synchronization latency. This is safe (prevents overflow/underflow) but affects peak throughput.
- **Wrap Bit in Gray Pointers:** In async FIFOs, detecting full requires comparing Gray-coded pointers where the two most significant bits are inverted and remaining bits match.

### Follow-ups
- Why must Gray code be used for async FIFO pointers? Gray code guarantees that only a single bit changes on each counter step, preventing catastrophic multi-bit sampling corruption in CDC synchronizers.
- Can depth be non-power-of-2 in an async FIFO? Yes, but standard Gray codes only wrap cleanly for powers of 2 ($2^N$); non-power-of-2 requires specialized Gray code counters.

title: Async FIFO Potential Problems
answer: Metastability, bad Gray encoding/wrap, pointer skew, premature full/empty, reset-domain inconsistency, lost/duplicated data. Use CDC review, constraints, assertions, randomized clock ratios/phases, and data-order scoreboarding.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy.

**Key idea:** Asynchronous FIFOs are prone to CDC metastability, multi-bit pointer skew, pointer wrap failures on non-power-of-2 depths, and reset-domain mismatches, all of which require Gray coding, 2-FF synchronizers, and cross-domain reset sequencing.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "wclk",         "wave": "p....." },
  { "name": "wptr_bin",     "wave": "=..===.", "data": ["0", "1", "2", "3"] },
  { "name": "wptr_gray",    "wave": "=..===.", "data": ["00", "01", "11", "10"] },
  { "name": "rclk",         "wave": "P......" },
  { "name": "sync_stage1",  "wave": "x..===.", "data": ["00", "01", "11"] },
  { "name": "sync_stage2",  "wave": "x...===.", "data": ["00", "01", "11"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "Gray Pointer CDC Synchronization across Asynchronous Clocks" } }
```

### Explanation
- **1. Metastability & Multi-Bit CDC Skew:**
  - If binary pointers are synchronized directly, multiple bits change simultaneously (e.g., `0111` to `1000`). Clock skew causes the receiving domain to sample intermediate invalid values (e.g. `0000`), generating false full/empty or data corruption.
  - *Fix:* Convert binary pointers to Gray code so only 1 bit transitions per increment, and pass through 2-stage flip-flop synchronizers.
- **2. Non-Power-of-2 Depth Wrap:**
  - Standard Gray codes wrap from $2^N-1$ to $0$ with a 1-bit Hamming distance. If depth is not a power of 2, wrapping between arbitrary endpoints changes multiple bits, reintroducing metastability.
  - *Fix:* Use symmetrical truncated Gray codes or restrict FIFO depths to $2^N$.
- **3. Reset Domain Asynchrony:**
  - If `wreset_n` and `rreset_n` deassert at different times, one domain starts operating while the other domain's synchronizers are held in reset, corrupting pointer tracking.
  - *Fix:* Implement coordinated reset sequencing: asynchronously assert, synchronously deassert in each respective clock domain.
- **4. Memory Write-to-Read Race:**
  - If read domain receives the updated write pointer before the dual-port SRAM write access has completed and settled, the read domain reads corrupted data.
  - *Fix:* Ensure pointer propagation path delay $\ge$ SRAM write-to-data-valid delay.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Pointer Comparison for Full:** In the write domain, FIFO is full when:
  `wptr_gray == {~rptr_gray_sync[ADDR_WIDTH:ADDR_WIDTH-1], rptr_gray_sync[ADDR_WIDTH-2:0]}`.
  Failing to invert the top two bits causes incorrect full detection.

### Follow-ups
- What is MTBF in CDC? Mean Time Between Failures, calculated using synchronizer clock frequencies, data toggle rates, and flip-flop setup/hold parameters.
- Why are full/empty flags conservative? Pointers take 2-3 destination clock cycles to cross; thus "full" indicates the FIFO was full 2 cycles ago, preventing overflow safely.

title: Simulation Runs Forever - Debug Strategy
answer: Check if simulation time progresses. A zero-delay loop freezes time; a running clock with no completion suggests objections, blocked handshakes, wait conditions, or missing responses. Inspect process stacks and objection traces (+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE). Add bounded watchdogs with state dumps.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy. **Key idea:** Debugging an infinite simulation begins by checking if simulation time is advancing: frozen time indicates zero-delay combinational or delta-cycle loops, while advancing time indicates leaked UVM phase objections, deadlocked handshakes, or hardware stalls. ```mermaid flowchart TD HANG["Simulation Runs Forever / Hangs"] --> TIME_CHK{"Is simulation time ($time) advancing?"} TIME_CHK -->|NO: Time is Frozen| DELTA["Zero-Delay Infinite Loop
- Unbounded while(1) loop
- Combinational feedback event loop (@*)
Debug: Interrupt with Ctrl+C, inspect stack trace"] TIME_CHK -->|YES: Time is Advancing| UVM_CHK{"Are UVM Phase Objections held?"} UVM_CHK -->|Objection Leaked| OBJ["Leaked Objection
- Component raised objection but never dropped it
- Sequence died before drop_objection()
Debug: Run with +UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE"] UVM_CHK -->|Objections Dropped| HW_STALL["Protocol / Hardware Deadlock
- Driver waiting for PREADY / valid-ready handshake
- Sequencer get_next_item blocked
Debug: Inspect waveform, enable watchdog timers"] ``` ### Explanation - **Step 1: Check Simulation Time Advancement** - *Time Frozen ($t$ constant, CPU 100%):* Caused by an infinite loop in a zero-delay procedural block (e.g. `while(cond)` without clock wait) or circular combinational evaluation (`always @(a) b = ~b`). Debug by sending `Ctrl+C` in simulator or using simulator profiler to display the active source line. - *Time Advancing ($t$ increases without terminating):* The simulator is executing clock cycles normally, but the termination condition is never reached. - **Step 2: Trace UVM Phase Objections** - Run the simulation with `+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE`. The UVM log will print every `raise_objection` and `drop_objection` event with component path and objection count. - Identify the component that raised an objection and failed to drop it before completion. - **Step 3: Investigate Protocol Deadlocks** - Check driver-sequencer interface: Driver called `seq_item_port.get_next_item()` but no sequence is generating items, or sequence called `start_item()` while driver is waiting on DUT pins. - Hardware deadlock: DUT interface waiting for `ready` handshake, credit exhaustion in flow-control buffer, or missing interrupt. - **Step 4: Implement Watchdogs** - Always configure a global phase timeout in the base test: `uvm_root::get().set_timeout(10ms, 1)`. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - **Silent Exception in Forked Thread:** A background thread created with `fork...join_none` terminates abnormally or crashes without dropping its objection, locking the phase indefinitely. - **Scoreboard Queue Accumulation:** Unmatched transactions accumulating in a scoreboard can consume all host memory, causing simulation to grind to a halt due to swapping. ### Follow-ups - How to inspect running threads in Questa or VCS? Use interactive commands `show threads` or `run -dump`. - What is a UVM heartbeat? A `uvm_heartbeat` monitor that monitors periodic events (e.g. transactions) and triggers an alert if no activity occurs within a defined window.

title: Cannot Reproduce Regression Bug
answer: Record seed, test/config, simulator version/options, RTL/TB revisions, inputs, and environment. Check race conditions, uninitialized data, thread ordering, and randomization stability. A seed alone does not reproduce a run when code or tool settings differ.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy.

**Key idea:** Inability to reproduce a failing regression run with the same seed is caused by environmental deltas, uninitialized 4-state variables, race conditions in non-deterministic simulator event scheduling, or git revision mismatches.

| Discrepancy Category | Root Cause Mechanism | Verification & Fix Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Environment & Toolchain | Different compiler flags, simulator minor release, OS env variables | Archive exact simulator command line, tool version, and LD_LIBRARY_PATH |
| Race Conditions | Delta-cycle non-determinism between concurrent `always` / `initial` blocks | Eliminate active-event races; use non-blocking (`<=`) in sequential logic |
| Uninitialized Variables | 4-state vs 2-state variable differences; X-optimism in logic | Enable `-xprop` and initialize all testbench and RTL variables on reset |
| PRNG Divergence | Unstable thread spawning alters `$urandom` sequence order | Use hierarchical object seeding; avoid calling `$urandom` in concurrent forks |
| Code Revision Drift | Local uncommitted changes vs regression git commit SHA | Log git commit hash (`git rev-parse HEAD`) directly in simulation banner |

### Explanation
- **Event Scheduling Races:** SystemVerilog IEEE 1800 defines a partial order for event regions. The execution order of processes within the Active Region (e.g., multiple `always` blocks sensitive to the same clock edge, or `fork...join_none` threads) is explicitly non-deterministic. Different tool versions or CPU load can reorder delta events, exposing hidden race conditions.
- **PRNG Seed Stability:** UVM provides a hierarchical random seeding mechanism (`uvm_seed_map`). However, if a testbench thread calls global `$urandom` or `$urandom_range` from dynamic threads whose creation order varies, the entire downstream random sequence diverges.
- **Uninitialized 4-State Variables:** Variables not explicitly initialized may take `X` in simulation, where RTL conditional expressions `if (x)` evaluate to false (X-optimism), whereas in gate-level or different simulator options they evaluate differently.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Dynamic File / Network Dependencies:** Testbenches reading from shared scratch directories where temporary files were overwritten by parallel regression jobs.
- **Plusarg Inconsistencies:** Regression scripts passing hidden default plusargs (e.g., `+UVM_VERBOSITY=UVM_LOW` or memory preloading flags) omitted during local reproduction.

### Follow-ups
- How to achieve stable random sequences? Use class-based `srandom(seed)` and isolate thread randomness from global `$urandom`.
- How can simulator race detection options help? Tools like VCS `-race` or Questa `check_races` detect conflicting read/write operations within the same time step.

title: Sources of X-Propagation in Simulation
answer: Uninitialized storage, conflicting drivers, incomplete assignments, out-of-range indices, power-off corruption, and gate-level timing violations. Trace the first X source. Use xprop modes to expose X-optimism.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy. **Key idea:** X-states originate from uninitialized flip-flops, multi-driver bus contention, gate-level timing violations, and out-of-bounds memory indexing, posing risks of X-optimism hiding real hardware bugs in RTL simulations. ```mermaid flowchart TD X_SRC["Sources of X (Unknown Value)"] --> S1["Uninitialized Registers / Flops before Reset"] X_SRC --> S2["Multi-Driver Bus Contention (0 and 1 driving wire)"] X_SRC --> S3["Gate-Level Timing Violations (Setup / Hold Violations)"] X_SRC --> S4["Out-of-Bounds Memory / Array Reads (mem[invalid_addr])"] X_SRC --> S5["Low Power Domain Isolation Failure (Unpowered domain driven active)"] X_SRC --> SIM_BEHAVIOR["Simulation Impact"] SIM_BEHAVIOR --> X_OPT["X-Optimism (RTL Simulation):
if (X) treated as FALSE -> Masks silicon bugs!"] SIM_BEHAVIOR --> X_PESS["X-Pessimism (Gate Simulation):
X on MUX input taints output even if both data inputs match"] SIM_BEHAVIOR --> REMED["Mitigation Strategies:
- Run simulator -xprop (forward/backward X-propagation)
- SVA assertions: assert (!$isunknown(bus))
- Complete synchronous / asynchronous reset trees"] ``` ### Explanation - **Root Causes of X in Simulation:** 1. *Uninitialized Storage:* 4-state flip-flops and registers power up with value `1'bx` until explicitly reset or written. 2. *Driver Contention:* Multiple active drivers driving opposite logic levels (`1'b0` and `1'b1`) onto a shared `wire` resolve to `1'bx`. 3. *Timing Violations:* In gate-level simulations with SDF back-annotation, setup or hold violations cause flip-flop UDP models to transition their outputs to `X`. 4. *Out-of-Bounds Indexing:* Reading an array or associative memory with an unmapped or X-valued index returns `X`. 5. *Power Gating:* Powered-down voltage domains without active isolation cells leak `X` into active logic. - **The X-Optimism Danger:** In RTL SystemVerilog, `if (cond)` executes the `else` branch whenever `cond` evaluates to `1'bx`. This masks silicon bugs where unknown control signals would actually cause hardware malfunction. - **Remediation:** - Compile with simulator `-xprop` flags to enforce accurate X-propagation through `if/case` constructs. - Place SVA assertions at key interfaces: `assert property (@(posedge clk) !$isunknown(valid))`. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - **X-Pessimism in GLS:** A 2-to-1 MUX where both input data lines are `1'b1` will output `1'bx` in gate-level simulation if the select line is `1'bx`, even though silicon hardware would deterministically output `1'b1`. ### Follow-ups - What is the difference between `-xprop=forward` and `-xprop=backward`? Forward propagates X through assignments; backward propagates X when conditions are ambiguous. - Why are 2-state types (`bit`, `int`) risky in testbenches? 2-state types automatically convert `X` to `0`, silently concealing DUT bugs.

title: SCB Design with Leading Drop and Garbage Bits
answer: Define framing, leading-drop count, alignment, and which bits are garbage. Reconstruct the valid payload from monitored bits, discard only the explicitly allowed regions, and compare the meaningful bits.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy. **Key idea:** A scoreboard handling streams with initial training patterns and padded garbage bits must incorporate a pre-comparison framing filter to discard the initial drop count and apply canonical bitmasks to compare only valid payload bits. ```mermaid flowchart LR RAW["Raw Monitored Stream
(contains training words & padded bits)"] --> FILTER["Pre-Scoreboard Filter / Intake"] FILTER --> DROP{"Leading Drop Counter < N?"} DROP -->|Yes| DISCARD["Discard Training Words
Increment drop_count"] DROP -->|No: Active Stream| MASK["Apply Payload Bitmask:
masked_data = data & DATA_MASK"] MASK --> FIFO["Push Normalized Transaction
into Scoreboard Match FIFO"] EXP["Reference Model
Expected Transactions"] --> FIFO_EXP["Expected FIFO"] FIFO --> COMP["Scoreboard Comparator"] FIFO_EXP --> COMP ``` ### Explanation - **Framing & Drop Counter:** - High-speed serial interfaces, Ethernet PHYs, and DSP pipelines often emit an initial sequence of training symbols, preamble bytes, or calibration pulses that do not represent valid application data. - The scoreboard (or subscriber pre-filter) maintains a state machine or integer counter: `if (drop_count < LEADING_DROP_COUNT) begin drop_count++; return; end` - Only after the calibration phase completes does the scoreboard begin pushing actual transactions into comparison queues. - **Bit Masking for Garbage/Padding Bits:** - Often, protocols pack 12-bit or 24-bit data into 32-bit words, leaving reserved upper bits uninitialized or filled with arbitrary hardware noise ("garbage bits"). - Do not use raw equality comparison (`act == exp`). - Implement a custom comparison method: ```systemverilog localparam bit [31:0] DATA_MASK = 32'h00FF_FFFF; // Upper 8 bits are garbage if ((actual.data & DATA_MASK) != (expected.data & DATA_MASK)) begin `uvm_error("SCB_MISMATCH", $sformatf("Mismatch: Act=0x%0h, Exp=0x%0h", actual.data, expected.data)) end ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - **Dynamic Drop Count:** If leading training length is negotiated dynamically (e.g. via handshake pins), the drop count cannot be a hardcoded constant; it must be driven by monitor sideband events. - **Garbage Bits in CRC:** If the protocol includes a CRC, verify whether the CRC is computed over raw words (including garbage bits) or over masked payload bits. ### Follow-ups - Where should the mask be applied? In the scoreboard comparator or inside a custom `do_compare()` method on the sequence item. - How to verify that garbage bits don't leak information? Implement a dedicated assertion ensuring garbage bits do not carry stale data from previous secure transactions.

title: Test Plan: Async FIFO Corner Cases & Verification
answer: Cover unrelated clock ratios/phases, near-equal clocks, burst traffic, full/empty, pointer wrap, simultaneous operations, stalls, and reset of each domain. Check no overflow/underflow, order, capacity, flag latency. Add CDC/STA checks.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy.

**Key idea:** Verifying an asynchronous FIFO requires stressing clock frequency extremes and phase drift, exercising continuous full/empty transitions, testing concurrent push/pop with pointer wrap, and verifying asynchronous reset recovery.

| Verification Dimension | Test Scenario | Stimulus Strategy | Checker & Success Metric |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clock Frequency Ratios | Extreme frequency differences ($f_W \gg f_R$ and $f_W \ll f_R$) | Independent clock generators with randomized frequencies | No underflow/overflow; data ordering preserved |
| Phase Drift / Jitter | Near-equal clocks ($f_W approx f_R$) with phase drift | Clocks with fractional period offsets and randomized jitter | CDC synchronizers reliably resolve CDC edges |
| Capacity Boundaries | Exact Full, exact Empty, full-to-empty continuous burst | Bursts of size $D$, $D+1$, and alternating single push/pop | SVA asserts `!full` on push, `!empty` on pop; flag timing correct |
| Pointer Wrap-Around | Continuous streaming past $2^N$ items | Long randomized bursts exceeding $4 imes$ FIFO depth | Gray-code wrap verified; zero data loss |
| Asynchronous Reset | Reset asserted during active push/pop bursts | Asynchronous reset pulse injected mid-transfer | Pointers reset to 0; empty=1, full=0; no residual data read |

### Explanation
- **Clock Ratio Verification:**
  - *Fast Write, Slow Read:* Stresses write full condition and backpressure handling.
  - *Slow Write, Fast Read:* Stresses empty detection and read latency.
  - *Mesochronous (Same frequency, drifting phase):* Stresses setup/hold windows of synchronizer flip-flops.
- **Data Integrity & Ordering Scoreboard:**
  - An independent scoreboard monitors `wdata` pushed on write clock edges and `rdata` popped on read clock edges.
  - Pushes `wdata` into an internal SystemVerilog queue `expected_q[$]` and pops on valid `rdata` to verify strict FIFO ordering, zero data corruption, and exact capacity limits.
- **Assertions (SVA):**
  - Check that write while full (`winc && wfull`) never corrupts existing memory.
  - Check that read while empty (`rinc && rempty`) never outputs valid data.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Simultaneous Read and Write:** Pushing and popping in the same cycle when the FIFO is almost full or almost empty must update internal pointer counters correctly without false flag toggles.
- **Reset Glitches:** Asynchronous reset deassertion must be synchronized to avoid metastability in write and read pointer registers.

### Follow-ups
- How to model CDC jitter in simulation? Add randomized micro-delays (`#($urandom_range(10, 100)*1ps)`) to clock generation edges.
- Why is functional coverage on Gray pointers important? To ensure every single-bit transition in the Gray sequence and the wrap-around boundary were hit.

title: Formal Verification - How It Works
answer: Formal tools explore state space symbolically to prove properties for all allowed traces or produce counterexamples. Assumptions restrict inputs; assertions specify guarantees; covers show reachability. Review vacuity and overconstraint; a bounded pass only proves the examined depth.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy. **Key idea:** Formal verification mathematically analyzes all reachable state spaces over all time steps using SAT/SMT solvers to prove design properties, utilizing `assert` for design guarantees, `assume` for input constraints, and `cover` to prevent vacuous proofs. ```mermaid flowchart TD SPEC["Design Specification & RTL Code"] --> FORMAL_TB["Formal Testbench (SVA)"] subgraph FORMAL_TB [Property Types] P1["assume property:
Restricts inputs to legal environment behavior"] P2["assert property:
Specifies design invariants & requirements to prove"] P3["cover property:
Checks scenario reachability (guards against vacuity)"] end FORMAL_TB --> ENGINE["Formal Model Checker (SAT / SMT / BDD)"] ENGINE --> RES{"Solver Result"} RES -->|Proof| PASS["FULL PROOF / BOUNDED PASS
Property holds mathematically for all reachable states"] RES -->|Violation| CEX["COUNTEREXAMPLE TRACE
Cycle-by-cycle waveform demonstrating bug"] RES -->|Unreachable Cover| OVER["OVER-CONSTRAINT ERROR
Assumptions accidentally eliminated valid design states"] ``` ### Explanation - **Principle of Formal Verification:** Unlike simulation, which tests specific stimulus vectors over time, formal verification converts the RTL and SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) into mathematical boolean formulas. Solvers search for any assignment of inputs over any number of cycles that can violate an assertion. - **Core Directives:** - `assert property`: Mathematical proof goal; states what the DUT must guarantee. - `assume property`: Constrains input stimulus to valid protocol behavior. The tool assumes these are always true when searching for assertion failures. - `cover property`: Proves that a specific state is reachable under the assumptions. Essential to detect *vacuity* (where over-restrictive assumptions inadvertently eliminate legal traffic). - **Bounded Model Checking (BMC) vs Full Proof:** - *BMC:* Unrolls the state transition relation up to $k$ cycles. Proves that no counterexample exists within depth $k$. - *Unbounded Proof (Induction):* Uses mathematical induction to prove the property holds for infinite depth. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - **Over-Constraining Inputs:** Adding an incorrect `assume` statement (e.g. `assume (ready == 1)`) makes assertions pass vacuously because the solver never explores the conditions where the bug exists. - **State Space Explosion:** Complex arithmetic units (multipliers, floating-point units) or large memories can cause formal tools to exhaust memory or run indefinitely without proving properties. ### Follow-ups - How to solve state-space explosion? Abstract large memories using black-boxing or read/write associative formal models. - What is a counterexample? The shortest cycle-by-cycle stimulus trace generated by the formal engine proving an assertion violation.

title: Scoreboard for Paired A/B Transactions with Timeout
answer: Use an associative table per pair ID with side-A/side-B data, arrival times, and duplicate flags. Match when both exist, expire unmatched entries, support either arrival order, and report leftovers at end of test.

title: Is Gate-Level Simulation Still Needed After RTL Verification?
answer: GLS checks reset/init behavior, scan configuration, library timing checks, SDF paths, and X behavior. STA/LEC/CDC cover much of the space more efficiently; choose targeted GLS cases.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy.

**Key idea:** Gate-level simulation remains necessary despite STA and LEC because it verifies asynchronous reset deassertion recovery, scan chain and DFT modes, clock gating cell timing, and multi-cycle/false-path timing exceptions.

| Verification Tool | What It Proves | What It Misses / Blind Spots | Why GLS Is Still Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| RTL Simulation | Functional & architectural logic correctness | Gate delays, physical cells, X-optimism | Cannot see netlist timing or cell dynamics |
| STA (Static Timing) | Setup and hold timing across all paths | Functional correctness of reset, multi-cycle logic | Verifies constraints but cannot validate if false-paths are truly safe |
| LEC (Equivalence) | Boolean logical equivalence of RTL vs Netlist | Dynamic timing, asynchronous reset deassertion | Proves logic equations match, ignoring all temporal timing |
| CDC Analysis | Clock domain crossing synchronization structures | Physical netlist implementation and placement delays | Validates synchronization intent, not physical gate delays |
| **GLS (Gate-Level)** | **Dynamic timing with SDF, reset recovery, DFT/scan, X-handling** | **Slow execution (100x-1000x slower than RTL)** | **Validates complete physical netlist with timing** |

### Explanation
- **Asynchronous Reset Recovery & Removal:** Static tools analyze reset paths, but dynamic gate-level simulation verifies that when reset deasserts asynchronously, all registers cleanly exit reset on the correct clock edge without glitching or entering unknown states.
- **Validating Timing Exceptions:** Designers manually declare `set_false_path` and `set_multicycle_path` in SDC timing constraints. If a timing exception was declared incorrectly, STA will ignore the violation, leading to silicon failure. GLS with SDF back-annotation exposes these erroneous assumptions.
- **DFT & Scan Chain Verification:** Tests that scan chains shift correctly, ATPG patterns run on actual silicon netlists, and memory BIST controllers function properly with physical library macros.
- **Clock Gating Cells (ICGs):** Verifies that enable signals to Integrated Clock Gating cells settle without glitching before the clock rising edge.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **X-Pessimism in GLS:** Gate-level UDP primitives often propagate `X` excessively on multiplexers and reset loops where silicon would settle cleanly, requiring manual zero-delay overrides or `$inhibit_xprop`.
- **Targeted GLS Strategy:** Due to low execution speed, do not run the full regression in GLS; select targeted boot-up, reset, DFT, and high-stress interface packets.

### Follow-ups
- What is an SDF file? Standard Delay Format file containing calculated cell delays and interconnect wiring delays from physical place-and-route.
- What are unit-delay gate-level simulations? Simulations run on the gate-level netlist without SDF delays, primarily used to verify scan chains and X-propagation before layout.

title: Serial-to-Parallel DUT - Driver, Monitor, Scoreboard
answer: Driver emits serial bits on accepted sampling events. Monitor independently captures and reconstructs words using specified bit order/framing. Scoreboard predicts parallel outputs after defined latency. Cover incomplete words, gaps, framing errors.
solution:
> Generated by Gemini via agy.

**Key idea:** A serial-to-parallel verification environment uses a driver that serializes parallel transactions with framing bits onto a single wire, dual monitors that independently capture the serial input and parallel output, and a scoreboard that verifies data deserialization and latency.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "sclk",        "wave": "p..........." },
  { "name": "sdata_in",    "wave": "01.0.1.1.0..", "data": ["start", "b0", "b1", "b2", "b3"] },
  { "name": "pready",      "wave": "1..........0" },
  { "name": "pvalid_out",  "wave": "0........1.0" },
  { "name": "pdata_out",   "wave": "x........=..", "data": ["4'hB"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "Serial-to-Parallel Conversion: 4 Serial Bits (1011 = 0xB) to Parallel Output" } }
```

### Explanation
- **Driver Architecture:**
  - Receives a high-level transaction containing an $N$-bit data word from the sequencer.
  - Generates protocol framing: drives an active START bit, sequentially drives data bits (either LSB-first or MSB-first per specification) on `sclk` edges, and optionally appends parity and STOP bits.
- **Monitor Architecture:**
  - *Serial Input Monitor:* Operates passively on the serial pin. Detects the framing start condition, shifts bits into an accumulator, and broadcasts the reconstructed word on an analysis port.
  - *Parallel Output Monitor:* Samples `pdata_out` when `pvalid_out && pready` are asserted on the parallel clock domain, broadcasting the captured parallel packet.
- **Scoreboard Architecture:**
  - Pushes transactions from the serial monitor into an `expected_queue[$]`.
  - Upon receiving transactions from the parallel output monitor, pops from `expected_queue` and asserts that:
    1. Data words match bit-for-bit.
    2. Conversion latency falls within the specified cycle window.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Framing Errors & Glitches:** Incomplete serial words (e.g. fewer than $N$ bits before reset) must not cause the parallel interface to emit false `pvalid` strobes.
- **Backpressure on Parallel Side:** If the parallel consumer deasserts `pready`, the DUT must either stall incoming serial reception or assert an overflow error flag.

### Follow-ups
- How to handle different clock domains? If serial clock and parallel clock are asynchronous, the testbench must model clock jitter and sample outputs with appropriate CDC domain crossing checks.
- What if bit order is configurable? Constrain the driver and monitor configuration objects to test both LSB-first and MSB-first modes.

title: Functional Coverage Not 100% - Analysis and Strategy
answer: Inspect unhit bins and map each to a requirement. Determine whether reachable, stimulus missing, sampling wrong, or overconstrained. Add directed constraints/sequences for reachable gaps and justify exclusions. Do not change bins simply to obtain 100%.
solution:
**Key idea:** Every unhit bin is a question to answer, not a number to fix. Classify each hole as *unreachable*, *not stimulated*, *sampled wrong*, or *over-constrained*, then close it with stimulus or a justified exclusion. Never reshape bins just to reach 100%. ```mermaid flowchart TD H["Unhit bin / cross"] --> R{"Is it legal and reachable per spec?"} R -->|No| EX["Exclude: ignore_bins / illegal_bins
plus a written waiver tied to the spec"] R -->|Yes| S{"Was the scenario ever driven?
(check stimulus logs, transaction dump)"} S -->|Yes, but bin not hit| SM["Sampling bug: wrong event, wrong clock,
sampled before update, iff gate wrong"] S -->|No| C{"Do constraints allow it?"} C -->|No| OC["Over-constrained: relax or add a
constraint mode / dist weight"] C -->|Yes, just rare| DS["Directed sequence or biased test
(dist, solve-before, more seeds)"] SM --> FIX["Fix covergroup, re-run, re-merge"] OC --> FIX DS --> FIX ``` ### Explanation 1. **Get the hole report** from the merged coverage database (all seeds, all tests). A hole in one test may be hit by another. 2. **Map each bin back to a verification-plan item.** If no requirement maps to it, the bin may be badly specified. 3. **Triage**: - *Unreachable* (e.g. a mode not supported in this config): exclude with `ignore_bins` or a tool exclusion, and have the designer or architect sign off on the waiver. - *Sampling bug*: e.g. `sample()` called on the wrong edge, `iff (valid)` where it should be `valid && ready`, or a cross sampled before both fields are updated. Fix the model, then re-check bins that were already hit, because they may also be wrong. - *Over-constrained*: a `soft` default never overridden, a `dist` weight of 0, or `solve...before` missing so the probability is close to zero. - *Rare but legal*: write a directed or weighted sequence and run more seeds. 4. **Re-run regression and re-merge.** Track closure over time and stop when the plan is met, not when the number reaches 100. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - 100% functional coverage with a weak covergroup means nothing. Also check code coverage for dead RTL that the plan never mentions. - Crosses blow up quickly. Use `binsof ... intersect` to keep only meaningful combinations. - An exclusion with no reason written down is a review finding. ### Follow-ups - *Code coverage 100%, functional 80%?* Stimulus reaches the logic, but the important combinations or sequences were not hit. Add targeted tests. - *Functional 100%, code 70%?* The plan is missing features. Add coverpoints or prove the code is dead. - *How do you prioritize holes?* By risk: a feature used by the customer plus the likelihood of a bug comes before cosmetic bins.

title: Multi-Channel DUT with Credit-Based Flow Control
answer: Track credits per channel: decrement on sends and increment on releases. Assert no send without credit, no over-return. Exercise simultaneous send/release, imbalance, delayed returns, reset, and starvation.
solution:
**Key idea:** Keep a **per-channel credit scoreboard** in the testbench: `credits[ch]` starts at the reset value, goes down by 1 on every send and up on every release. Check it every cycle: never send at 0 credits, never go above the maximum. Then stress the concurrency cases: send and release in the same cycle, all channels at once, and delayed returns.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",          "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "send[0]",      "wave": "01.0....1.0" },
  { "name": "release[0]",   "wave": "0...1.0.1.0" },
  { "name": "credit[0]",    "wave": "=.==.==....", "data": ["2","1","0","1","2"] },
  { "name": "stall (ch0)",  "wave": "0..1.0....." }
],
  "head": { "text": "max credits = 2; send blocked at 0; same-cycle send+release keeps count" } }
```

### Explanation
- **Reference model** (in a monitor-fed checker):
```systemverilog
class credit_model #(int NCH = 4, int MAXC = 8);
  int credits[NCH];
  function void reset(); foreach (credits[i]) credits[i] = MAXC; endfunction
  // call once per clock with all events seen that cycle
  function void step(bit [NCH-1:0] send, bit [NCH-1:0] rel);
    foreach (credits[i]) begin
      if (send[i] && credits[i] == 0 && !rel[i])
        `uvm_error("CREDIT", $sformatf("ch%0d sent with 0 credits", i))
      credits[i] += rel[i] - send[i];
      if (credits[i] > MAXC)
        `uvm_error("CREDIT", $sformatf("ch%0d over-return: %0d", i, credits[i]))
    end
  endfunction
endclass
```
- Decide early, from the spec, whether a release in the same cycle can be used by a send in that cycle (bypass). This is the most common mismatch between the model and the RTL.
- **SVA** on the interface: `assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) send[ch] |-> dut_credit[ch] != 0);`
- **Stimulus**: a slave-side responder with a random release delay (0 up to large), bursty senders, and per-channel independent rates.

### Scenarios to cover
| Scenario | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Send and release same cycle at 0 / MAX | off-by-one and bypass behavior |
| One channel starved (no releases) | others must keep flowing (no head-of-line blocking) |
| All channels saturate together | arbitration fairness, shared-pool limits |
| Release delay 0 and very long | pipeline and timeout behavior |
| Reset with credits outstanding | counters reinitialize, late releases ignored or flagged |
| Credit return of more than 1 per cycle | counter width and saturation |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Sample on the accepted handshake, not on `valid` alone.
- Check that at end of test every channel's credits are back to MAX (no leak).

### Follow-ups
- *Shared credit pool across channels?* Model a global counter as well and check that the sum is at most the pool size.
- *Why credits rather than ready/valid?* Credits tolerate long round-trip latency without combinational backpressure.

title: Constrained-Random Verification - How It Works
answer: Describe legal input space with constraints, randomize reproducibly, drive transactions, check with assertions/reference models, and use coverage to find gaps and guide constraints. Directed tests address rare boundaries.
solution:
**Key idea:** Constrained-random verification describes the **legal input space** with constraints, lets the solver pick many legal points, checks every result automatically (assertions plus a reference model or scoreboard), and uses **functional coverage** to measure what was exercised and steer the next round. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Verification plan
features to coverage"] --> C["Constraints
(legal space, dist weights)"] C --> R["randomize() with seed"] R --> D["Driver to DUT"] D --> M["Monitors"] M --> K["Checkers:
SVA, scoreboard, ref model"] M --> V["Functional coverage"] V -->|holes| A["Analyze holes"] A -->|tune constraints / directed tests| C K -->|fail| DBG["Debug with same seed"] ``` ### Explanation - **Constraints** encode the protocol and configuration rules (`addr` aligned, `len inside {[1:256]}`, mode-dependent fields). `dist` biases toward interesting values like boundaries. - **Reproducibility**: each run uses a logged seed. A failure is replayed with `+ntb_random_seed=` (VCS) or `-svseed` (Xcelium), and random stability keeps results the same when unrelated code changes. - **Self-checking is mandatory**. Random stimulus without an automatic oracle only exercises the design; nothing tells you when it is wrong. - **Coverage closes the loop**. Random testing finds the bugs nobody thought of, but only coverage tells you which planned scenarios actually happened. - **Directed tests** are still used for rare corners (e.g. exact FIFO-full plus error injection) and for bring-up. | | Directed | Constrained-random | | --- | --- | --- | | Effort per scenario | High | Low after the environment exists | | Unknown bugs found | Few | Many | | Needs coverage? | Implicit | Yes, explicitly | | Debuggability | Easy | Needs seeds and good logging | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Over-constraining hides bugs. Under-constraining wastes cycles on illegal stimulus or causes false failures. - Watch for solver distribution bias: use `solve a before b` when one variable determines another. ### Follow-ups - *When does random stop paying off?* When coverage stops growing. Then switch to directed tests or a formal check. - *What is coverage-driven verification?* Using coverage holes as the explicit metric that decides what to write next.

title: FP Multiplier ALU Verification Strategy
answer: Use a bit-accurate IEEE-754 reference. Cover normals, zeros, infinities, NaNs, subnormals, boundary exponents, rounding modes and ties, overflow/underflow, and exception flags.

title: FIFO Verification - What to Verify, How, Corner Cases
answer: Verify order, data integrity, capacity, empty/full flags, and reset. Exercise fill/drain, simultaneous push/pop, wraparound, bursts, overflow/underflow attempts. Use a queue reference model.
solution:
**Key idea:** A FIFO must preserve **order and data**, honor **capacity**, and produce correct **full/empty (and almost) flags**, including at reset and under simultaneous push and pop. Check it with a SystemVerilog queue as the reference model plus a few SVAs.

| What to verify | How | Corner cases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data integrity and order | queue model: push_back on write, pop_front and compare on read | wraparound of pointers many times |
| full / empty flags | compare to `model.size()` each cycle | exactly DEPTH and 0, 1 and DEPTH-1 |
| Overflow / underflow protection | write when full, read when empty | data must not be corrupted; error flag if specified |
| Simultaneous push and pop | random same-cycle requests | when empty (bypass?) and when full |
| Reset | assert mid-traffic | flags go to empty, old data never reappears |
| Async FIFO extras | random clock ratios, Gray pointers | flag latency is pessimistic but never wrong |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "wr_en", "wave": "01...0..." },
  { "name": "rd_en", "wave": "0...1...0" },
  { "name": "count", "wave": "=.===.===", "data": ["0","1","2","3","2","1","0"] },
  { "name": "full",  "wave": "0........" },
  { "name": "empty", "wave": "1.0.....1" }
],
  "head": { "text": "same-cycle push+pop keeps count constant" } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// Scoreboard core
bit [W-1:0] q[$];
always @(posedge clk) if (rst_n) begin
  if (rd_en && !empty) begin
    assert (q.size() > 0) else $error("read on model-empty");
    assert (rd_data == q.pop_front()) else $error("data mismatch");
  end
  if (wr_en && !full) q.push_back(wr_data);
  assert (full  == (q.size() == DEPTH));
  assert (empty == (q.size() == 0));
end

// Protocol assertions
a_no_ovf: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) full  && wr_en && !rd_en |=> count == DEPTH);
a_no_udf: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) empty && rd_en && !wr_en |=> count == 0);
a_flags : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) !(full && empty));
```
(Adjust the read-data timing for a registered output: compare one cycle after `rd_en`.)

- **Stimulus**: fill-to-full, drain-to-empty, random rates with bias toward 0 and 100% duty cycle, long runs to wrap pointers.
- **Coverage**: count in {0, 1, DEPTH-1, DEPTH}, cross of (wr, rd) × (empty, full), overflow and underflow attempts.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- In first-word-fall-through (FWFT) FIFOs data is valid before `rd_en`; the model timing differs.
- Async FIFO: flags are computed from synchronized pointers, so `full` may stay high a few cycles after a read. That is legal; model with tolerance, not exact equality.

### Follow-ups
- *Depth not a power of two?* Pointer wrap logic needs explicit compare; test the wrap boundary.
- *How do you check the async FIFO's CDC?* Structural CDC tools, Gray-code SVA (`$onehot0(ptr ^ $past(ptr))`), and random clock ratios.

title: Systolic Array UVM Testbench - PE Level and Sub-System Level
answer: At PE level, verify MAC arithmetic, saturation, enable/reset, latency. At array level, model data movement, wavefront scheduling, accumulation, and boundaries. Test matrix dimensions, stalls, tiling, flush.
solution:
**Key idea:** Verify bottom-up. At **PE level** prove the MAC arithmetic, saturation, enable and latency with a small block testbench. At **array level** feed real matrices, model the skewed wavefront and accumulation with a golden matrix multiply, and compare the whole output tile, under stalls, tiling and flush. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph PE_TB["PE-level env"] PS["rand a, b, psum, en"] --> PDRV["PE driver"] --> PE["PE: acc += a*b"] PE --> PMON["PE monitor"] --> PSB["Scoreboard: ref MAC with saturation"] end subgraph SYS_TB["Array-level env"] MS["Matrix seq: A(MxK), B(KxN), tiling cfg"] --> FEED["Skew feeder agents
(row i delayed i cycles)"] FEED --> ARR["NxN systolic array"] ARR --> OMON["Output drain monitor"] --> MSB["Scoreboard: C = A x B
(golden numpy/DPI)"] CFG["RAL / config agent"] --> ARR end PSB -.->|"reuse ref MAC"| MSB ``` ### PE level - Checks: `acc_next = sat(acc + a*b)` for signed/unsigned, bypass of a and b to neighbors with exactly one cycle latency, `en=0` holds state, `clear` resets the accumulator. - Corners: max × max, min × min (signed overflow), alternating signs to wrap the accumulator, enable toggling every cycle. - Small enough for **formal**: prove the MAC equation with a property, which is cheap and exhaustive. ### Array level - **Stimulus**: matrix sequences with random dimensions (1×1, exactly N×N, non-multiples that need padding, larger than the array to force tiling), special values (identity, all zero, all max, sparse). - **Model**: compute `C = A × B` with the same width and saturation rules; the scoreboard does not need to model the wavefront timing if it compares on output tile completion, keyed by tile ID. - **Timing checks**: SVA that row i input starts i cycles after row 0 (skew), that output valid appears after the expected `2N+K-2` style latency, and that back-pressure stalls the entire array consistently. - **Coverage**: dimensions × tiling mode × data class; stall position (start, middle, drain); flush during compute. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Stall in the middle of a wavefront: every PE must freeze at the same time or the skew breaks. - Accumulator reset between tiles; stale partial sums show up only on the second tile. - Weight-stationary vs output-stationary dataflow changes what the model compares and when. ### Follow-ups - *How to speed up array-level sims?* Smaller array parameter (e.g. 4×4) for most regressions, full size for a nightly subset. - *Where do bugs usually hide?* Edges of tiles, padding, and control (start/flush), not in the MAC itself.

title: 512-bit Transaction Split-Reassemble Over 64-bit Link
answer: Eight 64-bit beats. Define beat/byte order, IDs, last indication, backpressure. Reassemble only accepted beats, detect missing/duplicate/out-of-order pieces, compare the full payload.
solution:
**Key idea:** A 512-bit transaction is carried as **eight 64-bit beats**. Fix the beat order and byte order in the spec, tag each beat with an ID and `last`, and have the receive-side monitor reassemble **only accepted beats** (valid && ready), then compare the full 512-bit payload in the scoreboard.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p..........." },
  { "name": "valid", "wave": "01.........0" },
  { "name": "ready", "wave": "1...0.1....." },
  { "name": "data",  "wave": "x====..====x", "data": ["B0","B1","B2","B3","B4","B5","B6","B7"] },
  { "name": "last",  "wave": "0.........10" }
],
  "head": { "text": "B3 held during backpressure; only valid&&ready beats count" } }
```

| Beat | Payload bits (little-endian beat order) |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | `[63:0]` |
| 1 | `[127:64]` |
| ... | ... |
| 7 | `[511:448]`, `last = 1` |

### Explanation
- **TX monitor** records the 512-bit transaction at the source. **RX monitor** collects beats:
```systemverilog
bit [63:0] beats[$];
forever begin
  @(posedge vif.clk);
  if (vif.valid && vif.ready) begin
    beats.push_back(vif.data);
    if (vif.last) begin
      if (beats.size() != 8) `uvm_error("REASM", $sformatf("got %0d beats", beats.size()))
      else begin
        txn512 t = txn512::type_id::create("t");
        foreach (beats[i]) t.payload[i*64 +: 64] = beats[i];
        t.id = vif.id;
        ap.write(t);
      end
      beats.delete();
    end
  end
end
```
- **Checks**: exactly 8 beats per ID; `last` only on beat 7; data and ID stable while `valid && !ready` (SVA); no interleaving between IDs unless the protocol allows it (then keep `beats` in an associative array keyed by ID).
- **Scoreboard**: compare the reassembled 512-bit value against the expected, keyed by ID.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Backpressure on beat 0, beat 7, and every beat.
- Reset in the middle of a burst: partial beats must be discarded, not glued onto the next packet.
- Endianness mismatch between the model and the monitor produces a "rotated" payload. Use address-distinct data such as `beat_index` in each beat so it is obvious.

### Follow-ups
- *What if the link has byte strobes?* Merge with masks and compare only enabled bytes.
- *Missing `last`?* Detect with a beat counter: the 9th beat without a `last` is an error.

title: Out-of-Order Scoreboard - Track and Match with Associative Array
answer: Store expected transactions keyed by unique ID. On response, reject unknown IDs, compare, delete. Check ID reuse, duplicates, timeouts, reset, and leftovers. If multiple requests per ID are legal, use a queue per ID.

title: Debug Scoreboard Mismatch - Step-by-Step Approach
answer: Start at the first mismatch; confirm checker alignment, reference inputs, reset, acceptance events. Trace one transaction through driver, input monitor, DUT, output monitor, and model. Compare widths, signedness, masks, endian, latency, IDs. Classify DUT vs monitor vs model fault.
solution:
**Key idea:** Go to the **first** mismatch, not the last. Take that one transaction and trace it through each stage (stimulus, input monitor, model, DUT, output monitor), comparing values at every hop. The first stage where the value goes wrong is the culprit, and it is just as likely to be the testbench as the DUT. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["First mismatch:
time, ID, exp vs act"] --> B{"Input monitor saw
what driver sent?"} B -->|No| T1["Driver/monitor bug
(timing, sampling edge)"] B -->|Yes| C{"Ref model output
correct by hand calc?"} C -->|No| T2["Model bug or
spec misread"] C -->|Yes| D{"DUT pins in waveform
equal model?"} D -->|Yes| T3["Output monitor bug
(late/early sample, wrong field)"] D -->|No| E["Trace DUT internals
backwards from output"] E --> T4["RTL bug: file with
seed + minimal test"] ``` ### Explanation 1. **Reproduce**: same seed, same command line; dump waves around the first error only (`$dumpvars` from a time, or a probe window in Verdi). 2. **Check alignment** before content: Is the scoreboard pairing the right expected with the right actual? Off-by-one pairing produces a long chain of mismatches after a single dropped or extra item. Compare IDs and counts first. 3. **Check context**: reset applied the same way to model and DUT? configuration (RAL mirror) matches what the DUT holds? Mode and register values at that time? 4. **Diff the values smartly**: XOR expected vs actual. Typical patterns: | Diff pattern | Likely cause | | --- | --- | | Bytes swapped | endianness | | Upper bits wrong | width truncation, sign extension | | Off by a constant | rounding, saturation, offset | | Right data, wrong transaction | latency / ID alignment | | Masked bytes differ | byte-enable handling in model | 5. **Classify** the fault (DUT, monitor, model, stimulus, spec ambiguity), fix, then **add a check** (assertion or coverage) that would have caught it earlier, and rerun the regression. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Do not "fix" the model to match the DUT without checking the spec; that hides real bugs. - Async or multi-clock designs: confirm the monitor samples in the right clock domain. ### Follow-ups - *Mismatch only with one seed out of 1000?* Look at what that seed randomized differently (rare config, back-to-back, reset timing) and add coverage for it. - *Tools?* Transaction recording in Verdi or SimVision, `uvm_info` with IDs at each stage, `+UVM_VERBOSITY` per component.

title: Router UVM Testbench - Complete Design
answer: Ingress agents and egress monitors, an independent route/arbitration model, packet reconstruction, and a scoreboard for delivery and data integrity. Check flow control, buffer limits, multicast/drop rules, fairness, errors, and reset.
solution:
**Key idea:** One active **agent per ingress port**, one passive **monitor per egress port**, an **independent routing model** that predicts the destination(s) for every packet, and a **scoreboard with a queue per (src, dst) pair** that checks delivery, data integrity, ordering, drops, and that nothing is lost or duplicated. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph IN["Ingress agents x N"] S0["seq/sqr/drv/mon 0"] S1["seq/sqr/drv/mon 1"] end subgraph OUT["Egress agents x M"] E0["mon + ready driver 0"] E1["mon + ready driver 1"] end CFG["RAL: route table,
priorities"] --> RM S0 -->|pkt| RM["Route model
dst = f(hdr, table)"] S1 -->|pkt| RM RM -->|"exp[src][dst] queue"| SB["Scoreboard"] E0 -->|pkt| SB E1 -->|pkt| SB S0 --> DUT["Router DUT"] S1 --> DUT DUT --> E0 DUT --> E1 SB --> COV["Coverage:
src x dst x size x congestion"] ``` ### Explanation - **Transaction**: header (dst address, priority, length, multicast mask), payload, CRC; with knobs for error injection (bad CRC, illegal dst, oversize). - **Route model**: computed from the header and the programmed table (read through the RAL mirror), not from DUT internals. Outputs: list of destinations, or "drop with reason". - **Scoreboard**: per (src, dst) FIFO, because packets from one source to one destination must stay in order while different flows may interleave. Multicast puts one copy in each destination's queue. Drops are expected entries that must not appear. - **Egress ready driver**: randomizes backpressure to fill internal buffers. - **Checks via SVA**: valid/ready stability, no output on a disabled port, buffer counters within limits. - **End-of-test**: all queues empty, drop counters in the DUT match the model. | Scenario | Purpose | | --- | --- | | All sources to one destination | congestion, arbitration fairness, buffer full | | Every src to every dst | full routing matrix | | Minimum and maximum packet length | framing | | Multicast/broadcast | replication | | Bad CRC, illegal dst | drop rules and counters | | Reset under traffic | recovery, no stale packets | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Fairness: measure grants per source over a window and check the max-min difference is bounded (no starvation). - Route table changes while traffic is in flight: specify whether in-flight packets use old or new rules. ### Follow-ups - *Deadlock detection?* Watchdog: no egress progress for X cycles while packets are pending is an error. - *Scaling to 64 ports?* Parameterized agent arrays created in a loop from a config object.

title: req/ack Handshake Testbench with Latency Checking
answer: Generate requests, monitor requests and acks, measure latency. Check min/max latency, no extra ack, request stability, reset. Cover zero/min/max delay and back-to-back traffic.

title: Out-of-Order Packet Scoreboard with Reconstruction
answer: Collect fragments by packet ID and index, track a received bitmap, reconstruct once complete, then compare. Reject duplicates, invalid indices, unknown IDs, and late fragments.
solution:
**Key idea:** Buffer fragments per packet ID in an associative array, keep a **received bitmap** per packet, and only when every fragment index is present do you **reconstruct** the full packet and compare it to the expected. Reject unknown IDs, out-of-range indices, duplicates and fragments arriving after the packet is complete.

| Event | id | idx/total | bitmap after | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| frag | 5 | 2/4 | `0100` | store |
| frag | 5 | 0/4 | `0101` | store |
| frag | 9 | 0/2 | `01` | store |
| frag | 5 | 2/4 | `0101` | **duplicate, error** |
| frag | 5 | 1/4 | `0111` | store |
| frag | 5 | 3/4 | `1111` | **complete, reconstruct and compare** |
| frag | 5 | 1/4 | — | **late fragment, error** |

### Code
```systemverilog
class pkt_reasm_sb extends uvm_scoreboard;
  `uvm_component_utils(pkt_reasm_sb)
  typedef struct { int total; bit [7:0] frags[int]; } partial_t;  // simplified 1-byte frags
  partial_t     part[int];        // id -> partial packet
  bit [7:0]     exp_pkt[int][$];  // id -> expected bytes (from input side)
  bit           done[int];        // completed ids (to detect late fragments)

  function new(string n, uvm_component p); super.new(n, p); endfunction

  function void add_expected(int id, bit [7:0] bytes[$]);
    exp_pkt[id] = bytes;
  endfunction

  function void write_frag(int id, int idx, int total, bit [7:0] data);
    if (done.exists(id))        begin `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("late frag id=%0d", id)) return; end
    if (!exp_pkt.exists(id))    begin `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("unknown id=%0d", id)) return; end
    if (idx < 0 || idx >= total) begin `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("bad idx %0d/%0d", idx, total)) return; end
    if (!part.exists(id)) part[id].total = total;
    else if (part[id].total != total) `uvm_error("SB", "total changed between fragments")
    if (part[id].frags.exists(idx)) begin `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("dup frag id=%0d idx=%0d", id, idx)) return; end
    part[id].frags[idx] = data;
    if (part[id].frags.num() == total) reconstruct(id);
  endfunction

  function void reconstruct(int id);
    bit [7:0] got[$];
    for (int i = 0; i < part[id].total; i++) got.push_back(part[id].frags[i]);
    if (got != exp_pkt[id]) `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("payload mismatch id=%0d", id))
    part.delete(id); exp_pkt.delete(id); done[id] = 1;
  endfunction

  function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    foreach (part[id]) `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("id=%0d incomplete: %0d/%0d", id, part[id].frags.num(), part[id].total))
    foreach (exp_pkt[id]) if (!part.exists(id)) `uvm_error("SB", $sformatf("id=%0d never arrived", id))
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If IDs are reused, clear `done[id]` when a new request with that ID is issued, otherwise legal traffic looks late.
- Per-packet timeouts catch fragments that are lost forever.
- Real fragments are multi-byte; store `byte q[$]` per index and concatenate.

### Follow-ups
- *Why a bitmap instead of a counter?* A counter cannot tell a duplicate from a new fragment.
- *Ordering requirement?* If fragments must arrive in order, also check `idx == next_expected[id]`.

title: Credit Release Handshake Checker with SVA
answer: Maintain a checker credit count updated by sends/releases and assert legal bounds. SVA can check stable release metadata during stalls and ack latency. A boolean assertion alone cannot catch excess credits without state.

title: Lane Redundancy Remapping - SV Constraint Generator
answer: Constrain logical-to-physical lane indices in range, exclude failed lanes, require distinct mappings, and obey adjacency rules. Check enough healthy lanes exist.

title: PHY Link Training - Delay Code Sweep with PRBS Error Injection
answer: Sweep delay codes, wait for settling, apply PRBS, count errors per window. Find the passing eye and choose the center. Inject errors to verify thresholds, retraining, and reporting.

title: 12-Channel 32-bit Coverage Strategy
answer: Cover each channel for valid transfers, data patterns, boundaries, stalls, errors. Cross channel with mode/status. Avoid crossing all 32-bit values; use walking ones/zeros and toggle coverage for bit-level exercise.

title: UVM Backdoor Access - HDL Path and Usage
answer: Configure valid HDL paths, then use RAL backdoor or uvm_hdl_read/deposit/force. Consider simulator optimization/access flags (+acc). Force persists until release; deposit does not.
solution:
**Key idea:** A backdoor bypasses the bus and reads or writes the RTL storage directly through an **HDL path**. Set the paths in the register model (`configure` / `add_hdl_path_slice`), make sure the simulator keeps those signals visible (`+acc`/`-access +rwc`), then use `reg.peek/poke` or `mem.peek/poke` (or `uvm_hdl_read/deposit/force` for raw signals). ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Test / sequence"] -->|"write/read (frontdoor)"| RAL["uvm_reg_block"] RAL -->|"bus transaction"| ADP["adapter -> sequencer -> driver"] --> BUS["DUT bus I/F"] --> REG["RTL flop / memory array"] T -->|"peek/poke (backdoor)"| RAL RAL -->|"uvm_hdl_read / uvm_hdl_deposit
root + block + reg path"| REG ``` ### Explanation ```systemverilog // In the register block build() default_map = create_map("map", 'h0, 4, UVM_LITTLE_ENDIAN); ctrl = ctrl_reg::type_id::create("ctrl"); ctrl.configure(this, null, ""); ctrl.build(); ctrl.add_hdl_path_slice("u_regs.ctrl_q", 0, 32); // path relative to block add_hdl_path("tb_top.dut"); // block root path // In a test or sequence uvm_status_e st; uvm_reg_data_t v; regm.ctrl.poke(st, 32'h1); // deposit: no bus cycle, no side effects regm.ctrl.peek(st, v); // read actual flop value regm.ctrl.write(st, 32'h3, UVM_BACKDOOR); // backdoor write that also updates mirror // raw signal access if (!uvm_hdl_deposit("tb_top.dut.u_core.state_q", 2)) `uvm_error("BD", "bad path") uvm_hdl_force("tb_top.dut.irq", 1); // stays until released uvm_hdl_release("tb_top.dut.irq"); ``` | Method | Persists? | Typical use | | --- | --- | --- | | `uvm_hdl_deposit` / `poke` | No, the next driver update overwrites it | preload memories, set state quickly | | `uvm_hdl_force` | Yes, until `uvm_hdl_release` | error injection, tie off a signal | | `uvm_hdl_read` / `peek` | n/a | check storage without bus side effects | ### When to use - Preload large memories (firmware images) in zero time. - Check that a frontdoor write actually landed in the right flop (catches address decode bugs that a frontdoor read would cancel). - Read clear-on-read or FIFO registers without triggering their side effects. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Optimization removes or renames nets; compile with access flags or the path check (`uvm_reg::has_hdl_path`, `uvm_hdl_check_path`) fails. - Backdoor `poke` does not model side effects (W1C, RC); `write(..., UVM_BACKDOOR)` emulates field access policies in the RAL, but the RTL side effects (interrupts) do not happen. - Gate-level sims: paths change after synthesis; keep a separate HDL path set (`"GATES"` kind). ### Follow-ups - *Mirror vs desired?* Backdoor `peek` updates the mirror only if `predict` is called; `mirror(..., UVM_BACKDOOR)` does both. - *Why does a backdoor write need +acc=w?* Writing a signal from the PLI/VPI requires write access to it.

title: Firmware Writes 1 to enable_reg but Device Does Not Start - Debug
answer: Confirm the write reached the correct address with correct byte enables. Trace bus completion, decode, register storage, clock/reset/power state, prerequisite configuration, and start-event generation. Check self-clearing/edge semantics.
solution:
**Key idea:** Follow the bit from software to the state machine: **did the write happen, did it land in the right register bit, is that bit visible to the logic, and are all other start conditions true?** Check bus completion, address decode, byte enables, register storage, clock/reset/power domain, prerequisites, and the start-pulse semantics (level vs edge vs self-clearing). ```mermaid flowchart TD A["FW: write 1 to enable_reg"] --> B{"Bus transaction completed
with OKAY response?"} B -->|No| B1["Check address map, bus error,
security/privilege, clock to bus"] B -->|Yes| C{"Correct address and
byte enable (wstrb)?"} C -->|No| C1["Driver/compiler: wrong offset,
8-bit vs 32-bit write"] C -->|Yes| D{"Backdoor peek:
flop holds 1?"} D -->|No| D1["Decode bug, write mask, field is RO,
reset held, clock gated"] D -->|Yes| E{"Start logic sees it?
(CDC sync, domain powered)"} E -->|No| E1["Missing synchronizer, power domain off,
isolation clamps"] E -->|Yes| F{"Prerequisites met?
(config valid, clock locked, busy=0)"} F -->|No| F1["Programming sequence order"] F -->|Yes| G["Edge vs level / self-clear:
was it already 1? pulse missed?"] ``` ### Explanation - **Bus level**: check the bus monitor log for the transaction: address, `wstrb`, response. A `SLVERR`/`DECERR` or a write to an aliased address is common. - **Register level**: backdoor `peek` the register. If it reads back 0 after a frontdoor write, the decode or the write mask is wrong. Also check the field's access policy (RO, W1C, write-once lock). - **Logic level**: in the waveform, follow `enable_q` to the FSM. Typical issues: - The FSM starts on a **rising edge** of enable; firmware wrote 1 when it was already 1 (from a previous run) so no edge happened. - The bit is **self-clearing** and the FSM is in another clock domain; a one-cycle pulse was lost in CDC. - The block is held in **reset** or its **clock is gated** or the power domain is off. - A required **configuration register** (length, address) is still 0 so the FSM returns to IDLE immediately. - **Status**: read the status/error register; a block often reports "config error". ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Write posting: firmware writes enable and immediately reads status before the write reached the device. Add a read-back or barrier. - Endianness or byte lane: writing `0x01` to the byte that does not hold the enable bit. ### Follow-ups - *How would DV have caught this earlier?* A RAL bit-bash test, a backdoor check after frontdoor writes, and a cover property for "enable set while busy". - *What evidence do you send to designers?* Waveform of the bus write, register value, FSM state, and the spec rule for starting.

title: DV Environment for Software-Programmed Threshold Transaction Limiter
answer: Monitor programming writes and transactions. Model threshold meaning, update timing, comparison, and counter reset. Check limits 0/1/max, threshold changes while active, exact crossing, backpressure, interrupts.
solution:
**Key idea:** The environment watches two streams: **register writes** (to know the current threshold and when it takes effect) and **transactions** (to count them). An independent model predicts exactly which transaction must be blocked, throttled or flagged, and the scoreboard compares that with what the DUT did. The risky parts are the update timing and the exact crossing point. ```mermaid flowchart LR CFG["APB/AXI-Lite agent
(threshold, enable, window)"] --> RAL["RAL mirror"] CFG --> DUT["Limiter DUT"] TX["Traffic agent (in)"] --> DUT --> OUT["Monitor (out) + IRQ monitor"] RAL --> MDL["Limiter model:
count, threshold, window reset"] TX -->|"txn"| MDL MDL -->|"expected pass/block/irq"| SB["Scoreboard"] OUT --> SB ``` ### Explanation - **Model state**: `count`, `threshold_active`, `threshold_pending`, window timer. Read from the spec: does a new threshold apply immediately, at the next window, or only when idle? Is the comparison `count < thr` or `<=`? Does writing the threshold reset the count? - **Checks**: transaction N passes iff the model says so; the interrupt fires exactly once at the crossing; the status counter equals the model count; blocked transactions get the specified response (dropped, stalled, error). - **Stimulus**: thresholds 0, 1, MAX, random; traffic bursts that land **exactly** on threshold−1, threshold, threshold+1; threshold written during traffic (lower than the current count, higher, same); backpressure on the output so transactions are pending when the limit changes. | Scenario | Expected (example spec: block when count ≥ thr) | | --- | --- | | thr = 0 | everything blocked (or "limiter disabled" if spec says 0 = off) | | thr = 1 | first passes, rest blocked | | Exactly thr transactions | all pass, IRQ at the last one | | thr lowered below current count | next transaction blocked immediately (or at window end) | | Window reset | count returns to 0, traffic resumes | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Simultaneous register write and transaction in the same cycle: define ordering in the model. - Counter width: if the counter is 16 bits and the threshold 32 bits, the counter wraps. - Do not compute expected results from DUT internal signals; that only proves the DUT agrees with itself. ### Follow-ups - *Coverage?* threshold value class × crossing event × "threshold written while active" × backpressure. - *Assertion idea?* `count >= thr |-> !out_valid` (if blocking is immediate).

title: 128-bit Parallel Bus - Stuck-at Fault and Short Wire Test Patterns
answer: All-zero/all-one patterns for stuck-at faults. Walking-one and walking-zero patterns isolate lines and expose shorts. Unique per-wire temporal signatures can distinguish wires efficiently (log2 N patterns).
solution:
**Key idea:** **All-0 and all-1** find stuck-at faults. **Walking-1 and walking-0** isolate each wire and find shorts between any pair (128 + 128 patterns). The efficient method assigns each wire a **unique code** across a few patterns (a counting sequence without the all-0 and all-1 codes), so ⌈log2(N+2)⌉ = **8 patterns** detect stuck-at faults and pairwise shorts on 128 wires; diagnosis to the exact pair needs the walking patterns.

**Walking-1 (8-bit slice shown):**

| Pattern | b7..b0 | Fault exposed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `00000001` | b0 stuck-at-0, b0 shorted to any wire (wired-OR pulls it high) |
| 1 | `00000010` | same for b1 |
| ... | ... | ... |
| 7 | `10000000` | b7 |

**Counting-sequence codes (each column is one wire, each row one test pattern):**

| Pattern | w1 | w2 | w3 | w4 | w5 | w6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P0 (LSB) | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| P1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| P2 (MSB) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |

Wire *i* gets code *i* (1..6 here; 1..128 needs 8 bits since codes 0 and 255 are excluded). Every wire sees both 0 and 1 (stuck-at detected), and every two wires differ in at least one pattern, so a wired-AND or wired-OR short changes at least one of them.

### Explanation
- **Stuck-at-0/1**: each wire must be driven to both values and observed: all-0 then all-1 (2 patterns) is enough.
- **Short (bridging) between wire a and b**: drive them to **opposite** values. A walking-1 does this for the active wire versus all others; the receiver sees two 1s (wired-OR) or zero 1s (wired-AND).
- **Unique codes**: if wire a and wire b have different codes, some pattern drives them oppositely, so the short is detected.
- **Diagnosis**: the failing pattern plus which bits flipped points to the pair; walking-1/walking-0 makes this direct (bit *i* active, bit *j* also high → short i–j).

| Method | Patterns for 128 bits | Stuck-at | Detect all pairwise shorts | Diagnose pair |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All-0 / all-1 | 2 | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |
| Checkerboard 0x55/0xAA | 2 | ✔ | adjacent only | partial |
| Counting sequence | 8 (plus 2 for margin) | ✔ | ✔ | partial |
| Walking-1 + walking-0 | 256 | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Shorts can be dominant (one driver wins), not just AND/OR; walking both 1 and 0 covers both polarities.
- Aliasing: with only counting codes, a short of wire a with b may produce a code equal to a third wire's code. Using code plus its complement ("true/complement" sequence, 2⌈log2 N⌉ patterns) removes this.
- Opens behave like stuck-at or floating values; pull resistors decide which.

### Follow-ups
- *Why exclude codes 0 and all-1?* Those wires would never toggle, so stuck-at faults on them would hide.
- *How is this done in silicon?* Boundary scan (JTAG EXTEST) interconnect tests use exactly these sequences.

title: Using AI-Generated Code in Verification - Risks and Workflow
answer: Treat generated code as an untrusted draft: review against the spec, compile/lint, run edge cases, compare with an independent model. Do not use the same generated algorithm as both implementation and oracle.

title: Memory Debug - Frontdoor Write + Backdoor Peek to Find Swap Bug
answer: Write address-distinct patterns through the frontdoor, inspect physical locations via backdoor. Compare expected mapping to actual storage. Also read frontdoor because symmetric write/read swaps can cancel and hide a fault.

title: Memory Verification - Complete Strategy and UVM Environment
answer: Verify address/data integrity, masks, latency, collisions, initialization, ECC, reset. Use a sparse reference memory and monitor-driven checking. Apply address-distinct, walking-bit, checkerboard, random patterns plus concurrent accesses.
solution:
**Key idea:** Verify that **every address stores and returns the right data** under all access types and timing: address decode, data integrity, byte masks, latency, read/write collisions, initialization, ECC and reset. Use a **sparse associative-array reference model** fed by monitors, plus classic patterns (address-distinct, walking bits, checkerboard) and random concurrent traffic. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph ENV["UVM env"] A0["Port A agent
(rd/wr, mask, burst)"] A1["Port B agent"] RAL["RAL + uvm_mem
(backdoor path)"] MDL["Ref model:
bit [W-1:0] mem[addr_t]"] SB["Scoreboard
