- *T from JK?* J = K = T.

title: Convert a JK flip-flop into a D flip-flop
answer: J = D and K = D'.
solution:
**Key idea:** Make the JK flop either set or reset depending on D: **J = D, K = D'** (never 00 hold or 11 toggle).

| D | Desired Qn+1 | J | K | JK action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | reset |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | set |

Deriving from the JK excitation table (Qn → Qn+1: 0→0: J=0,K=x; 0→1: J=1,K=x; 1→0: J=x,K=1; 1→1: J=x,K=0) and minimizing gives J = D, K = D'.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["D"] -->|"J"| JK["JK flip-flop"]
  D --> INV["NOT"] -->|"K"| JK
  CLK["clk"] --> JK
  JK --> Q["Q"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Simpler alternative using don't-cares?* J = D, K = D' is already minimal (K could also be D' only when Q=1 matters; the inverter is the cheapest form).
- *JK to T?* J = K = T.

title: What is the difference between a synchronous counter and an asynchronous (ripple) counter?
answer: Synchronous counter: all flops share a common clock and change together (e.g., ring, Johnson counters). Asynchronous counter: only the first flop gets the clock; each subsequent flop is clocked by the previous flop's output (ripple).
solution:
**Key idea:** In a **synchronous** counter all flops share one clock and change together; in an **asynchronous (ripple)** counter only the first flop gets the clock and each later flop is clocked by the previous flop's output, so the count ripples through with accumulated delay.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "sync q0", "wave": "01010101" },
  { "name": "sync q1", "wave": "0.1.0.1." },
  { "name": "ripple q0", "wave": "01010101", "phase": -0.2 },
  { "name": "ripple q1", "wave": "0.1.0.1.", "phase": -0.4 }
],
  "head": { "text": "ripple counter bits settle one flop-delay after each other → transient wrong counts" } }
```

| Aspect | Synchronous | Asynchronous (ripple) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clock | common to all flops | output of previous stage |
| Speed | one Tcq + logic | N × Tcq ripple delay |
| Glitches/decoding | clean | transient invalid states (e.g., 0111→1000 passes 0110, 0100…) |
| Logic | needs next-state logic (AND chain) | minimal (T-flops toggling) |
| Power | all flops clocked | less clock power |
| Examples | binary sync counter, ring, Johnson counter | ripple up/down counter, clock dividers |

### Code
```systemverilog
// synchronous 4-bit counter
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) cnt <= '0; else cnt <= cnt + 1'b1;

// ripple counter bit i clocked by previous bit (avoid in synchronous ASIC design)
always_ff @(negedge q[i-1] or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) q[i] <= 1'b0; else q[i] <= ~q[i];
```

### Follow-ups
- *Why are ripple counters avoided in ASICs?* Generated clocks complicate STA/CDC and decoded outputs glitch.

title: What is the difference between a ripple carry adder and a carry look-ahead adder?
answer: RCA: each full adder waits for the previous carry, so carries ripple (slow). CLA: computes carries in advance using Generate Gi = AiBi and Propagate Pi = Ai^Bi with Ci+1 = Gi + PiCi, which is faster.
solution:
**Key idea:** A ripple-carry adder (RCA) chains full adders so each carry **waits for the previous one** – O(N) delay. A carry look-ahead adder (CLA) computes all carries in parallel from **generate** Gi = Ai·Bi and **propagate** Pi = Ai⊕Bi – O(log N) delay at the cost of more gates. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph RCA["Ripple carry"] FA0["FA0"] -->|"c1"| FA1["FA1"] -->|"c2"| FA2["FA2"] -->|"c3"| FA3["FA3"] --> CO["Cout"] end subgraph CLA["Carry look-ahead"] PG["Pi, Gi for all bits"] --> CLU["look-ahead unit
c1..c4 in parallel"] CLU --> SUM["Si = Pi xor ci"] end ``` | Carry | Look-ahead expression | | --- | --- | | c1 | G0 + P0·c0 | | c2 | G1 + P1·G0 + P1·P0·c0 | | c3 | G2 + P2·G1 + P2·P1·G0 + P2·P1·P0·c0 | | c4 | G3 + P3·G2 + P3·P2·G1 + P3·P2·P1·G0 + P3·P2·P1·P0·c0 | | Aspect | Ripple carry | Carry look-ahead | | --- | --- | --- | | Delay | ~2N gate levels | constant per 4-bit block, log N with tree | | Area | minimal | grows quickly (wide AND/OR) | | Use | small/slow adders | wide fast adders (hierarchical CLA, Kogge-Stone) | ### Code ```systemverilog module cla4 (input logic [3:0] a, b, input logic cin, output logic [3:0] s, output logic cout); logic [3:0] g, p; logic [4:0] c; assign g = a & b; assign p = a ^ b; assign c[0] = cin; always_comb for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) c[i+1] = g[i] | (p[i] & c[i]); // unrolls to look-ahead terms assign s = p ^ c[3:0]; assign cout = c[4]; endmodule ``` (Synthesis flattens the loop into the parallel sum-of-products shown in the table.) ### Follow-ups - *Other fast adders?* Carry-select, carry-skip, Brent-Kung, Kogge-Stone prefix adders.

title: What is the longest path (in gates) of an N-bit ripple carry adder?
answer: 2N + 1 gates (1-bit: 3 gates, 2-bit: 5 gates).
solution:
**Key idea:** **2N + 1 gates.** One XOR to form P0 (or the first carry term), then each bit's carry goes through 2 gate levels (AND then OR: c(i+1) = Gi + Pi·ci), and the final sum needs one more XOR.

| Adder width | Path | Gates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1-bit | A0→XOR(P0)→AND→OR(c1) … or A0→XOR→XOR(S0) | 3 |
| 2-bit | P0 → AND/OR (c1) → AND/OR (c2) | 5 |
| N-bit | 1 + 2N | 2N + 1 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A0["A0,B0"] --> P0["XOR P0"] --> A1["AND"] --> O1["OR c1"] --> A2["AND"] --> O2["OR c2"] --> D["..."] --> CN["OR cN"]
```

### Explanation
- Counting the critical path from the LSB inputs to the final carry-out: XOR (propagate of bit 0) + 2 per stage × N = 2N + 1. (Exact counts depend on the full-adder gate implementation, but the linear 2-gates-per-bit growth is the point.)

### Follow-ups
- *Delay of a 64-bit RCA with 20 ps gates?* ≈ 129 × 20 ps ≈ 2.6 ns – why CLA/prefix adders exist.

title: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous reset?
answer: Synchronous reset is sampled on a clock edge like any other input. Asynchronous reset can happen without a clock and has highest priority.
solution:
**Key idea:** A **synchronous** reset is sampled only on the active clock edge (it's just another data input). An **asynchronous** reset acts immediately, without a clock, and has highest priority.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "rst", "wave": "0.10..." , "phase": -0.3},
  { "name": "q (sync reset)", "wave": "=..0...", "data": ["5"] },
  { "name": "q (async reset)", "wave": "=.0....", "data": ["5"], "phase": -0.3 }
],
  "head": { "text": "async reset clears q as soon as rst rises; sync reset waits for the next clk edge" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// synchronous reset
always_ff @(posedge clk)
  if (rst) q <= '0; else q <= d;

// asynchronous reset (active-low), in the sensitivity list
always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
  if (!rst_n) q <= '0; else q <= d;
```

| Aspect | Synchronous | Asynchronous |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs clock | yes | no |
| Glitch filtering | yes (only sampled at edges) | no – glitch can reset the flop |
| Timing | reset is in the data path (setup/hold normal) | recovery/removal checks on de-assertion |
| Area | extra gate in D path | flop with reset pin |
| Typical | most datapaths | power-on / global reset |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Asynchronous assert, synchronous de-assert** (reset synchronizer: two flops) is the standard practice – avoids metastability on release.
- Sync reset requires the clock to be running and reset to be held ≥ 1 cycle.

### Follow-ups
- *Recovery vs removal?* Setup/hold analogues for reset de-assertion relative to the clock.

title: How many flip-flops are needed to implement a 32-bit register?
answer: 32 flip-flops – each stores one bit.
solution:
**Key idea:** One flip-flop stores one bit, so a 32-bit register needs **32 flip-flops** (all sharing clock, and usually enable/reset).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["d[31:0]"] --> R["32 x D-FF (shared clk, en, rst)"] --> Q["q[31:0]"]
  CLK["clk"] --> R
```

| Register width | Flip-flops |
| --- | --- |
| 8 | 8 |
| 32 | 32 |
| N | N |

### Code
```systemverilog
module reg32 (input logic clk, rst_n, en, input logic [31:0] d, output logic [31:0] q);
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n)  q <= '0;
    else if (en) q <= d;
endmodule
```

### Follow-ups
- *Contrast with state encoding:* an FSM with 32 *states* needs only log2(32) = 5 flops (binary) or 32 (one-hot).

title: What is the difference between a Mealy and a Moore finite state machine?
answer: Mealy: output depends on present state and present input. Moore: output depends only on present state.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Moore**: outputs depend only on the current state. **Mealy**: outputs depend on current state **and current inputs**.

| Aspect | Moore | Mealy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Output function | f(state) | f(state, input) |
| Response to input | one cycle later | same cycle (combinational) |
| Number of states | usually more | usually fewer |
| Glitch/timing | outputs clean (registered state) | input glitches can reach outputs |
| Diagram | output written inside states | output on transitions (in/out) |

Example: detect "11" on serial input `x`.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Mealy" as mealy {
    S0 --> S0: 0/0
    S0 --> S1: 1/0
    S1 --> S1: 1/1
    S1 --> S0: 0/0
  }
```

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  state "Moore (z inside state)" as moore {
    A_z0 --> A_z0: 0
    A_z0 --> B_z0: 1
    B_z0 --> C_z1: 1
    B_z0 --> A_z0: 0
    C_z1 --> C_z1: 1
    C_z1 --> A_z0: 0
  }
```

### Explanation
- Mealy needs 2 states, Moore needs 3, and Moore's output asserts one clock later than Mealy's.
- A Mealy output can be registered to make it glitch-free (then it behaves with Moore-like timing).

### Follow-ups
- *Which do you verify differently?* Mealy outputs need checks in the same cycle as the input (`|->`), Moore outputs one cycle later (`|=>`).

title: What is an excitation table? Give the excitation tables of D, T and JK flip-flops
answer: An excitation table shows the inputs required to move from a known present state Q(t) to a desired next state Q(t+1). D: D=Q(t+1). T: T=1 when state changes. JK: 0→0 J=0,K=X; 0→1 J=1,K=X; 1→0 J=X,K=1; 1→1 J=X,K=0.
solution:
**Key idea:** An excitation table is the inverse of a characteristic table: given **present state Q(t) and desired next state Q(t+1)**, it lists the **flop inputs required**. It is what you use when designing an FSM with a particular flop type.

| Q(t) → Q(t+1) | D | T | J | K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 → 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | X |
| 0 → 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | X |
| 1 → 0 | 0 | 1 | X | 1 |
| 1 → 1 | 1 | 0 | X | 0 |

### Explanation
- D: next state = D, so D = Q(t+1).
- T: toggle when the state must change: T = Q(t) ⊕ Q(t+1).
- JK: 0→0 can be "hold" (J=0,K=0) or "reset" (J=0,K=1) → K is don't-care; similarly for others. These X entries are why JK designs often minimize to simpler logic.

### Follow-ups
- *SR excitation?* 0→0: S=0,R=X; 0→1: S=1,R=0; 1→0: S=0,R=1; 1→1: S=X,R=0.

title: If given a choice, which flip-flop would you use to implement a synchronous circuit such as a sequence detector: D or JK?
answer: Depends: JK can give a simpler circuit because of many don't-care inputs; D flip-flops are easier since next state equals the input.
solution:
**Key idea:** It depends. **JK** has many don't-care inputs in its excitation table, which can yield simpler next-state logic in hand design; **D** is simplest to design with because D = next state (no excitation mapping) and needs one input per flop.

| Criterion | D flip-flop | JK flip-flop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Design effort | trivial: D = next state | need excitation table |
| Inputs per flop | 1 | 2 |
| Logic minimization | fewer don't cares | many don't cares → sometimes smaller logic |
| Library / synthesis support | universal | rarely used in ASIC libraries |
| Timing analysis | simple | simple |

### Explanation
- In a hand-design exam question, JK may give fewer gates. In RTL/ASIC practice the answer is D – synthesis optimizes the next-state logic anyway.

### Follow-ups
- *Which in practice?* D flip-flops (next question).

title: In practice, which flip-flop is used more often for implementing synchronous circuits: D or JK?
answer: D flip-flops: no excitation tables (next state = input), only one input, simpler to implement.
solution:
**Key idea:** **D flip-flops.** Next state = input (no excitation tables), only one input per flop, simpler/smaller cells, and they map directly onto `q <= d` in RTL and onto standard-cell libraries. | Reason | Detail | | --- | --- | | No excitation mapping | Q(t+1) = D | | One input | less routing, simpler timing | | Simpler cell | fewer transistors than JK | | Tool flow | synthesis infers D flops (with enable/reset variants) | ```mermaid flowchart LR RTL["always_ff: q <= next"] --> SYN["synthesis"] --> DFF["D flip-flop cells
(+ enable/reset variants)"] ``` ### Follow-ups - *How is JK behavior obtained then?* `q <= (j & ~q) | (~k & q);` – synthesized into logic in front of a D flop.

title: Design a sequence detector FSM that detects the pattern 10110 in a serial input stream, using D flip-flops
answer: States A (none), B (1), C (10), D (101), E (1011); key overlap transitions D->C on 0 and E->C on 0 (output 1). 3 D flops: A=000,B=001,C=010,D=011,E=100. Z = Q2Q1'Q0'X'; D2 = Q2'Q1Q0X; D1 = Q2Q1'Q0'X' + Q2'Q1Q0'X + Q2'Q0X'; D0 = Q2'Q1'X + Q2'Q0'X + Q1'Q0'X.
solution:
**Key idea:** Track the longest prefix of `10110` seen so far (5 states A–E), handle **overlaps** (on mismatch go to the state matching the longest suffix that is still a prefix), and assert Z (Mealy) on the final 0.

States: A = nothing, B = "1", C = "10", D = "101", E = "1011".

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  A --> A: 0/0
  A --> B: 1/0
  B --> B: 1/0
  B --> C: 0/0
  C --> D: 1/0
  C --> A: 0/0
  D --> E: 1/0
  D --> C: 0/0
  E --> C: 0/1
  E --> B: 1/0
```

| Present (Q2Q1Q0) | X=0 next | X=1 next | Z (X=0) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A 000 | A 000 | B 001 | 0 |
| B 001 | C 010 | B 001 | 0 |
| C 010 | A 000 | D 011 | 0 |
| D 011 | C 010 | E 100 | 0 |
| E 100 | C 010 | B 001 | **1** |

Equations (unused 101,110,111 = don't care):
- Z = Q2·Q1'·Q0'·X'  (= Q2·X')
- D2 = Q2'·Q1·Q0·X
- D1 = Q2·X' + Q1·Q0'·X + Q0·X'  (book: Q2Q1'Q0'X' + Q2'Q1Q0'X + Q2'Q0X')
- D0 = X·(Q1' + Q0')

### Code
```systemverilog
module det_10110 (input logic clk, rst_n, x, output logic z);
  typedef enum logic [2:0] {A, B, C, D, E} state_t;
  state_t st, nxt;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) st <= A; else st <= nxt;
  always_comb begin
    nxt = st;
    unique case (st)
      A: nxt = x ? B : A;
      B: nxt = x ? B : C;
      C: nxt = x ? D : A;
      D: nxt = x ? E : C;   // "1010": suffix "10" restarts at C
      E: nxt = x ? B : C;   // "10110": suffix "10" allows overlap
      default: nxt = A;
    endcase
  end
  assign z = (st == E) && !x;   // Mealy output
endmodule
```

### Trace (input 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 0)
| x | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| state before | A | B | C | D | E | C | D | E |
| z | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | **1** | 0 | 0 | **1** |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Forgetting D→C on 0 misses `1010110`; forgetting E→C on 0 misses overlapping `10110110`.

### Follow-ups
- *Moore version?* Add state F = "10110" with Z=1 → 6 states, output one cycle later.

title: What is the minimum number of flip-flops required to implement a synchronous circuit with 9 states?
answer: 4 flip-flops (3 flops give only 8 states; 4 give up to 16).
solution:
**Key idea:** N flops encode up to 2^N states, so you need ⌈log2 9⌉ = **4** flip-flops (3 flops give only 8 states).

| Flops | Max states |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 4 |
| 3 | 8 |
| **4** | **16** ≥ 9 |

### Explanation
- 7 of the 16 codes are unused – make sure the FSM recovers from them (`default` → reset state) for robustness.
- One-hot encoding would use 9 flops but simpler/faster next-state logic; Gray/Johnson are other options.

### Follow-ups
- *Johnson counter with 9 states?* Not possible exactly – an N-flop Johnson counter has 2N states (even).

title: Design a circuit that counts 1 every time another counter counts from 0 to 255
answer: Implement a divide-by-256 (f/256) circuit: increment the second counter when the first counter reaches 255 (carry-out/terminal count).
solution:
**Key idea:** This is a **divide-by-256**: increment the second counter on the cycle where the first (8-bit) counter wraps from 255 to 0, i.e., use the first counter's terminal count (carry-out) as the enable.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "cnt8", "wave": "=====.=", "data": ["253", "254", "255", "0", "1", "2"] },
  { "name": "tc (cnt8==255)", "wave": "0.10..." },
  { "name": "cnt_hi", "wave": "=..=...", "data": ["k", "k+1"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "cnt_hi increments when cnt8 wraps (terminal count)" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module div256_count (input logic clk, rst_n, output logic [7:0] cnt8, output logic [15:0] cnt_hi);
  logic tc;
  assign tc = (cnt8 == 8'hFF);          // terminal count / carry out
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) begin cnt8 <= '0; cnt_hi <= '0; end
    else begin
      cnt8 <= cnt8 + 8'd1;              // wraps 255 -> 0 naturally
      if (tc) cnt_hi <= cnt_hi + 16'd1; // one increment per 256 clocks
    end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- Equivalently this is one 24-bit counter whose upper bits are the "count of rollovers" – the low 8 bits divide the clock rate by 256.
- Use a clock **enable** (tc), not `cnt8[7]` as a clock, to keep the design synchronous.

### Follow-ups
- *Generate a clk/256 waveform?* Use `cnt8[7]` as a 50% duty output (but don't clock logic with it without CTS considerations).

title: Implement clock divide-by-2 and divide-by-4 using the minimum number of D flip-flops
answer: Divide by 2: one D flop with Q' fed back to D. Divide by 4: two such stages cascaded (or a 2-flop synchronous counter).
solution:
**Key idea:** Divide-by-2 = **one** D flop with Q' fed back to D (toggles every edge). Divide-by-4 = **two** flops – cascade two divide-by-2 stages (ripple) or build a synchronous 2-bit counter / 2-flop Johnson counter. ```wavedrom { "signal": [ { "name": "clk", "wave": "p.......", "period": 1 }, { "name": "clk/2 (q0)", "wave": "lhlhlhlh", "period": 1 }, { "name": "clk/4 (q1)", "wave": "l.h.l.h.", "period": 1 } ], "head": { "text": "q0 toggles every clk edge; q1 toggles every q0 rising edge" } } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR CLK["clk"] --> F0["DFF0
D = Q0'"] F0 -->|"Q0 = clk/2"| F1["DFF1 (clocked by Q0)
D = Q1'"] F1 -->|"Q1 = clk/4"| OUT["out"] ``` ### Code ```systemverilog // divide by 2 always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) if (!rst_n) q0 <= 1'b0; else q0 <= ~q0; // divide by 4, synchronous (preferred): 2-flop Johnson counter 00->01->11->10 always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) if (!rst_n) {q1, qa} <= 2'b00; else {q1, qa} <= {qa, ~q1}; // q1 is clk/4 with 50% duty ``` ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Ripple version skews q1 by an extra Tcq relative to clk; in an ASIC, generated clocks need `create_generated_clock` in STA. - Always reset the divider, or simulation shows X forever. ### Follow-ups - *Divide by 3 with 50% duty?* Needs a posedge and a negedge counter OR-ed together.

title: What is the difference between an ASIC, an ASSP and an SoC?
answer: ASIC: designed for a specific application/customer. ASSP: built with ASIC technology but sold to multiple companies for a wider market. SoC: integrates an entire subsystem (processor, memory, peripherals, custom logic) on a chip. ASICs/ASSPs may be SoC or non-SoC.
solution:
**Key idea:** **ASIC** = custom chip for one customer/application. **ASSP** = built with ASIC flows but sold as a standard part to many customers for one application domain. **SoC** = a chip integrating a whole system (CPU(s), memory, peripherals, interconnect, custom logic). An ASIC or ASSP may or may not be an SoC.

| Type | Customer | Example | Contains a processor? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ASIC | single company/system | a custom 24×24 10G switch for one system | optional |
| ASSP | many companies | audio/video codec chip | optional |
| SoC | any | smartphone application processor | yes – CPU + memory + peripherals |
| FPGA | any (reprogrammable) | prototyping, low volume | soft/hard cores optional |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph SOC["SoC"]
    CPU["CPU cores"] --- BUS["interconnect (AXI/NoC)"]
    MEM["SRAM / DDR ctrl"] --- BUS
    PER["peripherals (UART, SPI, USB)"] --- BUS
    ACC["custom accelerator"] --- BUS
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *Verification impact of SoC?* Adds integration/connectivity tests, HW/SW co-verification, interconnect performance, power-domain checks.

title: What are the different steps in a typical ASIC or SoC design flow?
answer: Specification, high-level design, low-level (micro-architecture) design, RTL coding, functional verification, logic synthesis (with equivalence checks), placement and routing (GDS), gate-level simulation/STA with SDF, fabrication, and post-silicon validation.
solution:
**Key idea:** Spec → architecture → micro-architecture → RTL → functional verification → synthesis (+ equivalence) → place & route → timing/gate-level sign-off → tape-out/fab → post-silicon validation.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  S["1. Specification"] --> HLD["2. High-level design (architecture)"]
  HLD --> LLD["3. Low-level design (micro-architecture)"]
  LLD --> RTL["4. RTL coding (Verilog/VHDL)"]
  RTL --> FV["5. Functional verification"]
  FV -->|"bugs"| RTL
  FV --> SYN["6. Logic synthesis + LEC"]
  SYN --> PNR["7. Place and route (CTS, routing) → GDS"]
  PNR --> GLS["8. STA + gate-level sim with SDF"]
  GLS --> FAB["9. Tape-out / fabrication / packaging"]
  FAB --> PSV["10. Post-silicon validation"]
```

| Step | Output / key checks |
| --- | --- |
| Specification | features, interfaces, performance/power targets |
| High-level design | block diagram, interfaces/protocols |
| Micro-architecture | FSMs, pipelines, FIFOs, registers |
| RTL | synthesizable HDL |
| Functional verification | test plan, testbench, coverage closure |
| Synthesis | gate netlist; equivalence check RTL vs netlist |
| Place & route | placement, clock tree, routing, GDSII |
| Sign-off | STA, gate-level sim (SDF back-annotation), DRC/LVS, power |
| Fabrication | silicon, packaging, manufacturing test |
| Post-silicon | lab bring-up with boards and software |

### Explanation
- Verification runs in parallel with design from the spec onward (test plan, VIP), and is the longest pole.
- FPGA flow is similar but ends with bitstream instead of GDS.

### Follow-ups
- *Where do formal tools fit?* Property checking during RTL; equivalence checking after synthesis/ECOs.

title: What is the difference between RISC and CISC architectures?
answer: RISC: fewer, simple fixed-length instructions, few addressing modes, ~1 cycle each, load/store, easy pipelining, more code. CISC: many complex variable-length instructions, memory-to-memory ops, multiple cycles, smaller code. E.g., CISC MULT M1,M2 vs RISC LOAD/LOAD/PROD/STORE.
solution:
**Key idea:** RISC = few, simple, fixed-length instructions, load/store architecture, ~1 cycle each, easy to pipeline (complexity in the compiler). CISC = many complex, variable-length instructions, memory-to-memory operations, multi-cycle (complexity in hardware/microcode).

| Aspect | RISC | CISC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Instruction count/complexity | small, simple | large, complex |
| Length | fixed | variable |
| Addressing modes | few | many |
| Memory operands | only load/store | ALU ops can access memory |
| Cycles per instruction | ~1 | multiple |
| Code size | larger | smaller |
| Performance lever | lower CPI | fewer instructions/program |
| Examples | ARM, RISC-V, MIPS | x86, VAX |

Example – M1 = M1 × M2:

| CISC | RISC |
| --- | --- |
| `MULT M1, M2` | `LOAD A, M1` ; `LOAD B, M2` ; `PROD A, B` ; `STORE M1, A` |

### Explanation
- Performance = instructions × CPI × cycle time; RISC attacks CPI, CISC attacks instruction count.
- Modern x86 cores decode CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-ops internally, so the distinction is mostly at the ISA level.

### Follow-ups
- *Why does RISC pipeline well?* Uniform length and simple decode give regular stage timing.

title: What is the difference between Von Neumann and Harvard architectures, and which would you prefer?
answer: Von Neumann: single memory and bus for data and instructions (unified cache). Harvard: separate memories/buses for instructions and data, allowing simultaneous access (separate I/D caches). Most modern architectures use Harvard (at least for caches).
solution:
**Key idea:** **Von Neumann**: one memory and one bus for both instructions and data (instruction fetch and data access compete – the "Von Neumann bottleneck"). **Harvard**: separate instruction and data memories/buses, so both can be accessed in the same cycle. Prefer Harvard (at least at the cache level) for performance. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph VN["Von Neumann"] C1["CPU"] <-->|"single bus"| M1["unified memory
code + data"] end subgraph HV["Harvard"] C2["CPU"] <-->|"I-bus"| IM["instruction memory"] C2 <-->|"D-bus"| DM["data memory"] end ``` | Aspect | Von Neumann | Harvard | | --- | --- | --- | | Memories | unified | separate I and D | | Simultaneous fetch + data access | no | yes | | Caches | unified | split I$ / D$ | | Flexibility | self-modifying code, flexible memory split | fixed split | | Use | general purpose (main memory) | DSPs, MCUs, L1 caches | ### Explanation - Most modern CPUs are **modified Harvard**: split L1 I$/D$ (Harvard) backed by unified L2/L3 and main memory (Von Neumann). - Harvard removes the structural hazard between IF and MEM pipeline stages. ### Follow-ups - *Why not separate main memories too?* Cost and the flexibility of a single address space.

title: Explain little-endian and big-endian formats in terms of memory storage
answer: Big endian stores the most significant byte at the smallest address; little endian stores the least significant byte at the smallest address. E.g., 0xDDCCBBAA at 0x1000: LE = AA,BB,CC,DD; BE = DD,CC,BB,AA.
solution:
**Key idea:** Endianness = byte order of a multi-byte word in byte-addressable memory. **Big-endian**: most significant byte at the lowest address. **Little-endian**: least significant byte at the lowest address.

Writing word 0xDDCCBBAA at address 0x1000:

| Address | Little-endian | Big-endian |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0x1000 | AA | DD |
| 0x1001 | BB | CC |
| 0x1002 | CC | BB |
| 0x1003 | DD | AA |

### Code (detect endianness in C)
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
int main(void) {
    uint32_t w = 0xDDCCBBAA;
    uint8_t *p = (uint8_t *)&w;          /* look at lowest address */
    printf("%s-endian\n", (*p == 0xAA) ? "little" : "big");
    return 0;
}
```

### Explanation
- x86 and most ARM configurations are little-endian; network byte order (TCP/IP) is big-endian.
- Verification impact: scoreboards/reference models must use the same byte ordering as the bus (e.g., AXI byte lanes are little-endian addressed); endianness bugs show up as byte-swapped data.

### Follow-ups
- *Byte swap in SV?* `{<<8{word}}` reverses byte order using the streaming operator.

title: What is the difference between SRAM and DRAM?
answer: DRAM stores data as charge in a capacitor (1T1C), needs refresh, is denser/cheaper, used for main memory. SRAM uses 6 transistors, retains data while powered without refresh, faster and costlier, used in caches.
solution:
**Key idea:** **SRAM** stores a bit in a 6-transistor cross-coupled latch – fast, no refresh, but large/expensive (caches). **DRAM** stores a bit as charge on a capacitor (1T1C) – dense and cheap, but leaks so it needs periodic refresh and is slower (main memory).

| Aspect | SRAM | DRAM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cell | 6T (cross-coupled inverters) | 1 transistor + 1 capacitor |
| Refresh | not needed | needed (every ~64 ms) |
| Read | non-destructive | destructive (restore after read) |
| Speed | fast (ns, on-chip) | slower (tens of ns) |
| Density / cost per bit | low / high | high / low |
| Power | leakage | refresh + access power |
| Typical use | registers files, caches | main memory (DDR) |
| Volatile? | yes | yes |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CPU["CPU"] --> L1["L1/L2/L3 caches (SRAM)"] --> DDR["Main memory (DRAM)"] --> DISK["Storage (Flash/disk)"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Why is DRAM read destructive?* Sensing shares the capacitor charge with the bit line; the sense amplifier then writes it back.

title: A computer has 256 KB of memory. How many address bits are needed if each byte is addressable?
answer: 256 KB = 2^8 x 2^10 = 2^18 bytes, so 18 address bits.
solution:
**Key idea:** Address bits = log2(number of addressable locations). 256 KB = 2^8 × 2^10 = 2^18 bytes → **18 address bits**.

| Memory size | Bytes | Address bits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 KB | 2^10 | 10 |
| 64 KB | 2^16 | 16 |
| **256 KB** | **2^18** | **18** |
| 4 GB | 2^32 | 32 |

### Explanation
- Address range: 0x00000 – 0x3FFFF.
- If the memory were word-addressed with 32-bit words, you'd need 18 − 2 = 16 bits.

### Follow-ups
- *How many bits for a 256K×32 memory addressed by word?* 18.

title: What are the different types of registers implemented in a CPU?
answer: Program Counter, Instruction Register, Accumulator, General Purpose Registers, Stack Pointer (plus status/flag registers).
solution:
**Key idea:** A CPU has special-purpose registers that control execution (PC, IR, SP, status) and general-purpose registers for data.

| Register | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Program Counter (PC) | address of the current/next instruction |
| Instruction Register (IR) | instruction being executed (fetched from memory[PC]) |
| Accumulator | holds intermediate ALU results (accumulator machines) |
| General Purpose Registers (GPRs) | operands/temporaries used by software; more GPRs → fewer memory accesses |
| Stack Pointer (SP) | top of stack (return addresses, local variables) |
| Status/flags (PSR) | zero, carry, overflow, negative, interrupt enable, mode |
| MAR / MDR | memory address / data registers on the memory interface |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  PC["PC"] -->|"address"| MEM["instruction memory"] --> IR["IR"] --> DEC["decode"]
  DEC --> RF["GPR file"] --> ALU["ALU"] --> ACC["accumulator / result"]
  ALU --> FL["flags"]
  SP["SP"] --> STK["stack in memory"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *What happens to PC on a CALL?* Return address (PC + instr size) is pushed using SP; PC loads the target.

title: Explain the concept of pipelining in computer architecture
answer: Pipelining splits instruction execution into stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back) so multiple instructions are processed concurrently. Increases throughput, not single-instruction latency.
solution:
**Key idea:** Pipelining splits instruction execution into stages (e.g., IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) so different instructions occupy different stages simultaneously – **instruction-level parallelism**. It raises **throughput** (ideally 1 instruction/cycle) but does **not** reduce the latency of a single instruction.

| Cycle → | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I1 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | | |
| I2 | | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| I3 | | | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB |

### Explanation
- Without pipelining 3 instructions take 15 cycles; pipelined they take 5 + 2 = 7.
- Speedup is limited by the slowest stage, pipeline register overhead, and hazards (structural, data, control) that cause stalls.

### Follow-ups
- *Deeper pipeline?* Higher clock frequency but bigger branch-mispredict penalty and more forwarding paths.

title: What is a pipeline hazard, and what are the different types of hazards in a pipelined microprocessor?
answer: A hazard is a condition where the next instruction can't execute. Types: structural (resource conflicts), data (RAW, WAW, WAR dependencies), and control (branches/jumps).
solution:
**Key idea:** A hazard prevents the next instruction from executing in its scheduled cycle. Three kinds: **structural** (resource conflict), **data** (dependency on another in-flight instruction – RAW, WAR, WAW), **control** (branches/jumps change the PC).

| Hazard | Cause | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structural | two instructions need one resource | single FP unit taking 2 cycles; one memory port for IF and MEM |
| Data – RAW (true) | read a value before a prior write completes | `add r1,r2,r3` → `sub r4,r1,r5` |
| Data – WAR (anti) | write a register before an earlier instruction reads it | `sub r4,r1,r5` → `add r1,r2,r3` (out-of-order) |
| Data – WAW (output) | two writes complete out of order | `div r1,..` → `add r1,..` |
| Control | branch outcome/target unknown | `beq` – fetched instructions may be wrong |

RAW stall without forwarding:

| Cycle | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| add r1 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| sub (uses r1) | | IF | stall | stall | ID | EX |

### Follow-ups
- *Which data hazards occur in a simple in-order 5-stage pipe?* Only RAW; WAR/WAW appear with out-of-order or variable-latency units.

title: What techniques can be used to avoid structural, data and control pipeline hazards?
answer: Structural: duplicate resources (separate I/D caches, multiple execution units, separate load/store units). Data: out-of-order execution, data forwarding. Control: branch prediction.
solution:
**Key idea:** Structural → duplicate/pipeline resources. Data → forwarding (bypass), out-of-order execution, register renaming, compiler scheduling. Control → branch prediction, delayed branches, early branch resolution.

| Hazard | Techniques |
| --- | --- |
| Structural | separate I$/D$, multiple execution units (INT/FP, load/store), pipelined units, multi-port register files |
| Data (RAW) | forwarding/bypass from EX/MEM/WB, stall (interlock) only when unavoidable (load-use), instruction scheduling |
| Data (WAR/WAW) | register renaming, in-order commit (ROB) |
| Control | static/dynamic branch prediction (BHT, BTB, return stack), speculative execution, branch delay slot, resolve branch in ID |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  EX["EX stage result"] -->|"forward"| MUX["ALU input mux"]
  MEM["MEM stage result"] -->|"forward"| MUX
  RF["register file"] --> MUX
  MUX --> ALU["ALU (dependent instruction)"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Which RAW can't be fully forwarded in a 5-stage pipe?* Load-use: data is available only after MEM → 1-cycle stall.
- *Verification angle:* write directed back-to-back dependency tests and cover every forwarding path × source stage.

title: A pipelined machine has 10 stages, each taking 1 ns. Assuming no hazards, how long does it take to process 100 data elements?
answer: First element takes 10 ns, remaining 99 take 1 ns each: 10 + 99 = 109 ns.
solution:
**Key idea:** The first element needs the full pipeline latency (10 ns); after that one element completes every cycle. Total = (k + n − 1) × t = (10 + 99) × 1 ns = **109 ns**.

| Element | Completes at |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 10 ns (pipeline fill) |
| 2 | 11 ns |
| … | … |
| 100 | 10 + 99 = **109 ns** |

```mermaid
gantt
  title First elements in a 10-stage pipeline (1 ns per stage)
  dateFormat X
  axisFormat %s
  section Element 1
  Stages 1-10 :0, 10
  section Element 2
  Stages 1-10 :1, 11
  section Element 100
  Stages 1-10 :99, 109
```

### Explanation
- Non-pipelined: 100 × 10 ns = 1000 ns → speedup = 1000/109 ≈ 9.2× (approaches 10× as n → ∞).

### Follow-ups
- *Throughput in steady state?* 1 element/ns = 1 G elements/s.

title: What are the different types of addressing modes for an instruction?
answer: Immediate (operand in instruction), direct (address in instruction), register (operands in registers), indexed (base register + offset).
solution:
**Key idea:** The addressing mode defines how an instruction finds its operand: as a constant in the instruction, in a register, at a fixed address, or at an address computed from registers.

| Mode | Example | Operand / effective address |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate | `add r0, r1, #0x12` | constant 0x12 in the instruction |
| Register | `mul r0, r1, r2` | contents of r1, r2 |
| Direct (absolute) | `load r0, 0x10000` | mem[0x10000] |
| Register indirect | `load r0, [r1]` | mem[r1] |
| Indexed / base+offset | `load r0, [r1 + 8]` | mem[r1 + 8] |
| PC-relative | `beq label` | PC + offset |
| Auto-increment | `load r0, [r1]+` | mem[r1], then r1 += size |

### Explanation
- RISC ISAs keep few modes (register, immediate, base+offset, PC-relative); CISC ISAs offer many.
- Indexed mode is how arrays/structs are accessed (base register + offset).

### Follow-ups
- *Which mode does a jump table use?* Indexed/indirect.

title: What is the principle of spatial and temporal locality of reference?
answer: Temporal locality: a recently referenced location is likely to be referenced again soon. Spatial locality: locations near a recently referenced location are likely to be referenced soon.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Temporal locality**: a location accessed now is likely to be accessed again soon (loop variables, stack). **Spatial locality**: locations near a recently accessed one are likely to be accessed soon (arrays, sequential code). Caches exploit both: keep recent data (temporal) and fetch whole lines (spatial).

```c
int sum = 0;                    /* 'sum' and 'i': temporal locality */
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    sum += a[i];                /* a[0], a[1], ... : spatial locality */
```

| Access trace | Locality |
| --- | --- |
| 0x100, 0x100, 0x100 | temporal |
| 0x100, 0x104, 0x108, 0x10C | spatial |
| 0x100, 0x9000, 0x4400 | neither (cache-unfriendly) |

### Follow-ups
- *Row-major array traversed by column?* Poor spatial locality – stride equals the row size, so each access may miss.

title: What are the different kinds of memories in a system?
answer: Registers, cache, main/primary memory, and secondary memory (magnetic/optical).
solution:
**Key idea:** Memory is a hierarchy trading speed for capacity and cost: registers → caches → main memory → secondary storage.

| Level | Technology | Typical size | Typical latency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Registers | flip-flops | < 1 KB | < 1 cycle |
| Cache (L1/L2/L3) | SRAM | KB – tens of MB | 1–40 cycles |
| Main/primary memory | DRAM | GB | ~100 cycles |
| Secondary memory | Flash/SSD, magnetic disk, optical | TB | µs – ms |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  R["Registers"] --> C["Cache (SRAM)"] --> M["Main memory (DRAM)"] --> S["Secondary storage (SSD/HDD/optical)"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Which are volatile?* Registers, caches, DRAM; secondary storage is non-volatile.

title: What is a cache?
answer: A cache is a small amount of fast memory between main memory and the CPU (often on the CPU chip).
solution:
**Key idea:** A cache is a small, fast memory (SRAM) between the CPU and main memory that holds copies of recently/nearby used memory blocks so most accesses avoid slow DRAM.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CPU["CPU"] <-->|"word transfer (fast)"| CACHE["cache"]
  CACHE <-->|"block / line transfer (slow)"| MEM["main memory"]
```

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Line/block | unit of transfer (e.g., 64 B) |
| Tag | identifies which memory block is in a line |
| Valid / dirty bits | line holds data / line modified (write-back) |
| Hit / miss | data found / not found in cache |

### Explanation
- Average memory access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty; e.g., 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 cycles vs 100 without a cache.

### Follow-ups
- *Where is the cache?* On the CPU die (L1/L2 per core, shared L3), sometimes off-chip.

title: Give an overview of cache operation. What is the principle behind the functioning of a cache?
answer: CPU checks cache first; on a hit data comes from cache. On a miss, a block is read from main memory into the cache and delivered to the CPU. Tags identify which memory block is in each slot. Based on locality of reference.
solution:
**Key idea:** On every access the cache is checked first (tag compare). Hit → data returned quickly. Miss → the whole block containing the address is fetched from memory into a cache line (evicting another if needed), then delivered. It works because of **locality of reference**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["CPU read address"] --> B{"tag match and valid?"}
  B -->|"hit"| C["return data from cache"]
  B -->|"miss"| D["choose victim line (LRU etc.)"]
  D --> E{"victim dirty?"}
  E -->|"yes"| F["write victim back to memory"]
  E -->|"no"| G["fetch block from memory"]
  F --> G
  G --> H["fill line, update tag/valid"] --> C
```

| Address field | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Offset | byte within line |
| Index | which set |
| Tag | compared with stored tag |

### Follow-ups
- *Write policies?* Write-through vs write-back; write-allocate vs no-write-allocate.

title: What is a cache hit and a cache miss?
answer: A cache hit is when the looked-up address is present in the cache; a miss is when it is not found.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Hit**: the requested address is present (valid line with matching tag) in the cache. **Miss**: it is not, so the block must be fetched from the next level.

| Access (direct-mapped, 4 lines, 1-word lines) | Index | Result | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| addr 0 | 0 | miss | cold/compulsory |
| addr 1 | 1 | miss | cold |
| addr 0 | 0 | **hit** | already cached |
| addr 4 | 0 | miss | conflict – evicts addr 0 |
| addr 0 | 0 | miss | conflict |

### Explanation
- Miss types (3 Cs): **compulsory** (first touch), **capacity** (working set > cache), **conflict** (too many blocks map to one set).
- Hit rate = hits / accesses; here 1/5.

### Follow-ups
- *How to reduce conflict misses?* Higher associativity or a victim cache.

title: Will a program that searches a value in a linked list perform differently from one that searches a vector on a machine with a cache?
answer: Yes: vector elements are contiguous, so cache-line fills bring adjacent elements and search is faster; linked-list nodes are non-contiguous and cause more misses.
solution:
**Key idea:** Yes. A vector is **contiguous**, so each cache-line fill (64–128 B) brings in many following elements (spatial locality) and hardware prefetchers detect the stride. Linked-list nodes are scattered, so almost every node visit can be a cache miss (pointer chasing). Vector search is faster.

| Aspect | Vector / array | Linked list |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Layout | contiguous | scattered heap nodes |
| Elements per 64 B line (4-B ints) | 16 | ~1 (plus pointer overhead) |
| Misses for 1024 elements (cold) | ~64 | up to ~1024 |
| Prefetching | effective (sequential) | ineffective (next address unknown until load completes) |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Vector
    L1["line: e0..e15"] --> L2["line: e16..e31"] --> L3["..."]
  end
  subgraph List
    N1["node @0x1000"] --> N2["node @0x8A40"] --> N3["node @0x3310"] --> N4["..."]
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *Both are O(n) – why care?* Constant factors: a DRAM miss costs ~100+ cycles, so the list can be 10× slower.

title: What are the different mechanisms for mapping memory to caches? Compare their advantages and disadvantages
answer: Direct mapping: block k maps to cache block k mod N (simple, one tag compare, but conflict evictions). Fully associative: any block anywhere (best utilization, but compares all tags – big, power hungry). Set associative: direct map to a set, any way within set (compromise). E.g., 64B line, 128 blocks, 32-bit address: direct = offset[5:0], index[12:6], tag[31:13]; 2-way 64 sets: index[11:6], tag[31:12].
solution:
**Key idea:** **Direct-mapped**: each memory block maps to exactly one line (block k → line k mod N). **Fully associative**: any block can go to any line. **N-way set-associative**: block maps to one set (k mod #sets) and to any way within it – the usual compromise.

Example: 32-bit address, 64 B lines, 128 lines (8 KB cache):

| Mapping | Tag | Index | Offset | Tag compares per lookup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direct-mapped (128 sets × 1) | [31:13] (19 b) | [12:6] (7 b) | [5:0] | 1 |
| 2-way (64 sets × 2) | [31:12] (20 b) | [11:6] (6 b) | [5:0] | 2 |
| Fully associative (1 set × 128) | [31:6] (26 b) | none | [5:0] | 128 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ADDR["address"] --> T["tag"]
  ADDR --> I["index → select set"]
  ADDR --> O["offset → byte in line"]
  I --> SET["set: way0 tag | way1 tag"]
  T --> CMP["parallel compare with each way"]
  SET --> CMP --> HIT["hit/miss + way select"]
```

| Mapping | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct | simplest, fastest hit, 1 comparator, lowest power | conflict misses (thrashing) even when cache is not full |
| Fully associative | no conflict misses, best utilization | N comparators, slow/power hungry, complex replacement; only for small structures (TLBs) |
| Set-associative | balances conflict misses vs cost | more comparators/muxing than direct; replacement policy needed |

### Follow-ups
- *Which addresses conflict in the direct-mapped example?* Any two whose bits [12:6] match, e.g., 0x0000 and 0x2000.

title: What is the disadvantage of having a cache with more associativity?
answer: More associativity needs bigger comparator logic to compare against tags in all ways of a set: more power and more hardware.
solution:
**Key idea:** More ways per set means more tags to compare **in parallel** on every lookup: more comparators, wider way-select muxes, more complex replacement state → more area, power and often a longer hit latency. Returns diminish beyond ~8–16 ways.

| Associativity (256 KB, 64 B lines) | Sets | Tag comparators per lookup | Conflict misses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1-way (direct) | 4096 | 1 | highest |
| 4-way | 1024 | 4 | lower |
| 16-way | 256 | 16 | lower still |
| Fully associative | 1 | 4096 | none |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  IDX["index"] --> W0["way0 tag"]
  IDX --> W1["way1 tag"]
  IDX --> WN["... wayN-1 tag"]
  W0 --> C0["=?"]
  W1 --> C1["=?"]
  WN --> CN["=?"]
  C0 --> HIT["OR → hit, N:1 data mux"]
  C1 --> HIT
  CN --> HIT
```

### Follow-ups
- *Replacement cost?* True LRU for N ways needs log2(N!) bits/set – why tree-PLRU is used.

title: A byte-addressable CPU with a 16-bit address bus has a direct-mapped cache with 1-byte blocks and a 4-bit index. How many blocks does the cache hold, and how many tag bits are stored per block?
answer: 4-bit index → 16 blocks; address[3:0] is the index and address[15:4] (12 bits) is the tag.
solution:
**Key idea:** Index bits select the line: 4 bits → 2^4 = **16 blocks**. Block size 1 B → 0 offset bits. Tag = 16 − 4 − 0 = **12 bits** (addr[15:4]).

| Field | Bits | Width |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tag | [15:4] | 12 |
| Index | [3:0] | 4 |
| Offset | – | 0 |

Worked example: address 0xA3C7 → index = 0x7 (line 7), tag = 0xA3C.

### Follow-ups
- *Total storage including valid bit?* 16 × (8 data + 12 tag + 1 valid) = 336 bits.

title: A 4-way set-associative cache is 256 KB with 64-byte lines. How many sets are there, and how many tag bits are needed for a 32-bit address?
answer: 4096 lines / 4 ways = 1024 sets. Offset [5:0], set index [15:6] (10 bits), tag [31:16] (16 bits).
solution:
**Key idea:** Lines = 256 KB / 64 B = 4096; sets = 4096 / 4 = **1024** → 10 index bits. Offset = log2 64 = 6 bits. Tag = 32 − 10 − 6 = **16 bits**.

| Field | Address bits | Width |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tag | [31:16] | 16 |
| Set index | [15:6] | 10 |
| Offset | [5:0] | 6 |

| Step | Calculation |
| --- | --- |
| Lines | 2^18 / 2^6 = 2^12 = 4096 |
| Sets | 4096 / 4 = 1024 = 2^10 |
| Tag bits | 32 − 10 − 6 = 16 |

### Follow-ups
- *8-way instead?* 512 sets → 9 index bits → 17 tag bits.
- *Tag array size?* 4096 lines × 16 bits = 64 Kbit (+ valid/dirty/LRU bits).

title: What is the difference between write-through and write-back caches? What are the advantages and disadvantages?
answer: Write-through writes every cache write to main memory too (simple, memory always up to date, but uses bandwidth). Write-back writes only to cache and defers memory update until eviction (saves bandwidth, but coherency is more complex).
solution:
**Key idea:** **Write-through**: every write updates the cache **and** memory (memory always current, costs bandwidth). **Write-back**: writes update only the cache and mark the line **dirty**; memory is updated on eviction (saves bandwidth, needs dirty tracking and coherence care).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant CPU
  participant Cache
  participant Mem as Memory
  Note over CPU,Mem: Write-through
  CPU->>Cache: write A=5
  Cache->>Mem: write A=5 (every time)
  Note over CPU,Mem: Write-back
  CPU->>Cache: write A=5 (dirty=1)
  CPU->>Cache: write A=6 (still dirty)
  Cache->>Mem: write back A=6 (only on eviction)
```

| Aspect | Write-through | Write-back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory up to date | always | only after eviction |
| Memory bandwidth | high (every store) | low (once per dirty line) |
| Complexity | simple (often + write buffer) | dirty bits, write-back on eviction |
| Coherence / I/O | simple | must snoop/flush dirty lines |
| Eviction cost | none | may require write-back |

### Follow-ups
- *Write-allocate?* On a write miss, fetch the line then write (usually paired with write-back); no-write-allocate pairs with write-through.

title: What is the difference between an inclusive and an exclusive cache?
answer: Inclusive: all L1 addresses are also in L2. Exclusive: an address is in at most one of L1/L2. Exclusive stores more data overall; inclusive makes snooping easier (only check L2).
solution:
**Key idea:** In a multi-level hierarchy, **inclusive**: every line in L1 is also in L2. **Exclusive**: a line lives in at most one of L1/L2. (Non-inclusive/NINE: no guarantee either way.)

| Aspect | Inclusive | Exclusive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effective capacity | L2 only (L1 duplicated) | L1 + L2 |
| Snoop filtering | check L2 only – miss in L2 means not in L1 | must check L1 and L2 |
| L2 eviction | must back-invalidate L1 copy | no back-invalidation |
| L1 eviction | just drop (copy in L2) | victim moves into L2 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Inclusive
    L1a["L1: A B"] --- L2a["L2: A B C D"]
  end
  subgraph Exclusive
    L1b["L1: A B"] --- L2b["L2: C D E F"]
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *Verification checks?* For inclusive caches, assert that every valid L1 tag exists in L2 (a great scoreboard/assertion invariant).

title: What are the different algorithms used for cache line replacement in a set-associative cache?
answer: LRU (age bits), MRU, Pseudo-LRU (one or two bits), LFU (frequency counts), Random replacement.
solution:
**Key idea:** When a set is full the replacement policy picks a victim: LRU, pseudo-LRU, MRU, LFU, FIFO/round-robin or random.

| Policy | State per set | Idea | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LRU | age bits per line | evict least recently used | best for temporal locality, costly for many ways |
| Pseudo-LRU (tree) | N−1 bits | binary tree points away from recently used | cheap approximation |
| MRU | age bits | evict most recently used | good for cyclic scans larger than the cache |
| LFU | counters | evict least frequently used | needs aging to adapt |
| FIFO / round-robin | pointer | evict oldest filled | simple |
| Random | LFSR | evict random way | no state, surprisingly good |

Worked LRU trace (2-way set, accesses A B A C):

| Access | Way0 | Way1 | LRU after | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | A | – | way1 | miss |
| B | A | B | way0 | miss |
| A | A | B | way1 | hit |
| C | A | **C** (evict B) | way0 | miss |

### Follow-ups
- *Tree-PLRU for 4 ways?* 3 bits: root picks a pair, child bit picks a way within the pair; on access, flip bits to point away.

title: What is the cache coherency problem?
answer: In SMP systems, multiple caches can hold copies of the same address; if processors update freely, reads on different processors can see different values – inconsistent view of memory.
solution:
**Key idea:** In a shared-memory multiprocessor each core has a private cache, so the **same address can have multiple copies**. If cores update their copies independently, different cores see different values for one location – an inconsistent view of memory.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P0 as P0 cache
  participant M as Memory (X=0)
  participant P1 as P1 cache
  P0->>M: read X → caches 0
  P1->>M: read X → caches 0
  P0->>P0: write X=1 (write-back, local only)
  P1->>P1: read X → still 0 (stale!)
```

| Requirement | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Write propagation | a write must eventually be visible to all cores |
| Write serialization | all cores see writes to one address in the same order |

### Explanation
- Solved by hardware coherence protocols (MESI/MOESI) using snooping or directories; software alternatives are cache flush/invalidate.

### Follow-ups
- *Coherence vs consistency?* Coherence concerns one address; memory consistency concerns ordering across different addresses.

title: What is the difference between snoop-based and directory-based cache coherency protocols?
answer: Snoop: requests broadcast to all processors, each snoops and responds – faster for small systems but doesn't scale. Directory: a directory tracks which processors cache which addresses; point-to-point requests – longer latency but scales better.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Snoop-based**: every request is **broadcast**; all caches snoop and respond. **Directory-based**: a directory tracks which caches hold each line; requests go to the directory, which sends **point-to-point** messages only to sharers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Snoop
    P0["P0"] -->|"broadcast"| BUS["shared bus / ring"]
    BUS --> P1["P1"]
    BUS --> P2["P2"]
    BUS --> P3["P3"]
  end
  subgraph Directory
    Q0["P0"] -->|"request"| DIR["directory: line X → {P2}"]
    DIR -->|"point-to-point"| Q2["P2"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Snoop-based | Directory-based |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Messaging | broadcast | targeted |
| Latency (small system) | low | extra directory lookup |
| Scalability | poor – traffic grows with cores | good – large SMP/NUMA |
| Storage | none extra | directory entries (presence bits) |

### Follow-ups
- *Hybrid?* Snoop filters: an inclusive tag directory filters broadcasts.

title: What is the MESI protocol?
answer: MESI: per-line states Modified (dirty), Exclusive (clean, only copy, can be written), Shared (clean, multiple copies, no write), Invalid. Reads serviced in any state except I; writes only in M or E.
solution:
**Key idea:** MESI is a write-back cache-coherence protocol with four per-line states: **M**odified (dirty, only copy), **E**xclusive (clean, only copy), **S**hared (clean, maybe other copies), **I**nvalid. Reads are serviced in M/E/S; writes only in M/E (S must first invalidate others).

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  I --> E: local read, no other sharer
  I --> S: local read, others have it
  I --> M: local write (RFO)
  E --> M: local write (silent)
  E --> S: snoop read
  S --> M: local write (invalidate others)
  M --> S: snoop read (supply data, write back)
  M --> I: snoop write / RFO
  S --> I: snoop write / RFO
  E --> I: snoop write / RFO
```

| State | Dirty? | Other copies? | Can read | Can write |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | yes | no | yes | yes |
| E | no | no | yes | yes (→ M silently) |
| S | no | possibly | yes | no – upgrade first |
| I | – | – | no | no |

### Follow-ups
- *Why E?* Lets a private line be written without a bus transaction – the main gain over MSI.

title: What are the MESIF and MOESI(F) protocols?
answer: Extensions of MESI. F (Forward): specialized S state; one cache is designated responder to forward data, reducing memory traffic. O (Owned): allows dirty data to be shared among caches without writing back to memory (line goes M→O when shared).
solution:
**Key idea:** Extensions of MESI. **F (Forward)** – one designated sharer of a clean shared line answers requests with data (cache-to-cache), cutting memory traffic (Intel MESIF). **O (Owned)** – a dirty line can be shared; the owner supplies data and is responsible for the eventual write-back, deferring the memory write (AMD MOESI).

| State | Dirty | Shared | Responds with data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | yes | no | yes |
| O | yes | yes (others in S) | yes – owner |
| E | no | no | yes |
| S | no | yes | no |
| F | no | yes | yes – designated forwarder |
| I | – | – | no |

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  M --> O: snoop read (share dirty data, no memory write)
  O --> M: local write (invalidate sharers)
  O --> I: snoop invalidate
  S --> F: becomes designated forwarder
  F --> S: forwarding duty passed to new requester
```

### Follow-ups
- *In MESIF, who gets F after a forward?* Usually the newest requester (most likely to keep the line).

title: What is an RFO (Read For Ownership)?
answer: RFO = Read For Ownership: a read with intent to write; combines read and invalidate broadcast, issued when writing to a line in S or I state; others invalidate their copies.
solution:
**Key idea:** RFO is a coherence transaction = **read + invalidate**. A core that wants to write a line it holds in S or I issues an RFO; it obtains the latest data and all other caches invalidate their copies, so the requester gets the line in E/M.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P0 as P0 (line in I)
  participant IC as Interconnect
  participant P1 as P1 (line in S)
  participant P2 as P2 (line in M)
  P0->>IC: RFO(X)
  IC->>P1: snoop invalidate
  IC->>P2: snoop invalidate
  P1-->>IC: ack (S→I)
  P2-->>IC: data (M→I)
  IC-->>P0: data, exclusive
  Note over P0: P0 writes X, state M
```

### Explanation
- If the requester already has valid data in S, an **upgrade** (invalidate-only) can be used instead of a full RFO.
- Write-heavy sharing causes RFO "ping-pong" (false sharing when different variables share a line).

### Follow-ups
- *How would you verify RFO?* Check that after completion no other cache holds the line valid, and data returned is the latest (scoreboard against a memory model).

title: What is the concept of virtual memory?
answer: Virtual memory lets a processor see a contiguous virtual address space even with small physical memory; OS manages mapping (paging) between virtual space, physical memory and secondary storage; MMU translates virtual to physical addresses.
solution:
**Key idea:** Each process sees a large, private, contiguous **virtual address space**; the OS and the MMU map virtual **pages** to physical frames (or to disk), so programs can be larger than physical RAM and are isolated from each other.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph VA["Process virtual pages"]
    V0["VP0"]
    V1["VP1"]
    V2["VP2"]
    V3["VP3"]
  end
  V0 --> F5["PF5"]
  V1 --> F1["PF1"]
  V2 --> DISK["on disk (swap)"]
  V3 --> F7["PF7"]
  subgraph PM["Physical memory frames"]
    F1
    F5
    F7
  end
```

| Benefit | How |
| --- | --- |
| Larger than RAM | inactive pages live on disk |
| Isolation/protection | per-process page tables, permission bits |
| Simplified linking/loading | every process starts at the same virtual addresses |
| Sharing | map the same frame into multiple processes |

### Follow-ups
- *Hardware involved?* MMU, TLB, page-table walker; page faults handled by the OS.

title: What is the difference between a virtual memory address and a physical memory address?
answer: Virtual address: used by a program/process within its address space. Physical address: the actual DRAM location after OS/hardware translation via paging; missing pages are brought from disk.
solution:
**Key idea:** A **virtual address** is what software/processes use; a **physical address** is what actually goes to DRAM. The MMU translates VA → PA through page tables (cached in the TLB); the page offset is unchanged.

| Field (4 KB pages, 32-bit VA) | Bits |
| --- | --- |
| Virtual page number (VPN) | VA[31:12] |
| Page offset | VA[11:0] |
| Physical address | {PFN from page table, VA[11:0]} |

Example: VA 0x0040_3ABC, page table maps VPN 0x00403 → PFN 0x1F2 → PA 0x001F_2ABC.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  VA["VA = VPN | offset"] --> TLB{"TLB hit?"}
  TLB -->|"yes"| PA["PA = PFN | offset"]
  TLB -->|"no"| PT["page table walk"] --> PA
  PT -->|"page not present"| PF["page fault → OS loads from disk"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Can two processes use the same VA?* Yes – they map to different PAs.

title: What is the concept of paging?
answer: Virtual address space is divided into pages (contiguous blocks, usually ≥ 4 KB; large pages 1–4 MB); a page is the minimum unit moved from secondary storage. Page tables translate virtual to physical addresses.
solution:
**Key idea:** Virtual and physical memory are divided into fixed-size **pages/frames** (typically 4 KB; large pages 2 MB/1 GB). A **page table** maps each virtual page number to a physical frame number plus permission/present bits. The page is the unit moved between disk and memory.

| VPN | Present | PFN | R/W/X |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x000 | 1 | 0x05 | R-X (code) |
| 0x001 | 1 | 0x01 | RW- |
| 0x002 | 0 | – (on disk) | RW- |
| 0x003 | 1 | 0x07 | RW- |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  VA["VA: VPN | offset"] --> PTBR["page table base reg"]
  PTBR --> PTE["PTE[VPN]"] --> PA["PFN | offset"]
```

### Explanation
- No external fragmentation (all pages same size); internal fragmentation in the last page.
- Multi-level page tables keep table memory proportional to used address space.

### Follow-ups
- *Why large pages?* Fewer TLB misses for big working sets.

title: What is a TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)?
answer: A TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical translations; on a hit the physical address is obtained quickly without a page-table walk; on a miss the page tables must be walked in memory.
solution:
**Key idea:** A TLB is a small (often fully/highly associative) **cache of recent VA→PA translations**. A TLB hit gives the physical address in ~1 cycle; a miss triggers a page-table walk (several memory accesses).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["virtual address"] --> B{"TLB lookup (VPN)"}
  B -->|"hit"| C["PA = PFN | offset → cache/memory"]
  B -->|"miss"| D["page table walk in memory"]
  D -->|"PTE valid"| E["refill TLB"] --> C
  D -->|"not present"| F["page fault exception → OS"]
```

| Event | Typical cost |
| --- | --- |
| TLB hit | 0–1 cycles |
| TLB miss, walk hits caches | 10–50 cycles |
| Page fault | millions of cycles (disk/OS) |

### Follow-ups
- *Context switch issue?* TLB entries belong to a process – flush or tag entries with ASIDs.
- *TLB reach?* entries × page size, e.g., 64 × 4 KB = 256 KB.

title: What is meant by a page fault?
answer: When a page mapped into virtual address space but not loaded in main memory is accessed, the MMU raises an interrupt called a page fault.
solution:
**Key idea:** A page fault is the exception the MMU raises when a program accesses a page that is mapped in its virtual address space but **not currently present in physical memory** (or violates permissions). The OS handles it: load the page from disk, update the page table, and restart the faulting instruction.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant CPU
  participant MMU
  participant OS
  participant Disk
  CPU->>MMU: load VA
  MMU-->>CPU: PTE present=0 → page fault
  CPU->>OS: trap to handler
  OS->>Disk: read page
  Disk-->>OS: page data
  OS->>OS: pick frame (evict if needed), update PTE
  OS-->>CPU: return, re-execute instruction
```

| Type | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| Minor/soft | page in memory but not mapped (e.g., shared/page cache) |
| Major/hard | page must be read from disk |
| Invalid | illegal address/permission → segmentation fault |

### Follow-ups
- *Fault or trap?* A page fault is a **fault** – handled before the instruction completes so it can be restarted.

title: If a CPU is busy executing a task, how can we stop it and run another task?
answer: By using external interrupt sources to interrupt program execution.
solution:
**Key idea:** Use an **interrupt**. An external (or timer) interrupt makes the CPU finish the current instruction, save context (PC, flags, registers), jump to the interrupt service routine / OS scheduler, which can then switch to another task.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant TaskA
  participant CPU
  participant Dev as Timer / device
  participant ISR as ISR / scheduler
  TaskA->>CPU: executing
  Dev->>CPU: IRQ asserted
  CPU->>CPU: finish current instruction, save PC/flags
  CPU->>ISR: vector to handler
  ISR->>ISR: save Task A context, choose Task B
  ISR-->>CPU: restore Task B context, return-from-interrupt
```

### Explanation
- Preemptive multitasking OSes use a periodic timer interrupt for time slicing.
- Interrupts can be masked; non-maskable interrupts (NMI) cannot.

### Follow-ups
- *Polling alternative?* The task itself checks a flag periodically – cooperative, wastes cycles, higher latency.

title: What are interrupts and exceptions, and how are they different?
answer: Interrupts: asynchronous events from external hardware, serviced after the current instruction. Exceptions: synchronous events from instruction execution (divide by zero, undefined instruction); types: faults (serviced before the faulting instruction), traps (after), aborts (severe errors).
solution:
**Key idea:** **Interrupts** are **asynchronous** events from outside the instruction stream (I/O, timers), serviced at an instruction boundary. **Exceptions** are **synchronous** events caused by the executing instruction (divide-by-zero, illegal opcode, page fault). Exceptions are classified as faults, traps and aborts.

| Aspect | Interrupt | Exception |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | external hardware | current instruction |
| Timing | asynchronous | synchronous, repeatable |
| Examples | keyboard, USB, timer, DMA done | divide by zero, undefined instruction, page fault, breakpoint |

| Exception class | When handled | Return to | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fault | before instruction completes | faulting instruction (re-execute) | page fault |
| Trap | after the instruction | next instruction | breakpoint, syscall |
| Abort | – | no reliable return | machine check, double fault |

### Follow-ups
- *Precise exceptions?* All earlier instructions completed, none later have changed state – required to restart after a fault (ROB in out-of-order CPUs).

title: What is a vectored interrupt?
answer: In a vectored interrupt, the interrupting device sends a unique code that directs the processor to the correct ISR. Non-vectored: first-level ISR reads status registers to decode the source.
solution:
**Key idea:** With a **vectored** interrupt the interrupting device supplies a unique code (vector) that directly selects its ISR address (via a vector table). With **non-vectored** interrupts a common handler must read status registers to find the source, then dispatch.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Vectored
    D1["device"] -->|"IRQ + vector 0x21"| VT["vector table[0x21]"] --> ISR1["specific ISR"]
  end
  subgraph NonVectored["Non-vectored"]
    D2["device"] -->|"IRQ"| GH["common handler"] --> RS["read interrupt status reg"] --> ISR2["dispatch to ISR"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Vectored | Non-vectored |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latency | lower | higher (software decode) |
| Hardware | vector delivery, table | simple |
| Examples | x86 IDT, ARM NVIC | simple MCUs, GIC with software dispatch |

### Follow-ups
- *Verification point?* Check each source maps to the correct vector, priority/nesting, and that pending/clear bits behave per spec.

title: What techniques are used to improve the performance of instruction fetching from memory?
answer: Instruction cache and prefetch (fetch ahead of decode/execute to hide latency) and branch prediction/branch target prediction (keep fetching along the predicted path).
solution:
**Key idea:** Hide memory latency in the front-end: **instruction cache + prefetching** (fetch ahead of decode) and **branch prediction + branch target prediction** (keep fetching down the predicted path without waiting for execution).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  BP["branch predictor + BTB"] -->|"next PC"| PC["PC"]
  PC --> IC["I-cache"]
  PF["prefetcher (next lines)"] --> IC
  IC --> FQ["fetch queue / buffer"] --> DEC["decode"]
```

| Technique | What it hides |
| --- | --- |
| I-cache | DRAM latency for hot code |
| Sequential prefetch / stream buffers | cold misses for straight-line code |
| Branch direction prediction | wait for branch resolution |
| Branch target buffer (BTB), return stack | wait for target computation |
| Fetch queue / decoupled front-end | short stalls |
| Wider fetch, trace/uop caches | fetch bandwidth |

### Follow-ups
- *Cost of a mispredict?* Flush everything fetched after the branch – roughly the pipeline depth in cycles.

title: What is meant by a superscalar pipelined processor?
answer: A superscalar processor exploits instruction-level parallelism by dispatching multiple instructions per cycle to different execution units; N instructions per cycle = N-way superscalar.
solution:
**Key idea:** A superscalar processor issues **more than one instruction per cycle** to multiple execution units (instruction-level parallelism). An N-way superscalar can fetch/decode/issue up to N instructions per cycle (ideal IPC = N).

| Cycle → | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I1 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| I2 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| I3 | | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB |
| I4 | | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB |

(2-way superscalar: two instructions in each stage per cycle.)

### Explanation
- Requires dependency checking among instructions issued together, multiple register file ports, multiple ALUs/load-store units; usually combined with out-of-order execution.
- Contrast: VLIW relies on the compiler to bundle independent instructions; superscalar does it in hardware.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is real IPC < N?* Dependencies, branch mispredicts, cache misses, limited execution units.

title: What is the difference between in-order and out-of-order execution?
answer: In-order: instructions are fetched, executed and completed in program order; a stall stalls all later instructions. Out-of-order: fetched in order, executed in any order, completed in order; independent instructions can proceed past a stalled one.
solution:
**Key idea:** **In-order**: instructions fetch, execute and complete in program order – one stall blocks everything behind it. **Out-of-order**: fetch in order, **execute when operands are ready** (any order), **retire/commit in order** – independent instructions bypass a stalled one.

Program: `I1: load r1,[r2]` (cache miss, 10 cycles), `I2: add r3,r1,1` (depends on I1), `I3: mul r4,r5,r6` (independent).

| Model | I3 executes | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In-order | after I1 and I2 | ~12 cycles |
| Out-of-order | immediately, during I1's miss | ~11 cycles (I3 hidden) |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F["fetch/decode (in order)"] --> RN["rename"] --> RS["reservation stations"]
  RS -->|"ready operands, any order"| EU["execution units"]
  EU --> ROB["reorder buffer"] -->|"commit in order"| ARF["architectural state"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Why commit in order?* Precise exceptions and correct architectural state on mispredicts.

title: What is the difference between a conditional branch and an unconditional branch instruction?
answer: Unconditional branch always branches (e.g., Jump <offset>). Conditional branch branches only if a condition is true (e.g., beq ra, rb, <offset>), otherwise continues sequentially.
solution:
**Key idea:** An **unconditional** branch always changes the program flow (`jump`, `call`, `return`). A **conditional** branch changes flow only if a condition holds (`beq ra, rb, offset` – branch if equal), otherwise execution falls through.

| Instruction | Type | Next PC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jump L1` | unconditional | L1 always |
| `beq ra, rb, L1` | conditional | L1 if ra == rb, else PC + 4 |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  B{"beq ra, rb, L1"} -->|"ra == rb (taken)"| L1["L1: target"]
  B -->|"ra != rb (not taken)"| N["PC + 4 (fall through)"]
  J["jump L2"] --> L2["L2: target"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Which needs direction prediction?* Conditional; unconditional only needs target prediction (BTB / return stack).

title: What is branch prediction and branch target prediction?
answer: Branch prediction predicts whether a conditional branch will be taken or not; branch target prediction predicts the target of a taken branch/jump before it is computed.
solution:
**Key idea:** A **branch (direction) predictor** guesses whether a conditional branch is taken or not-taken. A **branch target predictor** (BTB) guesses *where* a taken branch or jump goes, before execution computes it. Together they let fetch continue without stalls.

2-bit saturating counter (per branch history entry):

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  SNT --> WNT: taken
  WNT --> SNT: not taken
  WNT --> WT: taken
  WT --> WNT: not taken
  WT --> ST: taken
  ST --> WT: not taken
  SNT --> SNT: not taken
  ST --> ST: taken
```

| Structure | Predicts | Indexed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BHT / pattern table (2-bit counters) | taken / not-taken | PC (+ global history in gshare) |
| BTB | target address | PC of branch |
| Return address stack | return targets | call/return pairing |

### Follow-ups
- *Why 2-bit not 1-bit?* A loop branch mispredicts only once per loop exit instead of twice.

title: What is meant by memory-mapped I/O?
answer: MMIO: CPU uses the same address bus for memory and I/O devices; a region of the address map is reserved for device registers, and the device responds when those addresses are accessed.
solution:
**Key idea:** With memory-mapped I/O (MMIO), device registers and buffers occupy part of the **system address map**; the CPU accesses them with ordinary load/store instructions on the same address bus, and the device decoding that address responds.

| Address range | Target |
| --- | --- |
| 0x0000_0000 – 0x0000_03FF | UART / timer registers (MMIO) |
| 0x0000_0400 – 0x3FFF_FFFF | reserved / other peripherals |
| 0x4000_0000 – 0xFFFF_FFFF | DRAM |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CPU["CPU load/store"] --> DEC["address decoder / interconnect"]
  DEC -->|"0x0000_0xxx"| UART["UART regs"]
  DEC -->|"0x4000_0000+"| DDR["DRAM"]
```

### Explanation
- Alternative is port-mapped I/O (separate I/O address space and `in/out` instructions, x86).
- MMIO regions must be uncached/strongly-ordered (side effects on read, e.g., read-to-clear status).

### Follow-ups
- *Verification:* register access tests via the bus, address-map/decoder coverage, UVM RAL.

title: What is the advantage of using one-hot encoding in a design?
answer: In one-hot coding, no decode is needed to know the current state (one bit per state, two bits change per transition). Uses more flip-flops but less combinational logic, helping timing-critical logic.
solution:
**Key idea:** In one-hot encoding exactly one flop is 1 per state, so the current state is known **without decoding** – next-state and output logic are small and fast, at the cost of more flip-flops (N flops for N states). On each transition exactly two bits change (one clears, one sets).

| State | Binary (2 FFs) | One-hot (4 FFs) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IDLE | 00 | 0001 |
| REQ | 01 | 0010 |
| ACK | 10 | 0100 |
| DONE | 11 | 1000 |

### Code
```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [3:0] {IDLE=4'b0001, REQ=4'b0010, ACK=4'b0100, DONE=4'b1000} st_t;
st_t st;
// "is state ACK?" is a single bit, no comparator:
assign ack_out = st[2];
// sanity assertion
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $onehot(st));
```

| Aspect | Binary | One-hot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flops | log2 N | N |
| Decode logic | comparators | single bit |
| Speed | slower | faster (FPGAs love it) |
| Illegal states | few | many (2^N − N) → need recovery |

### Follow-ups
- *Detect corruption?* `$onehot` assertion / parity of state.

title: What is the difference between static and automatic variables, and between local and global variables?
answer: Scope distinguishes local (visible only in its block) and global (visible everywhere). Storage duration distinguishes static (lives for the whole program) and automatic (exists only while the block executes). A local static has local scope but keeps its value across calls.
solution:
**Key idea:** Two independent properties. **Scope** (local vs global) = *where* a name is visible. **Lifetime/storage duration** (static vs automatic) = *how long* the storage exists. A local static is visible only inside its function but keeps its value across calls.

| Variable | Scope | Lifetime | Copies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Global | whole program / class | whole program | 1 |
| Local automatic | its block/function | each call (re-created) | 1 per call (re-entrant) |
| Local static | its block/function | whole program | 1 shared by all calls |
| Class static member | class | whole program | 1 shared by all objects |

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class test_class;
  int        inst_int;        // one per object, lives as long as the object
  static int global_static;   // one for the class, lives for the whole simulation

  function void compute();
    static    int count;      // local scope, static lifetime: keeps value across calls
    automatic int sum = 0;    // local scope, automatic: fresh each call
    sum   = sum + 1;          // always 1
    count = count + sum;      // 1, 2, 3, ... on successive calls
    $display("sum=%0d count=%0d", sum, count);
  endfunction
endclass
```

| Call # | sum | count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 1 | 3 |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- In SystemVerilog, functions/tasks in **modules** are static by default (`task automatic` needed for recursion/re-entrancy); class methods are automatic by default.
- Static locals are not thread-safe across concurrent forked calls.

### Follow-ups
- *C equivalent?* `static int count;` inside a function; `static` at file scope means internal linkage instead.

title: What is an inline function?
answer: A function expanded inline at each call (compiler replaces call with body), avoiding call/return overhead; useful for small functions used often (e.g., max in C).

title: What is a regular expression?
answer: A special sequence of characters used to match or find other strings with a special syntax; powerful pattern matching used in Perl, Python, Tcl.
solution:
**Key idea:** A regular expression is a pattern language for matching/searching/replacing text. It is used heavily in Perl, Python, Tcl, grep/sed – e.g., to parse simulation logs.

| Pattern | Meaning | Example match |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.` | any char | `a.c` → abc |
| `*`, `+`, `?` | 0+, 1+, 0/1 of previous | `ab+` → abbb |
| `[0-9]`, `\d` | digit | 7 |
| `\w`, `\s` | word char, whitespace | x, space |
| `^`, `$` | start, end of line | `^ERROR` |
| `( )` | capture group | `(\d+)` |
| `{m,n}` | repeat m..n | `\d{2,4}` |

### Code (Python – extract UVM errors from a log)
```python
import re
pat = re.compile(r"^UVM_(ERROR|FATAL)\s+(\S+)\((\d+)\)\s+@\s+(\d+):\s+(.*)$")
with open("sim.log") as f:
    for line in f:
        m = pat.match(line)
        if m:
            sev, file, lineno, time, msg = m.groups()
            print(f"{sev} at t={time}: {msg}  ({file}:{lineno})")
```

### Follow-ups
- *Greedy vs non-greedy?* `.*` grabs as much as possible; `.*?` as little as possible.

title: What is the difference between a heap and a stack?
answer: Stack: stores temporary/local variables of functions, managed automatically, LIFO, limited size (stack overflow). Heap: memory managed by programmer/GC (allocate/free), slower, accessed via pointers, resizable, can fragment.
solution:
