**Key idea:** The **stack** holds function call frames (local automatic variables, return addresses) – allocated/freed automatically in LIFO order, fast, limited size. The **heap** holds dynamically allocated memory (`malloc`/`new`, objects) – managed by the programmer or a garbage collector, larger, slower, accessed through pointers, can fragment.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph Memory["Process address space"]
    TEXT["code (text)"]
    DATA["globals/static (data, bss)"]
    HEAP["heap ↓ grows up: malloc/new"]
    FREE["free space"]
    STACK["stack ↑ grows down: frames"]
  end
  TEXT --- DATA --- HEAP --- FREE --- STACK
```

| Aspect | Stack | Heap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allocation | automatic on function entry | explicit (`malloc`/`new`) |
| Deallocation | automatic on return | `free`/`delete` or GC |
| Speed | very fast (pointer bump) | slower (allocator) |
| Size | small, fixed (stack overflow) | large, can grow |
| Lifetime | until function returns | until freed |
| Fragmentation | none | possible |
| Typical contents | locals, args, return address | objects, dynamic arrays |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Returning a pointer to a local (stack) variable → dangling pointer.
- Deep recursion → stack overflow.

### Follow-ups
- *Where do SV class objects live?* On the simulator's heap; handles are references, memory is garbage-collected.

title: What is the difference between ++a and a++?
answer: ++a increments first and returns the new value; a++ returns the current value and then increments.
solution:
**Key idea:** Both increment `a`. **Pre-increment `++a`** increments first and yields the new value; **post-increment `a++`** yields the old value, then increments.

### Code (C)
```c
int a = 5, x, y;
x = ++a;   /* a = 6, x = 6 */
y = a++;   /* y = 6, a = 7 */
```

| Statement | a before | value used | a after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `x = ++a;` | 5 | 6 | 6 |
| `y = a++;` | 6 | 6 | 7 |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `i = i++ + ++i;` is undefined behavior in C/C++ (unsequenced modifications).
- In C++, prefer `++it` for iterators/objects (post-increment must copy the old value).
- SystemVerilog supports both too (`i++` in loops), with the same semantics.

title: What is meant by a memory leak?
answer: A memory leak occurs when dynamically allocated memory becomes unreachable without being freed (e.g., C++ objects not deleted). Languages with garbage collection (SystemVerilog, Java) are less prone.
solution:
**Key idea:** A memory leak happens when dynamically allocated memory is no longer reachable (the last pointer to it is lost) but was never freed, so it can't be reused. Common in C/C++; garbage-collected languages (SystemVerilog, Java, Python) reclaim unreachable objects automatically.

### Code (C++)
```cpp
#include <vector>
void leak() {
    int *p = new int[100];
    p = new int[100];        // first block now unreachable -> leaked
    delete[] p;              // frees only the second block
}
void no_leak() {
    std::vector<int> v(100); // RAII: freed automatically when v goes out of scope
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["pointer p"] -.->|"overwritten"| B1["block #1 (unreachable, leaked)"]
  P --> B2["block #2"]
```

### Explanation
- Detect with valgrind/ASan; avoid with RAII and smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`).
- In SV testbenches, "leaks" still occur when handles are kept in queues/associative arrays forever (e.g., scoreboard never pops matched items) – memory grows over a long simulation.

### Follow-ups
- *Dangling pointer vs leak?* Dangling = pointer to freed memory; leak = allocated memory with no pointer.

title: What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
answer: Compiler translates the whole program into machine code before execution (more analysis time, faster execution, errors after full scan; C/C++). Interpreter translates one statement at a time (less analysis time, slower execution, stops at first error; Perl/Python).
solution:
**Key idea:** A **compiler** translates the whole program into machine code ahead of time (then the hardware runs it fast). An **interpreter** translates/executes one statement at a time at runtime (slower, but immediate feedback, portable).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Compiler
    S1["source (C/C++)"] --> C["compiler"] --> B["machine code binary"] --> H["CPU executes"]
  end
  subgraph Interpreter
    S2["source (Perl/Python)"] --> I["interpreter (statement by statement / bytecode VM)"] --> H2["CPU runs interpreter"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Compiler | Interpreter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Translation unit | entire program | one statement at a time |
| Analysis time | longer | shorter |
| Output | machine-specific binary | no binary (or intermediate bytecode) |
| Execution speed | faster | slower |
| Errors reported | after scanning whole program | stops at first error |
| Examples | C, C++ | Perl, Python, Tcl |

### Follow-ups
- *Where do HDL simulators fit?* Modern simulators compile HDL to native code (compiled-code simulation); Python is compiled to bytecode then interpreted; JITs blur the line.

title: What is the difference between a statically typed language and a dynamically typed language?
answer: Statically typed: types fixed at compile time, variables declared with types before use (C, Java, SystemVerilog). Dynamically typed: types discovered at execution time (Python, VBScript).
solution:
**Key idea:** **Static typing**: variable types are fixed and checked at compile time (declare before use) – C, C++, Java, SystemVerilog. **Dynamic typing**: types are attached to values and determined at run time – Python, Perl, VBScript.

### Code
```c
/* C: static */
int count = 5;
count = "five";      /* compile-time error */
```
```python
# Python: dynamic
count = 5
count = "five"       # fine - the name now refers to a str
print(count + 1)     # TypeError only when this line runs
```

| Aspect | Static | Dynamic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type errors found | compile time | run time |
| Declarations | required | not required |
| Performance | typically faster | slower (runtime checks) |
| Flexibility | less | more (duck typing) |

### Follow-ups
- *Strong vs weak typing?* A different axis – whether implicit conversions are allowed (Python is dynamic but strong; C is static but fairly weak).

title: Which of the following is false about a stack? (1) Only push and pop apply (2) A stack implements a FIFO (3) Stacks are useful for nested loops and subroutine calls (4) Stacks are efficient for arithmetic expression evaluation
answer: Option (2) is false: a stack is LIFO, not FIFO.
solution:
**Key idea:** **(2) is false** – a stack is **LIFO** (last in, first out), not FIFO. A queue is FIFO.

| Operation sequence | Stack (LIFO) pops | Queue (FIFO) pops |
| --- | --- | --- |
| push 1, push 2, push 3 | 3, 2, 1 | 1, 2, 3 |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  P["push 3 / pop → 3 (top)"] --> T2["2"] --> T1["1 (bottom)"]
```

### Code (SystemVerilog queue as a stack)
```systemverilog
int stk[$];
initial begin
  stk.push_back(1); stk.push_back(2); stk.push_back(3);
  $display("%0d", stk.pop_back());   // 3 - LIFO
end
```

### Explanation
- Stacks naturally handle nested calls (return addresses), nested loops/parentheses, and postfix (RPN) expression evaluation.

title: What are the major differences between use and require in Perl?
answer: use is evaluated at compile time and implicitly calls import; require is evaluated at run time and doesn't import; use takes only a bareword while require can take a bareword or expression.
solution:
**Key idea:** `use` is processed at **compile time** and calls the module's `import` (exporting symbols); `require` happens at **run time**, doesn't import, and can take an expression/file path – useful for conditional loading.

| Aspect | `use Module;` | `require Module;` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When | compile time (`BEGIN` block) | run time |
| Calls `import` | yes | no |
| Argument | bareword only | bareword or expression (`require $file;`) |
| Failure | script won't compile | dies when executed (can be trapped with `eval`) |

### Code
```perl
use strict;
use List::Util qw(max);          # compile-time, imports max()
print max(3, 9, 4), "\n";

if ($ENV{USE_JSON}) {
    require JSON::PP;             # loaded only if needed, at run time
    print JSON::PP->new->encode({a => 1}), "\n";   # no import: use full name
}
```
- `use Module LIST;` is equivalent to `BEGIN { require Module; Module->import(LIST); }`.

### Follow-ups
- *Load a module only if installed?* `eval { require Foo; 1 } or warn "Foo missing";`

title: What is the difference between static and dynamic memory allocation?
answer: Static: allocated at compile time (stack/other sections), no need to free, fixed size, faster. Dynamic: allocated at run time on the heap, must be freed explicitly, resizable (realloc), slower.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Static** allocation: size fixed at compile time, memory in data segment/stack, freed automatically. **Dynamic** allocation: requested at run time from the heap (`malloc/new`), size can vary, must be freed explicitly.

| Aspect | Static | Dynamic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When allocated | compile/load time | run time |
| Where | data segment or stack | heap |
| Freeing | automatic | explicit (`free`/`delete`) or GC |
| Size change | fixed | resizable (`realloc`) |
| Speed | faster | slower |

### Code (C)
```c
#include <stdlib.h>
int table[256];                       /* static: fixed size */
void f(int n) {
    int *buf = malloc(n * sizeof *buf);  /* dynamic: size known only at run time */
    if (!buf) return;
    buf = realloc(buf, 2 * n * sizeof *buf);
    free(buf);
}
```

### Follow-ups
- *SV analogue?* Fixed-size arrays (static) vs dynamic arrays `new[n]`, queues, associative arrays, class objects (dynamic).

title: What are pre-processor directives?
answer: Lines starting with # are directives to the pre-processor, which modifies the source code before compilation; e.g., #define identifier value replaces identifier with value.
solution:
**Key idea:** Lines beginning with `#` are instructions to the **pre-processor**, which rewrites the source (macro substitution, file inclusion, conditional compilation) **before** compilation.

| Directive | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `#define N 16` | text/macro substitution |
| `#include "file.h"` | paste another file |
| `#ifdef/#ifndef/#if/#else/#endif` | conditional compilation |
| `#undef` | remove macro |
| `#pragma` | compiler-specific hints |

### Code (C)
```c
#ifndef FIFO_H            /* include guard */
#define FIFO_H
#define DEPTH 16
#define SQR(x) ((x) * (x))   /* parenthesize macro args! */
#ifdef DEBUG
#define LOG(msg) printf("%s\n", msg)
#else
#define LOG(msg)
#endif
#endif
```

### Follow-ups
- *SystemVerilog equivalent?* Compiler directives with a backtick: `` `define``, `` `include``, `` `ifdef``, `` `timescale``.

title: What is the function of 'using namespace std' in C++ code?
answer: A namespace groups entities under a name; std is the standard namespace containing the C++ library (string, cin, cout, vector). 'using namespace std' tells the compiler to use names from the standard library without the std:: prefix.
solution:
**Key idea:** The C++ standard library (string, vector, cout, cin…) lives in namespace `std`. `using namespace std;` imports all those names into the current scope so you can write `cout` instead of `std::cout`.

### Code
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;          // bring std:: names into scope
int main() {
    vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};   // instead of std::vector
    cout << v.size() << endl; // instead of std::cout / std::endl
}
```

| Style | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `using namespace std;` | short code | name clashes; never put it in headers |
| `using std::cout;` | selective | a little more typing |
| `std::cout` everywhere | explicit, safe | verbose |

### Follow-ups
- *Why do namespaces exist?* To group related names and avoid collisions between libraries (like SV packages).

title: What is the difference between 'int a;' and 'const int a;'?
answer: int a can be changed at different times in the program; const int a cannot be changed once initialized.
solution:
**Key idea:** `int a;` is a modifiable variable. `const int a = …;` is read-only after initialization – any later assignment is a compile error (and a const must be initialized at definition).

### Code
```cpp
int a;            // can be assigned any time
a = 5; a = 7;     // OK

const int b = 10; // must be initialized
// b = 11;        // error: assignment of read-only variable 'b'

const int *p1 = &b;   // pointer to const int: *p1 can't change, p1 can
int *const p2 = &a;   // const pointer to int: p2 can't change, *p2 can
```

| Declaration | Can change value? | Can change pointer? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int a` | yes | – |
| `const int a` | no | – |
| `const int *p` | no (*p) | yes |
| `int *const p` | yes (*p) | no |

### Follow-ups
- *SV equivalent?* `const int` / `localparam`; class property `const` can be set once in the constructor.

title: What does the keyword volatile mean in C?
answer: volatile tells the compiler the variable may change between accesses, so it must not optimize accesses (no caching in registers, no removal or reordering); mainly used for memory-mapped I/O.

title: What is a pointer? Explain the concept of a pointer
answer: A pointer is a variable whose value is the address of another variable. E.g., int a=10; int *b=&a; int c=*b; → b holds a's address (e.g., 4096), c = 10.
solution:
**Key idea:** A pointer is a variable whose **value is the address** of another variable. `&x` gives an address; `*p` dereferences (accesses the value at that address).

### Code (C)
```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int a = 10;
    int *b = &a;      /* b holds the address of a */
    int c = *b;       /* c = value stored at that address = 10 */
    printf("b=%p c=%d\n", (void *)b, c);
    *b = 20;          /* modifies a through the pointer */
    printf("a=%d\n", a);   /* 20 */
    return 0;
}
```

| Variable | Address (assumed) | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | 0x1000 | 10 (later 20) |
| b | 0x2000 | 0x1000 (= 4096) |
| c | 0x2008 | 10 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B["b @0x2000 = 0x1000"] -->|"points to"| A["a @0x1000 = 10"]
  C["c = *b = 10"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Pointer arithmetic?* `p + 1` advances by `sizeof(*p)` bytes.
- *SV analogue?* Class handles (references, no arithmetic) and `ref` arguments.

title: Explain pass by value and pass by reference in C
answer: Pass by value copies the value into a new local variable – changes don't affect the original (c stays 15). Pass by reference passes the address – changes via the pointer affect the original (c becomes 20).
solution:
**Key idea:** **Pass by value** copies the argument – changes inside the function don't affect the caller. **Pass by reference** (in C: pass a pointer to the variable) lets the function modify the caller's variable and avoids copying large data.

### Code
```c
#include <stdio.h>
void pass_by_value(int a)      { a = a + 5; }        /* modifies local copy */
void pass_by_reference(int *b) { *b = *b + 5; }      /* modifies caller's variable */

int main(void) {
    int c = 15;
    pass_by_value(c);
    printf("1. Value of C is %d\n", c);   /* 15 */
    pass_by_reference(&c);
    printf("2. Value of C is %d\n", c);   /* 20 */
    return 0;
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph ByValue["pass_by_value"]
    C1["c = 15 (caller)"] -->|"copy"| A1["a = 15 → 20 (local)"]
  end
  subgraph ByRef["pass_by_reference"]
    C2["c = 15 → 20"] 
    B2["b = &c"] -->|"*b += 5"| C2
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *Arrays in C?* Decay to pointers – effectively passed by reference.
- *SystemVerilog?* `ref` arguments (automatic tasks/functions), `const ref` for read-only large arrays; class handles are passed by value but refer to the same object.

title: What is the value and size of a NULL pointer?
answer: Value of a NULL pointer is 0; its size equals the pointer size of the machine – 4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 bytes on 64-bit.

title: What is a linked list? How many types of linked lists are there?
answer: A linked list is a group of nodes forming a sequence, each with data and a link to the next node. Types: singly (one-way) linked list and doubly (two-way) linked list (plus circular variants).

title: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search, binary search, insertion sort, merge sort and bucket sort?
answer: Linear search O(N), binary search O(log N), insertion sort O(N^2), merge sort O(N log N); bucket sort worst case O(N^2).
solution:
**Key idea:** Big-O keeps only the dominant term (5n^4 + 6n^2 + 1 → O(n^4)). Worst cases:

| Algorithm | Worst-case time | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear search | O(N) | may check every element |
| Binary search | O(log N) | halves the sorted range each step |
| Insertion sort | O(N^2) | reverse-sorted input shifts every element |
| Merge sort | O(N log N) | log N levels × N work per level |
| Bucket sort | O(N^2) | all elements in one bucket (average O(N + k)) |

Worked example – binary search for 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]:

| Step | low | high | mid | a[mid] | action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | 9 | 4 | 16 | go right |
| 2 | 5 | 9 | 7 | 56 | go left |
| 3 | 5 | 6 | 5 | 23 | found (3 steps ≤ log2 10 + 1) |

### Follow-ups
- *Best case of insertion sort?* O(N) on already-sorted input.

title: What is the space complexity of linear search, binary search, insertion sort, merge sort and bucket sort?
answer: Linear search O(1), binary search O(1), insertion sort O(N), merge sort O(N), bucket sort O(N) (N = list size).

title: Explain the difference between the & and && operators in C/C++
answer: & is bitwise AND (a=10, b=6 → 2); && is logical AND returning a boolean ((a==10) && (b==6) → true).
solution:
**Key idea:** `&` is **bitwise AND** (operates on each bit, returns an integer). `&&` is **logical AND** (treats operands as true/false, returns 0/1, and **short-circuits**).

| Expression (a=10, b=6) | Computation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a & b` | 1010 & 0110 | 0010 = **2** |
| `a && b` | true && true | **1** |
| `(a == 10) && (b == 6)` | 1 && 1 | 1 |
| `1 & 2` | 01 & 10 | 0 (false!) |
| `1 && 2` | true && true | 1 |

### Code
```c
int a = 10, b = 6;
int bw = a & b;                  /* 2 */
int lg = (a == 10) && (b == 6);  /* 1 */
if (p != NULL && p->valid) { }   /* short-circuit protects the dereference */
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `if (flags & MASK == MASK)` parses as `flags & (MASK == MASK)` – parenthesize.
- `&` does not short-circuit: both sides always evaluated.
- Same distinction exists in SystemVerilog (`&` bitwise / `&&` logical, plus unary `&` reduction).

title: How do a structure and a union differ in terms of memory allocation in C/C++?
answer: Structs allocate space for all members sequentially; unions allocate only enough for the largest member and all members share the same space (only one is used at a time).
solution:
**Key idea:** A **struct** allocates space for **all** members, laid out one after another (plus alignment padding); size ≥ sum of members. A **union** allocates space for its **largest** member only; all members overlay the same bytes, so only one is meaningful at a time.

```c
struct S { int i; char c[8]; };   /* i at offset 0, c at offset 4  → 12 bytes */
union  U { int i; char c[8]; };   /* i and c both at offset 0     →  8 bytes */
```

| Offset | struct S | union U |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–3 | i | i / c[0..3] |
| 4–7 | c[0..3] | c[4..7] |
| 8–11 | c[4..7] | – |
| sizeof | 12 | 8 |

### Explanation
- Unions are used for type punning, variant records, and saving memory; a tag field usually says which member is valid.
- Alignment matters: `struct { char a; int b; }` is 8 bytes, not 5 (3 bytes padding).

### Follow-ups
- *SV equivalents?* `struct packed` / `union packed` – a packed union lets one bit-vector be viewed as different formats (e.g., a bus word as header or payload).

title: How much memory is allocated for struct ID { int IntID; char CharID[8]; }?
answer: 12 bytes (4 for int + 8 for the char array).
solution:
**Key idea:** A struct holds all members: 4 (int) + 8 (char[8]) = **12 bytes** (no padding needed: char array has 1-byte alignment and 12 is a multiple of int's 4-byte alignment).

| Member | Offset | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IntID | 0 | 4 |
| CharID[8] | 4 | 8 |
| **Total** | | **12** |

```c
#include <stdio.h>
struct ID { int IntID; char CharID[8]; };
int main(void) { printf("%zu\n", sizeof(struct ID)); return 0; }   /* 12 */
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Reorder to `{ char c; int i; }` and padding appears; with `double` members alignment can grow to 8.
- Assumes 4-byte int (typical).

title: How much memory is allocated for union ID { int IntID; char CharID[8]; }?
answer: 8 bytes – memory is allocated only for the largest member (char[8]).

title: What is a stack and how does it differ from a FIFO?
answer: A stack is LIFO (last in first out); a FIFO is first in first out.
solution:
**Key idea:** Both are ordered buffers. A **stack** is **LIFO** – the last element pushed is the first popped (one access end). A **FIFO/queue** is **first in, first out** – elements leave in arrival order (write at tail, read at head).

| Push order | Stack pop order | FIFO pop order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A, B, C | C, B, A | A, B, C |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Stack
    IN1["push/pop"] <--> TOP["C (top)"] --- B1["B"] --- A1["A"]
  end
  subgraph FIFO
    W["write"] --> T["C"] --> M["B"] --> H["A"] --> R["read"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Stack | FIFO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Order | LIFO | FIFO |
| Pointers | 1 (top) | 2 (read, write) |
| Uses | call stack, expression evaluation, undo | buffering between producer/consumer, clock-domain crossing |

### Follow-ups
- *Hardware FIFO full/empty?* Compare read/write pointers with an extra wrap bit.

title: What is a kernel?
answer: A kernel is a program that manages I/O requests from software and translates them into CPU/hardware instructions – the core of the OS.
solution:
**Key idea:** The kernel is the core of an operating system: it manages CPU scheduling, memory, devices and system calls, translating software I/O requests into operations on the hardware.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  U["User applications"] --> SH["Shell / libraries"]
  SH -->|"system calls"| K["Kernel: scheduler, memory manager, file systems, drivers"]
  K --> HW["Hardware: CPU, memory, devices"]
```

| Kernel responsibility | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Process management | scheduling, context switches |
| Memory management | virtual memory, paging |
| Device drivers | disk, network, USB |
| File systems | ext4, NFS |
| System calls | `open`, `read`, `fork` |

### Follow-ups
- *Monolithic vs microkernel?* Linux is monolithic (drivers in kernel space); microkernels move services to user space.

title: What is UNIX and how is it different from Linux?
answer: UNIX is a multi-user, multi-tasking OS made of kernel, shell and programs. Linux is a free, open-source UNIX-like OS (e.g., Ubuntu) while UNIX versions are vendor-licensed (e.g., Solaris).
solution:
**Key idea:** UNIX is a family of multi-user, multitasking operating systems (originally AT&T), made of a kernel, a shell and programs; commercial variants are vendor licensed (Solaris, AIX, HP-UX). Linux is a free, open-source, UNIX-like kernel (plus GNU tools = distributions like Ubuntu, RHEL).

| Aspect | UNIX | Linux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin | AT&T Bell Labs (1969) | Linus Torvalds (1991) |
| License | proprietary per vendor (BSDs open) | GPL, free |
| Development | vendors | open-source community |
| Examples | Solaris, AIX, HP-UX, macOS (certified) | Ubuntu, RHEL/CentOS, Debian |
| Hardware | vendor-specific | almost anything |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  USER["user"] --> SHELL["shell (bash, csh, tcsh)"] --> KERNEL["kernel"] --> HW["hardware"]
  PROGS["programs/utilities (ls, grep, make)"] --> KERNEL
```

### Follow-ups
- *Why does DV care?* EDA tools run on Linux farms; scripting (shell, Perl/Python), LSF/grid, and file handling are daily work.

title: What does Perl stand for?
answer: Practical Extraction and Reporting Language.

title: Perl is an interpreted language. What does this mean?
answer: Perl translates source statement by statement into intermediate code interpreted by another program rather than producing a binary; it stops at the first error.
solution:
**Key idea:** Perl source is not compiled to a native binary ahead of time. The `perl` interpreter parses the script into an internal representation (op-tree/intermediate code) and executes it at run time; you run the source directly.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SRC["script.pl"] --> P["perl interpreter: parse → op-tree"] --> RUN["execute ops at run time"]
```

| Aspect | Interpreted (Perl) | Compiled (C) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run | `perl script.pl` | `gcc` then `./a.out` |
| Edit-run cycle | fast | slower |
| Execution speed | slower | faster |
| Portability | wherever perl exists | recompile per platform |
| Errors | syntax errors found when the whole file is parsed; runtime errors when reached | at compile time |

### Follow-ups
- *Detail:* Perl actually compiles the whole file before running (so `use` executes at compile time) – which is why syntax errors anywhere stop the script before it starts.

title: What are the different data types in Perl?
answer: Scalars ($: number, string, or reference), arrays (@: ordered lists of scalars, index from 0), hashes (%: unordered key/value pairs).
solution:
**Key idea:** Three core types identified by sigils: **scalars** `$` (number, string or reference), **arrays** `@` (ordered list, index from 0), **hashes** `%` (unordered key → value pairs).

### Code
```perl
use strict; use warnings;
my $name  = "fifo_test";              # scalar
my @seeds = (11, 42, 7);              # array
my %res   = (fifo_test => "PASS", axi_test => "FAIL");   # hash

print "$name first seed: $seeds[0]\n";       # element of array is a scalar: $
print "count: ", scalar(@seeds), "\n";       # 3
for my $t (sort keys %res) { print "$t => $res{$t}\n"; }
my $aref = \@seeds;                          # reference (scalar)
print "last: $$aref[-1] / $aref->[-1]\n";
```

| Type | Sigil | Element access | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scalar | `$` | – | `$x = 5` |
| Array | `@` | `$a[i]` | `@a = (1,2)` |
| Hash | `%` | `$h{key}` | `%h = (k => v)` |

### Follow-ups
- *Nested data?* Use references: `$h{list} = [1,2,3]`, access `@{$h{list}}`.

title: What is a cron job? When would you use one?
answer: A cron job is time-based job scheduling that runs jobs automatically at specified times/intervals, e.g., a script computing per-user disk usage run periodically.
solution:
**Key idea:** cron is the UNIX/Linux time-based scheduler. A cron job is a command/script that runs automatically at specified times/intervals, configured in a crontab.

```text
# ┌ min (0-59) ┌ hour (0-23) ┌ day-of-month ┌ month ┌ day-of-week (0=Sun)
# │            │             │              │       │
  0            2             *              *       *    /proj/scripts/nightly_regress.sh >> /proj/logs/nightly.log 2>&1
  */30         *             *              *       1-5  /proj/scripts/disk_usage.pl
```

| Field | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0 2 * * *` | nightly | 02:00 every day |
| `*/30 * * * 1-5` | every 30 min | weekdays |
| `0 9 * * 1` | weekly | Monday 09:00 |

### Explanation
- Edit with `crontab -e`, list with `crontab -l`.
- DV uses: nightly regressions, coverage merges, disk-usage reports, cleanup of old sim directories.

### Follow-ups
- *Pitfall?* cron runs with a minimal environment – source your setup (PATH, licenses) inside the script.

title: What is the use of the rsync command in UNIX/Linux?
answer: rsync (remote sync) copies/synchronizes files across disks, networks and machines, transferring only changed portions with compression; used for backups and mirroring.
solution:
**Key idea:** `rsync` (remote sync) copies/synchronizes files and directories locally or across machines, transferring **only the changed parts** (delta algorithm), optionally compressed – ideal for backups and mirroring.

### Code
```bash
# mirror a regression result tree to a backup server, preserving attributes
rsync -avz --delete /proj/regress/ backup:/archive/regress/
# dry run first to see what would change
rsync -avzn --exclude '*.vpd' /proj/regress/ backup:/archive/regress/
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-a` | archive: recursive, preserve perms/times/links |
| `-v` | verbose |
| `-z` | compress during transfer |
| `-n` | dry run |
| `--delete` | delete files at destination that no longer exist at source |
| `--exclude` | skip patterns |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Trailing slash matters: `src/` copies contents, `src` copies the directory itself.

### Follow-ups
- *rsync vs scp?* scp copies everything every time; rsync only differences and can resume.

title: True or false: variable names in C can contain alphanumeric characters as well as special characters
answer: False – C variable names may contain only letters, digits and underscore (not starting with a digit).
solution:
**Key idea:** **False.** C identifiers may contain only letters, digits and the underscore `_`; they cannot start with a digit and cannot be keywords. Special characters like `$`, `@`, `-`, `#` are not allowed (some compilers accept `$` as an extension).

| Identifier | Valid? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `count_1` | yes | letters, digit, underscore |
| `_tmp` | yes (reserved-ish at file scope) | leading underscore allowed |
| `1st_val` | no | starts with a digit |
| `data-out` | no | `-` is an operator |
| `rate$` | no (standard C) | `$` not portable |
| `int` | no | keyword |

### Follow-ups
- *SystemVerilog?* Simple identifiers may contain letters, digits, `_` and `$` (not first); escaped identifiers `\bus[0] ` allow any printable chars.

title: What is the use of the '\0' character in C/C++?
answer: It is the terminating null character marking the end of a string.
solution:
**Key idea:** `'\0'` (NUL, value 0) is the **string terminator**: C strings are char arrays that end at the first `'\0'`. All `str*` functions rely on it.

```c
char s[] = "DV";        /* stored as 'D' 'V' '\0' → sizeof(s) == 3, strlen(s) == 2 */
```

| Index | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| s[i] | 'D' (0x44) | 'V' (0x56) | '\0' (0x00) |

### Code
```c
size_t my_strlen(const char *s) {
    size_t n = 0;
    while (s[n] != '\0') n++;   /* stop at the terminator */
    return n;
}
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Forgetting space for `'\0'` (e.g., `char buf[2] = "DV";` in C has no terminator) → buffer overruns.
- `strncpy` doesn't always terminate.

title: What are binary trees?
answer: Binary trees extend linked lists: each node has a left and a right pointer, each of which can branch to further nodes.

title: How can you generate random numbers in C?
answer: Use the rand() function from <stdlib.h> (seeded with srand()).

title: What are special characters, quantifiers and anchors in regular expressions?
answer: Special characters are meta-characters with special meaning (\, ^, $, (), [], |). Quantifiers specify how often to match (*, +, ?, {}). Anchors specify where to match (^, $, <, >).
solution:
**Key idea:** **Special (meta) characters** have syntactic meaning; **quantifiers** say *how many times* the preceding item matches; **anchors** say *where* the match must occur (they match positions, not characters).

| Category | Tokens | Example | Matches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Special chars | `\ . ^ $ ( ) [ ] { } \| * + ?` | `a\.b` | literal "a.b" |
| Character class | `[abc]`, `[^0-9]`, `\d \w \s` | `[0-9a-f]+` | hex digits |
| Quantifiers | `*` (0+), `+` (1+), `?` (0/1), `{n}`, `{n,m}` | `x{2,3}` | xx, xxx |
| Anchors | `^` (line start), `$` (line end), `\b` (word boundary), `\<` `\>` (word start/end in grep/vim) | `^ERROR` | ERROR only at line start |

### Code (Perl)
```perl
while (my $line = <STDIN>) {
    # anchor ^, special (), quantifiers + and ?
    if ($line =~ /^UVM_ERROR\s+(\S+)\((\d+)\)\s*@\s*(\d+)/) {
        print "file=$1 line=$2 time=$3\n";
    }
}
```

### Follow-ups
- *Escape a metacharacter?* Prefix with backslash: `\$`, `\(`.

title: What is the difference between a class and an object?
answer: A class is a set of attributes and behavior grouped together; an object is an instance of the class representing a real entity (e.g., animal class; dog, cat objects).
solution:
**Key idea:** A **class** is a blueprint/type defining data members (attributes) and methods (behavior). An **object** is a concrete **instance** of the class created at run time with its own copy of the data.

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class animal;
  string name;
  int    legs;
  function new(string name, int legs); this.name = name; this.legs = legs; endfunction
  function void speak(); $display("%s has %0d legs", name, legs); endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    animal dog = new("dog", 4);   // object 1
    animal bird = new("bird", 2); // object 2
    dog.speak(); bird.speak();
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
classDiagram
  class animal {
    string name
    int legs
    new(name, legs)
    speak()
  }
```

| | Class | Object |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What | type definition | instance in memory |
| When | compile time | created at run time (`new`) |
| How many | one definition | many instances |

### Follow-ups
- *SV handle vs object?* `animal a;` is just a null handle; the object exists only after `a = new(...)`.

title: What is the difference between a class and a struct in C++?
answer: In C++ the only real difference is default access: class members are private by default, struct members public by default.
solution:
**Key idea:** In C++ they are almost identical (both can have members, methods, constructors, inheritance). The only language difference: **members and base classes are private by default in a class, public by default in a struct**.

```cpp
struct PointS { int x, y; };          // x, y public by default
class  PointC { int x, y; };          // x, y private by default

int main() {
    PointS s; s.x = 1;                // OK
    PointC c; // c.x = 1;             // error: 'int PointC::x' is private
}
```

| Aspect | struct | class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default member access | public | private |
| Default inheritance | public | private |
| Convention | plain data (POD) | encapsulated types with invariants |

### Follow-ups
- *Can a struct have virtual functions?* Yes in C++.

title: What is the difference between a class and a struct in SystemVerilog?
answer: In SV a struct is an integral type allocated when declared; a class is a dynamic type – declaring it gives a null handle and memory is allocated only when an object is created.
solution:
**Key idea:** A SV **struct** is an integral/value type – memory is allocated when it is declared, assignment copies the data, no methods. A **class** is a dynamic reference type – declaring it gives a **null handle**; memory is allocated only by `new()`; it supports methods, inheritance, polymorphism, randomization with `rand`.

### Code
```systemverilog
typedef struct packed { logic [7:0] addr; logic [31:0] data; } pkt_s;

class pkt_c;
  rand bit [7:0]  addr;
  rand bit [31:0] data;
  function void print(); $display("addr=%h data=%h", addr, data); endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  pkt_s s1, s2;      // storage exists already
  pkt_c c1, c2;      // null handles
  initial begin
    s1.addr = 8'h10; s2 = s1; s2.addr = 8'h20;   // s1.addr still 10 (copy)
    c1 = new(); c1.addr = 8'h10;
    c2 = c1;   c2.addr = 8'h20;                  // c1.addr is now 20 (same object)
  end
endmodule
```

| Aspect | struct | class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | value (integral if packed) | reference (handle) |
| Allocation | at declaration | at `new()` |
| Assignment | copies data | copies handle |
| Methods / inheritance | no | yes |
| Synthesizable | yes (packed) | no |

### Follow-ups
- *Can structs contain rand fields?* Yes, inside a class: `rand pkt_s s;`.

title: What are public, private and protected members of a class?
answer: Private members are accessible only within the class (not derived classes); public members are accessible inside and outside the class and in derived classes; protected members are accessible within the class and derived classes but not outside.
solution:
**Key idea:** Access qualifiers control visibility. **Public**: accessible everywhere. **Private** (`local` in SV): only inside the class itself, not derived classes. **Protected**: inside the class **and derived classes**, not outside.

| Accessed from | public | protected | private / `local` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Same class | yes | yes | yes |
| Derived class | yes | yes | **no** |
| Outside code | yes | **no** | **no** |

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class base;
  int            pub_cnt;       // public (default in SV)
  protected int  prot_cnt;
  local int      priv_cnt;      // 'local' = private
endclass

class derived extends base;
  function void f();
    pub_cnt++;      // OK
    prot_cnt++;     // OK - protected visible in derived
    // priv_cnt++;  // compile error - local
  endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    derived d = new();
    d.pub_cnt = 1;     // OK
    // d.prot_cnt = 1; // error - not visible outside
  end
endmodule
```

### Follow-ups
- *Default access in SV vs C++?* SV class members are public by default; C++ class members are private.

title: What is polymorphism?
answer: Polymorphism: ability of an entity to refer to objects of various classes at run time; achieved via inheritance and virtual functions in SV (and overloading in C++); the method of the actual object type is called.
solution:
**Key idea:** Polymorphism ("many forms") lets one handle/interface refer to objects of different classes and invoke the **right method for the actual object type at run time**. In SystemVerilog this comes from inheritance + `virtual` methods; C++ adds compile-time polymorphism (function/operator overloading, templates).

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class shape;
  virtual function real area(); return 0; endfunction
endclass
class square extends shape;
  real s; function new(real s); this.s = s; endfunction
  virtual function real area(); return s*s; endfunction
endclass
class circle extends shape;
  real r; function new(real r); this.r = r; endfunction
  virtual function real area(); return 3.14159*r*r; endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    shape list[$];
    square sq = new(2.0); circle ci = new(1.0);
    list.push_back(sq); list.push_back(ci);
    foreach (list[i]) $display("area=%f", list[i].area());  // 4.0, 3.14 - dynamic dispatch
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
classDiagram
  shape <|-- square
  shape <|-- circle
  class shape { +area() virtual }
  class square { +area() }
  class circle { +area() }
```

### Follow-ups
- *UVM use?* Factory overrides: a test replaces `base_driver` with `err_driver`; the env still calls through base handles.
- *What if `area` weren't virtual?* The base-class version would be called (static binding on handle type).

title: What are method overriding and method overloading, and how do they differ?
answer: Overloading: same function name defined multiple times with different parameters (e.g., add(int,int), add(int,int,int), add(float,float)). Overriding: derived class redefines a base-class virtual method. SV supports only overriding.

title: What is operator overloading?
answer: Operator overloading is redefining built-in operators for user-defined types (polymorphism); supported in C++, not SV. E.g., overload + to add data members of two Testclass objects.

title: What is a constructor method?
answer: A constructor is a special member function invoked automatically when an object is created; in C++ it has the class name, in SV it is new().

title: What is a destructor?
answer: A destructor is invoked automatically when an object goes out of scope; C++: class name with ~ prefix. SV has no destructor (automatic garbage collection).

title: What is the difference between composition and inheritance in OOP?
answer: Composition is a 'has-a' relationship (a class instantiates another class's object, e.g., ford has an engine); inheritance is an 'is-a' relationship (ford derives from car).
solution:
**Key idea:** **Inheritance** = "is-a" (a `ford` **is a** `car`; it derives from the base class). **Composition** = "has-a" (a `ford` **has an** `engine` object as a member).

```mermaid
classDiagram
  car <|-- ford : is-a (inheritance)
  ford *-- engine : has-a (composition)
  class car { +drive() }
  class ford { +engine e }
  class engine { +start() }
```

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class engine; function void start(); $display("vroom"); endfunction endclass
class car;    virtual function void drive(); $display("driving"); endfunction endclass

class ford extends car;        // is-a
  engine e;                    // has-a
  function new(); e = new(); endfunction
  virtual function void drive(); e.start(); super.drive(); endfunction
endclass
```

| Aspect | Inheritance | Composition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relation | is-a | has-a |
| Coupling | tight (depends on base internals) | loose |
| Reuse | extends behavior | delegates to contained object |
| UVM example | `my_driver extends uvm_driver` | env **has** agents, agent **has** driver/monitor |

### Follow-ups
- *Guideline?* "Favor composition over inheritance" unless there's a true is-a relation.

title: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy in object-oriented programming?
answer: Shallow copy: new object with copied values, but references to other objects copy only the handle. Deep copy: referenced objects' values are also copied, not just handles.
solution:
**Key idea:** **Shallow copy** creates a new object and copies the member values; for members that are handles to other objects, **only the handle is copied** – both copies share the sub-object. **Deep copy** also recursively copies the referenced objects, so the copies are fully independent.

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class A; int a, b; endclass

class B;
  int x;
  A   objA;
  function new(); objA = new(); endfunction
  function B deep_copy();
    deep_copy = new();          // new B with its own new A
    deep_copy.x = x;
    deep_copy.objA.a = objA.a;  // copy contents, not the handle
    deep_copy.objA.b = objA.b;
  endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    B b1 = new(), b2, b3;
    b1.objA.a = 5;
    b2 = new b1;            // SHALLOW: b2.objA == b1.objA (same object)
    b3 = b1.deep_copy();    // DEEP: separate A
    b1.objA.a = 9;
    $display("%0d %0d", b2.objA.a, b3.objA.a);   // 9 5
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Shallow
    B1["b1"] --> A1["A (a=9)"]
    B2["b2"] --> A1
  end
  subgraph Deep
    B1d["b1"] --> A1d["A (a=9)"]
    B3["b3"] --> A3["A copy (a=5)"]
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *In UVM?* Implement `do_copy()` to deep-copy nested objects; `clone()` = create + copy.

title: What are virtual functions in C++ or other OOP languages?
answer: A virtual function is declared in a base class with the virtual keyword and can be redefined in a derived class (method overriding); calls dispatch based on the object's actual type.

title: What is meant by multiple inheritance?
answer: Multiple inheritance lets a class inherit from more than one parent class; C++ supports it, SystemVerilog does not (single inheritance only).
solution:
**Key idea:** Multiple inheritance lets a class derive from **more than one parent class**, inheriting members of all. C++ supports it; SystemVerilog classes support only **single** inheritance (SV-2012 adds `interface class` + `implements` for multiple *interfaces*).

```mermaid
classDiagram
  Printer <|-- MultiFunction
  Scanner <|-- MultiFunction
  class Printer { +print() }
  class Scanner { +scan() }
```

### Code
```cpp
class Printer { public: void print() {} };
class Scanner { public: void scan()  {} };
class MultiFunction : public Printer, public Scanner {};   // C++ multiple inheritance
```
```systemverilog
interface class printable; pure virtual function void print(); endclass
interface class scannable; pure virtual function void scan();  endclass
class multi_function implements printable, scannable;       // SV-2012
  virtual function void print(); endfunction
  virtual function void scan();  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Diamond problem: two parents share a grandparent → ambiguity/duplicate base; C++ uses `virtual` inheritance to fix.

### Follow-ups
- *Single inheritance?* Exactly one parent (SV `extends`).

title: What is an abstract class?
answer: An abstract class has one or more abstract (declared, unimplemented) methods and cannot be instantiated; subclasses implement them. In SV, use 'virtual class' (e.g., virtual class BaseShape with get_num_edges implemented in Rectangle).

title: What are static methods inside a class?
answer: Static methods are declared with the static keyword and can be used without creating an object; only one copy is shared by all objects.
solution:
**Key idea:** A static method belongs to the **class**, not to an object: callable without creating an instance (`ClassName::method()`), only one copy shared by all objects, and it can access only static members (no `this`).

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class packet;
  static int count;          // shared by all packets
  int id;
  function new(); id = count++; endfunction
  static function int get_count();   // no 'this' available
    return count;
  endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    packet p1 = new(), p2 = new();
    $display("%0d", packet::get_count());   // 2 - called on the class
  end
endmodule
```

| Aspect | Static method | Instance method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs object | no | yes |
| Access to non-static members | no | yes |
| `this` | not available | available |
| Typical use | factories, singletons, counters, utilities | object behavior |

### Follow-ups
- *UVM:* `type_id::create()`, `uvm_config_db#(T)::set/get`, `uvm_root::get()` are static methods.
- *Static method vs method with static lifetime?* `static function` (class-level) differs from `function static` (static variables inside).

title: What is the 'this' pointer with reference to a class?
answer: 'this' is a special pointer/handle referencing the current object of a class inside the class scope.
solution:
**Key idea:** `this` is an implicit handle/pointer to the **current object** inside its non-static methods – used to disambiguate members from same-named arguments, or to pass the object itself to another function.

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class packet;
  bit [7:0] addr;
  function new(bit [7:0] addr);
    this.addr = addr;          // member = argument
  endfunction
  function void register(ref packet q[$]);
    q.push_back(this);         // pass self
  endfunction
endclass
```
```cpp
class Packet { int addr; public: Packet(int addr) { this->addr = addr; } };  // C++: pointer, so ->
```

| Language | Form |
| --- | --- |
| C++ | pointer: `this->x`, `*this` |
| SystemVerilog | handle: `this.x` |
| Static methods | `this` not allowed |

### Follow-ups
- *UVM:* `super.new(name, parent)` and passing `this` as parent when creating child components: `drv = my_driver::type_id::create("drv", this);`

title: What is type conversion and type casting in programming languages?
answer: Both change one data type to another: type conversion is implicit (compiler does it, e.g., assigning float to int), type casting is explicit by the programmer.
solution:
**Key idea:** Both change a value from one type to another. **Type conversion** is **implicit** (done automatically by the compiler, e.g., float assigned to int). **Type casting** is **explicit** (the programmer requests it).

### Code
```c
float f = 3.75;
int   i = f;            /* implicit conversion: truncates to 3 */
int   j = (int)f;       /* explicit cast: 3 */
double d = (double)7 / 2;   /* cast before divide → 3.5 instead of 3 */
```
```systemverilog
real r = 3.75;
int  i = r;                 // implicit: rounds to 4 in SV (real→int rounds!)
int  j = int'(r);           // static cast: 4
int  k = $rtoi(r);          // truncate: 3
typedef enum {RED, GREEN} color_e;
color_e c;
initial if (!$cast(c, 1)) $error("bad enum");   // dynamic cast with check
```

| Kind | Who | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Implicit conversion | compiler | `int i = f;` |
| Static cast | programmer, compile time | `(int)f`, `int'(r)` |
| Dynamic cast | programmer, checked at run time | `$cast(child_h, base_h)` |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- C truncates float→int; SystemVerilog rounds real→int on assignment.
- `$cast` for class handles fails if the object isn't actually of the target type.

title: What is the general method for calculating FIFO depth, and why can a FIFO only absorb bursty (not continuous) traffic?
answer: FIFO depth = number of data items left unread at the end of the write burst. FIFO only works for bursts; continuous faster writes need infinite depth.
solution:
**Key idea:** The FIFO must hold every item that is written but not yet read during the burst: depth = items written in the burst window - items the reader can drain in that same window. If writes are faster than reads forever, no finite depth works.

| Step | What you compute |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Effective write period T_w = (idle_w + 1) / f_A (time per written item) |
| 2 | Burst write time T_burst = B x T_w |
| 3 | Effective read period T_r = (idle_r + 1) / f_B |
| 4 | Items read during the burst N_r = floor(T_burst / T_r) |
| 5 | Depth = B - N_r (then add sync margin, round up to 2^n) |

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01.......0.."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.1010101010"}, {"name": "level", "wave": "=.==========", "data": ["0", "1", "1", "2", "2", "3", "3", "4", "4", "3", "3"]}], "head": {"text": "write burst fills faster than reads drain; level peaks at the end of the burst"}}
```

### Explanation
- A FIFO is a rate-matching buffer: it is needed when the producer is temporarily faster than the consumer.
- The peak occupancy happens at the moment the last item of the burst is written; that peak is the minimum depth.
- If the average write rate exceeds the average read rate over an unbounded time, occupancy grows without bound, so you need flow control (back-pressure), not a deeper FIFO.
- Ask the interviewer for: f_A, f_B, burst length, idle cycles (or enable duty cycles), and the gap between bursts (it must be long enough to drain).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Use the reader's rate *during the burst window*, not over the whole period.
- Round items read **down** (a partially completed read does not free an entry).
- Depth also needs margin for pointer-synchronizer latency in an async FIFO.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.
- *What is the closed-form?* Depth = B - B x (T_w / T_r) = B x (1 - rate_r / rate_w), rounded up.

source.name: FIFO Depth Calculation Made Easy (Putta Satish)

title: FIFO depth: writer at 80 MHz, reader at 50 MHz, burst of 120 items, no idle cycles on either side. What is the minimum depth?
prompt: f_A (write) = 80 MHz, f_B (read) = 50 MHz, burst length = 120, no idle cycles on write or read.
answer: Write 1 item = 12.5 ns, burst = 1500 ns. Read 1 item = 20 ns -> 75 read in 1500 ns. Depth = 120 - 75 = 45.
solution:
**Key idea:** Write time for the burst = 120 x 12.5 ns = 1500 ns; in 1500 ns the reader drains 1500/20 = 75 items, so 120 - 75 = **45** entries must be buffered.

| Time (ns) | Written (every 12.5 ns) | Read (every 20 ns) | Occupancy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 100 | 8 | 5 | 3 |
| 500 | 40 | 25 | 15 |
| 1000 | 80 | 50 | 30 |
| 1500 (burst ends) | 120 | 75 | **45 (peak)** |
| 2400 | 120 | 120 | 0 (drained) |

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A 80MHz", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01.........."}, {"name": "clk_B 50MHz", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.1........."}, {"name": "level", "wave": "=.=.=.=.=.=.", "data": ["0", "1", "2", "3", "4", "5"]}], "head": {"text": "back-to-back writes and reads; level grows by 3 every 100 ns (8 writes vs 5 reads)"}}
```

### Explanation
- T_w = 1/80 MHz = 12.5 ns, T_r = 1/50 MHz = 20 ns.
- Burst time = 120 x 12.5 = 1500 ns.
- Reads in 1500 ns = 1500 / 20 = 75.
- Depth = 120 - 75 = **45**.
- Closed form: 120 x (1 - 50/80) = 120 x 0.375 = 45.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Do not use the reader's time to read 120 items (2400 ns); the peak occurs at 1500 ns when the writer stops.
- A practical async FIFO would be 64 deep (power of two plus sync margin).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

title: FIFO depth: f_A = 80 MHz > f_B = 50 MHz, burst of 120, with "one clock cycle delay between two successive reads and writes". How does this change the answer?
prompt: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, one clock cycle delay between two successive reads and between two successive writes.
answer: Same as the no-idle case: one cycle between successive transfers = back-to-back. Depth = 45.
solution:
**Key idea:** It does not change anything: "one clock between successive transfers" just means one transfer per clock (back-to-back), identical to the no-idle case, so depth = **45**.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p........"}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01......."}, {"name": "wdata", "wave": "x=======x", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2", "D3", "D4", "D5", "D6"]}], "head": {"text": "successive writes are one clock apart = zero idle cycles"}}
```

| Wording | Items per clock | Equivalent idle cycles |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no idle cycles | 1 | 0 |
| one clock delay between successive writes | 1 | 0 |
| one idle cycle between writes | 1/2 | 1 |

### Explanation
- The time between the start of transfer *n* and transfer *n+1* is one clock period, i.e. continuous streaming.
- So T_w = 12.5 ns, T_r = 20 ns, burst = 1500 ns, reads = 75, depth = 120 - 75 = **45**.
- The question is a wording trap: distinguish "delay of one cycle between transfers" (period = 1 clk) from "one idle cycle between transfers" (period = 2 clk).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Clarify the spec with the interviewer: say out loud which interpretation you use and show both numbers if unsure (45 vs 83 for 1 idle write / 3 idle read).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

title: FIFO depth: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst of 120, 1 idle cycle between writes and 3 idle cycles between reads. Minimum depth?
prompt: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, idle cycles between writes = 1, idle cycles between reads = 3.
answer: T_w = 25 ns, burst = 3000 ns; T_r = 80 ns -> 37 reads. Depth = 120 - 37 = 83.
solution:
**Key idea:** One write every 2 clk_A cycles (25 ns) and one read every 4 clk_B cycles (80 ns). Burst lasts 120 x 25 = 3000 ns, reader completes floor(3000/80) = 37 reads, so depth = 120 - 37 = **83**.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "010101010101"}, {"name": "clk_B", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "010001000100"}], "head": {"text": "write: 1 of every 2 clk_A cycles; read: 1 of every 4 clk_B cycles"}}
```

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| T_w = 2 / 80 MHz | 25 ns |
| Burst time = 120 x 25 | 3000 ns |
| T_r = 4 / 50 MHz | 80 ns |
| Reads in 3000 ns = 3000/80 = 37.5 | 37 complete reads |
| Depth = 120 - 37 | **83** |

### Explanation
- Idle cycles stretch the effective period: (idle + 1) clock periods per item.
- Write rate = 40 Mitems/s, read rate = 12.5 Mitems/s; the gap is much larger than in the no-idle case.
- 37.5 is rounded **down** to 37 because half a read does not free an entry; that gives the safe (larger) depth 83.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Rounding 37.5 up to 38 would under-size the FIFO by one entry (82).
- Use 128 for a power-of-two async FIFO.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

title: FIFO depth: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst of 120, wr_en duty cycle 50% and rd_en duty cycle 25%. Minimum depth?
prompt: f_A = 80 MHz, f_B = 50 MHz, burst = 120, duty cycle of wr_en = 50%, duty cycle of rd_en = 25%.
answer: Equivalent to 1 idle write cycle and 3 idle read cycles -> depth 83. (Source typo: second duty cycle refers to rd_en.)
solution:
**Key idea:** A 50% wr_en duty cycle means one write every 2 clk_A cycles and a 25% rd_en duty cycle means one read every 4 clk_B cycles: the same as the 1-idle/3-idle case, so depth = **83**.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr_en (50%)", "wave": "101010101010"}, {"name": "clk_B", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "rd_en (25%)", "wave": "100010001000"}], "head": {"text": "duty cycle of an enable = fraction of clocks carrying a transfer"}}
```

| Spec form | Write period | Read period |
| --- | --- | --- |
| idle cycles 1 / 3 | 2 clk_A = 25 ns | 4 clk_B = 80 ns |
| duty cycle 50% / 25% | 2 clk_A = 25 ns | 4 clk_B = 80 ns |

### Explanation
- Effective rate = f x duty: writes 80 x 0.5 = 40 M/s, reads 50 x 0.25 = 12.5 M/s.
- Burst time = 120 / 40 M = 3000 ns; reads in that time = 3000 x 12.5 M = 37.5 -> 37.
- Depth = 120 - 37 = **83**.
- (The source lists the second duty cycle as wr_enb again; it is clearly rd_en.)

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Duty cycle only gives the *average* rate. If the 50% enable could be high for many consecutive cycles (e.g. high for 60 then low for 60), the worst case is a back-to-back burst: then use f_A directly and depth grows. Ask how the enable is distributed.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

title: FIFO depth: writer clock slower than reader clock (f_A < f_B), no idle cycles on either side. What depth is needed?
prompt: f_A < f_B, no idle cycles in write or read (one transfer per clock on each side).
answer: Reader is faster -> no data accumulates; FIFO depth of 1 is sufficient (plus sync latency margin in practice).
solution:
**Key idea:** The reader drains faster than the writer fills, so occupancy never builds up: logically a **depth of 1** (a single holding register) is enough; in an async FIFO you still need a few entries to cover pointer-synchronization latency.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A (slow)", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "0101010."}, {"name": "clk_B (fast)", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.101010"}, {"name": "level", "wave": "0101010."}], "head": {"text": "each item is read before the next one arrives: level stays at <= 1"}}
```

| Time | Event | Occupancy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| t0 | write D0 | 1 |
| t0 + T_B | read D0 | 0 |
| t0 + T_A | write D1 | 1 |
| ... | ... | <= 1 |

### Explanation
- Rate_write = f_A < Rate_read = f_B, so B - N_r <= 0 for any burst length.
- A single entry handles the clock-domain crossing.
- Real design: an async FIFO's empty flag is updated only after the write pointer passes a 2-FF synchronizer, so the reader cannot pop immediately. Depth must cover that round-trip latency (typically 4-8 entries) to keep the writer from stalling.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If the writer is back-pressured by a slow full-flag update, throughput drops even though average rates match; size for latency, not just rate.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

| T_w = 2 / 30 MHz | 66.67 ns (15 M items/s) |
| Burst time = 120 x 66.67 ns | 8000 ns |
| T_r = 4 / 50 MHz | 80 ns (12.5 M items/s) |

- Lesson: "f_A < f_B" alone does not mean depth 1; always compare *effective* rates.

title: FIFO depth: f_A = f_B (e.g. both 30 MHz), burst of 120, no idle cycles. Is a FIFO needed, and how deep?
prompt: f_A = f_B = 30 MHz, burst = 120, no idle cycles.
answer: No FIFO if clocks have no phase difference; depth 1 if there is a phase difference.
solution:
**Key idea:** Equal rates mean nothing accumulates. If the clocks are the same clock (no phase difference) no FIFO is needed; if they are asynchronous clocks of the same nominal frequency, a depth of **1** logically suffices (practically a small async FIFO to absorb sync latency and ppm drift).

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "01......"}, {"name": "wdata", "wave": "x=======", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2", "D3", "D4", "D5", "D6"]}, {"name": "clk_B", "wave": "p......."}, {"name": "rd_en", "wave": "0.1....."}, {"name": "rdata", "wave": "x.======", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2", "D3", "D4", "D5"]}], "head": {"text": "one in, one out per cycle: occupancy stays constant"}}
```

| Clock relationship | Needed buffering |
| --- | --- |
| same clock / same phase | none (direct register path) |
| same frequency, unknown phase | 1 entry logically; async FIFO in practice |
| same nominal frequency, ppm offset (plesiochronous) | elastic buffer sized for drift over the burst |

### Explanation
- Write rate = read rate, so B - N_r = 0 except for the initial offset.
- With a phase difference you still must cross clock domains safely; a single-entry handshake or a small async FIFO does that.
- For long streams between plesiochronous clocks (e.g. +/-100 ppm), drift accumulates: 120 items x 200 ppm is far below 1, but for packets of millions of items you need an elastic buffer with skip symbols.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An async FIFO's empty flag lags the write by ~2-3 read clocks, so the reader starts late; to stream at full rate the FIFO must cover that latency (~4 entries).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

title: FIFO depth: writer delivers 80 data per 100 clocks (any 20 cycles idle, randomly placed), reader consumes 8 data per 10 clocks, same clock, burst size 160. Minimum depth?
prompt: Writing data = 80 DATA / 100 clocks (20 idle cycles placed randomly). Outgoing data = 8 DATA / 10 clocks. Burst size = 160. Write and read frequencies are equal.
answer: Worst case: 160 written in 160 consecutive cycles (back-to-back windows). Reads in 160 cycles = 128. Depth = 32.
solution:
**Key idea:** Worst case is two back-to-back write windows: the 80 writes of window 1 placed at its end and the 80 writes of window 2 at its start give **160 writes in 160 consecutive clocks**. The reader takes only 160 x 8/10 = 128 in that time, so depth = 160 - 128 = **32**.

| Placement of the 20 idle cycles | Cycles to write 160 items |
| --- | --- |
| idle at start of both windows | 200 |
| idle at end of both windows | 200 |
| idle split 10/10 in each window | 180 |
| window 1 idle first, window 2 idle last (worst case) | **160** |
| idle in the middle of both windows | 200 |

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "window", "wave": "=...=...", "data": ["100 clocks", "100 clocks"]}, {"name": "wr_en", "wave": "0.1...0."}, {"name": "rd_en (8 of 10)", "wave": "1......."}, {"name": "burst", "wave": "x.=...x.", "data": ["160 writes in 160 clks"]}], "head": {"text": "worst case: 20 idle | 80 writes || 80 writes | 20 idle"}}
```

### Explanation
- Write side: 160 items in 160 clocks (rate 1/clk) in the worst case.
- Read side: 8 per 10 clocks -> 0.8/clk -> 128 items in 160 clocks.
- Depth = 160 - 128 = **32**.
- Always pick the *maximum* instantaneous write rate and the *minimum* read rate the spec allows.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The read side can also be bursty (8 of 10 clocks); worst case it reads at the end of its window. Using floor over each 10-cycle window still gives 128 over 160 cycles, so 32 holds if the reader's windows align; a fully adversarial reader alignment can add up to 2 more entries, so a careful answer is 32-34 -> choose 34 or simply 64 (power of two).

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

title: FIFO depth: f(clk_A) = f(clk_B)/4, period(en_B) = 100 x period(clk_A), duty cycle(en_B) = 25%. A writes every clk_A cycle; B reads every clk_B cycle while en_B is high. How deep must the FIFO be to avoid overflow and underflow?
prompt:
Frequency(clk_A) = frequency(clk_B) / 4
Period(en_B) = period(clk_A) x 100
Duty cycle(en_B) = 25%
answer: Assume clk_B = 100 MHz, clk_A = 25 MHz. Burst = 100 items in 4000 ns. Reading is enabled for 1000 ns only; items written in the other 3000 ns = 3000/40 = 75. Depth = 75.
solution:
**Key idea:** Pick numbers: clk_B = 100 MHz, clk_A = 25 MHz. In one en_B period (4000 ns) A writes 100 items; B can read only during the 1000 ns window. The 3000 ns with en_B low accumulates 3000/40 = **75** items, which is the minimum depth.

```wavedrom
{"signal": [{"name": "clk_A (25MHz)", "wave": "p..........."}, {"name": "wr (every clk_A)", "wave": "1..........."}, {"name": "en_B (25%)", "wave": "0........1.."}, {"name": "level", "wave": "=..=..=..=.=", "data": ["0", "25", "50", "75 peak", "0"]}], "head": {"text": "en_B low 3000 ns: 75 items pile up; en_B high 1000 ns: B (4x faster) drains 75 + 25 new"}}
```

| Interval | Writes (every 40 ns) | Reads (every 10 ns) | Level at end |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0-3000 ns, en_B = 0 | 75 | 0 | **75** |
| 3000-4000 ns, en_B = 1 | 25 | up to 100 | 0 |
| Per 4000 ns period | 100 | 100 | balanced |

### Explanation
- The burst length is implied: one en_B period = 100 clk_A cycles = 100 writes.
- Reader capacity in the window = 1000 ns / 10 ns = 100 = writes per period, so the system is balanced (no long-term growth).
- Worst-case occupancy is at the moment en_B rises: 75 items -> depth **75** (practically 128 for async Gray pointers, or 75 + sync margin).
- The source says "items read in 3000 ns = 3000/40"; it really means items *written* while reading is disabled.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If en_B's high window can start at any phase relative to the writes, the answer is still 75 because the low phase is 3000 ns long.
- If clk_B were only 2x clk_A, the reader could not drain 100 items in 1000 ns and the FIFO would overflow regardless of depth.

### Follow-ups
- *Would you round the depth up to a power of two?* Yes for an async FIFO with Gray pointers (e.g. 45 -> 64), because Gray-code pointer wrap only works cleanly for 2^n depths.
- *What about synchronizer latency?* The full/empty flags are seen 2-3 destination cycles late, so add a few entries of margin on top of the computed number.

source.name: FIFO Depth Calculation Made Easy (Putta Satish)

title: Write a parameterized synchronous FIFO. How do you detect full and empty?
answer:
Use pointers one bit wider than the address. Equal pointers = empty; only the MSB (wrap bit) differs = full.
Follow-ups: non-power-of-2 depth → wrap by hand at D-1 and keep an occupancy counter (full = count == D).
Read+write together when full: this design blocks the write; some specs allow it, check which one.
The memory has no reset: saves area, and the empty flag already hides stale data.
solution:
**Key idea:** make each pointer one bit wider than the address. The low bits index the RAM; the extra MSB is a *wrap bit* that flips each time the pointer laps the buffer. Equal pointers mean **empty**; same index but different wrap bit means the writer is exactly one lap ahead, i.e. **full**.

Trace for `D = 4` (AW = 2, pointers are 3 bits):

| Event | wptr | rptr | empty | full |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| reset | 000 | 000 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 writes | 100 | 000 | 0 | 1 (index 00 = 00, MSB differs) |
| 1 read | 100 | 001 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 reads | 100 | 100 | 1 | 0 |
| 4 writes | 000 (wrapped) | 100 | 0 | 1 |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "wr_en", "wave": "01.0...." },
  { "name": "wdata", "wave": "x==x....", "data": ["A", "B"] },
  { "name": "rd_en", "wave": "0...1.0." },
  { "name": "rdata", "wave": "x....==.", "data": ["A", "B"] },
  { "name": "empty", "wave": "1.0...1." }
],
  "head": { "text": "registered read: rdata is valid one cycle after rd_en" } }
```

### Solution
- `do_wr = wr_en && !full`, `do_rd = rd_en && !empty`: never move a pointer on an illegal access, so overflow and underflow are impossible by construction.
- Pointers have an async reset; the storage array and `rdata` have none (keeps reset out of the data path).
- Occupancy, if needed, is simply `wptr - rptr` in AW+1 bits.

### Code
```systemverilog
module sync_fifo #(parameter int W = 8, D = 16, localparam int AW = $clog2(D)) (
  input  logic         clk, rst_n, wr_en, rd_en,
  input  logic [W-1:0] wdata,
  output logic [W-1:0] rdata,
  output logic         full, empty
);
  logic [W-1:0] mem [D];
  logic [AW:0]  wptr, rptr;                  // extra MSB = wrap bit
  logic         do_wr, do_rd;

  assign empty = (wptr == rptr);
  assign full  = (wptr[AW] != rptr[AW]) && (wptr[AW-1:0] == rptr[AW-1:0]);
  assign do_wr = wr_en && !full;
  assign do_rd = rd_en && !empty;

  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)  // pointers: async reset
    if (!rst_n) begin
      wptr <= '0; rptr <= '0;
    end else begin
      if (do_wr) wptr <= wptr + 1'b1;
      if (do_rd) rptr <= rptr + 1'b1;
    end

  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin             // storage: no reset
    if (do_wr) mem[wptr[AW-1:0]] <= wdata;
    if (do_rd) rdata <= mem[rptr[AW-1:0]];   // valid 1 cycle after rd_en
  end
endmodule
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The wrap-bit trick needs `D` to be a power of 2 (and at least 2). For other depths, wrap each pointer at `D-1` by hand and keep a counter: `full = (count == D)`.
- **Read and write in the same cycle while full:** this design rejects the write. Some specs allow it, since a slot frees up that cycle (`do_wr = wr_en && (!full || rd_en)`). Check which one the spec wants.
- While empty, a simultaneous read is rejected: there is no fall-through. A first-word-fall-through (FWFT) FIFO needs extra output logic.

### Follow-ups
- *almost_full / almost_empty?* Compare `wptr - rptr` with a threshold, and register it if timing is tight.
- *Why no reset on the memory?* It saves area and reset routing. The empty flag already stops anyone from reading stale data.
- *How would you verify it?* Use a queue reference model and SVA on the flags (see "How would you verify a FIFO?").

title: Draw an async FIFO. Why use Gray-code pointers, and how are full and empty generated?
answer:
Gray code changes one bit per increment, so a synchronizer sampling mid-transition gets the old or the new pointer, never a wrong one.
Write pointer (Gray) → 2 flops → read domain, where empty is computed. Read pointer (Gray) → 2 flops → write domain, where full is computed.
Empty: read Gray == synchronized write Gray. Full: top two bits inverted, rest equal.
Flags are pessimistic: they assert on time and deassert 2-3 cycles late, which is safe. Data needs no synchronizer: it is stable before the pointer says it is written.
Depth must be a power of 2. Constrain the Gray bus with set_max_delay -datapath_only / set_bus_skew. Know binary↔Gray conversions.
solution:
**Key idea:** each side keeps its own pointer and only sees a *synchronized, slightly stale* copy of the other side's pointer. Pointers cross as **Gray code**: only one bit changes per increment, so a 2-FF synchronizer that samples mid-change sees either the old or the new value, never a value the pointer never held.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph WD["write domain (wclk)"]
    WP["wbin / wgray"] --> FULL["full logic"]
    WS["wq2_rgray (2-FF sync)"] --> FULL
  end
  subgraph RAMB["dual-port RAM"]
    RAM["mem (2^AW entries)"]
  end
  subgraph RDOM["read domain (rclk)"]
    RP["rbin / rgray"] --> EMPTY["empty logic"]
    RS["rq2_wgray (2-FF sync)"] --> EMPTY
  end
  WP -->|waddr| RAM
  RP -->|raddr| RAM
  WP -->|wgray| RS
  RP -->|rgray| WS
```

Gray pointers for D = 4 (3-bit pointers, extra wrap bit):

| binary | 000 | 001 | 010 | 011 | 100 | 101 | 110 | 111 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gray | 000 | 001 | 011 | 010 | 110 | 111 | 101 | 100 |

After 4 writes and no reads, wgray = `110` and rgray = `000`. Invert the top two bits of rgray to get `110`, which equals wgray, so the FIFO is **full**. One lap apart in binary (MSB differs) shows up in Gray as *both* top bits differing.

### Explanation
- **Empty** (read domain): `rgray_next == rq2_wgray`.
- **Full** (write domain): `wgray_next == {~wq2_rgray[AW:AW-1], wq2_rgray[AW-2:0]}`.
- Both flags are registered from the *next* pointer values, so they update in the same cycle as the pointer.

### Code
```systemverilog
module async_fifo #(parameter int W = 8, AW = 4) (    // depth = 2**AW, AW >= 2
  input  logic         wclk, wrst_n, winc,
  input  logic [W-1:0] wdata,
  output logic         wfull,
  input  logic         rclk, rrst_n, rinc,
  output logic [W-1:0] rdata,
  output logic         rempty
);
  logic [W-1:0] mem [2**AW];
  logic [AW:0]  wbin, wgray, rbin, rgray, wbin_next, wgray_next, rbin_next, rgray_next;
  logic [AW:0]  wq1_rgray, wq2_rgray, rq1_wgray, rq2_wgray;

  // ---------------- write domain
  assign wbin_next  = wbin + (winc & ~wfull);
  assign wgray_next = (wbin_next >> 1) ^ wbin_next;
  always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n)
    if (!wrst_n) begin
      wbin <= '0; wgray <= '0; wfull <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
      wbin  <= wbin_next;
      wgray <= wgray_next;
      wfull <= (wgray_next == {~wq2_rgray[AW:AW-1], wq2_rgray[AW-2:0]});
    end
  always_ff @(posedge wclk)
    if (winc && !wfull) mem[wbin[AW-1:0]] <= wdata;
  always_ff @(posedge wclk or negedge wrst_n)          // rgray -> wclk domain
    if (!wrst_n) {wq2_rgray, wq1_rgray} <= '0;
    else         {wq2_rgray, wq1_rgray} <= {wq1_rgray, rgray};

  // ---------------- read domain
  assign rbin_next  = rbin + (rinc & ~rempty);
  assign rgray_next = (rbin_next >> 1) ^ rbin_next;
  always_ff @(posedge rclk or negedge rrst_n)
    if (!rrst_n) begin
      rbin <= '0; rgray <= '0; rempty <= 1'b1;
    end else begin
      rbin   <= rbin_next;
      rgray  <= rgray_next;
      rempty <= (rgray_next == rq2_wgray);
    end
  assign rdata = mem[rbin[AW-1:0]];                    // first-word fall-through read
  always_ff @(posedge rclk or negedge rrst_n)          // wgray -> rclk domain
    if (!rrst_n) {rq2_wgray, rq1_wgray} <= '0;
    else         {rq2_wgray, rq1_wgray} <= {rq1_wgray, wgray};
endmodule
```

Conversions you should be able to write on the spot:
```systemverilog
assign g_out = b_in ^ (b_in >> 1);                     // binary -> Gray
always_comb begin                                      // Gray -> binary
  b_out[N-1] = g_in[N-1];
  for (int i = N-2; i >= 0; i--) b_out[i] = b_out[i+1] ^ g_in[i];
end
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Flags are pessimistic, and that is safe.** Each flag *asserts* on time, because the pointer that causes it is local. It *deasserts* 2–3 cycles late, because the other pointer is stale. The FIFO can't overflow or underflow, but it gets a little less throughput, so add a few entries of depth.
- **No synchronizer on the data:** the reader only reads an entry after the synchronized pointer says it was written, and by then the data has been stable for 2 or more cycles.
- **Depth must be a power of 2,** or the Gray sequence is no longer one-bit-change at the wrap. Other depths need a special Gray sequence.
- **Timing constraint:** add `set_max_delay -datapath_only` or `set_bus_skew` on the Gray bus, so the skew between its bits stays under one source clock period. Otherwise two bits could change in the same sampling window.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not synchronize a binary pointer?* 0111→1000 flips 4 bits. If they resolve on different cycles, the receiver could see 1111, a false pointer far ahead.
- *How do you verify it?* Sweep the clock ratios (fast/slow/equal), reset each domain on its own, add an SVA that the Gray pointer changes by `$onehot0` per cycle, and run formal CDC.

title: How does a 2-FF synchronizer work? Why can't you use it for a multi-bit bus?
answer:
The first flop may go metastable; it gets a full clock cycle to settle before the second flop samples it. MTBF = e^(tr/tau) / (T0 * fclk * fdata); a third flop multiplies MTBF by about e^(T/tau).
Multi-bit bus: each bit may resolve on a different cycle, so the receiver can see a value that never existed.
Fixes: Gray code (counters stepping ±1), req/ack handshake or async FIFO, mux recirculation with a synchronized enable.
Fast-to-slow pulse: stretch it, or convert to a toggle and edge-detect after syncing.
Same frequency, different phase: one PLL with a fixed known offset is STA-timed (synchronous); unknown or drifting phase is a CDC.
solution:
**Key idea:** the first flop may sample a changing input and go **metastable**. It gets almost one full destination clock period to resolve before the second flop samples it, so the probability that metastability reaches the logic drops exponentially. It works per *bit*, so a bus whose bits resolve on different cycles can show a value that never existed.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk_dst",       "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "d (async)",     "wave": "0.1....." },
  { "name": "q1",            "wave": "0..x1..." },
  { "name": "q2 (to logic)", "wave": "0...1..." },
  {},
  { "name": "bus src",       "wave": "=..=....", "data": ["01", "10"] },
  { "name": "bus after sync","wave": "=...==..", "data": ["01", "11", "10"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "q1 may go metastable but settles within a cycle; bus bits settle on different cycles and show 11" } }
```

### Explanation
