```systemverilog
  // :=  weight applies to EACH value:   0 -> 1;  1, 2, 3 -> 2 each
  // :/  weight is SPLIT over the range: 4..15 share 7 in total
}
```

| Value | Weight | Probability (total weight 14) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 1 | 1/14 ≈ 7.1% |
| 1, 2, 3 | 2 each | 2/14 ≈ 14.3% each |
| 4 … 15 | 7/12 each | ≈ 4.2% each (50% together) |

### solve…before
```systemverilog
rand bit       mode;
rand bit [7:0] len;
constraint c_dep { mode -> len == 0; }
constraint c_ord { solve mode before len; }
```

| | Legal (mode, len) pairs | P(mode = 1) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no ordering | 256 with mode = 0, plus 1 with mode = 1 = **257**, all equally likely | 1/257 |
| `solve mode before len` | the same 257 pairs | **1/2** (mode is picked first, uniformly) |

### Explanation
- The default solver is uniform over **all legal solutions together**, so a rarely-legal value of one variable becomes rare.
- `solve a before b` makes the solver pick `a` first (uniformly over its feasible values), then `b` given `a`. The legal set doesn't change.
- `dist` is a soft weighting, not a hard limit: values outside the `dist` list are still legal unless another constraint excludes them. Pair it with `inside` if needed.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `randc` variables can't appear in `solve…before`, because they're always solved first anyway.
- `dist` can't be used on `randc` variables.
- Weight 0 (`5 := 0`) excludes a value from the distribution.

### Follow-ups
- *Another way to get 50/50 mode?* `mode dist {0 := 1, 1 := 1};` gives the same effect here.
- *Implication vs if-else?* `a -> b` is the same as `if (a) b;`, and both are bidirectional for the solver.

title: Make array elements unique without using the unique keyword
answer:
Pairwise constraint: foreach (arr[i]) foreach (arr[j]) if (i < j) arr[i] != arr[j]; (O(N^2) constraints).
Alternative: fill 0..N-1 (or any distinct set) in post_randomize() and call arr.shuffle() — O(N), and also a way to get randc-like behavior without randc.

title: Constrain a dynamic array so that its elements sum to 20
answer:
rand bit [7:0] da[]; constraint c_size { da.size() inside {[4:8]}; } constraint c_sum { da.sum() with (int'(item)) == 20; }
Trap: sum() computes at the element width, so 8-bit values can overflow and wrap; the int'(item) cast fixes it.
The size is solved before the elements — always bound size().
Count matching elements: da.sum() with (int'(item > 200)) >= 2. Resize and keep data: da = new[16](da).
solution:
**Key idea:** constrain the **size** (bounded!) and the **sum**, and widen the sum so it can't overflow at the element width.

```systemverilog
class sum20;
  rand bit [7:0] da[];
  constraint c_size { da.size() inside {[4:8]}; }               // always bound the size
  constraint c_sum  { da.sum() with (int'(item)) == 20; }       // sum in 32 bits
endclass
```

Why the cast matters: without it, the sum is computed at 8 bits.

| da | true sum | 8-bit `sum()` | passes `== 20` without cast? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5, 5, 5, 5 | 20 | 20 | yes (correct) |
| 200, 76, 0, 0 | 276 | 276 mod 256 = **20** | **yes (wrong!)** |
| 255, 255, 22, 0 | 532 | 532 mod 256 = **20** | **yes (wrong!)** |

With `int'(item)` the sum is 32 bits, so only true sums of 20 pass.

### Explanation
- The solver fixes `size()` first, then solves the elements. An unbounded size can make the solver pick huge arrays or fail.
- `with (expr)` maps each element before summing. It works for counting too:
```systemverilog
constraint c_cnt  { da.sum() with (int'(item > 200)) >= 2; }   // at least two elements > 200
constraint c_even { da.sum() with (int'(item[0] == 0)) == da.size(); }  // all even
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `item` is the implicit iterator name; `da.sum(x) with (int'(x))` names it explicitly.
- `product()` overflows even faster: cast to `longint` and bound the elements.
- To resize at run time and keep the old data: `da = new[16](da);`.

### Follow-ups
- *Each element non-zero?* `foreach (da[i]) da[i] > 0;` (then size ≤ 20).
- *Sum of a 2-D array?* Constrain each row's sum, then a separate sum over a helper array of row sums.

title: Randomize a 16-bit value that has exactly one run of consecutive 1s
answer:
Randomize start position and length, then derive x: len in [1:16], start in [0:15], start + len <= 16, x == ((17'h1 << len) - 1) << start.
Bit-trick check: x is one contiguous run iff x != 0 and x + (x & -x) is a power of 2 (computed in 17 bits).
One-hot without $countones: x != 0; (x & (x-1)) == 0. Exactly N ones: helper rand bit b[16], b.sum() with (int'(item)) == N, pack into x.
solution:
**Key idea:** describe the shape, not the bits. A single run of 1s is fully defined by **where it starts** and **how long it is**, so randomize those two and derive `x`.

```systemverilog
class one_run;
  rand bit [15:0]   x;
  rand int unsigned start, len;
  constraint c_run {
    len   inside {[1:16]};
    start inside {[0:15]};
    start + len <= 16;
    x == ((17'h1 << len) - 1) << start;    // len ones, shifted up by start
  }
endclass
```

Worked example: `start = 3`, `len = 4` → `(1 << 4) - 1 = 0b1111` → `<< 3` → `x = 16'b0000_0000_0111_1000` (0x0078).

Bit-trick check (handy in a checker or as a follow-up):

| x | `x & -x` (lowest 1) | `x + (x & -x)` | power of 2? | one run? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0111_1000 | 0000_1000 | 1000_0000 | yes | yes |
| 0101_1000 | 0000_1000 | 0110_0000 | no | no |
| 1111_1111_1111_1111 | 1 | 1_0000_0000_0000_0000 (17 bits) | yes | yes |

Adding the lowest set bit makes a contiguous run carry all the way through, leaving a single 1. Compute it in 17 bits so the all-ones case doesn't wrap to 0.

### Related patterns
```systemverilog
constraint c_onehot { x != 0; (x & (x - 1)) == 0; }       // one-hot without $countones

rand bit b[16];                                           // exactly N ones, without $countones
constraint c_n  { b.sum() with (int'(item)) == N; }
function void post_randomize(); foreach (b[i]) x[i] = b[i]; endfunction
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `start + len <= 16` uses `int unsigned`, which can't wrap here because both are bounded. Always bound helper variables.
- The distribution is uniform over (start, len) pairs, so short runs are more common than in a uniform choice over all legal `x` values. Add `solve` or `dist` if that matters.

### Follow-ups
- *Exactly two runs?* Two (start, len) pairs with a gap of at least 1 between them.
- *Run of 0s?* Constrain `~x` the same way.

title: Randomize non-overlapping memory regions (aligned, inside a 1 KB space)
answer:
rand int unsigned base[4], size[4]; bound base < 1024, size in [1:64], base % 32 == 0, base + size <= 1024; for every pair i<j: (base[i]+size[i] <= base[j]) || (base[j]+size[j] <= base[i]).
Watch wrap-around: with bit [9:0], base+size wraps at 1024; with an unbounded int unsigned, a base near 2^32 wraps too. Either way an out-of-range or overlapping region can pass, so bound base explicitly.
solution:
**Key idea:** two regions don't overlap when **one ends before the other starts**. Constrain every pair with that OR, and bound every value so the additions can't wrap.

```systemverilog
class mem_regions;
  rand int unsigned base[4], size[4];
  constraint c_region {
    foreach (base[i]) {
      base[i] < 1024;                    // bound it, or base + size can wrap at 2^32
      size[i] inside {[1:64]};
      base[i] % 32 == 0;                 // 32-byte aligned
      base[i] + size[i] <= 1024;         // stay inside 1 KB
    }
    foreach (base[i]) foreach (base[j])
      if (i < j) (base[i] + size[i] <= base[j]) || (base[j] + size[j] <= base[i]);
  }
endclass
```

One possible solution:

| region | base | size | end (exclusive) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0x060 | 40 | 0x088 |
| 1 | 0x200 | 64 | 0x240 |
| 2 | 0x000 | 17 | 0x011 |
| 3 | 0x3E0 | 32 | 0x400 |

```text
0x000 [2]--)    0x060 [0]----)        0x200 [1]------)          0x3E0 [3]---) 0x400
```

### Explanation
- `(end_i <= start_j) || (end_j <= start_i)` is the standard interval non-overlap test, with ends exclusive.
- The `i < j` guard avoids comparing a region with itself (which would be unsatisfiable) and halves the constraints.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Wrap-around:** if `base` and `size` were both `bit [9:0]`, then 1000 + 40 would wrap to 16 and pass the checks. With unbounded `int unsigned`, a base near 2^32 wraps the same way. Either way an out-of-range or overlapping region slips through, so bound `base` explicitly.
- Too many regions or sizes for the space makes the constraint unsatisfiable. Check the randomize result.

### Follow-ups
- *Sorted regions?* Add `base[i] + size[i] <= base[i+1]` for consecutive i instead of all pairs (O(N) constraints).
- *Allow touching but not overlapping?* That's already the case (`<=`). Use `<` to require a gap.

title: How do you override a parent class constraint in a child class? Give three methods
answer:
1) Same constraint name in the child replaces the parent's. 2) Turn it off: tr.c_len.constraint_mode(0), then add new constraints inline. 3) Make it soft in the parent: constraint c_len { soft len < 16; } so an inline with {len == 100;} wins instead of failing.
An inline with can't relax a hard constraint; a conflict makes randomize() return 0.
solution:
**Key idea:** constraints are **inherited like virtual methods by name**, can be **switched off** per object, and `soft` constraints **give way** to any conflicting hard constraint.

```systemverilog
class base_tr;
  rand bit [7:0] len;
  constraint c_len  { len inside {[1:15]}; }
  constraint c_def  { soft len < 8; }               // method 3: soft default
endclass

class long_tr extends base_tr;                      // method 1: same name replaces it
  constraint c_len { len inside {[100:200]}; }
endclass

base_tr t = new();
t.c_len.constraint_mode(0);                         // method 2: turn it off for this object
if (!t.randomize() with { len == 250; }) `uvm_error("RND", "failed")
// c_def (soft) yields to the inline len == 250
```

| Method | Scope | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same name in the child | every object of the child class | parent's `c_len` replaced |
| `constraint_mode(0)` | one object, at run time | constraint ignored until turned back on |
| `soft` in the parent | wherever it conflicts | dropped silently when a hard constraint disagrees |

### Explanation
- A child constraint with a **different** name is *added* to the parent's, so both must hold.
- `soft` constraints are resolved by priority: later and more specific (inline, child) beats earlier (parent).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- An inline `with {}` **can't relax** a hard constraint: `with { len == 250; }` while `c_len` (1..15) is active makes `randomize()` return 0.
- Calling `constraint_mode(0)` on a name that doesn't exist is a compile error. Calling it on the class handle affects only that object.
- In UVM, a factory override to `long_tr` changes the constraints for every item a sequence creates, with no change to the sequence.

### Follow-ups
- *Disable all constraints?* `t.constraint_mode(0);` on the object.
- *Turn off randomization of one field?* `t.len.rand_mode(0);`.

title: Randomize a 300-element array with values 0–5, each appearing exactly 50 times, and no two 0s in a row
answer:
rand bit [2:0] arr[300]; each element inside [0:5]; for each value v: arr.sum() with (int'(item == v)) == 50; foreach i>0: !(arr[i] == 0 && arr[i-1] == 0).
With this many elements the solver gets slow. For performance build the multiset in post_randomize(), shuffle it, and repair any 0–0 pairs.

title: Constrain a dynamic array so that any 5 consecutive values are all different (sliding window)
answer: foreach (da[i]) if (i + 4 < da.size()) unique {da[i], da[i+1], da[i+2], da[i+3], da[i+4]};

title: More constraint patterns: strictly increasing array, alternating read/write transactions, Sudoku
answer:
Strictly increasing: foreach (a[i]) if (i > 0) a[i] > a[i-1].
Alternate READ/WRITE across randomize calls: keep the last value in a static variable, constrain is_wr != last_wr, update it in post_randomize.
Sudoku: g[r][c] inside [1:9]; each row unique; for every pair of cells in the same column or same 3x3 box (r < r2), values differ.

title: What does the solver do when you call a function inside a constraint?
answer:
Random variables passed as function arguments are solved BEFORE the function runs (an implicit solve-before); the function result is only checked afterwards, so count_big(a) == 2 usually fails.
Use an array method the solver handles in both directions: a.sum() with (int'(item > 100)) == 2.
Functions in constraints can't have output or ref arguments (const ref is fine) and shouldn't have side effects.
solution:
**Key idea:** the solver can't "see inside" a function. Random arguments are solved **first**, as if with `solve args before result`, then the function is evaluated once and the constraint is just checked. The solver can't steer the arguments to make the result come out right.

```systemverilog
rand bit [7:0] a[8];

constraint c_sym { foreach (a[i]) if (i < 4) a[i] == a[7-i]; }   // relations: no function needed

function int count_big(bit [7:0] arr[8]);
  int n = 0;
  foreach (arr[i]) if (arr[i] > 100) n++;
  return n;
endfunction
constraint c_fn  { count_big(a) == 2; }                          // RISKY: usually fails

constraint c_ok  { a.sum() with (int'(item > 100)) == 2; }       // solver understands this
```

| Step | With `count_big(a) == 2` | With `a.sum() with (...) == 2` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | solve `a` with no knowledge of the target | build one combined problem over `a` |
| 2 | evaluate `count_big(a)`, e.g. 4 | solver picks `a` so exactly 2 elements are > 100 |
| 3 | 4 != 2: **randomize fails** (or retries, tool-dependent) | success |

### Explanation
- Functions are fine for things that depend only on **state variables** or on variables solved earlier on purpose, e.g. `len == calc_len(mode)` where `mode` should be picked first.
- Array reduction methods (`sum`, `product`, `and`, `or`, `xor` with `with`) and `foreach` are expanded into real constraints, so they work in both directions.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Functions called in constraints can't have `output` or `ref` arguments (`const ref` is fine) and shouldn't have side effects. They may be called several times.
- The implicit ordering can create circular-dependency errors if two functions use each other's results.
- `$countones(x)` is understood by most solvers, but interviewers often ban it. Know the `sum()` form.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you check symmetry with a function safely?* Call the function in `post_randomize()` as a self-check, not as a constraint.

title: What's the difference between an immediate and a concurrent assertion?
solution:
**Key idea:** an **immediate** assertion is a procedural `if` that reports an error, evaluated once, right now. A **concurrent** assertion is a temporal property, clocked, sampled race-free in the Preponed region, and able to span many cycles.

|   | Immediate | Concurrent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | inside procedural code: `assert (x);` | stand-alone (module, interface, checker): `assert property (...)` |
| Timing | evaluated when the statement executes | sampled in Preponed, evaluated in Observed, every clock |
| Spans cycles | no | yes (`##`, `[*]`, `$past`, `|=>`) |
| Typical use | `randomize()` result, scoreboard values, function arguments | protocol rules on DUT signals |
| Formal tools | rarely | yes (assert / assume / cover) |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p....." },
  { "name": "req",   "wave": "01.0.." },
  { "name": "gnt",   "wave": "0.10.." },
  { "name": "assert property: req |=> gnt", "wave": "x.=x..", "data": ["pass @3"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "a concurrent assertion samples req at edge 2 and checks gnt at edge 3" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// immediate: procedural
always_comb assert (!(rd_en && wr_en)) else $error("simultaneous rd/wr");
if (!tr.randomize()) `uvm_error("RND", "fail")   // preferred over assert(tr.randomize())

// concurrent: temporal, clocked
module fifo_sva (input logic clk, rst_n, full, wr_en);
  a_no_overflow: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) full |-> !wr_en);
endmodule

// attach to the RTL without editing it
bind sync_fifo fifo_sva u_sva (.*);
```

### Explanation
- **Deferred immediate** assertions (`assert #0` / `assert final`) wait until the end of the time step, which avoids false failures from zero-delay glitches in `always_comb`.
- `bind` instantiates the checker module inside every instance (or one instance) of the DUT module, so verification code stays out of the RTL files.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A concurrent assertion inside a class is illegal. Put it in the interface or a bound checker.
- Immediate assertions in `always_comb` can fire on transient values during delta cycles. Use deferred ones.

### Follow-ups
- *Can a concurrent assertion be placed in procedural code?* Yes, as a *procedural concurrent* assertion inside `always @(posedge clk)`; it inherits the clock and the enclosing `if` condition.

title: What's the difference between |-> and |=>? What is a vacuous pass?
answer:
a |-> b: check b in the same cycle a holds (overlapping). a |=> b: check b in the next cycle; equals a |-> ##1 b.
Vacuous pass: when the antecedent is false the property passes trivially, so an assertion that never fails may never have been exercised. Pair every important assert with a cover property on its antecedent.
solution:
**Key idea:** `|->` (overlapping) checks the consequent **in the same cycle** the antecedent matches; `|=>` (non-overlapping) checks it **one cycle later**. `a |=> b` is exactly `a |-> ##1 b`.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",       "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "a",         "wave": "0100100" },
  { "name": "b",         "wave": "0100010" },
  { "name": "a |-> b",   "wave": "x=xx=xx", "data": ["pass", "FAIL"] },
  { "name": "a |=> b",   "wave": "xx=xx=x", "data": ["FAIL", "pass"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "a at cycles 1 and 4; b at cycles 1 and 5" } }
```

| Cycle | a | b | `a \|-> b` | `a \|=> b` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | pass | starts, checks b at 2 |
| 2 | 0 | 0 | vacuous | **fail** (b = 0) |
| 4 | 1 | 0 | **fail** | starts, checks b at 5 |
| 5 | 0 | 1 | vacuous | pass |

### Vacuous pass
- When the antecedent is false, the implication is **true by definition**. Most cycles of most assertions are vacuous passes.
- Danger: an assertion whose antecedent never happens (wrong signal name, a feature never stimulated, reset never released) passes in every test and proves nothing.
- Fix: pair every important assertion with a **cover** of its antecedent (or the whole scenario), and check the cover count in the regression.

```systemverilog
a_hold: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready |=> valid);
c_hold: cover  property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready);   // proves it was exercised
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `disable iff (!rst_n)` stops evaluation during reset. Without it, assertions fire on X or reset values.
- Many simulators report vacuous successes separately; some count them as passes. Look at the "real" (non-vacuous) success count.

### Follow-ups
- *`a |-> ##[1:3] b`?* b must arrive 1 to 3 cycles after a.
- *`a #-# b` / `a #=# b`?* Followed-by operators: like implication, but they *fail* if the antecedent never matches (used in covers and formal).

title: Write an assertion: valid must stay high, with stable data, until ready (AXI / stream handshake)
solution:
**Key idea:** once the source raises `valid`, it can't take it back or change the payload until the handshake (`valid && ready` on a clock edge). So: whenever `valid` is high and `ready` is low, next cycle `valid` must still be high **and** `data` unchanged.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "valid", "wave": "01..0.1.0" },
  { "name": "ready", "wave": "0..10..10" },
  { "name": "data",  "wave": "x=..x.==x", "data": ["D0", "D1", "D2"] },
  { "name": "check", "wave": "x.==x..=x", "data": ["ok", "ok", "FAIL"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "D0: held until ready (ok). D1 changes to D2 while ready is low: $stable fails" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_valid_hold;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  valid && !ready |=> valid && $stable(data);
endproperty
a_valid_hold: assert property (p_valid_hold)
  else `uvm_error("SVA", "valid dropped or data changed before ready")

c_backpressure: cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready);
c_long_stall:   cover property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) valid && !ready [*4]);
```

### Explanation
- `|=>` checks the **next** edge: if there was no handshake this edge (`!ready`), the beat is still pending next cycle.
- `$stable(data)` compares the sampled value with the previous edge's value. For AXI, include every payload field (`{addr, len, size, burst, id}`).
- The cover proves backpressure actually happened. Without it, a TB with `ready` always high passes vacuously.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Don't write `valid |-> ##[0:$] ready`: that's a liveness property (ready eventually), which is different and unbounded in simulation.
- `$stable` on X data: X to X counts as stable. Add `valid |-> !$isunknown(data)` as a separate check.
- After reset, `valid` must be low (AXI rule): `$rose(rst_n) |-> !valid`.

### Follow-ups
- *Ready may depend on valid?* Yes, the rule is one-way: the source must not wait for ready, and the sink may wait for valid.
- *Liveness with a bound:* `valid |-> ##[0:100] ready` catches a stuck sink in simulation.

title: Write assertions for a req/ack handshake: ack within 1–3 cycles, req held until ack, and no ack without req
answer:
p_ack_in_time: $rose(req) |-> ##[1:3] ack. p_req_hold: req && !ack |=> req. p_no_orphan: $rose(ack) |-> req (ack may only rise while req is high).
4-phase handshake: add $fell(req) |-> ##[1:$] $fell(ack) and !req |=> !$rose(ack).
solution:
**Key idea:** split the protocol into **one property per rule** (timing, stability, causality) so a failure message tells you exactly which rule broke.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "req", "wave": "01...0....." },
  { "name": "ack", "wave": "0..1.0....." },
  {},
  { "name": "phase", "wave": "x=.=.=....x", "data": ["req up, wait 1-3", "ack: done", "both low (4-phase)"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "req rises, ack follows 2 cycles later, req drops, then ack drops" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_ack_in_time;  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $rose(req) |-> ##[1:3] ack;                  endproperty
property p_req_hold;     @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  req && !ack |=> req;                         endproperty
property p_no_orphan;    @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  $rose(ack) |-> req;                          endproperty  // ack only rises while req is high

a_ack_in_time: assert property (p_ack_in_time) else $error("ack not within 1-3 cycles");
a_req_hold:    assert property (p_req_hold)    else $error("req dropped before ack");
a_no_orphan:   assert property (p_no_orphan)   else $error("ack without req");

// 4-phase (return-to-zero) handshake additions
a_ack_falls:   assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $fell(req) |-> ##[1:$] $fell(ack));
a_no_new_ack:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) !req |=> !$rose(ack));

c_ack_at_3:    cover property (@(posedge clk) $rose(req) ##3 ack);   // slowest legal response
```

| Rule | Property | Typical bug it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| timing | `$rose(req) \|-> ##[1:3] ack` | slave too slow / stuck |
| stability | `req && !ack \|=> req` | master gives up early |
| causality | `$rose(ack) \|-> req` | spurious ack |
| return to zero | `$fell(req) \|-> ##[1:$] $fell(ack)` | ack stuck high |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `##[1:$]` is unbounded: in simulation, a missing `$fell(ack)` only shows up as an *incomplete* assertion at the end of the test. Use a bound (`##[1:16]`) if the spec has one.
- `$rose(req)` needs a defined previous value; use `disable iff` so the first cycle after reset doesn't false-trigger.
- If ack can arrive in the same cycle as req, the window is `##[0:3]`.

### Follow-ups
- *Formal:* make the req rules `assume`s and the ack rules `assert`s when verifying the responder.

title: Write APB protocol assertions: PSEL → PENABLE → PREADY
answer:
Setup phase is followed by the access phase: psel && !penable |=> psel && penable.
While waiting, controls are held stable: psel && penable && !pready |=> penable && $stable({paddr, pwrite, pwdata}).
Transfer ends and PENABLE drops: penable && pready |=> !penable.

title: Write an assertion: B toggles exactly 2 cycles after A toggles
answer: assert property (@(posedge clk) $changed(a) |-> ##2 $changed(b));
solution:
**Key idea:** "toggles" means the value changed since the last clock: `$changed(x)` (equivalent to `!$stable(x)`). Every change of A must be followed, exactly 2 cycles later, by a change of B.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",        "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "a",          "wave": "0.1...0.." },
  { "name": "b",          "wave": "0...1...1" },
  { "name": "$changed(a)","wave": "0.10..10." },
  { "name": "check",      "wave": "x...=...=", "data": ["pass", "pass"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "a changes at cycles 2 and 6; b changes at cycles 4 and 8" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
a_b_follows_a: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 $changed(a) |-> ##2 $changed(b));

// stricter: b changes ONLY 2 cycles after a change of a
a_b_only_then: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
                 $changed(b) |-> $past($changed(a), 2));

c_toggle: cover property (@(posedge clk) $changed(a) ##2 $changed(b));
```

| Requirement | Property |
| --- | --- |
| every A toggle causes a B toggle 2 cycles later | `$changed(a) \|-> ##2 $changed(b)` |
| B never toggles on its own | `$changed(b) \|-> $past($changed(a), 2)` |
| both | use both properties |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- After reset, `$changed` compares with the reset-time sampled value; `disable iff` avoids a false trigger on the first cycle.
- If A toggles on consecutive cycles, B must also toggle on consecutive cycles; the properties handle it because each A change starts its own thread.
- "Toggle" for a bus means any bit changed; for a 1-bit signal it's a rise or fall (`$rose(a) || $fell(a)`).

### Follow-ups
- *B toggles 2 to 4 cycles later?* `$changed(a) |-> ##[2:4] $changed(b)`.
- *Equivalent with `$past`?* `$changed(b) == $past($changed(a), 2)` checked every cycle covers both directions at once.

title: Write an assertion: after cat rises, dog is high for 3 or 4 consecutive cycles. Explain the repetition operators
answer:
assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(cat) |=> dog[*3:4] ##1 !dog);
[*n] repeats on consecutive cycles; [->n] is goto: the nth occurrence (may be spread out), match ends on that occurrence; [=n] is non-consecutive: like goto but the match may extend past the last occurrence.
solution:
**Key idea:** `dog[*3:4]` matches a run of 3 or 4 consecutive `dog` cycles. Following it with `##1 !dog` pins the run's **end**, so a run of 5 or more fails.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p..........." },
  { "name": "cat", "wave": "010......10." },
  { "name": "dog", "wave": "0.1..0...1.." },
  { "name": "result", "wave": "x....=....x.", "data": ["pass (3 dogs)"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "cat rises, then 3 consecutive dogs, then dog low: pass" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
a_cat_dog: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
             $rose(cat) |=> dog[*3:4] ##1 !dog);
```

### Repetition operators
For a sequence `start ##1 b[…] ##1 end_sig`, with `b` high on the marked cycles:

| Operator | Meaning | `b` pattern `1 1 1` | `b` pattern `1 0 1 0 1 0 0` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `b[*3]` | 3 **consecutive** cycles | match (ends on the 3rd 1) | no match |
| `b[->3]` | goto: 3rd occurrence, gaps allowed, match **ends on** the 3rd 1 | match | match, ends on the 3rd 1 |
| `b[=3]` | non-consecutive: 3 occurrences, match may **extend** past the last one while b stays 0 | match | match, ending on the 3rd 1 or any later 0 cycle |

### Explanation
- In the consequent, `dog[*3:4]` starts one thread per length. The property passes if **any** thread matches: with 4 dogs, the 3-thread fails on `!dog` but the 4-thread passes.
- `[->n]` is common in protocols: `req |-> ack[->1] ##1 done` means "at the first ack, then done next cycle".

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Without `##1 !dog`, `dog[*3:4]` passes as soon as 3 dogs are seen, so 10 dogs would also pass.
- `[*0]` (empty match) in an antecedent can cause surprising vacuous passes. Avoid it unless needed.

### Follow-ups
- *Unbounded run:* `dog[*1:$]` (one or more), or `[+]` shorthand in SV-2009.
- *Cover each length:* `cover property ($rose(cat) ##1 dog[*4] ##1 !dog);`.

title: Write assertions that check a clock period within ±5% and detect glitches shorter than 2.5 ns
answer:
Use a local variable to capture time at one edge and compare at the next:
p_period: realtime t; @(posedge clk) (1, t = $realtime) |=> ($realtime - t >= 0.95*PERIOD) && ($realtime - t <= 1.05*PERIOD).
p_no_glitch: realtime t; @(posedge sig) (1, t = $realtime) |-> @(negedge sig) ($realtime - t >= 2.5ns).
If PERIOD comes from another domain, sample it into a stable variable, or do the check in a monitor instead of SVA.

title: Write an assertion that an AHB burst must not cross a 1 KB boundary
answer: assert property (@(posedge hclk) htrans == NONSEQ && hburst == INCR4 |-> (haddr[9:0] + (4 << hsize)) <= 11'd1024);
solution:
**Key idea:** check once, at the **first beat** (`HTRANS == NONSEQ`). The burst's last byte is `start + beats × 2^HSIZE − 1`, and it must stay in the same 1 KB block. With the offset inside the block `haddr[9:0]`: `offset + beats × 2^HSIZE ≤ 1024`.

| HSIZE (bytes) | HBURST | start `haddr` | offset + bytes | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 (4 B) | INCR4 (16 B) | 0x3F0 | 0x3F0 + 0x10 = 0x400 | **ok** (ends exactly at the boundary) |
| 2 (4 B) | INCR4 (16 B) | 0x3F8 | 0x3F8 + 0x10 = 0x408 | **fail** (crosses 0x400) |
| 3 (8 B) | INCR8 (64 B) | 0x7C0 | 0x3C0 + 0x40 = 0x400 | ok |
| 2 (4 B) | INCR16 (64 B) | 0xBD0 | 0x3D0 + 0x40 = 0x410 | **fail** |

```text
1 KB block:  0x000 ........................ 0x3F0 0x3F4 0x3F8 0x3FC | 0x400 0x404
INCR4 @0x3F8:                                         [beat0][beat1] | [beat2][beat3]  <- crosses
```

### Code
```systemverilog
localparam logic [1:0] NONSEQ = 2'b10;
localparam logic [2:0] INCR4 = 3'b011, INCR8 = 3'b101, INCR16 = 3'b111;

function automatic int unsigned beats(logic [2:0] hburst);
  case (hburst)
    INCR4:   return 4;
    INCR8:   return 8;
    INCR16:  return 16;
    default: return 1;          // SINGLE, INCR (undefined length): checked per beat elsewhere
  endcase
endfunction

a_no_1kb_cross: assert property (@(posedge hclk) disable iff (!hresetn)
  htrans == NONSEQ && hready && hburst inside {INCR4, INCR8, INCR16} |->
    (int'(haddr[9:0]) + (beats(hburst) << hsize)) <= 1024)
  else $error("AHB burst crosses a 1 KB boundary at %h", haddr);
```

### Explanation
- `beats << hsize` = beats × 2^HSIZE = total bytes in the burst.
- Cast to `int` so the sum can't wrap at 10 or 11 bits.
- Sample the address phase only when `hready` is high (when the address phase is actually accepted).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- WRAP bursts never cross by construction (they wrap inside their own aligned window), so they don't need this check.
- Undefined-length INCR may legally cross only if the master ends the burst first; check each SEQ beat (`haddr[9:0] != 0` for SEQ beats) if the spec forbids crossing.
- AXI's equivalent rule is 4 KB (`addr[11:0]`).

### Follow-ups
- *Why 1 KB?* It's the minimum address space given to one AHB slave, so a burst can't spill into a different slave.

title: How do you check data through a pipeline with SVA? Which built-in functions do you know? assert vs assume vs cover?
answer:
Carry data with a local variable: (in_vld, v = in_data) |-> ##3 (out_vld && out_data == v + 1).
$rose(start) |-> busy throughout (##[1:10] done): busy high from start until done, done within 10 cycles.
Built-ins: $rose/$fell, $stable/$changed, $past(x,n), $onehot/$onehot0, $isunknown, $countones.
assert: must hold (sim reports failures, formal proves). assume: constrains inputs in formal, checked like an assert in sim. cover: scenario can happen (formal witness, sim hit count).
JasperGold: assumes for input protocol, asserts for outputs; a wrong assume over-constrains and hides bugs — back assumptions with covers.
solution:
**Key idea:** a **local variable** captures the input when it enters, and the property checks the matching output N cycles later. Each input starts its own thread with its own copy of the variable, so overlapping transactions are handled automatically.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",      "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "in_vld",   "wave": "01.0....." },
  { "name": "in_data",  "wave": "x==x.....", "data": ["5", "9"] },
  { "name": "out_vld",  "wave": "0...1.0.." },
  { "name": "out_data", "wave": "x...==x..", "data": ["6", "10"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "latency 3, out = in + 1: each input spawns its own thread with its own v" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_latency3;
  logic [31:0] v;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
  (in_vld, v = in_data) |-> ##3 (out_vld && out_data == v + 1);
endproperty
a_latency3: assert property (p_latency3);

// busy is high from the start cycle until done, and done arrives within 10 cycles
a_busy: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
          $rose(start) |-> busy throughout (##[1:10] done));
```

| Function | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$rose(x)` / `$fell(x)` | x went 0→1 / 1→0 since the last clock |
| `$stable(x)` / `$changed(x)` | x is the same as / different from the last clock |
| `$past(x, n)` | x as sampled n clocks ago |
| `$onehot(x)` / `$onehot0(x)` | exactly one bit set / at most one bit set |
| `$isunknown(x)` | any bit is X or Z |
| `$countones(x)` | number of 1 bits |

| Directive | Simulation | Formal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assert property` | reports failures | tries to prove it for all legal inputs |
| `assume property` | checked like an assert | **constrains** the inputs (the environment's rules) |
| `cover property` | counts hits | finds a witness trace, or proves it unreachable |

### Explanation
- In **JasperGold** (or any formal tool): write `assume`s for the input protocol the block can rely on, and `assert`s for its outputs. A wrong or too-strong assume over-constrains the inputs and hides real bugs, so back every important assumption with covers showing interesting behavior is still reachable.
- `throughout` requires the left expression on **every** cycle of the right sequence.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Variable latency: use `##[1:$]` with a terminating condition, e.g. `(in_vld, v = in_data) |-> ##[1:20] (out_vld && out_data == v + 1)`. With in-order outputs, a tag or counter is needed to match the right output.
- Local variables can't be used to check *ordering* across threads; use a scoreboard for that.

### Follow-ups
- *`$past` with an enable?* `$past(x, 1, en)` samples only on cycles where `en` was high.
- *`sequence` vs `property`?* Sequences describe patterns over time and can be reused inside properties; properties add implication, `not`, `disable iff`.

title: What is the difference between |-> and |=> in SVA?
answer: Consequent starts in the same cycle (overlapping, `|->`) vs the next cycle (non-overlapping, `|=>`). `a |=> b` is equivalent to `a |-> ##1 b`.
solution:
**Key idea:** both are implications that only check the consequent when the antecedent matches. `|->` (overlapping) starts the consequent **in the same cycle** the antecedent ends; `|=>` (non-overlapping) starts it **one cycle later**. `a |=> b` is exactly `a |-> ##1 b`.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",           "wave": "p..." },
  { "name": "a",             "wave": "10.." },
  { "name": "b for a |-> b", "wave": "1x.." },
  { "name": "b for a |=> b", "wave": "x1x." }
],
  "head": { "text": "|-> checks b in the same cycle as a; |=> checks the next cycle", "tick": 1 } }
```

| | `a \|-> b` | `a \|=> b` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | overlapping | non-overlapping |
| b checked at | cycle of a | cycle after a |
| Equivalent | | `a \|-> ##1 b` |
| Typical use | combinational response, same-cycle rules (`valid \|-> !$isunknown(data)`) | registered response (`wr_en \|=> !empty`, `req \|=> ack`) |

### Explanation
- Both pass **vacuously** when the antecedent is false, so add a `cover property` on the antecedent.
- If the antecedent is a multi-cycle sequence, `|->` starts the consequent on the antecedent's **last** cycle.

```systemverilog
a_same : assert property (@(posedge clk) valid |-> !$isunknown(data));
a_next : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) wr_en && !full |=> !empty);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `|->` when the design responds a cycle later (registered output) gives false failures: draw the waveform first.
- `a ##1 b |-> c` checks `c` at b's cycle, not a's.

### Follow-ups
- **Response within 1 to 3 cycles?** `a |-> ##[1:3] b` (or `a |=> ##[0:2] b`).
- **Is `|=>` allowed in a sequence?** No, implication is a property operator; it can't be nested inside a sequence.

title: What is a vacuous pass, and how do you detect it?
answer: Antecedent false: the implication passes without checking anything. Add a `cover property` on the antecedent and check the hit count (and the tool's vacuous-pass statistics).
solution:
**Key idea:** for `A |-> C`, every clock where `A` does not match counts as a **vacuous success**: nothing was checked. A property whose antecedent never fires passes the whole simulation and proves nothing. Pair every implication with a `cover` of its antecedent.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",               "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "wr_en (antecedent)", "wave": "0......" },
  { "name": "empty",             "wave": "1......" },
  { "name": "a_wr result",       "wave": "=======", "data": ["vac", "vac", "vac", "vac", "vac", "vac", "vac"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "wr_en |=> !empty: wr_en is never 1, so every attempt passes vacuously" } }
```

| Statistic (VCS/Xcelium report) | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| attempts | clocks where an evaluation started |
| real (non-vacuous) successes | antecedent matched and consequent held |
| vacuous successes | antecedent did not match |
| failures | antecedent matched, consequent failed |

### Explanation
```systemverilog
a_wr : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) wr_en |=> !empty);
c_wr : cover  property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) wr_en);   // must be > 0
// Stronger: cover the full scenario, not just the trigger
c_wr_full : cover property (@(posedge clk) full ##1 rd_en ##1 wr_en);
```
- A cover hit count of 0 means the check was **never exercised**: a stimulus or coverage hole.
- In formal, an unreachable cover means dead logic or over-constrained assumptions.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A wrong signal name or polarity in the antecedent (`rst_n` vs `rst`) produces silent vacuity.
- `disable iff` held true for the whole sim makes everything "disabled", not checked.

### Follow-ups
- **How do you report vacuity automatically?** Track real-success counts in the coverage report or use the simulator's vacuity reporting; review covers with zero hits.
- **Is a property without implication ever vacuous?** No: `assert property (!(full && empty))` is checked every cycle.

title: Why are concurrent assertions race-free?
answer: Values are sampled in the Preponed region, before any updates in that time step; properties are evaluated in the Observed region and action blocks run in Reactive.
solution:
**Key idea:** a concurrent assertion **samples** its signals in the **Preponed** region (before anything changes in that time step) and **evaluates** in the **Observed** region. It sees the same pre-edge values a flip-flop does, so `<=` updates on the same edge can't race it. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Preponed
SAMPLE values for assertions"] --> B["Active
RTL always blocks, blocking assigns"] B --> C["Inactive
#0 events"] C --> D["NBA
nonblocking updates"] D --> E["Observed
EVALUATE properties"] E --> F["Reactive
action blocks, program code"] F --> G["Postponed
$strobe, assert final"] ``` ```wavedrom { "signal": [ { "name": "clk", "wave": "p...." }, { "name": "q (RTL, <=)", "wave": "0.1..", "node": "..a" }, { "name": "q sampled (Preponed)", "wave": "0..1.", "node": "...b" } ], "edge": [ "a~>b seen one edge later" ], "head": { "text": "q updates at edge 2, but assertions at edge 2 still sample 0", "tick": 0 } } ``` ### Explanation - Sampling happens once per time step, before Active, so the order of `always` blocks doesn't matter. - Evaluation in Observed means the property uses only sampled values (except `disable iff`, which uses current values). - Action blocks (`else $error`) run in Reactive, after the design has settled. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The flip side: an assertion sees a value **one edge later** than the RTL update: `d` driven at edge *n* is visible to the property at edge *n+1*. - Immediate assertions inside `always_comb` are **not** race-free; use deferred (`assert #0` / `assert final`) to filter glitches. - Testbench drives without clocking blocks can still race the *DUT*; the assertion is fine, the stimulus isn't. ### Follow-ups - **Which value does `$rose(x)` compare?** The sampled value at this clock vs the sampled value at the previous clock. - **What uses current (not sampled) values?** `disable iff` and the clocking event itself.

title: What is the difference between [->3] (goto) and [=3] (non-consecutive) repetition?
answer: Goto `[->3]` ends ON the 3rd occurrence; non-consecutive `[=3]` matches the 3rd occurrence and may extend until just before the next occurrence. Interview line: [->n] = "on the nth one"; [=n] = "after the nth one, before the next one".
solution:
**Key idea:** both count non-consecutive occurrences of `b`. **Goto `b[->3]`** ends exactly **on** the 3rd `b`. **Non-consecutive `b[=3]`** matches on the 3rd `b` *and every following cycle until (not including) the next `b`*. The difference only shows when something follows the repetition.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",            "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "b",              "wave": "010101001" },
  {},
  { "name": "b[->3] matches", "wave": "000001000" },
  { "name": "b[=3] matches",  "wave": "000001110" },
  { "name": "b[*3] matches",  "wave": "000000000" }
],
  "head": { "text": "[->3] ends ON the 3rd b; [=3] can stretch until just before the 4th b; [*3] needs 3 consecutive", "tick": 1 } }
```

| Operator | Expansion | Ends |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `b[*3]` | `b ##1 b ##1 b` | after 3 consecutive b |
| `b[->3]` | `(!b[*0:$] ##1 b)[*3]` | on the 3rd b |
| `b[=3]` | `b[->3] ##1 !b[*0:$]` | on the 3rd b or any later cycle before the next b |

### Explanation
With `c` after the repetition (start at cycle 1):
- `b[->3] ##1 c` requires `c` **exactly** the cycle after the 3rd `b` (cycle 7 here).
- `b[=3] ##1 c` accepts `c` at cycle 7, 8 or 9, as long as no 4th `b` came first.

```systemverilog
// exactly the cycle after the 4th beat, the burst must end
a_burst_end : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(start) |-> beat[->4] ##1 done);
// 3 writes some time before the commit, no extra write before it
a_commit    : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(open) |-> wr[=3] ##1 commit);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `[->1]` is the common "wait for the next occurrence": `req |-> ack[->1] ##0 data_ok`.
- Unbounded repetitions in an antecedent spawn many threads; wrap with `first_match` or bound them.

### Follow-ups
- **`b[->1:3]`?** Ends on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd occurrence (multiple matches).
- **Equivalent of `b[=3]` with goto?** `b[->3] ##1 !b[*0:$]`.

title: What is the difference between the sequence operators and and intersect?
answer: `and`: both sequences start together; the composite matches when both have matched, ending at the later end. `intersect`: same start and the same end (same length).
solution:
**Key idea:** both require two sequences to start at the same cycle and both to match. `s1 and s2` ends when the **later** of the two ends (lengths may differ). `s1 intersect s2` requires them to **end on the same cycle** (same length).

Example, all attempts start at cycle 1: `s1 = a ##[1:3] b` (b true at cycles 2 and 4), `s2 = c ##2 d` (ends at cycle 3).

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p...." },
  { "name": "a",   "wave": "010.." },
  { "name": "b",   "wave": "00101" },
  { "name": "c",   "wave": "010.." },
  { "name": "d",   "wave": "00010" }
],
  "head": { "text": "cycles 1..4: s1 can end at 2 or 4, s2 ends at 3", "tick": 0 } }
```

| Composite | Matches end at | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `s1 or s2` | 2, 3, 4 | any match of either |
| `s1 and s2` | 3, 4 | pairs (2,3) end at 3 and (4,3) end at 4 |
| `s1 intersect s2` | none | s1 ends at 2 or 4, s2 at 3: never the same cycle |

### Explanation
- `intersect` is the tool for **length constraints**: `(req ##[1:$] ack) intersect (1'b1 [*1:8])` means ack arrives within 8 cycles.
- `within` is built from `intersect`: `s1 within s2` = `(1[*0:$] ##1 s1 ##1 1[*0:$]) intersect s2`.
- `throughout` too: `e throughout s` = `(e[*0:$]) intersect s`.

```systemverilog
// handshake must complete in at most 6 cycles
a_len : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(req) |->
          (req ##[1:$] ack) intersect (1'b1 [*2:6]));
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- With `and`, the composite keeps waiting for the slower sequence: an unbounded `s2` makes the whole thing unbounded.
- `and`/`or` on *properties* are different operators (property conjunction/disjunction) from the *sequence* ones, though they read the same.

### Follow-ups
- **What does `first_match(s1 and s2)` add?** Keeps only the earliest end (cycle 3 here), killing the extra thread.

title: How do you check that output data equals input data from N cycles ago?
answer: `$past(in, N)` for a fixed latency (with an enable/valid qualifier, `$past(x, n, en)` for stalls); use a local variable if the latency is variable.

title: How do you check that a response matches its request ID when the latency is variable?
answer: Use a local variable to capture the ID in the antecedent and compare it in the consequent: `(arvalid && arready, id = arid) |-> ##[1:32] (rvalid && rid == id)`.
solution:
**Key idea:** a **local variable** in the property captures the ID when the request handshakes; each attempt is its own thread with its own copy, so many requests can be in flight and each waits for *its* ID.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",     "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "arvalid", "wave": "010....." },
  { "name": "arid",    "wave": "x=x.....", "data": ["5"], "node": ".a" },
  { "name": "id (local)", "wave": "x=......", "data": ["5"] },
  { "name": "rvalid",  "wave": "0..1.10." },
  { "name": "rid",     "wave": "x..=x=x.", "data": ["3", "5"], "node": ".....b" }
],
  "edge": [ "a~>b match rid == id" ],
  "head": { "text": "capture arid=5; rid=3 is ignored; rid=5 at cycle 5 satisfies the attempt", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_id_resp;
  logic [3:0] id;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (arvalid && arready, id = arid)
      |-> ##[1:32] (rvalid && rready && rlast && rid == id);
endproperty
a_id_resp : assert property (p_id_resp)
  else $error("[%0t] no response for ARID %0d within 32 cycles", $time, $sampled(arid));
c_id_resp : cover  property (p_id_resp);
```

### Explanation
- Syntax: `(expression, var = value)` assigns the local variable when that subsequence matches.
- `##[1:32]` bounds the wait (a safety property, good for simulation and formal). For an unbounded wait use `s_eventually` / `strong(##[1:$] ...)`.
- Local variables can also be used for data integrity: capture the write data with the address and compare on the read.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Two outstanding requests with the **same** ID can both be satisfied by one response: SVA threads don't "consume" matches. Counting outstanding transactions per ID needs an aux model or the scoreboard.
- Only R beats with `rlast` should close a burst; matching any beat passes too early.

### Follow-ups
- **Response must not arrive for an ID that was never requested?** Needs per-ID outstanding counters: aux logic (`cnt[id]`) plus `rvalid |-> cnt[rid] != 0`.

title: Can SVA check in-order completion of many outstanding transactions?
answer: Not cleanly: each attempt is an independent thread. Use an auxiliary counter/queue model (modeling code next to the assertions) or the scoreboard.
solution:
**Key idea:** not with pure SVA. Each attempt is an **independent thread**, so assertions can say "every request eventually gets a response" but not "responses come back **in request order**" or "never more than N outstanding". Add a small **auxiliary model** (a tag FIFO / counter in RTL-style code) and assert against it, or leave ordering to the scoreboard. ```mermaid flowchart LR REQ["req_fire, req_id"] --> AUX["aux tag FIFO
wr_ptr / rd_ptr"] RSP["rsp_fire, rsp_id"] --> AUX AUX -->|head_id, count| SVA["a_in_order: rsp_fire implies rsp_id == head_id"] AUX --> SVA2["a_max_out: count never exceeds N"] ``` ### Code (formal-friendly: fixed array, no queues) ```systemverilog module inorder_sva #(parameter int IDW = 4, parameter int DEPTH = 8) ( input logic clk, rst_n, input logic req_fire, rsp_fire, input logic [IDW-1:0] req_id, rsp_id ); localparam int AW = $clog2(DEPTH); logic [IDW-1:0] tag_mem [DEPTH]; logic [AW:0] wr_ptr, rd_ptr; // extra bit tells full from empty wire [AW:0] count = wr_ptr - rd_ptr; always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) if (!rst_n) begin wr_ptr <= '0; rd_ptr <= '0; end else begin if (req_fire) begin tag_mem[wr_ptr[AW-1:0]] <= req_id; wr_ptr <= wr_ptr + 1; end if (rsp_fire) rd_ptr <= rd_ptr + 1; end default clocking @(posedge clk); endclocking default disable iff (!rst_n); a_no_spurious : assert property (rsp_fire |-> count != 0); a_in_order : assert property (rsp_fire |-> rsp_id == tag_mem[rd_ptr[AW-1:0]]); a_max_out : assert property (count <= DEPTH); c_full : cover property (count == DEPTH); endmodule ``` | Check | Pure SVA | Aux model | Scoreboard | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | each req gets a rsp within N | yes | | yes | | response ID matches a request | weak (no consumption) | yes | yes | | in-order completion | no | yes | yes | | data transformation correct | limited | | yes | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Request and response in the same cycle: the aux model must update both pointers (it does here). - Queues and class objects are not allowed in concurrent assertion expressions; keep aux logic static for formal. ### Follow-ups - **AXI (in order per ID only)?** One tag FIFO per ID, or a per-ID counter plus a scoreboard.

title: What does disable iff do to an in-flight assertion attempt?
answer: Aborts it: the attempt counts as neither pass nor fail. `disable iff` is asynchronous and uses current (not sampled) values. Use `default disable iff (!rst_n);`.
solution:
**Key idea:** when the `disable iff` condition becomes true, every attempt in progress is **aborted** and reported as *disabled*: neither a pass nor a failure. The condition is checked **asynchronously** with **current** values, not sampled ones.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "rst_n", "wave": "1..0.1." },
  { "name": "req",   "wave": "010...." },
  { "name": "ack",   "wave": "0......" },
  { "name": "attempt (req |-> ##[1:4] ack)", "wave": "x=.=x..", "data": ["waiting", "DISABLED"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "reset asserts mid-window: the attempt is aborted, not failed", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
module blk_sva (input logic clk, rst_n, req, ack);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);       // applies to every assertion below

  a_req_ack : assert property ($rose(req) |-> ##[1:4] ack);

  // $past right after reset can see pre-reset values: guard it
  a_hold : assert property ($past(rst_n) && $past(req && !ack) |-> req);
endmodule
```
- Without it, assertions fire false errors during reset (X on signals, `$past` returning reset/X values).
- Because it is asynchronous, a one-cycle reset glitch between edges still kills in-flight attempts.

| Outcome | Counted as |
| --- | --- |
| antecedent false | vacuous pass |
| consequent holds | real pass |
| consequent fails | failure |
| `disable iff` true during attempt | disabled (neither) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `disable iff` is only allowed at the top of a property (not nested).
- Too broad a disable condition (e.g. tied to a debug mode always on) silently disables checking: watch the disabled count.
- `accept_on` / `reject_on` are the newer alternatives that turn the abort into a pass or fail.

### Follow-ups
- **Assertion on reset behavior itself?** Write it without `disable iff`: `$rose(rst_n) |-> count == 0`.

title: Why use bind for assertions?
answer: Adds checkers without editing RTL; the designer owns the RTL, the verifier owns the checkers; the same checker binds into every instance and is reused directly in formal (JasperGold).
solution:
**Key idea:** `bind` instantiates a checker module **inside** a design module (or specific instances) from outside the RTL source. The RTL stays untouched, the checker sees internal signals through port connections, and the same checker runs in simulation and formal.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  RTL["fifo.sv (designer owned)"] --> I1["u_fifo_a"]
  RTL --> I2["u_fifo_b"]
  SVA["fifo_sva.sv (verifier owned)"] --> BIND["bind fifo fifo_sva u_sva (.*)"]
  BIND -->|instantiated inside| I1
  BIND -->|instantiated inside| I2
  BIND --> FV["same bind file in JasperGold"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// every instance of module fifo gets a checker
bind fifo fifo_sva #(.DEPTH(DEPTH)) u_fifo_sva (.*);

// only selected instances
bind fifo: top.u_core.u_fifo_a, top.u_core.u_fifo_b fifo_sva u_fifo_sva (.*);

// explicit connections when names differ
bind fifo fifo_sva u_fifo_sva (.clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .wr_en(push), .rd_en(pop),
                               .full(full), .empty(empty));
```

| Approach | Edits RTL? | Reuse across instances | Sees internals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| assertions inline in RTL | yes | yes | yes |
| assertions in TB via hierarchical paths | no | no (paths per instance) | yes |
| **bind** | no | yes | yes (via ports) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `.*` needs matching names in the target scope; parameters can reference the target's parameters (`DEPTH`).
- Checker ports should all be **inputs**: a checker must never drive design signals.
- Keep bind files in the verification file list, not compiled into synthesis.

### Follow-ups
- **Bind to an interface?** Yes, `bind` works on modules, interfaces and specific instances.
- **`checker ... endchecker`?** SV's dedicated checker construct, also bindable; plain modules are more common in practice.

title: What do assert, assume and cover mean in formal verification?
answer: Prove / constrain / show reachable. In simulation, assume is checked like assert; cover counts matches.
solution:
**Key idea:** **assert** = a proof target, **assume** = a constraint on inputs (the legal environment), **cover** = a reachability goal that must produce a trace. In simulation `assume` is just checked like `assert`, and `cover` counts hits.

| Directive | Simulation | Formal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assert property` | checks, reports failures | must hold on all reachable states; a failure gives a CEX trace |
| `assume property` | checked like an assert (catches a bad stimulus) | restricts input values the tool may choose |
| `cover property` | counts matches (functional coverage) | proves the scenario is reachable and shows a trace |
| `restrict property` | ignored | formal-only state-space pruning |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ENV["assume: legal inputs"] --> DUT["DUT under proof"]
  DUT --> AS["assert: proven or CEX"]
  DUT --> CV["cover: reachable or unreachable"]
  CV -->|unreachable| WARN["dead logic or over-constrained assumes"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// Environment rule: the upstream master never drops valid before ready
m_vld_hold : assume property (@(posedge clk) valid && !ready |=> valid);
// DUT promise
a_no_ovf   : assert property (@(posedge clk) full |-> !push_accepted);
// Sanity: can we actually fill the FIFO?
c_full     : cover  property (@(posedge clk) full);
```
- **Assume-guarantee**: the same property is an `assert` on the block that drives a signal and an `assume` on the block that consumes it.
- Always run covers alongside asserts: a proof is only meaningful if the interesting states are reachable.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Over-constraining** with assumes makes proofs pass trivially and hides bugs; a conflicting set of assumes can make *everything* pass.
- An assumption on an output of the DUT constrains the design itself: assume inputs only.

### Follow-ups
- **Bounded vs full proof?** Bounded = holds up to N cycles from reset; full = holds for all reachable states.

title: How do you make an eventuality property fail at the end of simulation?
answer: Wrap it in `strong(...)` or use `s_eventually`; `##[1:$]` is weak by default, so an attempt still waiting when the sim ends does not fail.

title: What is the difference between an immediate and a deferred immediate assertion?
answer: Deferred (`assert #0` / `assert final`) reports after zero-delay glitches settle in the time step; simple immediate reports as soon as the statement executes. `assert final` reports in the Postponed region.
solution:
**Key idea:** a **simple immediate** assertion checks the expression the instant the statement executes, so in `always_comb` it can fire on a **zero-delay glitch** while signals are still settling. A **deferred** assertion (`assert #0` or `assert final`) queues its report and only reports the result of the **last** evaluation in that time step.

| Event within one time step | `sel` | simple `assert` | `assert #0` | `assert final` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| comb logic evaluates first input | 3 (glitch) | **fails** | pending (flushed) | pending (flushed) |
| second input settles | 1 | passes | pending | pending |
| Observed / Reactive | 1 | | reports pass | |
| Postponed | 1 | | | reports pass |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p..." },
  { "name": "sel (with 0-delay glitch)", "wave": "=.=.", "data": ["0", "3 then 1"] },
  { "name": "simple assert", "wave": "x.=x", "data": ["false error"] },
  { "name": "assert #0 / final", "wave": "x.=x", "data": ["pass"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "the glitch to 3 exists only inside one time step" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
always_comb assert (!(rd_en && empty)) else $error("read on empty");   // simple: glitch-prone
always_comb assert #0   (sel inside {[0:2]});      // observed deferred
always_comb assert final ($onehot0(grant));         // final deferred, Postponed region
```

### Explanation
- `#0` deferred: report scheduled in the Reactive region; `final`: in Postponed, after everything (including program code) settled.
- Deferred assertions are allowed outside procedural code too (`assert #0 (...)` at module level acts like an `always_comb`).
- Action blocks of deferred assertions may contain only a single subroutine call.

### Follow-ups
- **Immediate vs concurrent?** Immediate: no clock, current values, one point in time. Concurrent: clocked, sampled values, temporal.

title: Write assertions: valid must stay high and data must stay stable until ready (valid/ready handshake)
prompt: For a valid/ready (AXI-style) channel: once `valid` is asserted it must not drop until `ready` is seen, and `data` must hold while stalled. Write the must-have protocol assertions plus covers, as a bindable checker.
answer: `valid && !ready |=> valid`, `valid && !ready |=> $stable(data)`, plus `valid |-> !$isunknown(data)` and a cover for a stall.

title: Write an assertion: a Gray-coded pointer changes at most one bit per clock
prompt: An async FIFO passes its write pointer to the read domain in Gray code. Write an assertion that the Gray pointer changes at most one bit per clock (in its own clock domain).
answer: `$past(rst_n) |-> $countones(gray_ptr ^ $past(gray_ptr)) <= 1` (equivalently `$onehot0(gray_ptr ^ $past(gray_ptr))`), clocked in the pointer's own domain.
solution:
**Key idea:** XOR the current and previous pointer values: the result has a 1 for each bit that changed. A Gray pointer must change **0 or 1** bits per clock, so `$countones(...) <= 1` (or `$onehot0(...)`). Clock it on the **source** domain and skip the first cycle out of reset.

| wr_bin | gray = bin ^ (bin >> 1) | gray ^ $past(gray) | ones |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 000 | | |
| 1 | 001 | 001 | 1 |
| 2 | 011 | 010 | 1 |
| 3 | 010 | 001 | 1 |
| 4 | 110 | 100 | 1 |
| 7 -> 0 (wrap) | 100 -> 000 | 100 | 1 |
| bug: binary 3 -> 4 sent | 011 -> 100 | 111 | **3: fail** |

### Code
```systemverilog
module gray_sva #(parameter int W = 4) (
  input logic         wclk, wrst_n,
  input logic [W-1:0] wptr_gray
);
  a_gray_1bit : assert property (@(posedge wclk) disable iff (!wrst_n)
                  $past(wrst_n) |-> $countones(wptr_gray ^ $past(wptr_gray)) <= 1)
    else $error("[%0t] gray pointer changed %0d bits", $time,
                $countones(wptr_gray ^ $past(wptr_gray)));

  // equivalent form
  a_gray_oh0  : assert property (@(posedge wclk) disable iff (!wrst_n)
                  $past(wrst_n) |-> $onehot0(wptr_gray ^ $past(wptr_gray)));

  // the pointer actually moves (non-vacuous)
  c_gray_move : cover property (@(posedge wclk) wptr_gray != $past(wptr_gray));
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- Why it matters: the read domain samples the pointer through a 2-flop synchronizer. If only one bit changes, a metastable sample resolves to either the old or the new value; both are safe. Multi-bit changes can produce a torn value that was never a real pointer.
- `$past(wrst_n)` guard avoids comparing against the reset value on the first cycle.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Clock it on the **write** clock: sampling on the read clock can legitimately see multiple increments between samples.
- The *synchronized* copy in the read domain may change by more than one bit between read clocks if wclk is faster; check the source register, not the sync output.
- The pointer must also be **registered** (no glitchy combinational Gray logic crossing the domain): a structural CDC check, not an assertion.

### Follow-ups
- **Non-power-of-two depth?** Plain Gray wrap breaks the one-bit rule; this assertion catches it.

title: Write assertions: a FIFO never overflows or underflows (as a bound checker)
prompt: A synchronous FIFO module `fifo` has ports `clk, rst_n, wr_en, rd_en, full, empty` and parameter `DEPTH`. Write a checker that the FIFO never overflows or underflows and that its flags are consistent, and attach it without editing the RTL.
answer: Checker module with `default clocking` and `default disable iff`: `full |-> !wr_en`, `empty |-> !rd_en`, `!(full && empty)`, `cover ($rose(full))`; attach with `bind fifo fifo_sva #(.DEPTH(DEPTH)) u_fifo_sva (.*);`.

title: Assertions vs scoreboard: when do you use which?
answer: SVA for local, cycle-accurate protocol rules (catches the bug at the cycle and location). Scoreboard for end-to-end data correctness, ordering and transformations.
solution:
**Key idea:** **assertions** check *local, cycle-accurate rules* right where and when they are broken; a **scoreboard** checks *end-to-end data correctness* (ordering, transformations, missing/extra transactions) at the transaction level. Real environments use both.

| | SVA | Scoreboard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level | signals, cycles | transactions |
| Best for | handshakes, stability, one-hot, timeouts, Gray, FIFO flags | data integrity, ordering, reference model compare |
| Catches the bug | at the exact cycle and signal | later, at the comparison point |
| Location | bound to the RTL block (reused in formal) | UVM env |
| Reuse | block, subsystem, formal | block to SoC with the agent |
| Weak at | many outstanding transactions, complex math | cycle-level timing rules |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  DUT["DUT"] -->|pins| SVA["bound SVA: protocol rules at each cycle"]
  DUT -->|pins| MON["monitor"]
  MON -->|transactions| SCB["scoreboard: expected vs actual"]
  REF["reference model"] --> SCB
```

### Explanation
- Example: an AXI crossbar sends W data to two slaves at once. A one-hot assertion on `s_wvalid` fires at **that cycle**; a scoreboard would only notice a wrong memory value at the end of the test.
- Conversely "read returns the last written data after reordering" is natural in a scoreboard and painful in SVA.

### Follow-ups
- **Overlap?** Fine: an assertion can catch the root cause earlier while the scoreboard confirms end-to-end correctness.
- **Where do you check reset values?** Assertions (`$rose(rst_n) |-> ...`) or a reset sequence in RAL.

title: How do assertions contribute to coverage?
answer: `cover property` hits are functional coverage. Assertion pass/fail/vacuous counts appear in the coverage report (VCS/Verdi) and map to verification plan items.
solution:
**Key idea:** `cover property` / `cover sequence` statements are **functional coverage points** that count temporal scenarios, and every assertion's attempt/pass/fail/vacuous statistics land in the coverage database. Both can be linked to verification-plan items.

| Construct | Counts | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cover property (p)` | each successful match of p | temporal scenarios: stall then transfer, back-to-back |
| `cover sequence (s)` | every match, including multiple per attempt | counting occurrences |
| assertion statistics | attempts, real passes, vacuous passes, failures | proving checks were exercised |
| covergroup | value bins / crosses | data-value coverage |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  COV["cover property hits"] --> DB["coverage DB (vdb / ucdb)"]
  ASTAT["assert pass / fail / vacuous counts"] --> DB
  CG["covergroups"] --> DB
  DB --> VP["vplan items in Verdi / vManager"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// Temporal scenarios that a covergroup can't express easily
c_stall_xfer : cover property (@(posedge clk) valid && !ready [*2:$] ##1 valid && ready);
c_full_empty : cover property (@(posedge clk) full ##[1:$] empty);
// Antecedent cover keeps an implication honest
c_req        : cover property (@(posedge clk) $rose(req));
```

### Explanation
- Assertion coverage tells you a check was **non-vacuously exercised**; it is not the same as "the feature works".
- In formal, a cover returning *unreachable* is a strong signal of dead logic or over-constraint.

### Follow-ups
- **Cover property vs covergroup?** Cover property for sequences over time; covergroups for values and crosses (can be sampled from a sequence match via a function call in the match item).

title: Compare immediate and concurrent assertions
answer: Immediate: procedural, evaluated when the statement executes, current values, `assert (expr)`. Concurrent: clocked, temporal, sampled (Preponed) values, `assert property`, in module/interface/program/bind.
solution:
**Key idea:** an **immediate** assertion is a procedural `if` with reporting: no clock, checked when the statement runs, using current values. A **concurrent** assertion is clocked and temporal: it samples values at the clock edge and can span many cycles.

| | Immediate | Concurrent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | procedural code (`always`, `initial`, tasks, class methods) | module, interface, program, checker, `bind`; also in `always` (inferred clock) |
| Timing | when the statement executes | every clock edge, across cycles |
| Values | current (glitch-prone) | sampled in Preponed |
| Keyword | `assert (expr)` | `assert property (...)` |
| Temporal operators | no | `##`, `[*]`, `\|->`, `$past`... |
| Use | single-point checks in a checker/scoreboard/model | protocol rules over time |

```systemverilog
// Immediate (simple) and deferred
always_comb assert (!(rd_en && empty)) else $error("read on empty");
always_comb assert final ($onehot0(grant));

// In a UVM scoreboard (classes can only use immediate assertions)
assert (tr.addr inside {[0:'hFFF]}) else `uvm_error("SB", "addr out of range")

// Concurrent
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |-> ##[1:4] ack);
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q{"Does the rule involve time or a clock?"} -->|no| IMM["immediate assert (deferred if in always_comb)"]
  Q -->|yes| CONC["concurrent assert property"]
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Concurrent assertions are **not allowed in classes**; use immediate ones or put SVA in an interface.
- Simple immediate assertions in `always_comb` can fire on delta glitches: use `assert #0` / `assert final`.

### Follow-ups
- **Concurrent assertion inside an `always @(posedge clk)` block?** Allowed; the clock is inferred from the block and the enclosing `if` becomes part of the antecedent.

title: Explain the anatomy of an SVA check: sequence, property and directive
answer: sequence = a pattern over time; property = clock + reset + implication around sequences; directive = assert / assume / cover (restrict for formal). Name every directive and give it an action block.
solution:
**Key idea:** three layers. A **sequence** describes a pattern over cycles, a **property** adds the clock, reset and implication (the rule), and a **directive** (`assert`, `assume`, `cover`, `restrict`) says what the tool should do with it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SEQ["sequence s_req_ack: req ##[1:3] ack"] --> PROP["property p_handshake: clock + disable iff + implication"]
  PROP --> A["assert: check, report failure"]
  PROP --> M["assume: constrain inputs"]
  PROP --> C["cover: did it happen?"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
sequence s_req_ack;
  req ##[1:3] ack;                       // a pattern over time
endsequence

property p_handshake;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    $rose(req) |-> s_req_ack;            // implication + clock + reset
endproperty

a_handshake : assert property (p_handshake)
  else `uvm_error("SVA", "ack not seen within 3 cycles of req")
c_handshake : cover  property (p_handshake);

// Parameterized and reusable
property p_resp_within(logic trig, logic resp, int unsigned max);
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) trig |-> ##[1:max] resp;
endproperty
a_rd : assert property (p_resp_within(rd_req, rd_ack, 8));
```

| Layer | Contains | Can be reused |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sequence | `##`, repetition, `and/or/intersect`, local vars | in other sequences and properties |
| property | clock, `disable iff`, `\|->`/`\|=>`, `not`, `strong` | by several directives |
| directive | `assert` / `assume` / `cover` / `restrict` + label + action block | n/a |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Label every directive (`a_handshake:`); unlabeled assertions get tool-generated names that are hard to waive or control.
- A `sequence` with a clock can be used standalone with `cover sequence`, and its `.triggered` can be used elsewhere.

### Follow-ups
- **Live-coding process?** 1) draw the waveform, 2) pick `|->` or `|=>`, 3) write the assertion with `default clocking` / `default disable iff`, 4) add a cover for the antecedent.

title: Explain SVA delay and consecutive repetition operators (##n, ##[m:n], [*n], ##[1:$])
answer: `a ##2 b` b exactly 2 cycles after a; `a ##[1:3] b` 1 to 3 cycles; `a ##[1:$] b` eventually (weak by default); `a[*3]` = a a a consecutive; `a[*2:4]` 2 to 4 consecutive cycles.
solution:
**Key idea:** `##` moves forward in clock cycles; `[*n]` repeats a sequence on **consecutive** cycles. Ranges (`##[1:3]`, `[*2:4]`) create several possible matches (one thread each), and `$` means unbounded.

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `a ##2 b` | b exactly 2 cycles after a |
| `a ##[1:3] b` | b 1 to 3 cycles after a |
| `a ##[1:$] b` | b eventually (weak by default) |
| `a ##0 b` | b in the same cycle a ends (fusion) |
| `a[*3]` | a a a, consecutive |
| `a[*2:4]` | a for 2 to 4 consecutive cycles |
| `a[*0:$]` | zero or more cycles of a |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "a",   "wave": "01..0.." },
  { "name": "b",   "wave": "0....10" },
  {},
  { "name": "a[*3] matches", "wave": "0..10.." },
  { "name": "a[*3] ##2 b",   "wave": "0....10" }
],
  "head": { "text": "a is high 3 consecutive cycles (1-3), b two cycles after the last a", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// busy must stay high 2 to 4 cycles after start, then done
a_busy : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(start) |-> busy[*2:4] ##1 done);
// grant 1 to 3 cycles after request
a_gnt  : assert property (@(posedge clk) req |-> ##[1:3] gnt);
// a pulse is exactly one cycle wide
a_pulse: assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(p) |=> !p);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `##[1:$]` in an **antecedent** spawns a new thread every cycle: slow sims; use `first_match` or a bound.
- `##[1:$]` in a consequent is **weak**: a hang doesn't fail (use `strong` or a bound).
- `a[*0]` is an empty match; `a[*0] ##1 b` behaves like `b`, which surprises people.

### Follow-ups
- **Non-consecutive repetition?** `[->n]` (goto) and `[=n]`.

title: Explain the SVA sampled-value functions: $rose, $fell, $stable, $changed, $past
answer: $rose LSB 0->1, $fell LSB 1->0, $stable unchanged, $changed = !$stable, $past(x,n) value n clocks ago, $past(x,n,en) counting only enabled clocks. Others: $onehot, $onehot0, $isunknown, $countones. Pitfall: $rose checks only the LSB of a vector.
solution:
**Key idea:** these functions compare **sampled** values at the current clock with those at the previous clock. They make edge and stability rules one-liners, but `$rose/$fell` look only at the **LSB** of a vector.

| Function | True when (sampled values) |
| --- | --- |
| `$rose(x)` | LSB of x went 0 -> 1 since the last clock |
| `$fell(x)` | LSB of x went 1 -> 0 |
| `$stable(x)` | x unchanged since the last clock |
| `$changed(x)` | `!$stable(x)` |
| `$past(x, n)` | x from n clocks ago (default 1) |
| `$past(x, n, en)` | x from n clocks *where `en` was true* |
| `$onehot(x)` / `$onehot0(x)` | exactly one / at most one bit set |
| `$isunknown(x)` | any bit X or Z |
| `$countones(x)` | number of 1 bits |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",        "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "x",          "wave": "0.1..0." },
  { "name": "$rose(x)",   "wave": "0.10..." },
  { "name": "$fell(x)",   "wave": "0....10" },
  { "name": "$stable(x)", "wave": "1.01.01" }
],
  "head": { "text": "evaluated at each edge from the sampled values", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// Pipeline with 2-cycle latency
a_pipe : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
           out_valid |-> out_data == $past(in_data, 2) + 1);

// Bus pitfall: $rose(state) only sees state[0]
a_bad  : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(state) |-> ...);          // wrong for a bus
a_good : assert property (@(posedge clk) (state == BUSY && $past(state) != BUSY) |-> ...);
// Or: $changed(addr) for any change on a bus
a_addr : assert property (@(posedge clk) valid && !ready |=> !$changed(addr));
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `$rose(x)` is also true when x goes X -> 1 on the first sampled clock; combine with reset guards.
- `$past` in the first cycles after reset returns pre-reset values: guard with `$past(rst_n)`.
- `$stable` treats X -> X as stable; add `!$isunknown` where it matters.

### Follow-ups
- **Use these outside assertions?** Yes, with a clocking event argument: `$rose(x, @(posedge clk))` in procedural code.

title: Explain throughout, within, first_match and .triggered in SVA
answer: `e throughout s`: e holds every cycle of s. `s1 within s2`: s1 occurs entirely inside s2's span. `first_match(s)`: only the earliest match (kills extra threads). `s.triggered`: s has ended in the current cycle (use in another property).

title: Write request/acknowledge assertions with a timeout
prompt: A requester raises `req` and must hold it until `ack`. The responder must answer within 8 cycles. Write the assertions (with covers).
answer: `$rose(req) |-> ##[1:8] ack` (ack within 8 cycles) and `req && !ack |=> req` (req held until ack).
solution:
**Key idea:** two rules, one per side. **Responder**: `ack` within 1..8 cycles of a new request (bounded, so a hang fails at cycle 8). **Requester**: `req` must not drop before `ack`.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "req", "wave": "01...0....." },
  { "name": "ack", "wave": "0...10....." },
  { "name": "window", "wave": "0.=.......0", "data": ["ack allowed in cycles 2..9"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "$rose(req) at cycle 1; ack at cycle 4 satisfies ##[1:8]; req held until ack", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module req_ack_sva (input logic clk, rst_n, req, ack);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);

  a_req_ack  : assert property ($rose(req) |-> ##[1:8] ack)
    else $error("[%0t] ack timeout (> 8 cycles)", $time);
  a_req_hold : assert property (req && !ack |=> req)
    else $error("[%0t] req dropped before ack", $time);
  a_no_spur  : assert property (ack |-> req);          // no ack without a request

  c_fast : cover property ($rose(req) ##1 ack);
  c_slow : cover property ($rose(req) ##8 ack);        // hit the boundary
endmodule
```

| Assertion | Owner side | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a_req_ack` | responder | ack later than 8 cycles (or never) |
| `a_req_hold` | requester | req withdrawn early |
| `a_no_spur` | responder | ack with no request |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `req` instead of `$rose(req)` in the antecedent starts a new attempt every cycle req is high; each attempt has its own 8-cycle window, which may hide a slow response.
- If `ack` can come in the same cycle, use `##[0:8]`.
- Four-phase protocol: also check `!req && ack |=> !req` (don't re-request until ack drops).

### Follow-ups
- **Unbounded but must eventually happen?** `$rose(req) |-> s_eventually ack`.

title: Write arbiter assertions: one-hot grant, grant only to requesters, and no starvation
prompt: An N-requester arbiter has `req[N-1:0]` and `gnt[N-1:0]`. Write assertions that: at most one grant is active, a grant only goes to an active requester, and no requester waits more than 16 cycles.
answer: `$onehot0(gnt)`; `|gnt |-> |(gnt & req)` (only grant a requester); `req[0] |-> ##[1:16] gnt[0]` (fairness bound).
solution:
**Key idea:** three classic arbiter properties: **mutual exclusion** (`$onehot0`), **validity** (grant implies request), and **fairness** (bounded wait). Generate the fairness check per requester.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",    "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "req[0]", "wave": "01....0" },
  { "name": "req[1]", "wave": "01..0.." },
  { "name": "gnt[0]", "wave": "0...1.0" },
  { "name": "gnt[1]", "wave": "0.1.0.." }
],
  "head": { "text": "grants never overlap; req[0] waits 3 cycles (within the 16-cycle bound)", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module arb_sva #(parameter int N = 4) (
  input logic         clk, rst_n,
  input logic [N-1:0] req, gnt
);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);

  a_onehot  : assert property ($onehot0(gnt));
```
